<meta>This page continues a discourse on the various branches of knowledge, transitioning here into a critique of Magic and its subdivisions. The text follows a classical and Renaissance tradition of distinguishing between "Natural Magic" (based on physical properties) and "Ceremonial Magic" (involving spirits).</meta>

<page-num>24</page-num>
<header>ON VANITY</header>

### ON VANITY

<margin>Magic beyond nature.</margin>
Magic consists of motion, numbers, figures, voices, harmonies, lights, the affections of the mind, and words. Thus the *Psylli* and *Marsi* <note>Ancient North African and Italian tribes famed for their power over snakes.</note> used to summon serpents, while others would put them to flight by suppressing them. *Orpheus* calmed the storm of the *Argonauts* with a hymn, and *Homer* relates that *Ulysses’* blood was stanched by words <note>original: "sanguine uerbis reftrictum"; a reference to the Odyssey where a wound is healed by an incantation.</note>. Furthermore, in the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, c. 450 BCE.</note>, a punishment was established for those who had "charmed away" the harvests <note>original: "messes excantassent"; the crime of using magic to steal a neighbor's crops.</note>, so that there is no doubt that magicians—not unknowingly using words, emotions, and other similar things—produce some wonderful effect not only in foul ways, but often upon external objects. They believe that all these things pour out an innate power into other things, drawing those things toward themselves, or repelling them away, or affecting them in some way; just as the magnet draws iron and amber draws chaff, or as the diamond and garlic repel the magnet. Thus, through this gradual and concatenated "sympathy" <note>In this context, 'sympathy' refers to a hidden natural connection or "agreement" between different objects in the universe.</note> of things, they claim that not only natural and celestial gifts, but even intellectual and divine ones, can be received from above, according to the opinion of magicians such as *Iamblichus, Proclus*, and *Synesius* <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote on the soul and theurgy.</note>. *Proclus* concludes from this that magicians were accustomed to successfully summon spirits <note>original: "numina"; divine powers or spirits.</note> through sacrifice and magic by means of this "consensus" or agreement of things. Indeed, some of them have fallen into such madness that they think an image—constructed from various constellations of the stars, through intervals of time and duly observed proportions—will receive a spirit by the power of the intellect of the heavens, which would then respond to those agreements and reveal the secrets of hidden truth. From this it is clear that this "Natural Magic" sometimes reclines into *Goetia* and *Theurgy* <note>Goetia refers to "low" or black magic involving demons; Theurgy refers to "high" magic intended to invoke gods or good spirits.</note>, and very often creeps in through the deceptions and errors of evil demons.

<margin>GOETIA.</margin>
<margin>THEURGY.</margin>
<margin>NECROMANCY.</margin>
<margin>DIVINATION.</margin>
<margin>...CY.</margin>
->¶ The parts of Ceremonial Magic, however, are *Goetia* and *Theurgy*. *Goetia* is entangled in dealings with unclean spirits, composed of the rituals of nefarious curiosity, illicit songs, and charms; it has been exterminated and execrated by the decrees of all laws. To this class belong those whom we today call *Necromancers* <note>Those who communicate with the dead.</note> and *Evildoers* <note>original: "Maleficos"; often used specifically for witches or practitioners of harmful magic.</note>: A race hated by the Gods, clever at defiling the Heavens, whom Nature brought forth as an evil; who, by swearing, fixed the stars of the World, established them, and then overturned them.<-

For

<summary>This page defines Magic as a manipulation of natural sympathies and words, citing classical examples like Orpheus and Roman law. It warns that "Natural Magic" often descends into the illicit and condemned practices of Goetia and Necromancy.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the title page of Henry Cornelius Agrippa’s "De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum" (On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences). Having established his credentials as a knight and counselor, Agrippa now presents a playful yet defiant introductory poem to the reader, setting a skeptical and satirical tone for the chapters to follow.</meta>

<page-type>preface</page-type>

### To the reader.

Among the Gods, there are none whom Momus does not criticize: <note>Momus was the Greek god of satire and mockery, famous for finding fault even with the work of the other gods.</note>
Among the Heroes, Hercules hunts down every monster:
Among the Demons, Pluto, the king of Erebus, is angry at all the Shadows: <note>Erebus refers to the personification of darkness or the dark region of the underworld; the "Shadows" are the spirits of the dead.</note>
Among the Philosophers, Democritus laughs at everything: <note>Democritus was known as the "laughing philosopher" due to his habit of mocking human follies.</note>
Conversely, Heraclitus weeps for all things: <note>Heraclitus, the "weeping philosopher," was seen as the melancholic opposite of Democritus.</note>
Pyrrho knows nothing of anything: <note>original: "Pyrrhus"; referring to Pyrrho of Elis, the father of the Skeptical school of philosophy, which taught that certain knowledge is impossible.</note>
And Aristotle thinks he knows everything:
Diogenes despises all things: <note>The famous Cynic philosopher who rejected social conventions and lived in a barrel.</note>
Agrippa spares no one here,
He despises; he knows, he knows not; he weeps, he laughs; he is angry, he hunts;
he finds fault with everything:
He himself is philosopher, demon, hero, god, and everything.

---

->To know nothing is the happiest life. <note>original: "Nihil scire felicissima vita"; this is the central paradox of the book, suggesting that intellectual pride leads to misery, while humble ignorance is a state of grace.</note><-

<summary>This preface uses a series of classical archetypes to characterize Agrippa's skeptical project, positioning the author as a multifaceted critic who embodies all philosophical attitudes to challenge the certainty of human knowledge.</summary>

The tone shifts from the previous page's satirical defiance to a display of "learned humility" and gratitude.</meta>

<page-type>dedication</page-type>

<meta>catchword: sive</meta>

# TO THE DISTINGUISHED 
## Gentleman, Lord Agostino Furnario, citizen of 
## Genoa, Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa 
## von Nettesheim 
## sends his fondest greetings. <note>original: "P. S. D." — an abbreviation for *Plurimam Salutem Dicit*, a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

As I was considering, most honorable Agostino (you who, through your zeal for doing good, have made me a perpetual debtor of gratitude), with what devotion, reverence, pledge, or mental effort I might testify to my respect for you, it was my intention to honor you with some beautiful and great gift—for you are most worthy of the most beautiful and greatest things. I wished to offer you books drawn from the innermost depths of both divine and human literature, written with both the most polished integrity of speech and the richest dignity of subject matter, along with the weightiest gravity of thought. 

But since I am far inferior to my own great intentions in both learning and talent, and since I follow far behind in eloquence and elegance of language, I find nothing in the storehouse of my wit that I can offer, except for a notable ignorance. My very talent lies cast down, dejected by the indignation of my fortune; indeed, out of that very indignation, I have almost been turned into a dog—just as that Trojan Hecuba was—and I possess no strength... <note>Hecuba was the Queen of Troy who, according to Greek myth, was transformed into a dog out of grief and rage after the fall of her city and the death of her children. Agrippa uses this vivid image to describe his own bitterness and sense of defeat regarding his career and social standing.</note>

<summary>This page contains the formal dedication of the book to Agostino Furnario. Agrippa uses self-deprecating language to contrast his "notable ignorance" and poor fortune with the high intellectual quality of the gift he originally intended to give.</summary>
<keywords>Agostino Furnario, dedication, gratitude, Hecuba, humility, Genoa, patronage</keywords>

--- Page 5 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter to Agostino Furnario. Agrippa, having previously compared his bitter state of mind to the grief-stricken Hecuba who was transformed into a dog, now explains how this "canine" disposition led him to write his famous critique of human knowledge.</meta>

...to speak well, I remember nothing more except how to bite, to bark, to curse, and to revile. Thus, being in such a state of mind, I have written in these days a quite sizable volume, to which I have given the title *On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences*. In this work, I have so barked at that whole **Battle of the Giants** <note>original: "Gigantomachiæ" — referring to the mythological war where Giants tried to overthrow the gods; here, Agrippa uses it to describe the arrogant structures of human knowledge.</note> of the sciences and arts, and I have nipped at all those most robust **Hunters** <note>original: "Venatores" — likely a reference to the biblical Nimrod, "a mighty hunter before the Lord," often interpreted by medieval and Renaissance writers as a type of tyrant or an aggressive, prideful scholar.</note> of the sciences and arts with such powerful bites, that whenever I revisit the work itself, I marvel at myself for being such a **Dog** in the form of a man—one who lacks nothing canine except for the habit of flattery, though that is a thing quite necessary for a **Courtier**. <note>original: "Aulico" — Agrippa is being sarcastic, suggesting that while dogs are usually loyal, the "human dog" (the courtier) uses flattery to survive, a trait Agrippa prides himself on lacking.</note> 

Therefore, lest I should seem to be a deserter of the respect I owe you—since I am unable to bestow fertile gifts worthy of you and drawn from the treasures of the sciences—I now offer you this **Cynic declamation** <note>original: "Cynicā declamationē" — The word "Cynic" comes from the Greek word for "dog-like." The Cynic philosophers were known for their biting criticism of social norms.</note> from that same workshop of my ignorance and indignation. I present you with this gift and establish it as dedicated to you, intending to freely show the greatness of my spirit toward you. 

I wish to show what a vigilant guardian, what a keen-eyed scout, what a bold soldier, and what a magnanimous leader you have acquired in me. For I am one who, as if from a high watchtower, announces the approach of enemies from afar, so that the citizens of divine letters <note>Agrippa refers to those who study the Bible and true theology as "citizens of divine letters," contrasting them with the "giants" of worldly philosophy.</note> may retreat to safer places. Then, for the safety of them all, I offer myself up to be torn apart by everyone, and I am the first to fight hand-to-hand in the front of the battle line: by which deed...

<meta>catchword: so much</meta>

<summary>Agrippa explains that his bitter mood led him to write a scathing critique of all human arts and sciences, which he dedicates to Furnario as a "Cynic" gift. He portrays himself as a protective watchdog for "divine letters," barking at the arrogance of worldly scholars to protect true believers.</summary>

<keywords>De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum, Cynicism, flattery, courtiers, divine letters, satire, defense of faith</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter to Agostino Furnario. Having previously justified his "canine" (Cynic) and biting tone as a necessary response to his personal misfortunes and the corruption of human learning, Agrippa now presents himself as a defender of the truth and hints at his future works.</meta>

So far am I from fearing envy that I believe gratitude is owed to me by all; for, in service of the public good, I act as both scout and soldier—denouncing and attacking those things by which human well-being is endangered. Moreover, I offer myself as a guide to those who, emerging from the labyrinth of the human sciences, strive toward the citadel of truth. <note>Agrippa characterizes the various academic disciplines as a "labyrinth"—a common Renaissance metaphor for confusing, man-made systems—contrasted with the "citadel" of divine or absolute truth.</note> Accept now, most venerable Augustine, <note>Agostino Furnario, to whom the work is dedicated.</note> this Declamation, such as it is, and hold it as your own by right. For I know that if you are a Hunter and love dogs, <note>Continuing the metaphor from the previous page where Agrippa described himself as a barking dog and scholars as "hunters" after prideful knowledge.</note> it cannot fail to be most pleasing to you.

But I shall now migrate from a Dog into a Crocodile, or a Dragon, or some other fire-breathing serpent, and I will immediately finish the **Pyrography** <margin>The book of *Pyrography*</margin> (a work such as our age has not yet seen, but which would be of use only to some famous destroyer of the world). <note>original: "Pyrographiam" — Literally "Fire-writing." This refers to a lost or perhaps never-completed work by Agrippa, likely dealing with pyrotechnics, artillery, or the more destructive aspects of natural magic.</note> Then I will sprinkle myself with sacred water and wash in a living stream, so that, finally stripped of these fatal masks, I may return once more to being a man; lest, by "Pythagorizing" <note>original: "Pythagorissans" — Referring to the philosopher Pythagoras and his doctrine of metempsychosis, or the transmigration of souls into different animal bodies.</note> too much and migrating into such various beasts, I might—like Lucian and Apuleius—turn into a philosophizing Ass. <note>A reference to the famous ancient satires, Lucian’s *The Ass* and Apuleius’s *The Golden Ass*, in which the protagonist is transformed into a donkey but retains his human reason.</note> But for now, fare you most happily, and remem-

->ber, when you read these words of ours,<-
->that to know nothing<-
->is the happiest<-
->life.<-

<summary>Agrippa concludes his dedication by framing his critique as a public service and teasing a future, more "destructive" work on the secrets of fire. He ends with his signature skeptical motto: that the happiest life is found in "knowing nothing."</summary>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's critique of various intellectual and occult disciplines, moving from a condemnation of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) and early Christian heresies to the mechanics of magical illusions.</meta>

### ON VANITY

<margin>Heresies arisen from the <term>Kabbalah</term><note>A form of Jewish mysticism involving the esoteric interpretation of Scripture.</note>.</margin> Leaving behind the substance and gasping at its shadow, they have lost their food. So too this treacherous and <term>stiff-necked</term><note>original: "duræ ceruicis." A biblical idiom for stubbornness.</note> race of men, always preoccupied with the shadows of Scripture and artfully applying their skills to those vanities for the sake of a superstitious Kabbalah, loses the bread of eternal life; feeding on empty names, they lose the word of truth. From this Jewish leaven of Kabbalistic superstition emerged the pure <term>Ophites</term><note>A Gnostic sect that gave special importance to the serpent in the Garden of Eden.</note>, <term>Gnostics</term><note>Early Christian groups who believed in "gnosis" or secret, salvific knowledge.</note>, and <term>Valentinian</term> heretics. They, along with their disciples, also devised a certain "Greek Kabbalah," perverting all the mysteries of the Christian faith and extending their heretical depravity to Greek letters and numbers. From these, they constructed a "body" which they call "of Truth," teaching that without these mysteries of letters and numbers, the truth cannot be found in the writings of the Gospels. They argue the Gospels are various and sometimes contradictory, mostly written in parables so that "those seeing may not see, and those hearing may not hear, and those understanding may not understand." Instead, they claim the Gospels were presented to the blind and the erring according to their capacity for blindness and error, while the sincere truth lying beneath them was entrusted only to the "perfected"—not through writing, but pronounced through a succession of the living voice. They believe this to be that "Alphabetic and
<margin>Mark 4:11</margin> Arithmetic Theology" <note>original: "Alphabetariam & Arithmeticam Theologiam." This refers to Gematria and similar practices where numerical values are assigned to letters.</note> which Christ manifested in secret to the Apostles, and which Paul says he speaks only among the 
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:6</margin> perfected. Since these are the highest mysteries, they claim they were neither written down nor should they be written, but preserved in silence among the Wise in secret, guarding those things within themselves. Among such people, however, no one is considered "Wise" unless he knows how to manufacture the greatest monsters of heresy. 

But let us return to Magic, a small part of which is also the Art of
<margin>ILLUSIONS</margin> <term>Prestidigitation</term><note>original: "PRAESTIGIAE." Meaning the art of sleight-of-hand or deceptive illusions.</note>, that is, of illusions which occur according to appearances. Through these, <term>Magi</term><note>Magicians or practitioners of the occult.</note> produce <term>Phantasms</term><note>Illusions or ghostly apparitions.</note>, perform many miracles through the frauds of traveling performers, and threaten dreams. This is done not so much by <term>Goetic</term><note>original: "Goeticis." Furthermore, they use rings, images, mirrors, and similar drugs and instruments of the magical art...

### Preface. Folio IX.

### HENRY CORNELIUS

<margin>The twelve labors of Hercules.</margin>
Will it not seem to you, studious reader, that this deed of mine is high-minded, daring, and almost Herculean? To take up arms against that entire <term>gigantomachia</term><note>original: "gigantomachiam." Literally a "war of giants," referring to the mythological battle between the gods and giants; here it represents the massive, entrenched system of all human sciences.</note> of all sciences and arts, and to challenge all those most robust hunters of knowledge and art into the arena? The arrogance of the Doctors, the erudition of the Licentiates, the authority of the Masters, the efforts of the Bachelors, the zeal of all the Scholars, and the rebellion of the craftsmen will roar against me. If I defeat them, will it not be equal to or greater than striking the Nemean Lion with a club, killing the Lernaean Hydra with fire, slaying the Erymanthian Boar, or capturing the stag in the Maenalian grove that wears golden horns? Or piercing the Stymphalian birds in the clouds with arrows, crushing Antaeus within my arms, fixing the Pillars in the Ocean, conquering the three-headed Geryon, driving off the cattle, or slaying the Bull? <margin><term>Agonia</term><note>original: "Αγωνία." A Greek term meaning a struggle or a singular contest.</note>, that is, in a singular contest.</margin> Or overcoming Achelous in single combat, leading away the horses of Diomedes, dragging Cerberus bound in a chain, stealing the golden apples of the Hesperides, and more deeds of that kind performed by Hercules through great labor and no less danger? For it is no less labor, and indeed the greatest danger, to overcome these monsters of the <term>gymnasia</term><note>The ancient Greek term for schools or training grounds; Agrippa uses it to refer to the universities of his time.</note> and the wrestling-pits. Indeed, I clearly see what a bloody battle I must enter here hand-to-hand, and how full of danger this war is, since I am surrounded by an army of such powerful enemies. Oh, with how many siege engines they will attack me, with how many assaults they will strike me, with how many disgraces they will pursue me! First, the lice-ridden Grammarians will clamor: they will fix a "gouty" name upon Agrippa from their etymologies <note>Agrippa is playing on a pun between his name and the Latin "podagricus" (gouty), suggesting the grammarians will mock his name to imply he has "pain in the feet" or is slow-witted.</note>. The peddling Historiographers will defame me even more than they did Pausanias or <term>Herostratus</term><note>A man who burned the Temple of Artemis to ensure his name would live on in history; Agrippa implies historians will treat him as a villainous seeker of infamy.</note>. The loud-mouthed Orators, with angry eyes, terrible countenances, thunderous voices, and dreadful gestures, will accuse me of <term>high treason</term><note>original: "perduellionatus." A legal term for a crime committed against the state or the majesty of the law.</note>.

# Preface. Leaf XI.

...[that I was] led by error to write these things; neither has a sacrilegious desire, nor the arrogance of a wicked mind driven me to this. Instead, the cause of all this is as just as it is true: namely, that I see many people so deeply rooted in human disciplines and sciences that they look down upon and despise the eloquence of the sacred scriptures and the canonical writings of the Holy Spirit as if they were rustic and uneducated. They do this because these scriptures lack the ornaments of words, the strength of logical syllogisms, affected persuasions, and the foreign learning of the **Philosophers**, being instead established simply in the operation of power and naked faith; for this reason, they not only despise them but even pursue them with a certain contempt.

We see others also, although they seem more pious to themselves, who strive to prove and confirm the laws of Christ by the decrees of the **Philosophers**, giving more credit to them than to the holy Prophets of God, the Evangelists, and the Apostles, even though these two groups are more than a <term>disdiapason<note>original: "disdiapason." A Greek-derived musical term referring to a double octave; Agrippa uses it here to express a vast, irreconcilable distance.</note></term> apart. Furthermore, in many and almost all **Universities**<note>original: "Gymnasiis." Referring to the high schools and universities of the period.</note>, a perverse custom and damnable habit has grown up: they compel students about to be initiated into study to take an oath that they will never oppose **Aristotle**, or **Boethius**, or **Thomas** [Aquinas], or **Albert** [the Great], or any other of their scholastic gods. If anyone thinks differently from these authorities by even a <term>fingernail's breadth<note>original: "latum unguem." A Latin idiom meaning the slightest possible distance or a tiny hair’s breadth.</note></term>, they proclaim him a heretic, a creator of scandal, an offense to pious ears, and someone to be consumed by fire and flames. 

Therefore, these rash Giants and enemies of the sacred scriptures must be attacked; their camps and citadels must be stormed. It must be shown how great the blindness of men is, who, with so many sciences and arts, and with so many masters and authors for each, always wander away from the knowledge of truth. How great also is the temerity, how arrogant the presumption, to prefer the schools of **Philosophers** to the Church of Christ, and to place—or even equal—the opinions of men before the Word of God! Finally, what an impious tyranny it is to imprison the minds of students to predetermined authors, and to take away from disciples the freedom of investigating and following the truth. 

Since all these things are so manifest that they cannot be denied, pardon must be granted if I seem to speak more freely and perhaps more bitterly against certain kinds of disciplines or their professors. Farewell.

<header>ON VANITY</header>

# OF THE NOBLE MAN
## HENRY CORNELIUS AGRIP-

->pa, <term>Knight of the Golden Spur<note>original: "Equitis aurati." A title of imperial knighthood bestowed by the Holy Roman Emperor.</note></term>, and <term>Doctor of both Laws<note>original: "utriusque Iuris Doctoris." Meaning he held doctorates in both Civil Law and Canon (Church) Law.</note></term>,<-
->Councilor to his Sacred Imperial Majesty and<-
->Keeper of the Archives, a Declamation on the<-
->Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences<-
->and the Arts.<-

---

It is an ancient opinion, and the nearly concurrent and unanimous sentiment of all who practice philosophy, who judge that any branch of knowledge brings a certain touch of divinity to man himself—according to the capacity and worth of each—so that such knowledge can often transport them beyond the limits of humanity into the <note>original: "Deorum beatorum choros." Agrippa uses classical Roman phrasing ("choirs of the blessed gods") to describe a state of divine enlightenment.</note>choirs of the blessed gods. From this have emerged those various and innumerable <term>encomiums<note>original: "encomia." Formal speeches or pieces of writing that highly praise someone or something.</note></term> of the sciences, in which every man strives to prefer those arts and disciplines in which he has sharpened the powers of his own intellect through long practice, placing them above all others and exalting them even above the heavens themselves, in a speech no less ornate than it is long. 

I, however, being persuaded by reasons of a different kind, judge that nothing more ruinous, nothing more pestilential, can happen to the life of men and the salvation of our souls than these very arts and these very sciences. Therefore, I believe I must act in a reverse order; it is my opinion that the sciences themselves should not be extolled with such great proclamations of praise, but should, for the most part, be condemned. Neither is there any science that lacks a just censure of reproach, nor again any that earns any praise from itself, unless it is borrowed from the integrity of the possessor. 

Furthermore, I wish this opinion of mine to be received by you with such modesty that you do not think I wish to rebuke others who feel differently, nor that I arrogantly claim anything for myself. Therefore, you will grant me pardon for dissenting from the rest in this matter, until we begin this judgment through each of the faculties of letters in order—not merely with common arguments taken from the surface of things, but with the firmest reasons drawn out from the very innermost guts of the matter.

<header>OF THE SCIENCES. XXII.</header>

I do not bring any of the clever eloquence of Demosthenes <note>The most famous of the ancient Greek orators.</note> or Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his dialectic skill; Agrippa implies that high-flown logic can be a distraction from faith.</note>, which would only be a source of shame for me as a professor of sacred scripture, or show me to be a lover of flattery, if I were to chase after the deceptions of rhetoric. For it is fitting for a teacher of holy texts to speak accurately rather than eloquently, and to focus on the truth of the subject rather than the beauty of the speech. For the seat of truth is not in the tongue, but in the heart. Nor does it matter what kind of language we use when speaking the truth. A lie requires eloquence and <term>ornamental trappings<note>original: "phaleratis." This term refers to the decorative metal disks on a horse's harness, implying that eloquent words are just external "bling" for a lie.</note></term> so that it may creep into the minds of men; but the language of truth, as Euripides <note>A famous Greek playwright.</note> writes, is simple in nature, seeking neither deception nor pigments. 

Therefore, if the task I have undertaken offends your most delicate ears because it lacks the bloom of eloquence (which will now be stripped bare, even though it should not be entirely neglected by us), I pray that you bear it with the same patience that a certain Roman Emperor once showed when he halted his army to listen to a poor woman. Likewise, King Archelaus sometimes wished to hear men with hoarse and unpleasant voices so that, after listening to them, he might find more delight in the eloquent. Remember that saying of Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle.</note>, that even unrefined men can speak before the greatest and most elegant people, provided they speak with integrity and reason. 

And so that I do not leave you hanging with your ears open as if yawning, I shall now bring into the light the tracks and signs by which I have—like a hunter with dogs—tracked down and caught this opinion of mine. But first, let me warn you: all sciences are as much evil as they are good, and they bring us no divine happiness beyond the limit of our humanity, except perhaps that which the ancient <margin>Genesis 3</margin> serpent promised to our first parents, saying: *You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.* In this serpent, therefore, those people glory who boast that they possess knowledge. We read that the <margin>Ophites</margin> <term>Ophite heretics<note>A Gnostic sect that believed the serpent in Eden was actually a bringer of knowledge (gnosis) rather than a tempter.</note></term> did this very thing, for they worshipped the serpent in their sacred rites, saying that he had introduced the knowledge of virtue in Paradise. Plato’s history agrees with this, stating that a certain <term>demon<note>original: "daemonem." In the classical Greek sense, a spirit or lesser deity, not necessarily an evil "demon" in the modern sense.</note></term> named Theuth, who was hostile to the human race, first invented these sciences—which are no less harmful than they are useful—as Thamus, the king of all Egypt, most wisely argued concerning the inventors of sciences and letters. Hence it is that since the serpent...

# OF VANITY

### OF THE SCIENCES. Folio XIII.

<margin>Knowledge in a fool</margin>
Even if the sciences fall into the hands of someone who is not necessarily evil but simply a fool, nothing is more insolent or troublesome than he is. For in addition to the natural folly he already possesses, he now defends that folly with the authority of learning. He possesses the tools of literature to protect his own madness—tools which other fools lack, and thus their insanity is milder. As Plato says regarding the Rhetorician <note>In his dialogues, such as the *Gorgias*, Plato often criticized rhetoricians for prioritizing persuasion over truth.</note>: the more foolish and unlearned he is, the more he will prattle on and imitate everything, believing nothing to be beneath him. Therefore, nothing is more destructive than to be mad with reason <note>original: "cum ratione insanire." This phrase suggests the danger of using logical tools to justify irrational or nonsensical behavior.</note>. 

However, if a good and wise man should possess these sciences, perhaps they will be good and useful to the Commonwealth; yet they will make their possessor not one bit happier. For, as Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who emphasized spiritual ascent over mere book-learning.</note> say, happiness is not found in the accumulation of words or the multitude of disciplines. Such happiness receives no increase based on the quantity of arguments or words. If it were so, nothing would prevent those who have gathered all the disciplines from being truly happy, while those who lack them would not be; thus, Philosophers would be happier than Priests.

<margin>True happiness.</margin>
For true happiness <note>original: "beatitudo." In this context, it refers to the highest state of human well-being or "blessedness."</note> does not consist in the knowledge of good things, but in a good life; not in understanding, but in living by the intellect. It is not a good intelligence, but a good will that joins men to God. Nor do the disciplines studied from without achieve anything, except perhaps to provide us with a certain purgatorial condition <note>A state of cleansing or preparation.</note> that leads somewhat toward happiness; however, they are not the actual means by which our happiness is fulfilled, unless a life transformed into the very nature of the Good is also present. 

For it is very often discovered (as Cicero says in his speech *For Archias*) that nature without learning has been more effective for praise and virtue than learning without nature. Therefore, there is no need to imbue the soul with a discipline of all the sciences that is so long, so difficult, and—as the <term>Averroists<note>Followers of the Islamic philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), known for their highly complex and intellectualized approach to Aristotelian philosophy.</note></term> contend—hardly ever fully searchable. Even Aristotle himself says that happiness is something very common, which all can easily attain through a certain discipline and diligence. He calls this an easy and almost universal faculty for contemplating the most noble object: namely, God, who is indeed so easy and common to all...

<margin>Ecclesiastes 8</margin>
Which Ecclesiastes seems to affirm to me here, when he says: "I understood that of all the works of God, man can find no reason for those things done under the sun; and the more he labors to seek, the less he finds: even if the Wise Man says he knows, he will not be able to find it." 

<margin>Nothing more pestilential than knowledge</margin>
Nothing more pestilential can happen to man than knowledge: this is that true plague which subverted the whole and entire human race to a man, which spat out all innocence, and made us subject to so many kinds of sins and to death; it is that which extinguished the light of faith, casting our souls into the profound darkness of conscience, and which, condemning truth, placed errors on the highest throne. And there is a free expanse, such that it cannot be demonstrated by the speculations of any science, nor by any pressing judgment of the senses, nor by any arguments of the logical artisan, nor by any evident proof, nor by any syllogism, nor can it be apprehended by any discourse of human reason, except by faith alone. Folio XV.
### OF THE SCIENCES

Among the Jews, letters were perhaps not originally in these characters which they use today; these are thought to be the invention of Ezra, <margin>Polydore Vergil, *On Inventors*, Book 1, chapter six.</margin> whom they consider the writer of almost all the books of the Old Testament. For the Latins, however, a woman named Nicostrata, surnamed Carmenta <note>An Italian prophetess and goddess; tradition says she adapted the Greek alphabet to create the Latin one.</note>, handed down their letters.

Seven various types of letters were preeminent in antiquity: Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Syrian, Chaldean, Egyptian, and Getic <note>Refers to the Goths; the Getae were often conflated with Goths in early modern scholarship.</note>. > Moses was the first to scribe the Hebrew letters.
> With sagacious mind, the Phoenicians established the Attic ones.
> Those which we Latins write, Nicostrata brought forth.
> Abraham discovered the Syrian, and likewise the Chaldean.
> Isis, with no less skill, produced the Egyptian.
> Gulfila <note>Also known as Ulfilas, the 4th-century missionary who created the Gothic alphabet to translate the Bible.</note> brought forth the last ones of the Goths, which we see.

# [OF THE] SCIENCES.
Folio XVI.

...so that there are no letters, no languages today that recognize or understand the form of their own antiquity. But from these so unstable and ever-changeable principles, I do not say only letters and languages, but first **Grammar**, and then the rest of the arts of speaking well which we have mentioned, came forth. 
<margin>Grammar.</margin>
For since it seemed of little use to know letters unless they were joined together in a certain formed order, and from letters syllables, and from those finally words and phrases were formed, and joined together for the understanding of speech, ingenious men dared to set down rules of speaking—namely, of construction, governance, and meanings—and as it were to put a bit <note>original: "frenum"; literally a horse's bridle or bit, used here as a metaphor for control or restraint.</note> upon the tongue, so that whatever was said according to those rules would be "well said," and this would be the art of speaking well; and they called this art **Grammar**.

<margin>The inventor of Grammar.</margin>
Its inventor among the Greeks is first said to be **Prometheus**. One **Crates of Mallus** <note>A Greek grammarian and Stoic philosopher of the 2nd century BCE.</note> first brought it to Rome, sent to the Senate by Attalus between the second and third Punic wars. 
<margin>Palaemon’s arrogance.</margin>
Which art afterwards **Palaemon** <note>Quintus Remmius Palaemon, a famous but notoriously arrogant Roman grammarian of the 1st century CE.</note> professed with such great pride that he gave his own name to the art, calling it the "Palaemonian Art." He was a man so exceedingly arrogant that he boasted that letters were born with him and would perish with him; he was so haughty that he held all the most learned men of his age in contempt, and even dared to call **Marcus Varro** <note>A prolific Roman scholar often called "the most learned of the Romans."</note> a "pig."

<margin>Greek letters serve the Latin.</margin>
Nevertheless, Latin Grammar itself is so impoverished and so beholden to Greek literature <note>original: "obnoxia"; meaning liable or indebted to.</note> that anyone who is not skilled in the latter should be immediately cast out from the number of grammarians. Therefore, the whole system of literature or Grammar consists in nothing but the custom of our ancestors and their authority, by which it pleased them that a thing should be called so, written so, and that words should be composed and constructed thus and so—which they now call "speaking well." 

<margin>Grammar is falsely called the art of speaking correctly.</margin>
Whence Grammar boasts itself to be the art of speaking correctly, but falsely. Since we learn that very thing far better from our mothers or common nurses than from grammarians. **Cornelia** <note>Cornelia Africana, mother of the Gracchi, famously cited by Roman authors as the primary influence on her sons' legendary eloquence.</note>, the mother, shaped the language of the **Gracchi** (who were considered the most eloquent of men). Istria the mother taught the Greek language to **Scythes**, the son of Aripithes, King of Scythia. It is well known that in many provinces where colonies of foreign nations were introduced, the sons born there always retained the speech of their mothers. Hence **Plato** and **Quintilian** [wrote] about choosing [the right nurses] for children...

We read that **Claudius Caesar** was so devoted to Greek letters that he invented three new letters for that language, which as prince he did not neglect. And 

<margin>German Grammar.</margin>
**Charlemagne** <note>Carolus Magnus (742–814 CE), King of the Franks and Holy Roman Emperor.</note> devised a Grammar of the German language, and gave new names to the months and the winds. And up to this very day, work continues day and night; they write *Commentaries*, *Elegancies*, *Questions*, *Annotations*, *Scholia*, *Observations*, *Corrections*, *Centuries*, *Miscellanies*, *Antiquities*, *Paradoxes*, *Collectanea*, *Additions*, *Lucubrations* <note>Literally "works produced by lamplight," referring to late-night scholarly labor.</note>, and repeated and reiterated editions. And meanwhile, there are born to us as many Grammars as there are Grammarians. 

Yet not one of them, whether Greek or Latin, has given a definitive account of how the parts of speech are to be distinguished, or what order must be kept in their construction. Are there only fifteen pronouns, as **Priscian** thinks, or more, as **Diomedes** and **Phocas** <note>Latin grammarians of the 4th and 5th centuries CE.</note> wished? 

<margin>Controversies of the Grammarians.</margin>
Does a **Participle** <note>A word formed from a verb and used as an adjective.</note> placed by itself sometimes remain a Participle? Whether **gerunds** <note>Verb forms functioning as nouns.</note> are nouns or verbs? Why among the Greeks do neuter plural nouns join with a singular verb? By what logic is it permitted for the Latins to produce names ending in *a* and in *us* as *um*, such as *margarita* [pearl] becoming *margaritum*, or *ponctus* [point] becoming *punctum*. How the nominative **Jupiter** produces the genitive **Jovis**. And by what reasoning some admit **neuter verbs** <note>original: "verba neutralia"; today usually called intransitive verbs, which do not take a direct object.</note> and others exclude them. 

Why some write many Latin words with a Greek diphthong <note>A sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable.</note> and others do not, such as *fœlix* [happy] or *quæstio* [question]. And whether the Latin diphthongs *æ* and *œ* are only written and not pronounced, or if both vowels are expressed under one syllable just as they are written? Similarly, why in many Latin words some use only the Greek *y* and others the Latin *i*, as in *considero* [I consider]. Likewise why in some words certain...

...to obey <note>original: "parere". This completes the sentence from the previous page, likely discussing how scholars expect language to "obey" their arbitrary rules.</note>. Some double their letters, and some do not, as in the words **cause** or **religion**. They argue why the word **caccabus** <note>original: *caccabus*; a three-legged cooking pot. Agrippa is mocking the intense focus on syllable length in obscure vocabulary.</note>, though it has its first syllable lengthened by the doubled "cc," is nevertheless mostly shortened by many poets. Likewise, they debate whether **Aristotle’s** soul should be written as **endelechia** with a *delta*, or **entelechia** with a *tau* <note>A famous Renaissance intellectual debate: *entelecheia* refers to "perfection" or "actuality," while *endelecheia* refers to "continuity" or "duration." The choice of letter changed the fundamental definition of the soul.</note>. I pass over their infinite and never-ending contentions regarding accents, spelling, the pronunciation of letters, figures, etymologies, analogies, and the rest of their precepts and rules, inflections, and modes of signifying, the changing of cases, and the variety of tenses, moods, persons, numbers, and the various impediments and the order of sentence construction. Finally, they argue about the very number of Latin letters and their genealogy, and whether **h** is a letter or not, and many things of this sort. Thus, not only in words and syllables, but even in the very elements of speech, they disagree with one another without any reason given. <margin>Lucian, in the *Judgment of the Vowels*.</margin> Lucian of Samosata <note>A 2nd-century Syrian satirist who wrote in Greek.</note> mocked this kind of battle between the **S** and **T** consonants in a most witty little book, an example of which can be seen in the words **thalassa** and **thalatta** <note>The Greek words for "sea"; different dialects used "ss" or "tt." Lucian’s satire features letters of the alphabet suing each other in court for the theft of sounds.</note>. A certain **Andreas of Salerno** also described a "Grammar War" <note>Andrea Guarna (c. 1470–1517), whose *Bellum Grammaticale* was a popular work personifying the parts of speech as rival armies.</note> with scholarly eloquence. 

But these are small and trivial matters. <margin>The destruction of the Republic resulting from the corrupt and depraved interpretation of names.</margin> We could say more and greater things about the depraved interpretations of names, by which they greatly deceive the whole world. From these, first of all, no small evils proceed in the **Republic** [the state], when they explain "subjection to laws" as **slavery**. They interpret the "liberty of citizens" as that state where everyone may do as they please, and they call it **isonomia** <note>Greek: *isonomia*, meaning "equality of political rights" or "equality before the law." Agrippa argues the term is misused to justify chaos or unfairness.</note>—that is, equality of law—where the same law, the same honor, and the same reward are given to all without distinction. In a similar way, they say a "tranquil empire" is one where everything yields to the **lust of the prince**; and the "happiest" state is where the people overflow with luxury and idleness. By quite similar follies, **Medicine**, and **Laws**, and **Church Canons** are corrupted by these expositions. By these, they even force the **Sacred Scriptures** themselves, and **Christ** himself, to disagree with one another, twisting them not according to the sense of the **Holy Spirit**, nor for the common salvation of men, but for their own profit. From this matter, the gravest dangers have often loomed, as an error in words is wont to [breed] error...

...discordant, so that it is necessary for most of them to be liars; those who trust most in their instructions are the ones who speak correctly the least of all. For the entire law of speech resides not with the Grammarians, but with the people, and it derives the practice of speaking well from common custom. However, once the vigor of the Latin language ceased to belong to the people after the Barbarians grew in power, its logic was to be sought not from Grammarians, but from suitable and learned writers—such as Cicero, Cato, Varro, both Plinys, Quintilian, Seneca, Suetonius, Quintus Curtius, Titus Livy, Sallust, and their like. In these men alone remain the ancient delights of Latinity and the practice of speaking correctly. It is not found among the "literatores" <note>Agrippa uses "literatores" as a derogatory term for pedants who obsess over letters rather than meaning.</note>—those Grammarians who, with their rules on the inflections of words and cases, compositions, and deponent verbs, impose so much upon Latinity itself. They very often construct such words that it would be a sin for a Latin man to use them, unless perhaps the Sorbonne of Paris <note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris, often the target of Agrippa’s criticism for their rigid and complex definitions.</note> should include them among their articles of faith.

If anyone should say that one must not trust Grammarians regarding the truth of the Latin language, these same "literatores" and Grammarians nevertheless set themselves up as the sole censors, judges, and interpreters of all writers. They even arrogate to themselves the right to reorganize all authors and books, or to remove them from the Canon. No author of such excellent genius has ever existed who escaped their evil-speaking tongue, whom they have not criticized, or in whom they have not found much to blame. They complain of confusion in Plato and find his order lacking—about whose faults George of Trebizond <note>original: *Georgius Trapezuntius* (1395–1486), a Greek scholar who famously attacked Plato in favor of Aristotle.</note> composed books.

There was once Servius, who deserved well of the Latin language among Grammarians, yet Beroaldus attacked him; eventually, later Grammarians shunned him entirely as a "Barbarian."

<margin>Lying Poetry <note>original: *Mēdax Poesis*</note>.</margin> ...except to soothe the ears of foolish men with wanton rhythms, the counting and weighing of syllables, and the empty noise of names, while deceiving their minds with the charms of fables and patchwork quilts of lies <note>original: *mendaciorunq; centonibus*; a "cento" was a poem made of various fragments of other poems, here used to imply a stitched-together falsehood</note>. For now, from Chaos itself, she begins the introductions of her stories: she tells of the mutilations of Heaven <note>original: *Cœli sectiones*; the myth of Saturn castrating his father Uranus</note>, the births of Venus, the war of the Titans, the infancy of Jupiter, the deceptions of Rhea and the substitution of the stone <note>the myth in which Rhea tricked Saturn into swallowing a stone instead of the baby Jupiter</note>, the chains of Saturn, the rebellion of the Giants, the theft and punishment of Prometheus, the wanderings of Delos, the labors of Latona, the slaughter of the Python, the treachery of Tityos, the floods of Deucalion, and the origin of men from stones. # OF THE SCIENCES.
## Folio 20.

...loves, pandering, lusts, fornications, adulteries, intercourse with both men and beasts, and things even more absurd and wicked than these. By weaving them with the poisonous charms of words <note>original: *uenenosis uerborum leporibus*</note> and the harmful sweetness of song, she not only deceives and infects those present, but also passes down these frenzied sorceries <note>original: *ueneficia*; literally "poisonings" or "witchcraft"</note>, preserved in beautiful little verses and meters, to posterity. Like the bite of a rabid dog, she compels whoever she once infects with her lies and dogmas to rave with a similar madness. Indeed, her lies are fashioned with such art that they frequently take precedence over true histories—as is evident in the forged story of Dido’s adultery with Aeneas, and the account of the capture of Troy by the Greeks.

<margin>Divine powers falsely attributed to poetry.</margin>
There are some, however, who have reached such a pitch of insane frenzy that they believe certain shares of divinity <note>original: *diuinitatis sortes*</note> reside within it, because demons once gave their responses in poetic verse. For this reason, they call poets "prophets" and "seers" <note>original: *prophetas ac uates*</note>, inspired by a divine spirit, and they use the most trifling verses of poets as if they were oracles for divination.

<margin>The Homeric and Virgilian Lots.</margin>
Hence, among the ancients, these were known as the "Homeric Lots" <term>sortes Homericæ; a practice of opening a book of poetry at random and taking the first line seen as a prophecy</term>, from the verses of Homer, just as from the songs of Virgil came the "Virgilian Lots," which Spartianus <note>Aelius Spartianus, one of the purported authors of the *Augustan History*</note> mentions in his *Life of Hadrian*. This superstition has today even been transferred to the Sacred Scriptures and the verses of the Psalms, with many teachers of our own religion not even disapproving of it.

<margin>Poetry to be banished from the Republic.</margin>
But let us return to Poetry. Augustine commands her to be exiled from the City of God; the pagan Plato expelled her from his Republic; Cicero forbids her to be admitted. Socrates warns that if anyone cares greatly for his reputation and desires to keep it unsullied, he should take care not to have a poet for an enemy, because they possess no power so great in praising as they do in slandering and reviling. King Minos, a most just man celebrated by Hesiod and Homer, incited the tragic poets against himself because he waged war on the Athenians; they, in turn, banished him to the underworld <note>where he was cast as a judge of the dead</note>. Penelope, whom Homer portrayed as a woman of singular chastity, is described by Lycophron <note>a Greek poet known for his intentionally obscure and dark style</note> as having slept with several suitors. Dido, the founder of Carthage and a most continent widow, was first depicted as having fallen in love with Aeneas by the poet Ennius while he was singing of the deeds of Scipio—even though, based on the calculation of the dates... <note>Agrippa is noting the chronological impossibility, as Dido and Aeneas lived centuries apart</note>

Likewise, they dispute concerning the "thefts" of Virgil <note>A common Renaissance critique regarding Virgil's heavy borrowing from Homer.</note>, and in what month of the year he died, and which author first published the short Elegies.

<margin>Horace in *The Art of Poetry*.</margin>
> The grammarians dispute, and the case is still before the judge. <note>original: "Grammatici certant, & adhuc sub iudice lis est." A quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica* regarding unresolved scholarly debates.</note>

<margin>Poets are full of flattery and madness.</margin>
Moreover, all the songs of the Poets are full of fables, sung for nothing but the delight of fools under the pretext of flattering virtues or detesting the worst vices. Whatever the Poets do—whether they narrate, praise, or invoke—they flatter with their fables. On the other hand, whether they rail, bite, or accuse, they rave with their fables; but they are always truly insane. Therefore, Democritus rightly calls this not an art, but madness. And it is the opinion of Plato: in vain did anyone in his right mind knock upon the doors of Poesy. For indeed, the Poets sing admirable things only when they are clearly insane or drunken.

<margin>Poetry is madness.</margin>
Hence Augustine calls Poetry the "wine of error," <note>original: "uinum erroris"</note> poured out by drunken teachers. Jerome calls it the "food of demons." <note>original: "dæmonum cibum"</note> Furthermore, it is a very thin and naked art, which in itself is an entirely tasteless thing unless it be clothed and seasoned by some other discipline; it is a starving and ever-famished art, eating another's bread like mice. And yet, I know not how, amidst trifles and fables, it dares to promise immortal glory of name—along with Tithonus’s cicadas, the frogs of the Lycians, and the ants of the Myrmidons <note>Refers to various mythological transformations; the author implies that the "immortality" promised by poets is as strange or insignificant as these creatures.</note>—and to say:

> Live happy, if my songs have any power,
> No day shall ever remove you from mindful time. <note>original: "Viuite felices, si quid mea carmina possunt, / Nulla dies unquam memori uos eximet æuo." A paraphrase of Virgil’s *Aeneid* (IX, 446-447).</note>

Which in truth is either nothing, or will be of no benefit. ¶ But the Historians will say that this duty of granting immortality belongs not to the Poets, but to themselves.

<margin>HISTORY.</margin>
History is the narration of deeds done, recorded with praise or blame; it sets before the eyes the counsels, actions, and outcomes of great affairs, and the deeds of kings and great men, with the order and description of times and places, like a kind of living picture. Therefore, almost everyone considers this to be the mistress of life <note>original: "uitæ magistram"</note> and most useful for its instruction, because [it teaches] by the examples of many things...

# OF THE VANITY
## OF THE SCIENCES
### [Page 22]

...[History] by examples, since it spurs all the best men to every noble deed for the sake of the immortal glory of their name and praise, and likewise deters the impious and the wicked from vices through the fear of perpetual infamy. However, this matter very often results in the opposite; for many, as Livy said of Manlius Capitolinus, would rather have a great reputation than a good one. Indeed, most people, what they cannot achieve through virtues, wish to become known for through their crimes and to be inscribed in the histories. 

This is seen in the case of Pausanias, the young Macedonian, famous for the murder of King Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great.</note>, as Justin recounts from Trogus; and in the case of Herostratus (who burned the Temple of Diana at Ephesus <note>One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>, the most magnificent work of all, built by all of Asia over two hundred years), as narrated by Gellius, Valerius, and Solinus. And although it was provided by the most severe laws that no one should ever name that man by voice or in writing, he nevertheless achieved the end for which he perpetrated the crime: namely, his fame and name have been carried down to us through so many centuries. 

But let us return to history. 

<margin>
The Vanity of Histories
</margin>
Although this discipline, above all others, demands a sequence of events, credibility, consistency, and truth, yet it provides these least of all. So much do the historians disagree among themselves, and they hand down such various and diverse accounts of the same things, that it is impossible for most of them not to be the greatest of liars <note>original: "mendacissimos"</note>. I do not speak only of the beginning of the world, of the universal flood, or of the founding of the City <note>Rome</note>—from which beginnings they profess to know the deeds done—since they all are ignorant of the first, not all believe the second, and the third remains uncertain among them. Since these things are most remote and not received by all with equal reason, they might be forgiven for those errors. 

But regarding more recent times, the guilt of lying cannot but be imputed to them. 

<margin>
Causes of lies in Histories.
</margin>
The causes of such great discord among them are many: for most, because they were not present at the times, places, persons, or deeds narrated, collecting popular rumors from the reports of others, write nothing certain, nothing consistent. For this vice, Eratosthenes, Metrodorus of Scepsis, Posidonius, and Patrocles the geographer are censured by Strabo <note>The Latin text reads "Stratone," likely a variant or error for the geographer Strabo, who famously critiqued these authors for their inaccuracies.</note>. There are others who, though they have seen a part of the events, perhaps while in military transit, or under the pretext of religious vows, or as physicians running through provinces by way of hospitals <note>original: "xenodochia," referring to hostels or places of rest for strangers and the sick.</note>, begin to write...

There are also those who turn true events into fables, such as Ctesias of Cnidus, Hecataeus, and many other ancient historians. There are many others who, shamelessly boasting of the title of "Historiographers," presume to write with a wordy novelty about unknown and inaccessible provinces—so as not to seem ignorant of anything or merely repeating what others have said—yet they have handed down nothing but elegant trifles and monstrous lies. Of this sort are the things we read concerning the Arimaspians <note>A legendary tribe of one-eyed people in northern Scythia.</note>, Griffins, Pygmies and Cranes, the Dog-headed people, the Mouthless people <note>original: "Astomoris"; a legendary race said to survive only on the scent of food and flowers.</note>, the Horse-footed people, the Phanesii <note>People with ears so large they could wrap themselves in them.</note>, and the Cave-dwellers. And Arrian the Greek, who asserts that the dwellings of the Germans are not far from the Ionian Sea, to whom may be added Dionysius in the false accounts he gave concerning the Pyrenees mountains. ...among the errors of more recent historians and geographers, Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Coccio (1436–1506), known as Sabellicus, a Venetian historian.</note> falsely derives the Alans from the Alemanni, and falsely claims the Hungarians are descended from the Huns. He also claims that Pliny made mention of the Bernese Helvetians, though they were first established much later by Berthold, Duke of Zähringen <note>Berthold V founded the city of Bern in 1191, long after Pliny the Elder's death in 79 AD.</note>.

<margin>
Conrad’s error
</margin>
Similarly, Conrad Celtes <note>A famous German Renaissance humanist and poet (1459–1508).</note> considers the Dacians to be the same as the Cimbri, and the Cherusci to be the same as the Cerusi. He even thinks the Riphean Mountains <note>A mythical mountain range supposed by ancient Greeks to exist in the far north.</note> are located in Sarmatia, and relates that amber <note>original: "electrum"; Agrippa refers to the ancient debate on whether amber was a mineral or a tree resin.</note> is a gum flowing from a tree.

There are still others among historians who bear the guilt of much greater lies; those who, despite having been present at the events or otherwise knowing the facts as they truly happened, are nevertheless overcome by favoritism and the desire to please. Flattering their own side, they confirm falsehoods against the truth. There are those who, having set out to tell histories to accuse or defend the causes of others, relate only those things that support their argument, while concealing, omitting, or downplaying the rest. Thus they write crippled and corrupt histories. For this vice, Biondo <note>original: "Blondus"; Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), an Italian historian often considered a founder of archaeology.</note> censures Orosius <note>Paulus Orosius, a 5th-century historian and student of St. Augustine.</note>, because Orosius remained silent about that massive slaughter of Italy—in which the Goths plundered Ravenna, Candanum, Aquileia, Ferrara, and nearly all of Italy—so as not to weaken the point of his own argument.

Furthermore, there are those who, corrupted by fear, jealousy, or hatred of others, detract from the truth. Others, while wishing to extol the deeds of their own people, downplay the achievements of others and cast them into lowliness. They write not what is, but what they desire, what they want, and what pleases them; they are confident that there will be no lack of companions and patrons for their lies, nor lack of witnesses among those they have so exceptionally flattered. This vice was familiar to Greek writers in ancient times; but today, the chroniclers of almost every nation suffer from it: such as Sabellicus and Biondo in their histories of the Venetians, and Paolo Emilio <note>An Italian historian who wrote a history of the French monarchy.</note> and Robert Gaguin in their accounts of the Franks, whom...

...Princes do not support scholars for any other benefit than that which Plutarch <note>A Greek biographer and essayist (c. 46–120 AD) known for his "Parallel Lives."</note> describes: so that, by employing men of good talent as servants, they might stifle the merits of others and elevate their own deeds above the dignity of history using trifles and fictions. In this way, the Greek historians, when writing about the inventors of things, wanted to claim everything for themselves—but not for their own people <note>original: "nō suæ uendicare uoluerunt"; implying they claimed credit for inventions that belonged to other nations.</note>. There is also another most corrupt type of flatterer who, when they attempt to extend the origin of their princes back to the most ancient kings, find they cannot reach that far within their own lineage; they then resort to foreign origins and fables, making up names of kings and places, and there is nothing they will not invent. Of this sort is that barbarian Hunibaldus <note>A legendary, apocryphal historian of the Franks, now known to be a medieval fabrication.</note>, who, in writing the history of the Franks, invented Scythia, Sicambria, and a "Priam the Younger," along with other names of places and kings that no previous historian ever mentioned. And yet, men of similar intellect followed his trifles—namely Gregory of Tours, Regino, Sigebert, and many others. Of this same grain is Widukind <note>Widukind of Corvey (c. 925–973), a Saxon chronicler.</note>, who says the Saxons were the most ancient and original inhabitants of Germany, yet also claims they are the offspring of Macedonians and derived from the remnants of Alexander the Great’s army; many others follow him in this error.

Furthermore, many write histories not so much to report the truth, but to delight the reader, or to express and fashion the image of an excellent Prince in whatever way they please. If anyone should accuse these writers of lying, they say that they look not so much at the actual event as to the benefit of posterity and the fame of their own talent; therefore, they do not tell everything as it happened, but as it is expedient to tell it. They argue they do not wish to stubbornly defend the truth where fiction and falsehood serve the common good, citing as a witness Fabius <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, the Roman rhetorician.</note> who said that such a lie is not to be blamed if it leads toward the persuasion of virtue. Besides, since they write for future generations, they claim it does not matter much under whose name or in what sequence the example of a good Prince is set before the public. Such indeed was Xenophon’s description of Cyrus <note>Referring to Xenophon's "Cyropaedia," a fictionalized biography of Cyrus the Great intended as a manual on leadership.</note>—not describing him as he actually was, but as he ought to have been, as a model and archetype <note>original: "archetypon"</note> of the best Prince. He wrote it as a clever and elegant story, but without the faithfulness of truth. From here at last

<header># LIFE</header>

It has come to pass that many people—suited both by their natural temperament and by their diligent effort for lying—have written fabled histories based on contrived arguments. Examples include the tales of Morgana, Maguelonne, Melusine, Amadis, Florandus, Tirant, Conomor, Arthur, Uther, Lancelot, and Tristan <note>The author lists famous heroes and heroines from medieval chivalric romances, which he considers "ravings" compared to serious history.</note>. These, I say, are entirely fabled and unlearned ravings, more mythical than even the comedies and plays of poets. Among the learned, however, Lucian <note>A 2nd-century satirist known for "A True Story," a parody of travel tales.</note> and Apuleius <note>Author of "The Golden Ass."</note> held the highest rank in such works. Indeed, as Cicero says, there are innumerable fables even in Herodotus, the "Father of History," as well as in Diodorus and Theopompus; they themselves are full of lies. In their works, we read of rivers drunk dry when the Mede <note>original: "Medo prandente"; a reference to the Persian King Xerxes, whose army was said to be so large it drank entire rivers dry.</note> was dining, and of ships sailing through Mount Athos.

<margin>
Juvenal,
Satire 10.
</margin>

> And whatever lying Greece 
> dares in history.

And these are the reasons why a truly accurate trustworthiness is nowhere to be found in history; although we seek it most in this field, the judgment needed for discernment is most difficult to achieve. For since there were no public descriptions of deeds performed which could teach the truth of events and expose liars, everyone was left to their own opinion. From this they gained the power to err and to lie, whence such great discord was born among historiographers that even Josephus <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> (as he says in his work *Against Apion*) notes that they rebuke each other in their books and write very contrary things about the same matters.

<margin>Josephus</margin>

In how many places (he says) does Hellanicus differ from Acusilaus <note>Ancient Greek chroniclers whose works are mostly lost.</note> regarding genealogies? In how many places does Acusilaus correct Herodotus? And how Ephorus shows Hellanicus to be a liar in many things, while Timaeus does the same to Ephorus, and those who came after him to Timaeus—and indeed everyone to Herodotus! Nor did Timaeus deign to agree on individual points with Antiochus, Philistus, or Callias. In many things even Thucydides <note>The Athenian historian of the Peloponnesian War, usually praised for his objectivity.</note> is accused as if he were deceptive, although he seems to have written a most scrupulous history. Josephus writes these things about others, yet our own Hegesippus <note>original: "Aegefippus"; a 4th-century Latin author who adapted Josephus's "Jewish War."</note> corrects Josephus himself. Furthermore, many of the historiographers relate many things, but not all are to be approved, and some are not approved at all...

<header># OF THE SCIENCES. BOOK I.</header>

...most people propose the worst examples to be imitated and approved. For those who paint Hercules, Achilles, Hector, Theseus, Epaminondas, Lysander, Themistocles, and finally Xerxes, Cyrus, Darius, Alexander, Pyrrhus, Hannibal, Scipio, Pompey, and Caesar with wonderful praises—what have they described but great and raging robbers and famous plunderers of the world? Granted, they may have been excellent commanders, but they were certainly the worst and most wicked of men. Now, if someone should tell me that prudence is chiefly obtained from the reading of histories, I would not deny it, provided he also concedes that the greatest ruin is also drawn from them; for, as Martial <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis, a 1st-century Roman poet known for his witty epigrams.</note> sings in one of his verses: "There are many good things, there are some middling things, and there are many bad things" <note>original: "Sunt bona multa, sunt mediocria, sunt mala multa." (Martial, Epigrams 1.16).</note>.

<margin>RHETORIC.</margin>
Indeed, regarding **RHETORIC**, which is very closely related to these matters, there is a dispute among the most serious men as to whether it is an art or not, and the case is still before the judge <note>original: "adhuc sub iudice lis est"; a legal phrase from Horace indicating that a matter is still undecided.</note>. For Socrates himself, in the works of Plato, contends with very strong arguments that it is neither an art nor a science, but a certain shrewdness—and one that is neither noble nor honorable, but rather a shameful, ungentlemanly, and servile flattery. Furthermore, Lysias, Cleanthes, and Menedemus were of the opinion that eloquence cannot be contained within any art, but proceeds solely from nature. Nature, they argue, teaches anyone, whenever there is a need, how to flatter, how to explain their affairs, how to strengthen their points with arguments, and how to employ proper delivery, memory, and a beautiful method of invention—all of which proceed from nature alone. This very thing was seen in Antonius <note>Marcus Antonius (Mark Antony), whom the author here calls the "leader of Roman orators."</note>. Moreover, although before Tisias, Corax, and Gorgias <note>Three of the earliest Greek teachers of rhetoric in the 5th century BCE.</note> no one had yet written about or taught the art of rhetoric, many were nevertheless extremely eloquent by the goodness of their own talent. Additionally, since an "art" is defined as a collection of precepts tending toward a single end, the rhetoricians still argue

<margin>Controversy over the goal of rhetoric.</margin>

over what that goal might be: whether it is to persuade, or to speak well. They do not even agree on true causes, but instead devise new and fictional ones. Furthermore, they have invented so many theses, hypotheses, figures, colors <term>colors: "colores," or rhetorical embellishments used to put a particular "spin" or perspective on a legal or moral case</term>, guides, styles, suasories <term>suasories: practice speeches or "suasoriae," intended to persuade a historical figure toward a specific decision</term>, controversies, declamations, introductions, insinuations, methods for winning goodwill <note>original: "beneuolentiæ captationes"; the "captatio benevolentiae" is a standard rhetorical device to make the audience receptive at the start of a speech.</note>, and highly artificial narrations, that it is hardly possible to count them; and yet...

# ON VANITY

<margin>
Rhetoric was not approved by the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, famous for their "laconic" or brief and direct way of speaking.</note>.
</margin>
They deny that an end or fixed goal has been established for Rhetoric. The Lacedaemonians rejected it entirely, judging that the speech of honest men ought to be seen as proceeding from the heart, not from an art. Even the ancient Romans admitted rhetoricians into the City quite late; and when, after much controversy, Cicero attempted to show that the faculty of speaking proceeds not so much from art as from prudence—and for that reason wrote a work on the "perfect Orator"—nevertheless, that Orator, whom he fashioned there as a model, was not approved by everyone.

<margin>
Cicero was suspected by Brutus <note>Marcus Junius Brutus, the Roman statesman and philosopher, known for his strict moral integrity.</note> on account of rhetoric.
</margin>
Indeed, even to Brutus himself, a man of singular integrity, Cicero seemed quite suspect; and the opinion always prevailed that the precepts of the rhetoricians for "speaking well" do more to hinder the lives of men than to benefit them. And, to tell the truth, it is certain that this entire discipline of Rhetoric is nothing other than the art of fawning, flattery, and (as some say more boldly) of lying, so that you might use the varnish of speech <note>original: "fuco orationis"; literally the "dye" or "makeup" used to color a speech.</note> to persuade someone of that which you cannot achieve through the truth of the matter.

<margin>
Pericles's faculty of speaking.
</margin>
This is just as Archidamus said regarding the Sophist Pericles (as Eunapius <note>The original Latin reads "Ennapius," likely referring to Eunapius, the 4th-century Greek historian and rhetorician.</note> is the authority). When asked whether he was better than Pericles, Archidamus replied: "Even if Pericles were defeated by me in war, he is nevertheless gifted with such eloquence that when he argues about the matter, he appears not as the loser, but as the winner." And Pliny says of Carneades <note>A Greek skeptical philosopher known for his ability to argue any side of a debate with equal force.</note> that while he was arguing, what was true could hardly be discerned.

<margin>
Carneades.
</margin>
It is recorded of the same man that, after he had publicly discussed many things elegantly and wisely in favor of Justice, on the following day he spoke against Justice with no less learning and abundance. There was in Syracuse a rhetorician named Corax <note>Tradition identifies Corax as the legendary founder of Greek rhetoric in the 5th century BCE.</note>, a man of sharp wit and a ready tongue, who taught this art for a fee. Tisias approached him, and since he did not have the fee ready, he promised to pay double after Corax had taught him Rhetoric. Corax accepted him and taught him on this condition. When Tisias had learned the art, seeking to cheat his master out of the price, he asked Corax: "What is Rhetoric?" When Corax replied that it was "the worker of persuasions," Tisias argued against his teacher thus: "Whatever I say regarding the fee, if I persuade you that I owe you nothing, I owe nothing, because I have persuaded you of my non-indebtedness."

For this reason, Socrates himself judged that Rhetoricians are worthy of no esteem, nor should they hold any power in a well-ordered Republic. <meta>This page continues the author's critique of rhetoric, moving from theoretical paradoxes to historical examples of how famous orators used their skills to destabilize their nations and subvert justice.</meta>

# ON VANITY <note>This refers to the "Vanity of the Sciences," a theme explored by the author Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa to show that human knowledge is often deceptive or harmful.</note>

Cato the Censor was himself accused forty times, and he brought charges against others seventy times and more, disturbing the tranquility of the Republic throughout his entire life with his restless declamations. The other Cato, he of Utica, by provoking Caesar, fundamentally overturned Roman liberty. Cicero no less provoked Antony to the ruin of the Republic, and Demosthenes provoked Philip to the detriment of the Athenians. Finally, no state of the Republic has ever been exempt from being overturned by this artifice <note>referring to the "art" of rhetoric</note>; none has remained unhurt by the vice of eloquence if it lent an ear. Thus, the confidence of eloquence carries great weight in legal judgments: with this as its protector, bad causes are defended, and a guilty defendant is snatched from the danger of the law. With this as the accuser, the innocent have often been condemned, nor has anyone ever emerged so well-defended by that artifice that the opposing party was not harmed. Marcus Cato, the wisest of the Romans, forbade those three Athenian orators—Carneades, Critolaus, and Diogenes—from being admitted to public hearing in the City of Rome, because they were endowed with such sharp wits, such fluency of speech, and such powerful eloquence that they could easily persuade people of both just and unjust things.

<margin>
Demosthenes' skill in persuasion.
</margin>
It is well known that Demosthenes once boasted among his friends that he could, whenever he pleased, turn the verdicts of the judges to his own will by the artifice of his speech; at his whim, the Athenians were often at war or at peace with Philip. Such was the power of his eloquence in stirring up and calming the passions of minds and wills that, as if holding sovereignty over his fellow citizens, he turned them wherever he wished by speaking.

<margin>
Cicero called king.
</margin>
For a similar reason, Cicero was called "king" by many in Rome, because he could turn the Senate wherever he wished by speaking, ruling all things with his oration.

<margin>
What Rhetoric is.
</margin>
From this, it appears that Rhetoric is nothing other than the art of persuading and moving the emotions, using subtle eloquence, exquisite disguise <note>original: "fuco"; literally "red dye" or "makeup," used here metaphorically for deceptive ornamentation</note>, and a deceitful appearance of truth <note>original: "verisimilitudine"; the quality of seeming true or "verisimilar" without actually being so</note> to snatch away the minds of the unwary and lead them into the captivity of error, perverting the sense of truth.

But if, by the benefit of nature, nothing is expressed except with a true voice, what is more pestilential than the study of counterfeit words? The speech of truth is simple, but living and penetrating, a discerner of the intentions of the heart, and like an axe and a sword...

Even if they could speak more elegantly about the virtues, we see they are far more refined and possess a more successful eloquence for defending errors, sowing strife, exciting factions, and heaping up insults, curses, and slanders than for promoting peace, harmony, and tranquility, or for preaching charity, faith, and religion.

<margin>
Lutherans skilled in rhetoric.
