Are their authors not highly eloquent men, skilled in speech and the elegance of the pen? We saw them a few years ago so praised for their mastery of languages, their refined speech, and their readiness in speaking and writing that nothing more could be added to their praise; yet today we see them as the heads and leaders of the heretics.

<margin>
Ciceronians.

Those who study Aristotle and Plato too intensely become, in the first case, superstitious, and in the second, impious. All those who pour idle speeches into the ears of men, instead of the simple words of truth, will stand at the judgment seat to give an account for the vain conjectures and lies they uttered against God.

<page-num>XXVII.</page-num>
<header>OF THE SCIENCES. Folio XXVII.</header>

...it might hand down a method by which true and false things may be judged. Furthermore, these **Dialecticians** <term>practitioners of Dialectic, the formal art of logical argument and reasoning</term> promise that they can find the essential definition (as they call it) of any thing. Yet, they can never provide a definition in any words so clear that the mind does not remain equally ignorant. Indeed, if one says to an unlearned person, instead of "man," that he is "a rational, mortal animal," that person will understand less than if he had simply said "man."

More has been written on these subjects among the Latins by **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose translations and commentaries on logic became the standard textbooks of the Middle Ages.</note>, whose works are not fully preserved, though they surpass all that **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (4th century BC) whose "Organon" defined the rules of logic for nearly two millennia.</note> wrote in his *Categories*, *Refutations*, *Topics*, *On Interpretation*, *Analytics*, and the rest. Following him, the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named after the covered walkways (peripatoi) where they traditionally met.</note> are of the opinion that nothing is stable, or can be known, unless it is proven through a **syllogism** <term>a form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises</term> by means of a demonstration—specifically, the kind that Aristotle describes.

However, Aristotle never actually observed this in his own teachings; all his arguments are deduced from his own presuppositions, whatever they might have been. To this day, all these promisers of the sciences have given no true demonstrations, or at least very few—

<margin>
No true demonstrations, or very few.
</margin>

—not even in the study of nature. Instead, they derive all their conclusions from pre-accepted ideas, either from their master Aristotle or from someone else who spoke before them. They have held the authority of these men as the principles of their demonstration. Yet Aristotle himself teaches that a true demonstration, which ought to produce certain knowledge, is that which is done through **quiddities** <term>from the Latin "quidditas," meaning the "whatness" or true essence of a thing</term>, using the specific differences of things which are hidden and unknown to us. He says, moreover, that a demonstration must be made from causes—from things that are "of themselves," "through themselves," and "according to themselves." These propositions, since they are convertible (each implying the other), led him to say that circular demonstration from causes is neither given nor allowed. 

If, therefore, the principles of demonstration are for the most part unknown, and circular reasoning is not permitted, then certainly no science, or very little and that quite uncertain, can be obtained from it. For it will be necessary to believe in things "demonstrated" through certain fragile principles, which we agree to either because of the preceding authority of wise men (treating them as known terms) or which we prove by experience through the senses. For all knowledge (as they say) has its

<margin>
Knowledge arises from the senses.
</margin>

# ON VANITY

...is also more true when multiple senses agree upon it. Thus, by their opinion, we are led by the hand from **sensible things** <note>original: "sensibilibus"; things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note> to all those things that can be known by us. Yet, since all senses are often deceptive, they certainly cannot prove any pure experience to us. Furthermore, since the senses are unable to reach an intellectual nature, and the causes of lower things (from which their natural effects, properties, or passions ought to be demonstrated) are by everyone's consent deeply unknown to our senses, is it not proved that the way of truth is closed off to the senses? Therefore, all those deductions and sciences that are fundamentally rooted in the senses themselves will be uncertain, erroneous, and deceptive. What use then is **Dialectic** <term>the formal art of logical argument</term> now? What fruit is there in that scientific demonstration derived from principles and experiments? Since it will be necessary to agree to these as if they were already known terms, will not those very principles and experiences be known more through intuition than through being demonstrated? But this art must now be revisited by us from a bit further back.

<margin>The Categories</margin>
Dialecticians number ten **Predicaments** <term>also called Categories; a classification of all possible things that can be the subject or predicate of a proposition</term>, which they call the most general types. These are: **Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Time, Place, Position, Possession, Action,** and **Passion** <note>original: "Passio"; in this context, it refers to the act of being acted upon or "undergoing," the opposite of "Action."</note>. They believe that all things consist of these, and that whatever is contained in the whole and universal circular world can be understood through them.

<margin>The Predicables</margin>
They teach, moreover, five things that may be predicated <note>stated or asserted</note> of these categories and their parts: **Genus, Species, Difference, Property,** and **Accident**. For this reason, these are named the **Predicables** <term>the five ways in which a predicate can be related to its subject</term>.

<margin>The Causes of things</margin>
Furthermore, they have identified four causes for any thing: the **material**, **formal**, **efficient**, and **final** causes <note>Aristotle’s framework: what it's made of (material), its essence/shape (formal), what made it (efficient), and its purpose (final).</note>. From these, they judge they can discover the truth or falsehood of all things through a certain "infallible" (as they think) demonstration—that is, the **syllogism**. This must be arranged in one of the three "figures" (as they call the patterns of argument) and across more than nineteen modes.

<margin>The Syllogism</margin>
They compose every syllogism or demonstration from three terms. The first is the subject of the question, called the **minor**; the second is the predicate of the question, called the **major**; the third is the **middle term**, which participates between the two. Based on these, they form two propositions which they call **premises**—the major and the minor—from which finally...

Folio 28.

### OF THE SCIENCES
D iij
<meta>Catchword: they prove.</meta>

...a conclusion is born, namely from one extreme to the other, running forward as if from a boundary toward a goal. This entire process is that "noble artifice," and these are its extreme borders, by which they believe they can combine, divide, and conclude all things. They rely on certain axioms <term>self-evident truths or principles</term> which they think are impossible to refute. These are the monstrous and deep mysteries of the logical craft, sought out with great labor by deceitful masters. These matters are treated like hidden secrets and arcane mysteries which not everyone is permitted to profess, nor to learn, except for those who can provide the proper levels of payment for them, and who have purchased this authority among the scholastics at great expense. Finally, these are their hunting dogs and those nets with which (in their opinion) they hunt for truth in all things—whether those subject to nature, as in **Physics**, or those accompanying nature itself, as in **Mathematics**, or even those which in some way surpass nature itself, as in **Metaphysics**. Yet, with this very artifice, according to the proverb of Publius Clodius and Varro, they lose the truth by arguing too much. These are merely the boundaries of the ancient dialecticians.

<margin>
SOPHISTRY
</margin>

But we are producing far more: for look at the monstrosities that the more recent school of **SOPHISTS** <term>scholars who use clever but fallacious arguments</term> has added to these things. They include: the properties of terms, the infinite, comparatives, superlatives, "differing from another," "beginning and ending," formalities, **haecceities** <note>original: "ecceitatibus"; a philosophical term for the "this-ness" or individual essence of a thing</note>, instants, ampliations, restrictions, distributions, intentions, **suppositions** <note>the way a term stands for an object in a sentence</note>, appellations, obligations, consequences, insolubles, exponibles, reduplicatives, exclusives, instances, cases, particularizations, supposits, mediated and immediate things, complete and incomplete, complex and incomplex, and other monstrous and vain words. These are handed down in their "Little Logicals" <note>referring to *Parva Logicalia*, the standard medieval textbooks on logic</note>, by which they will easily convince anyone that everything false and impossible is true—and conversely, whatever is true, they will devastate with a sudden fire and ruin of words, as if bursting forth from these machines like a Trojan horse. There are 

<margin>
Controversies of the Sophists.
</margin>

those who accept only three predicaments, and only two figures of syllogisms, and only eight of their modes...

### ON VANITY
<meta>Catchword: nor</meta>

...they prove. Moreover, they mock **modal propositions**, and further, **concrete and abstract terms**; nor are there lacking those who count an eleventh **category** <term>also known as a predicament; the classifications of all things according to Aristotle</term>, and a fourth figure of the **syllogism** <term>a form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term>. They have increased the number of "predicables" <note>the ways in which a predicate can be related to a subject</note> and causes, and have introduced so many inventions and **Scotist subtleties** <note>original: "Scoticas subtilitates"; referring to the notoriously complex logic of Duns Scotus and his followers</note>, that the cleverness of **Cleanthes** and **Chrysippus** <note>famous Stoic logicians of antiquity</note>, along with the little traps of **Daphitas**, **Euthydemus**, and **Dionysodorus**, will seem entirely thick and rustic if they are compared with these new inventions of our modern **Sophists**.

<margin>The fruits of Sophistry.</margin>

In these inventions, almost the entire crowd of Scholastics is now occupied everywhere with miserable labor and damnable zeal. They seem to do nothing more than learn how to err, and through perpetual "sword-clashes" of words, they render the truth—which ought to be explained—more obscure, or they lose it entirely. Their whole discipline is nothing other than a kind of snare, which, by a deceitful trickery of perverted wording, subverts the proper use of speech and does violence to the tongue of the ignorant. It turns well-worn truth into a "plausible" exposition. Their glory is situated in nothing but contention and noise, as they do not desire victory so much as the struggle itself. 

<margin>Who is best among the Sophists.</margin>

They have no purpose of finding the truth, but only of quarreling, so much so that among them, the first place is held by whoever is loudest, most impudent, and boldest in the clatter of his tongue. Of these people, **Petrarch** says: whether it is out of shame for their writing style or a confession of ignorance, they are relentless with their tongues but do not struggle with the pen. They do not want it to appear how frivolous the things are with which they adorn themselves, and therefore, in the **Parthian manner** <note>referring to the ancient Parthian tactic of firing arrows while retreating</note>, they engage in a fugitive battle. Tossing out flying words, they commit their sails, as it were, to the winds. 

For these are the ones of whom **Quintilian** says: they are wonderfully clever in disputing, but once they leave that trickery, they are no more capable in any serious action than certain small little animals which, while nimble in narrow spaces, are easily caught in an open field. Thus they fear the "open field" <note>meaning the open arena of serious scholarship or public life</note>. It is a true saying that diversions and winding paths are the refuge of weakness; just as those who are not strong enough to run well elude others by turning, so these Sophists fear to fight by quoting books and authors. Instead, they wish to contend only by the strength of memory and tongue, with fugitive shouts, aiming not at the pen but at ears prone to forgetting.

# THE SCIENCES. Folio XXIX.

...nor do they think it matters what reasoning anyone uses, provided he gives an **instance** <term>an 'instantia' or formal objection used to block an opponent's argument</term>, nor do they care what he feels or says, so long as he speaks and contends vigorously: <margin>Wordy Sophists</margin> For whoever is more wordy, he is seen as more learned among them; with these deceptions they circle the schools and the streets, and seek out rivals, whom they invite, press, and leap upon to engage in battle; if the rival engages and pushes back, they slip away into diversions, and seek hiding places, and return to their usual tricks, making so many twists and turns, as if it were necessary to circle a labyrinth. <margin>The Sophists' lust for arguing</margin> But if anyone is unwilling, or finds it tedious to fight with them, they attack with some deceitful interrogation about something which that person has not investigated with the best knowledge, so that in this way, they might either convict the respondent of an error by surprise, or, if he denies knowing it, make him guilty of shame and drive him out <note>literally "explode" him; in a theatrical sense of hissing someone off a stage</note>, while they themselves claim the glory of learning for both sides of the issue. 

But let us look at what fruits **Dialectic** <term>the formal art of logical discussion and investigation</term> with its Sophists has produced and is producing for us in the Church of Christ; those who, not submitting to divine tradition, confound it with composed reasons derived from fallacious senses. By trusting these too much, as the light of truth recedes, darkness grows, in which these false teachers—wrapped up and blinded—and leaders of the blind, drag many with them into the pit with false arguments and "plausible" reasons, always swimming in a deep sea of ignorance and error. 

Slippery in the manner of serpents, and slinking in with words of fraud and seduction, they seduce the unskilled into believing their fictions; and extolling these, they dare to persuade others that the most sacred **Theology**, without Logic, without Dialectic, without strife, without altercation, and without Sophists, cannot stand. <margin>How far Logic is useful</margin> I do not deny that Logic contributes to scholastic exercise, but what it contributes to the contemplation of Theology, I do not see—the highest "Logic" of which consists in prayer. For it was not with a vain promise that Christ pledged to us, saying, "Ask and you shall receive." <note>A reference to Matthew 7:7 or John 16:24</note> And so, before these contentious **Scholastics** <note>university-trained theologians and philosophers of the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> learn their own dialectic, those faithful to Christ obtain all necessary truth from the Master of Truth <note>original: "magistro veritatis"; referring to Christ</note> himself. Furthermore, Logic, through various circuitous paths, finally does not [another]...

# ON VANITY

<margin>
Logic is the strength of heretics.
</margin>

...can reach higher, not through philosophy, but through faithful prayer; by this straight and most certain way, one ascends to the highest wisdom of both divine and human affairs. Therefore, all those who say that this **Dialectic** <term>the formal art of logical argument</term> is the most powerful engine for overturning heretics are in error, when in truth it is the very strength of all heretics. Relying on this art, the heretics **Arius** and **Nestorius** <note>Arius (d. 336) argued that Jesus was not co-eternal with God the Father; Nestorius (d. c. 450) was accused of separating Christ's human and divine natures</note> once acted so impudently foolish: the former asserted that there were different substances in the Trinity, divided by rank and time; the latter denied that the Virgin Mary was the *Mother of God* <note>original: "theotocon"; the Greek term 'Theotokos' emphasizes that Mary gave birth to God in human form</note>. They did this because they presumed to measure divine operations by logical sophisms, paying more attention to the logical traps of **Aristotle** than to the divine words of Scripture. For all the dogmas of heretics (as **Jerome** says) find their seat and rest among the thickets <note>original: "spineta"; literally 'thorn-bushes' or 'brambles'</note> of **Aristotle** and **Chrysippus** <note>Chrysippus was a leader of the Stoic school known for his rigorous logic</note>. From those thickets **Eunomius** <note>a radical Arian bishop</note> brings forth the idea that "that which was born did not exist before it was born." From there, the **Manichaean** <note>followers of a dualistic religion that saw the world as a struggle between Light and Dark</note>, in order to free God from the responsibility of evil, introduces another "author" of evil. From there, **Novatus** <note>a 3rd-century priest who held a rigorous view against readmitting Christians who had lapsed during persecution</note> withdraws the hope of pardon so that he might take away the possibility of repentance. 

All the dogmas of Heretics draw the streams of their arguments from those fountains. For since there is no speech that does not admit contradiction, and no argument that cannot be subverted by another, it follows that men can reach no end of knowledge and no realization of truth through logical disputes. Instead, it happens that many turn away from the truth into heresies, believing they have found a "stronger" appearance of truth through logical arguments, or they refute heretics in such a way that they themselves establish nothing healthier in their place. For this reason, **Plato** himself was very reluctant for his "Guardians" <note>the ruling class in Plato's ideal Republic</note> to touch Dialectic until late in life, because it argues for both sides and makes one's reasoning regarding what is honorable or dishonorable less firm. So much for Dialectic.

<margin>THE ART OF MEMORY</margin>
¶ Among these arts is also numbered **MEMORY**, which (as **Cicero** says) is nothing other than a certain induction and a method of instruction, consisting of "places" and "images" <term>The Method of Loci: a mnemonic technique where one mentally "places" items to be remembered in specific locations within a building</term> as if they were parchment and characters. Nevertheless, whatever its nature, it cannot exist at all without natural memory, which it often overwhelms with so many monstrous images. Instead of a tenacious memory, it sometimes induces Mania and Phrensy <note>historical terms for madness or inflammation of the brain</note>; by overloading the natural memory with images of innumerable things and words, it makes those not content with the limits of nature go mad through art. Thus, when Simonides or someone else offered this art to **Themistocles** <note>An Athenian statesman and general</note>, he replied that he would rather have the art of forgetting: "For," he said, "I remember many things I would not want to, and I cannot forget what I would wish." And **Quintilian** said of Metrodorus: "It was certainly vanity and boasting, for one to glory in his memory more by art than by nature." **Cicero** wrote about it in his books on the *New Rhetoric* <note>original: "Rhetoricorum nouorum"; referring to the *Rhetorica ad Herennium*, which in the Renaissance was attributed to Cicero</note>, as did **Quintilian** in his *Institutes*, and **Seneca**, and among more recent authors, **Francesco Petrarch**, **Mareolus of Verona**, **Peter of Ravenna**, and **Hermannus Buschius**, and many others, though many are obscure men and unworthy of a catalog. And these disciplines, although they have produced few or no heresies in the Church, nevertheless, as **Augustine** says, pertain nothing to salvation, but rather lead into error and call one away from God; and as **Jerome** says, they are not sciences of piety.

It deals with harmonic and geometric numbers, and with various properties <note>original: "passionibus"; literally "passions," a technical term for the characteristics or "behaviors" of numbers</note> and subtractions of numbers, and the method of calculation.

### ON VANITY

<margin>**PYTHAGOREAN** Lots <note>The practice of "sortes" or lots involved using chance or mathematical systems to predict the future.</note>.</margin>
Nor do I think I should pass over that which the **PYTHAGOREANS** asserted, and which others believe Aristotle himself credited: that the elements of the alphabet possess their own fixed numbers. From these, they would divine using men's proper names by collecting the numbers of each letter into a total. By comparing these sums, they awarded the palm <note>A symbol of victory.</note> to the one whose total exceeded the other—whether the question concerned war, lawsuits, marriage, life, or any other similar matter. By this reasoning, they say Patroclus was conquered by Hector, and Hector in turn was overcome by Achilles. Terentianus <note>Terentianus Maurus, a Roman grammarian of the 2nd century AD who wrote a famous treatise on letters and syllables.</note> handed down this tradition in these verses:

> *And they say names are so bound to letters,*
> *That some are of greater numbers, others of lesser:*
> *Whenever they face the uncertain dangers of battle,*
> *Where the greater number stands, victory favors,*
> *While the smallest sum reveals the omens of death:*
> *Thus they say Patroclus perished by Hector’s hand,*
> *And thus they say Hector soon fell to Achilles.*

<margin>Horoscopes through lots.</margin>
There are also those who, by similar calculation, promise that they can determine horoscopes, just as some man named Alexandrinus <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, though here described as an "obscure philosopher."</note>—an obscure philosopher said to be a disciple of Aristotle—wrote on the matter. Furthermore, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> records that even this discovery is attributed to **PYTHAGORAS**: that an odd number of vowels in a person's proper name portends blindness in the eyes, lameness, or similar misfortunes.

<margin>The parts of Music.</margin>
The ancients divided this into the **Enharmonic**, **Chromatic**, and **Diatonic** genera. The first (namely the **Enharmonic**), because of its excessively obscure difficulty and the impossibility of its investigation, they abandoned; the second [the **Chromatic**], however, they despised and rejected due to its reputation for lewdness; but the third type alone [the **Diatonic**] they admitted, being persuaded that it was consistent with the composition of the world <note>The "composition of the world" refers to the *Musica Mundana*, the ancient belief that the movements of celestial bodies followed harmonic proportions.</note>. There are also among the ancients those who distinguished musical modes by the names of nations, such as the **Phrygian**, **Lydian**, and **Dorian**, which are established to have been the oldest types among **Polymestes** and **Sacadas of Argos**; to these, **Sappho of Lesbos** (as **Aristoxenus** says) added a fourth, namely the **Mixolydian**, whose inventor others think was **Terpander**, or others **Pithoclydes** the flute-player: **Lysias** named **Lamprocles of Athens** as its author. The authority of the ancients noted these four modes as famous and called their structure the **Encyclopedia** <note>original: *Encyclopaediã*; literally the "circle of learning." The author suggests music was once considered the core of a universal education.</note>, as if it were a circle of sciences, because Music embraces all disciplines; just as **Plato** says in the first book of the *Laws*, music cannot be handled without universal learning. 

<margin>The Phrygian modulation.</margin>
Among these four modes, however, they do not approve of the **Phrygian**, because it distracts and ravishes the soul; **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry was a 3rd-century Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote extensively on the "harmonics" of Ptolemy.</note> calls it "barbaric" because it is only suitable for exciting fury and battles. Others for that reason call it "Bacchic" <note>Referring to Bacchus, the god of wine and frenzy.</note> as being frenzied, impetuous, and disturbed; by its modulation, which they express with the anapaest foot <note>The anapaest is a poetic and musical rhythm (short-short-long) often used for driving, martial movements.</note>, we read that the **Spartans** and **Cretans** were stirred to arms. With this same mode, **Timotheus** incited King **Alexander** to arms; and a young man of **Tauromenium** (as **Boethius** tells) <note>Boethius relates a famous anecdote where Pythagoras used a different musical mode to calm a drunken youth who, driven mad by the Phrygian mode, was attempting to burn down a house.</note>, being excited by the **Phrygian** sound, rushed to burn down the house where a prostitute was hiding. 

**Plato** also reproves the **Lydian** mode, as it is high-pitched and, departing from the modesty of the **Dorian**, suited for lamentations. Yet (as it pleases some) it is also suitable for those who are cheerful and pleasant by nature. Hence they say the **Lydians** are a cheerful and very pleasant people, delighted by these modulations.

...which even the Tuscans, as descendants of the Lydians, used for their choral dances. 

<margin>The Dorian mode of modulation.</margin>
However, they preferred the **Dorian** mode above all others, as it was considered more serious and honorable, modest in every respect, and suited for the weightier affections of the soul and movements of the body—being useful for living rightly and well. For this reason, it was held in great veneration among the Cretans, the Lacedaemonians <note>The Lacedaemonians are the Spartans, known for their disciplined and austere lifestyle.</note>, and the Arcadians. Even the general **Agamemnon**, when about to set out for the Trojan War, left a Dorian musician at home to keep his wife **Clytemnestra** in a state of modesty and integrity by means of the **spondee** <note>original: *spondæo pede*; the spondee is a slow, steady musical or poetic foot consisting of two long syllables, believed to have a calming and moralizing effect on the listener.</note>. Consequently, she could not be corrupted by **Aegisthus** until he had first impiously removed that musician from her presence.

<margin>Mixolydian modulation.</margin>
But they say the **Mixolydian** mode, being suitable for tragedies and lamentations, possesses the power to both incite and restrain the spirit, and holds dominion over grief. To these four modes, there are some who have added others which they call "collaterals"—namely, the **Hypodorian**, **Hypolydian**, and **Hypophrygian**—so that there are seven in total, corresponding to the seven planets. To these, **Ptolemy** adds an eighth, the **Hypermixolydian**, which is the sharpest (highest) of all and is attributed to the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars in the ancient geocentric model of the universe.</note>. Yet **Lucius Apuleius**, in the first book of his *Florida*, describes five modes: the **Aeolian**, which is varied; the **Ionian**, which is plaintive; the **Phrygian**, which is warlike; and the **Dorian**, which is religious. Following the tradition of **Aristoxenus**, **Martianus Capella** also counts five principal modes and ten collateral ones.

<margin>The utility of music.</margin>
And although people admit that this art possesses no small degree of sweetness, the common opinion—and indeed the experience known to everyone—is that music is an exercise for unfortunate and intemperate minds, and for those who hold no reason for either beginning or ending. This is much like what is read concerning the flute-player **Archabius**, who had to be paid more to stop than he was paid to play. Concerning such troublesome musicians, **Horace** writes thus in his *Satires*:

<margin>Horace, in his Satires.</margin>
> This is a vice common to all singers: among friends,
> They can never bring themselves to sing when asked,
> But when unbidden, they never stop.

<margin>
Musical parasites
</margin>
...no serious, modest, chaste, or brave man has ever professed this art. Therefore, the Greeks called them by a common name: "Craftsmen of Father Liber" <note>Father Liber is an ancient Roman god of fertility and wine, often identified with the Greek Dionysus or Bacchus.</note> or (as Aristotle says) "Dionysian craftsmen" <note>original: *Dionysiacos technitas*</note>—that is, artists of the Bacchanalia. These individuals were mostly accustomed to having wicked characters, spending much of their lives in lack of restraint and often in poverty—vices which the art of music both gives birth to and increases. The kings of the Persians and Medes counted musicians among parasites and stage actors; they took pleasure in their work but held the performers themselves in contempt.

<margin>
Antisthenes' saying about the flute-player.
</margin>
The wise Antisthenes, when he heard that a certain Ismenias was considered an excellent flute-player <note>The *tibicen* played the *tibia*, a double-piped reed instrument often translated as a flute or oboe.</note>, said: "He is a worthless man; for if he were a man of integrity, he would not be a flute-player." For as they say, that art does not belong to a sober and upright man, but to one who is idle and reckless. Scipio, Aemilianus, and Cato rejected this art as being foreign to Roman customs. Hence, it was a source of shame for Augustus and Nero that they pursued music too eagerly. However, Augustus, having been corrected, stopped; but Nero, pursuing it even more extensively, was held in contempt and became a laughingstock for it.

<margin>
Philip's aphorism on music
</margin>
When King Philip heard that his son [Alexander the Great] had sung quite sweetly in a certain place, he rebuked him: "Are you not ashamed," he said, "that you know how to sing so well?" For it is enough and more for a prince to have leisure to listen while others sing. In the Greek poets, Jupiter does not sing, nor does he play the lyre; the learned Pallas <note>Pallas is another name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom, who in myth famously threw away the flutes because they distorted her face.</note> detests the flutes. In Homer, the lyre-player plays while Alcinous and Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> listen. In Virgil, Iopas sounds and sings while Dido and Aeneas listen. While Alexander the Great was once singing, his tutor Antigonus broke the lyre and threw it away, saying: "At your age, it is fitting to rule, not to sing." Even the Egyptians (according to Diodorus) forbade their youths to learn music, as it effeminates the minds of men. And Ephorus (witnessed by Polybius) taught that it was invented for nothing but to mock and deceive men. But in truth, what is more useless, what more contemptible, what more to be shunned than these flute-players, singers, and other kinds of musicians? ->Argus had a head surrounded by a hundred eyes:<-

Therefore, Anaxilas <note>A Greek poet of Middle Comedy.</note> said not wrongly: "By the gods, Music—just like Libya <note>A common ancient proverb: "Libya always brings forth something new."</note>—every year brings forth some new wild beast." Athanasius banned this art from the churches because of its vanity; but Ambrose, more eager for ceremonies and display, established the practice of singing and chanting in the churches. Augustine, however, hesitating in the middle, records in his *Confessions* that a not insignificant doubt arose for him from this. <margin>The dangers of dances.</margin>
Often there the matron (as Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the Italian poet and scholar who often wrote on moral philosophy</note> says) has lost her long-preserved honor; often the unhappy young girl has learned there what she would have been better off never knowing. The reputation and shame of many perish there. Many have returned home from such things unchaste, even more have returned with their virtue in doubt, but not one has ever returned more chaste. We see modesty often laid low, and always pushed and attacked by dances. Yet some Greek writers have praised this art, just as they have praised many other foul and ruinous things.

<margin>Where dances originated.</margin>
They say that the very beginnings of dancing proceeded divinely from the highest heavens, from the motions of the stars and constellations—their progress and retreat, their embrace and order—like a certain harmonic heavenly dance born together with the creation of the World. Others say it was an invention of the Satyrs <note>Nature spirits in Greek myth, often associated with riotous dancing and wine</note>. They also say that Bacchus <note>The god of wine and ecstasy</note> defeated the Tyrrhenians, Indians, and Lydians—most warlike peoples—with this art. From here, finally, dance itself was brought into religious practice, and by the Corybantes <note>Armed priests in Phrygia who worshipped the goddess Cybele with loud music and dancing</note> in Phrygia...

Among the Ethiopians as well, and the Egyptians, Thracians, and Scythians, dancing was held among the sacred ceremonies, since it had been established by Orpheus and Musaeus <note>Mythical figures associated with the origins of music, poetry, and religious mysteries.</note>, who were themselves the best of dancers. The Spartans, the most excellent of the Greeks, having thoroughly learned to dance from Castor and Pollux, were accustomed to perform all things with dances. In Thessaly, it was held in such high esteem that the leaders and standard-bearers of the people were honored with the title of "foremost dancers." Even Socrates himself, judged the wisest of all men by the oracle, did not blush to learn to dance even when he was older in age; indeed, he extolled it with the highest praises and counted it among the serious disciplines. To him, the matter seemed too weighty to be judged simply, as it was entirely divine, born with the creation of the World, and came forth into light alongside the most ancient God, Love.

But what wonder is it that the Greeks philosophize in this way? They are a people who attribute adulteries, rapes, parricides, and indeed every kind of crime to the Gods as their authors. Many have written books about dancing, which categorize all its types, forms, and rhythms, listing their names, the nature of each, and by whom they were invented; therefore, I will refrain from saying more about them here. The ancient Romans, men grave in wisdom and authority, rejected all dances,

### OF THE SCIENCES. Folio 46.

[so that he] may understand. Such is the excellence of the **Art of Acting** <term>Histrionica: the ancient Roman art of dramatic stage performance, often involving mimicry and gesture</term> that there is no need for interpreters at all; for it represents the old man, the boy, the woman, the male servant, the female servant, the drunkard, the angry man, and the differences and emotions of all characters with such pleasant gesturing that even a spectator at a distance who does not hear the play can understand its plot solely from the Actor's dance. 

<margin>Cicero’s competition with the actor Roscius.</margin>
Hence we read that Actors were held in no small esteem; and it is established (on the authority of Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius, a Roman provincial writer of the early 5th century</note>) that Cicero used to compete with the actor Roscius (who was also very dear to the dictator Sulla), to see whether the actor could express the same meaning more often through various gestures, or whether Cicero himself could deliver it through his abundance of eloquence in different speech. This challenge led Roscius to write a book in which he compared eloquence with the Art of Acting. 

However, the city of Marseille <note>original: "Massiliensium civitas"</note> (according to Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman historian of the 1st century AD</note>) stood as such a guardian of dignity that it allowed no entrance to Actors or Mimes. This was because their plots for the most part contained acts of adultery <note>original: "stuprorum"</note>, and they feared that the habit of watching such things might create the license to imitate them. 

Furthermore, practicing the Art of Acting is not only a shameful and wicked occupation, but it is also scandalous even to watch and take pleasure in it, since finding delight in a lewd mind falls into the category of a crime. Finally, no name was once more infamous than that of Actors, and by the laws themselves, anyone who had danced in a play in the Theater was barred from holding honors <note>original: "ab honoribus," referring to public offices or social status</note>.

<margin>Rhetorical dance.</margin>
There was also a **Rhetorical dance**, not unlike the Art of Acting but more restrained, which Socrates, Plato, Cicero, Quintilian, and most of the Stoics considered very useful and extremely necessary for an orator. This consisted of a certain fitting gesture of the body, a composed arrangement of the face and limbs, the vigor of the eyes, the gravity of the expression, and a sound of voice adapted to individual words and sentences, with effective movement of the body toward those things being expressed—but only so far as gesturing is concerned. 

However, this dancing or Acting style of Rhetoric eventually began to be banished by certain Orators, after Augustus warned Tiberius to speak with his mouth, not with his fingers <note>original: "ore, non digitis loqueretur"</note>. Now it has been entirely abolished, except perhaps by a few scenic little brothers <note>original: "fraterculis," likely a dismissive reference to certain friars or minor clergy who maintained theatrical gestures in their preaching</note> who still [cherish it]...

### OF VANITY. Folio 46.

<margin>Actors were once expelled from the Church.</margin>
[The art of acting] is cultivated (even though actors were once driven out by the Church and even denied the holy sacrament of communion). Today we see some who, with a strange straining of their voices, multifaceted expressions, wandering and impudent eyes, flailing arms, dancing feet, swaying hips, and various movements, turnings, rotations, tossings-back, leaps, and the whole body gesturing—the shifting soul, of course, turning itself over—proclaim popular sermons to the common people from the pulpit. They are perhaps mindful of the opinion of Demosthenes <note>The most famous orator of ancient Greece</note>, who (as recorded in Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus, a 1st-century Roman author</note>), when asked what was most effective in speaking, replied: "hypocrisy" <note>original: "hypocrisis." In the classical Greek sense used here, this refers to 'delivery' or 'acting' rather than moral insincerity</note>. When asked a second and third time, he said the same, claiming that almost the entire power of speaking is owed to this. But let us not stray too far from Mathematics; let us now hasten toward Geometry.

<margin>GEOMETRY.</margin>
Geometry itself, which Philo Judaeus <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria</note> calls the leader and mother of all disciplines, possesses this praise above all other studies: while there are great and countless conflicts among the sects of almost every other discipline, all Geometricians everywhere agree with one another. No contention ever arises among them regarding their field, except that they still dispute over points, lines, and surfaces—specifically, whether these are divisible or indivisible. Otherwise, they do not differ from one another in doctrine or tradition; rather, each strives to surpass the other with new or more subtle inventions, such as no one else has ever devised. 

Yet, no Geometrician has yet found the true **squaring of the circle** <term>squaring the circle: the ancient mathematical challenge of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle, proven impossible in the 19th century</term>, nor has anyone provided a line equal to the side [of a square]. Although Archimedes of Syracuse <note>The renowned Greek mathematician and inventor</note> once thought he had discovered these, and many successors up to these present times have attempted the same thing, they have, in a way, labored in vain—even if they seem to have come close to the truth. Yet such is their ambition that they never rest satisfied with the traditions of their predecessors; thinking they can find something more in such matters than their masters did, they drive themselves into such a madness that all the hellebore <note>A plant used in antiquity as a medicinal treatment for insanity</note> in the whole world would not be enough to purge them.

<margin>The fruits of Geometry.</margin>
Beyond the fact that Geometry investigates lines, forms, intervals, magnitudes, bodies, dimensions, and weights, there depend whatsoever <note>original: "uæcunq" (quaecunque). The sentence breaks here at the page's end.</note>

### FO. XXXVII.

->OF THE SCIENCES<-

whatever organic, ingenious works, and artistic instruments there are, such as the art of lifting machines <term>Manganaria</term>, machine-making <term>Mechanopoetica</term>, and siegecraft <term>Poliorcetica</term>—which are suited for the uses of war, architecture, and other needs. These include battering rams, tortoises <note>protective sheds for soldiers</note>, mines, catapults, scorpions <note>engines for shooting arrows</note>, drawbridges, siege-engines <note>original: "sambucæ," a ladder-like device</note>, scaling ladders, levers for lifting men, mobile towers, "city-takers" <note>original: "heliopoles," massive siege towers</note>, ships, triremes, bridges, and mills. Likewise, there are two-horse, three-horse, and four-horse chariots, pulleys, screws, wheels, levers, and all those devices by which immense weights are pulled or lifted with very little force. Furthermore, there are those things which function by weight, or water, or air, or by sinews and cords—such as clocks that move by weights, and musical organs that sound by the impulse of the wind; also any hydraulic and pneumatic instruments, even those which are built for nothing but pleasure and wonder. These include balls that jump on their own, lamps that produce their own wicks, and suction-cups or gourds that blow fire by themselves. Then there is the kind of animal that Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a leading Renaissance scholar and poet</note> describes, which, while it is being carved at the table, drinks in the meantime and imitates the movements and voices of a living creature. It was perhaps by such a craft that Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with ancient wisdom</note> says the Egyptians fashioned statues of the gods so they could utter articulated speech and walk. Even Archytas of Tarentum <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician</note> constructed a wooden dove according to geometric principles in such a way that it rose into the air and flew. And indeed, we read that Archimedes was the first to build a brass heaven <note>An orrery or mechanical model of the solar system</note> with such great artistic skill that the movements of all the planets could be most clearly observed therein, along with the rotations of each of the individual celestial spheres; we have even seen such a thing built in these recent days. From this art also come various kinds of engines of war, cannons, and other fire-vomiting instruments. I recently composed a special book about these under the title of *Fire-Writing* <note>original: "pyrographia," referring to the art of artillery or gunpowder</note>, which I now finally regret, since it teaches nothing but a most destructive mastery. Finally, whatever skill there is in painting, in surveying <term>cosmimetria</term>, in agriculture, in the art of war, in metal-casting, in molding, in sculpture, in carpentry, in architecture, or in metallurgy—all of this, or the greatest part of it, comes from Geometry.

# OF VANITY

Then follow Proportion <term>Consimimetria</term> and Architecture. As for Perspective—which we also call Optics—it deals with the three ways of seeing: direct, reflected, and refracted. It teaches us what light is, what shadows are, and the nature of distances. It discovers the causes of visible things that appear false due to distance, and it investigates the projection of rays through one or more transparent objects <note>original: "perspicua"</note> across various shapes of bodies. It also studies the formations of shadow and light, as well as the phenomena that occur to the objects themselves, to our sight, and to the medium between them. Furthermore, it demonstrates how both the object and the vision are affected in different ways by variations in that medium.

Regarding the method of seeing, <margin>Various opinions of the philosophers on the method of seeing</margin> there are diverse and conflicting opinions. For **Plato** believes that sight occurs through "clarity"—namely, by that light which comes from the eyes flowing out to the external air and meeting the light coming from bodies. This external air, being easily spread and moved, becomes an extension of the fire-like power of sight. **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> agrees with Plato, but **Hipparchus** says that rays are sent out from the eyes until they touch bodies—almost like a kind of feeling or palpation—and return the perception of them to the sight. 

The **Epicureans**, however, assert that "images" <note>original: "simulachra"; in Epicurean philosophy, these were thin films of atoms shed by objects</note> of visible things force themselves into the eyes. **Aristotle** thinks that these images are not physical bodies, but rather a change in quality <note>Aristotle's theory of "intentional species" or alterations in the medium</note> that travels through the surrounding air from the visible object to the sight. **Porphyry**, on the other hand, says that neither rays, nor images, nor anything else is the cause of seeing; instead, it is the soul itself, which recognizes itself as visible, and being the one soul of all things, recognizes itself in everything that exists. 

Yet **Geometers** and **Opticians**, following Hipparchus to some extent, write that cones are formed from the meeting of rays emitted through the eyes. This explains why the sight can grasp many visible things at once, though those where the rays coincide are seen most clearly. But **Al-Kindi** <note>original: "Alchindus," a 9th-century Arab polymath who wrote "De Aspectibus" on optics</note> teaches something entirely different regarding appearances. Finally, to **Augustine**, it seems that the power of the soul performs something in the eye—a matter which students of wisdom must investigate thoroughly.

<margin>The fruits of Optics.</margin> 
This science, therefore, is used to detect the variation, distance, size, and motion of the celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions, through many...

Fo.XXXVIII.

-> OF THE SCIENCES <-

[Perspective] is useful: it also serves Architecture in measuring buildings. However, it provides the greatest ornament and benefit to the art of painting and the manufacture of mirrors, so much so that these arts cannot be perfected without it. For it demonstrates how we should create images that are neither disproportionate nor deformed, which are often perceived as such because of varying distances and heights.

<margin>PAINTING</margin>

### PAINTING
Painting is therefore an extraordinary art <note>original: "monstrosa", used here in the sense of marvelous or prodigious</note>, consisting of the imitation of natural things through the most accurate drawing of lines and the proper application of colors. This art was once held in such high esteem that it held the first rank among the liberal arts <note>The "liberal arts" were the subjects considered essential for a free person to master, such as grammar, logic, and rhetoric</note>. Indeed, it is no less a "free" or noble art than poetry, as Horace <note>The original refers to "Flaccus," the Roman poet Quintus Horatius Flaccus</note> so well sang:

> To painters and to poets, 
> The power to dare whatever they wish has always been equal.

<margin>The kinship between painting and poetry.</margin>
Painting is said to be nothing other than silent poetry, while poetry is a speaking picture, so closely related are they to one another. For just as poets do, so painters fashion stories and myths; they express images of all things, as well as light, brilliance, shadows, highlights, and depths.

<margin>Optical painters.</margin>
Furthermore, Painting borrows from Optics the ability to deceive the sight, so that in a single image, by varying the viewing position, it presents several different appearances to the eyes of the viewers. It reaches where sculpture cannot: it paints fire, rays, light, thunders, thunderbolts, lightning, sunset, dawn, twilight, mists, and the emotions of man, the feelings of the mind, and expresses almost the voice itself. Through the dimensions and proportions of the mind, it makes things that do not exist appear as if they do, or makes things that are not a certain way seem as though they are.

<margin>The contest of Zeuxis and Parrhasius.</margin>
Just as historians tell of the painters **Zeuxis** and **Parrhasius**, who, when they entered a contest for artistic supremacy, the former brought forward painted grapes with such likeness that birds flew down to them. The other brought forward a painted curtain, feigning reality so well that Zeuxis—puffed up by the judgment of the birds—demanded that the curtain be drawn aside to show the painting. Finally, realizing his error, he was forced to yield the prize to his rival, since he had deceived birds, but Parrhasius had deceived the artist himself. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist</note> also recounts that during the games of Claudius, there was great admiration for painting when birds flew toward the likeness of roof tiles <note>original: "regularum"; likely referring to the painted stage scenery</note>, deceived by their image.

Truly, it was discovered by a famous experiment of the triumvirate <note>Agrippa likely refers to a story from Pliny the Elder's *Natural History* involving a competition between famous painters</note> (as Pliny tells it) that the singing of birds was silenced by the sight of a painted dragon. <margin>
STATUARY
</margin>

### STATUARY
Painting is accompanied by **STATUARY**, as well as Modeling, Casting, and Engraving—crafts of a restless mind—which can nevertheless be included under the umbrella of Architecture. **Statuary** manufactures "idols" <note>original: "idola", meaning images or representations</note> of things from stone, wood, and ivory; the **Modeler** fashions the same from clay. The art of **Casting** expresses these in a mold from bronze and other metals. The **Engraver**, on the other hand, carves into stones and gems.

Pomponius Gauricus <note>A Neapolitan humanist who wrote *De sculptura* in 1504</note> among the moderns has written about these, but all these arts—along with painting—were, I believe, invented by evil demons for the sake of vanity, lust, and superstition. Their craftsmen were those who first (according to the words of <margin>Romans 1</margin> Paul) "changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed beasts, and creeping things." These men, acting against the divine <margin>Deuteronomy 5</margin> commandment that forbids a graven idol and the likeness of anything in heaven above or on the earth below, introduced that idolatry most hateful to God.

Regarding these, the Wise Man <note>Referring to the author of the biblical Book of Wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon</note> says: <margin>Wisdom 14</margin> "The idol itself is cursed, and he who made it; both the maker and the work shall suffer torment." For the vanity of men (as the same author says) "invented these arts as a temptation to the souls of men and a snare for the feet of the foolish; and the wonder felt for them is the corruption of life." 

Nevertheless, we Christians are so foolish beyond all other nations that we are not ashamed to keep this corruption of life and morals everywhere in our courtyards, houses, and bedrooms, <margin>The danger of idolatry in statues.</margin> so that our matrons and daughters are invited to lewdness by these lustful images. Indeed, we even bring these things into temples, chapels, and onto the altars of God with great veneration, not without the danger of idolatry. 

But we shall discuss this more at length under the heading of Religion. However, I once learned in Italy that no small authority resides in pictures and statues. For when the Augustinian friars, together with the Canons Regular, were before the Roman Pontiff...

...concerning the habit of Saint Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity. Different monastic orders later claimed him as their founder, leading to disputes over his historical clothing.</note>, specifically whether he wore a black cloak over a white tunic, or a white one over a black one. They fought over this stubbornly, and since nothing could be found in the Scriptures to settle the dispute, it seemed best to the Roman judges to delegate the whole matter to the Painters and Sculptors. They decided that whatever evidence these artists could bring forward from ancient paintings and statues would have the force of a legal verdict.

Strengthened by this example, while I was once investigating the origin of the monk’s hooded cowl <note>original: "cucullæ". A hood or cowl associated with monastic orders.</note> with tireless diligence, and could find nothing about it in the Scriptures, I finally turned to the painters. I searched for the matter in those processions and porches belonging to the brothers, where stories from both the Old and New Testaments are seen depicted in great number. In the entire Old Testament, I found not one of the Patriarchs, nor the Priests, nor the Prophets, nor the Levites—nor even Elijah himself (whom the Carmelites <note>A Catholic religious order that claims spiritual descent from the prophet Elijah on Mount Carmel.</note> claim as their patron)—to be hooded. 

Turning then to the New Testament, I found there Zacharias, Simeon, John the Baptist, Joseph, Christ, the Apostles, Disciples, Scribes, Pharisees, High Priests, Annas, Caiaphas, Herod, Pilate, and many others; yet nowhere did I see a hooded cowl. Then, examining everything one by one from the beginning again, suddenly, right at the forefront of the story, there appears a hooded devil: specifically, the one who was tempting Christ in the desert. I rejoiced greatly that I had found in paintings what I had hitherto been unable to find in literature—namely, that the devil was the first author of the hooded cowl. From him, I suppose, the rest of the monks and brothers later borrowed this garment in various colors, or perhaps they received it as if it were left to them by hereditary right.

# ON VANITY

...he easily made himself a master of obscenity through mirrors of that kind <note>The author likely refers to Hostius Quadra, a Roman mentioned by Seneca who used magnifying mirrors to enlarge the appearance of sexual acts.</note>, which returned images far larger than they truly were, so that a finger might exceed the measure of an arm in both length and thickness. There is also a mirror made in which one sees the image of another person, rather than their own. And another which, when placed in a certain spot, reflects no images at all, but when moved elsewhere, brings images into view. Likewise, there is one that returns images upside down; and another that returns many images of a single thing. There is even one which, contrary to the custom of other mirrors, reflects the right side on the right and the left on the left <note>A "non-reversing" or "true" mirror.</note>.

And burning mirrors are made that reflect from both the front and the back; and another kind which does not represent the received image within itself, but casts it further out, away from itself into the air, making it appear there like an airy phantom <note>original: "aereum simulachrum". This describes a "Pepper’s Ghost" style projection or a real image formed by a concave mirror.</note>. By gathering the rays of the Sun into itself, it can strike fire into any combustible material across distant spaces. We have seen many such things and know how to manufacture them ourselves.

Transparent mirrors <note>original: "perspicua specula". Here referring to lenses or glass used for magnification and refraction.</note> also have their own deceptions: namely, making a large thing appear small, and conversely, making the smallest things appear large. They can make things that are far off seem near, or things that are near seem remote. They can make those things beneath our feet appear above us, and those above us appear at the very bottom, or present themselves to our sight in some other orientation. There are also lenses through which one thing is seen as many, and others that represent the things themselves in various colors, as in a rainbow, or under different and dissimilar shapes to deceive the sight, and other things of this sort.

I myself know how to construct mirrors in which, when the Sun is shining, everything illuminated by its rays can be seen most fully across the farthest distances—I believe as far as three or five miles. There is also this wonder in flat mirrors: no matter how small they are, they represent the object on a smaller scale according to their size; yet, no matter how large the mirror is, it never renders the object larger than it truly is. Considering this while writing to Nebridius, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD). Nebridius was one of his close friends and frequent correspondents on philosophical matters.</note> believed that some hidden mystery lay beneath this fact. 

Yet, in the end, all these things are vain and superfluous, invented for nothing but ostentation and idle delight. Many Greeks and Latins alike have written about mirrors, but one man, Vitellius <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1280), a Polish friar and physicist whose work "Perspectiva" was the standard medieval textbook on optics.</note>, stands above them all.

Fo. XI.
# [OF THE] SCIENCES.

<margin>COSMOMETRY.</margin>
Next, let us briefly discuss **COSMOMETRY** <note>literally "measurement of the world"</note>; this is divided into Cosmography and Geography. Both measure and distinguish the world, but the former measures the positions of lands and the places subject to them according to celestial calculations and their distinctions, using measurements of degrees and minutes. It teaches, through mathematical calculations for each specific location, the systems of climates, the differences between days and nights, the cardinal directions of the winds, the various Risings of the stars, the elevations of the poles, parallels and meridians, the shadows cast by gnomons <note>The gnomon is the part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>, and all other such matters. The latter science, however, uses no celestial calculations; it measures the world by stadia <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note> and miles, and distinguishes it by mountains, forests, lakes, rivers, seas, and shores. It points out nations and peoples, kingdoms, provinces, cities, ports, and other noteworthy things:

> And it explains all the ancestral customs and the character of places,
> What each region produces, and what each refuses to bear,
> And through a kind of imitation of painting, following the principles
> Of Geometry and Perspective, it shapes the whole world onto a globe
> Or a flat map,
> Painting the whole world in a small volume.

Under these categories, some include **Chorography** <note>The description or mapping of a particular region or district in great detail.</note>, which, by exploring certain partial locations separately, depicts them with an even more perfect and, as it were, finished image.

> Distinct in all its parts with varied ornament,
> With vines and forests, with the springs of meadows and fields,
> With the flowing rivers that water the sea; and where it sinks
> Into low valleys, or where it rises high,
> Lifting mountains with lofty peaks toward the heavens.

<margin>The disagreement of Geographers.</margin>
<margin>The navel of the Earth.</margin>
Cosmometry itself promises us all these things, and those we mentioned before. But the authors who are to teach us these things fight among themselves with nothing but discord, greatly disagreeing with one another regarding boundaries, longitudes, latitudes, magnitudes, measurements, distances, climates, and their conditions. Eratosthenes describes them one way, Strabo another, Marinus another, Ptolemy another, Dionysius another, and the moderns <note>original: "iuniores"</note> yet another.

The author highlights that even the most famous ancient and modern geographers cannot agree on the basic measurements and boundaries of the Earth.</summary>

# DE VANITATE
### [OF VANITY]

distinguish: Nor do they agree among themselves about the navel of the earth <note>The "omphalos" or center point of the world.</note>, which **Ptolemy** places under the equinoctial circle <note>The equator.</note>: **Strabo** believed it to be Parnassus, a mountain of Greece, in which **Plutarch** and **Lactantius** the grammarian agree, thinking that during the time of the flood it was the boundary of the height of the waters, just as **Lucan** sings of this:

> This peak alone emerged by submerging the lands in the flood,
> And was a boundary between the Sea and the Stars.
> <note>original: "Hoc solum fluctu terras mergendo cacumen / Emicuit, Pontoque fuit discrimen & Astris."</note>

But if this reasoning is enough to refute them, the navel of the earth will be not in the Parnassus of Greece, but in the Gordicus mountain of Armenia <note>Likely referring to the mountains of Gordyene, associated with the landing of Noah's Ark.</note>, which (**Berosus** being witness) first emerged from the deluge and received Noah’s Ark. Others bring forward other theories, such as how the center of the earth was found by the flight of eagles <note>Refers to the myth of Zeus releasing two eagles from the ends of the earth to see where they would meet (Delphi).</note>. There are also Theologians who, thrusting their sickle into this harvest <note>A metaphor for meddling in a field of study not strictly their own.</note>, wish for Jerusalem to be the center of the earth, because it is written by the Prophet: "God has worked salvation in the midst of the earth" <note>Psalm 74:12.</note>. Added to this judgment are **Lucretius**, **Lactantius**, and **Augustine**, who so constantly denied the Antipodes <note>People living on the opposite side of the globe, whose feet would be "opposite" ours.</note>. And those, moreover, who denied that there was any other habitable world outside of Europe, Asia, and Africa: which things, however, by the navigations of the Spaniards and Portuguese, have been found otherwise by us of later generations, who have also shown that the entire zone under the zodiac <note>The Torrid Zone or tropics, which Aristotle believed was too hot for human life.</note> is inhabited, contrary to the trifles of the Poets and the false opinion of **Aristotle**. Furthermore, we have recounted many other errors of the Geographers above among the Historians. 

Truly this art, while it tries to teach us of the immense earth, the inscrutable seas, the locations, boundaries, and insignias of all islands and regions, and likewise the unknown origins, rites, customs, and distinctions of innumerable nations, we perceive no other fruit from it, except that while we greedily scrutinize the affairs of others, we learn to be ignorant of ourselves; and (as **Augustine** says in his *Confessions*) men go to admire the heights of mountains, and the massive waves of the sea, and the widest flows of rivers, and the circuit of the Ocean, and the revolutions of the Stars, and they leave themselves behind. **Pliny** also says it is madness to measure the earth, for while we measure it, we most often exceed the measure.

ARCHI-
TE-

<margin>
The
disease
of
building
</margin>

Architecture, however, undoubtedly brings many benefits and ornaments to both public and private buildings. It provides us with walls and roofs, mills <note>original: *pistrinas*, specifically gristmills for grinding grain</note> and vehicles, bridges and ships, shrines, temples, sanctuaries, city walls, towers, and all kinds of machines (by which human affairs are protected and adorned both publicly and privately). It is a discipline that would otherwise be entirely necessary and honorable, were it not that it so greatly fascinates the minds of mortals that almost no one can be found (provided they do not lack the means) who does not entirely desire to always add some new construction even to buildings already well-constructed. From this insatiable zeal and desire for building, it has come to pass that there is no limit or end to this activity. Hence, cliffs are cut away, valleys are filled, mountains are leveled, rocks are drilled through, and promontories are opened to the sea; the very guts of the earth are excavated, rivers are diverted, seas are joined to seas, lakes are exhausted, marshes are drained, the oceans are restrained, and the depths of the sea are searched; new islands are created, and others are restored back to the mainland. All of these things, and more besides, though they fight against nature itself, have nonetheless often brought no small convenience to the entire world.

But let us compare these to those things which are of no other use to mortals than to be wondered at and looked upon, and (as **Pliny** says) were constructed at enormous expense for the idle and foolish display of money. Of this sort are the superstitious miracles of the works of the Egyptians, Greeks, Etruscans, Babylonians, and certain other nations: the Labyrinths, Pyramids, Obelisks, Colossi, Mausoleums, and the monstrous statues of **Porsenna**, **Solomon**, and **Amasis**. And then there is that marvelous Sphinx, in which **King Amasis** <note>Amasis II, a Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty; though the Sphinx is much older, ancient writers often associated such monuments with later kings.</note> is thought to be buried. For it was (as **Pliny** says) fashioned from natural red stone; the circumference of the monster's head around the brow measures one hundred and two feet, and its length is one hundred and forty-three feet. But there are works even greater than these: the work of **Memnon** and **Semiramis** in the middle of a Babylonian mountain, a vast image of seventeen stades <note>A stade was an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters; seventeen stades would be nearly two miles, an obvious exaggeration by the author's sources.</note>. To this same vanity belong the temples built for our own **Saints** <note>original: *Divis*</note> with the most proud gables, piled up to a wondrous height with a massive weight of stones, and those towering bell-towers <note>campanilia</note> funded by many sacred funds and lavished alms. Meanwhile, many of Christ’s poor—who are the true temples of God and His living images—are left perishing from hunger, thirst, cold, sickness, and poverty; they could have been more rightly "built up" and sustained by those funds which are instead being neglected <note>original: *deserentiq*, likely referring to the neglect of the poor in favor of stone</note>.

Furthermore, how much destruction this art very often brings to men is witnessed by hostile fortresses, machines of war, armored engines <note>original: *cataphractæ*</note>, scorpions <note>a type of Roman bolt-throwing engine</note>, ballistae <note>large stone-throwing engines</note>, and other instruments for the subversion of human life, as well as the peoples conquered through the ingenuity of these things. Nor is this limited to the land, since architecture has also taught us to build ships like camps and fortresses, in which we do not so much sail the dangerous seas as inhabit them; and while the seas are by nature infested with a thousand dangers for us, we make them more dangerous with these vessels, committing robberies and waging wars in them just as on solid ground.

On the subject of **Architecture**, **Agatharchus** of Athens wrote first, followed by **Democritus** and **Anaxagoras**, then **Silenus**, **Archimedes**, **Aristotle**, **Theophrastus**, **Cato**, **Varro**, **Pliny**, and finally **Vitruvius** Nigrigenitus <note>literally "the Black-born," possibly a reference to a specific medieval lineage or nickname for the famous Roman architect</note>. ### ON VANITY

<margin>The discovery of metals.</margin>
Pliny says <note>original: "ait Plinius"; referring to Pliny the Elder’s Natural History</note> that these discoveries have made the lands so much more harmful that men are no less reckless than those who seek pearls from the depths of the sea. The invention of these metals is attributed to many different, and indeed disagreeing, historians. The foremost authorities record that lead <note>original: "plūbum"</note> was first found in the islands called the Cassiterides <note>The "Tin Islands," likely referring to the Scilly Isles or Cornwall</note>, situated opposite Celtiberia <note>Ancient North-Central Spain</note>. However, copper <note>original: "aes"</note> was found in Cyprus, iron in Crete, and gold and silver at Mount Pangaeum in Thrace. Eventually, these metals infected the whole world. Only the Scythians—as Solinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman geographer</note> reports—condemned the use of gold and silver forever, renouncing themselves from this public greed. Regarding the excess of gold, there was once a caution among the Romans by an ancient decree; there was a Censor’s law regarding the local gold mines which (as Pliny says) in the territory of Vercelli <note>A city in Northern Italy</note> provided that the tax-collectors should not have more than five thousand men working there. Would that men were carried toward heaven with the same zeal with which they Scrutinize the bowels of the earth, lured only by a vein of riches! These riches are so far from being able to make a man blessed that many—and not rarely—repent of the labor they spent on them.

<margin>ASTROLOGY.</margin>
¶ In the highest place, **ASTROLOGY** now presents itself, which is also called Astronomy. It is entirely deceptive and much more trivial than the fables of the Poets. Its masters are bold, professing men and authors of portents. Through their impious curiosity and according to their own whim, they fabricate celestial spheres, measurements of stars, movements, figures, images, numbers, and harmonies above the human lot—much like the heretic Basilides <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic teacher</note> fabricated his "Abraxas" <note>A mystical word/deity representing the 365 heavens in Gnosticism</note>. They depict these things as if they had recently fallen from the heavens and had lived there for some time. They believe that through these things all things stand, happen, and can be known. Yet, they disagree significantly among themselves, being contrary and even now fighting each other. Thus, I would not hesitate to say with Pliny that the very inconsistency of this art openly proves that it is nothing at all. For the Indians feel one way about its principles, the Chaldeans another, the Egyptians another, the Moors another, the Jews another, the Arabs another, the Greeks another, the Latins another, the Ancients another, and the Moderns another still.

<margin>Controversy regarding the eighth sphere.</margin>

Because of this, they believe the fixed stars do not always incline toward the same part of the world, but sometimes return to where they began. # ON VANITY

<margin>Controversy regarding the double motion of the eighth sphere</margin>
...or Astronomers attribute a triple motion to the eighth sphere: one proper to it, which we have called **trepidation** <note>original: "trepidationis"; a theoretical oscillation or "shaking" of the equinoxes</note>, which is completed once every seven thousand years. Another, which they call **gyration** <note>rotation</note>, derived from the ninth sphere, whose revolution is finished in no less than forty-nine thousand years. The third is from the tenth orb, which they call the **motion of the prime mover** <note>original: "primi mobilis"</note>, or the **sweeping motion** <note>original: "motum raptus"; the force that pulls the lower spheres along with the highest one</note>, or the **daily motion**, which returns to its starting point every day within a natural day. Furthermore, those who have attributed a double motion to the eighth sphere do not all agree among themselves. For almost all the **Moderns** <note>original: "Recentiores"; referring here to late medieval and Renaissance scholars</note>, and those who admit the motion of trepidation, argue that it is snatched along by a higher sphere. But **Al-Battani** <note>Albategni</note>, **Abufiafien**, **Alfraganus** <note>Al-Farghani</note>, **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd</note>, **Rabbi Levi** <note>Gersonides</note>, **Abraham Zacuto**, and **Agostino Ricci** believe that the daily motion—which others think is the "sweeping motion"—is not the property of any specific sphere, but is caused by the whole Heaven. Averroes himself also says that **Ptolemy**, in a certain book of his (which he titled *Narrations*), denies the motion of gyration; and Rabbi Levi says that he agreed with Averroes that the daily motion is caused by the whole Heaven. 

<margin>Disagreement over the measurement of the movement of the eighth orb of fixed stars</margin>
Again, they now agree no better regarding the measurement of the movement of the eighth orb and the fixed stars. For **Ptolemy** thinks the fixed stars move one degree in a hundred years. **Al-Battani** contends this happens in sixty-six Egyptian years; with him agree **Rabbi Levi**, **Rabbi Zacuto**, and **Alfonso** <note>King Alfonso X of Castile</note> in the correction of his tables. **Al-Zarqali** <note>Azarcheles Maurus</note> the Moor says they move one degree in seventy-five years; **Hipparchus** in seventy-eight Hebrew years; many others—such as **Rabbi Joshua**, **Rabbi Moses Maimonides**, **Rabbi Ibn Ezra**, and after them **Ali ibn Ridwan** <note>Haly Benrodiam</note>—say in seventy years. **Johannes Regiomontanus** <note>Ioannes de Monte Regio</note> says in eighty. **Agostino Ricci** holds a middle ground between the opinions of Al-Battani and the Hebrews, believing that the fixed stars move through one part of Heaven no faster than sixty-six years, nor slower than seventy years. But even **Rabbi Abraham Zacuto** (as Ricci relates) testifies from the tradition of the **Indians** <note>original: "Indorum"; likely referring to ancient Sanskrit astronomical texts known to the Arabs</note> that there are still two stars in the Heaven diametrically opposed to each other...

A maidservant timely rebuked these astronomers, these servants of Anaximenes <note>Anaximenes of Miletus (c. 585 – c. 528 BC), a Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher</note>,

I too drank in this art from my parents as a boy; later, I lost no small amount of time and labor on it, until finally I learned that this entire field rests on no other foundation than mere trifles and the figments of imagination. I am weary of it and repent of the effort once spent; I would desire to strip away every memory and use of it. I cast it from my soul long ago, nor would I ever take it up again, were it not that the violent prayers of powerful people (who are often accustomed to abuse even great and honest talents for unworthy arts) often [compelled me]
