Fo. XLV.

### OF THE SCIENCES.

...would compel me to strike back again, and domestic utility persuaded me that I ought sometimes to enjoy their foolishness, and comply more with those who so greatly desire trifles. I say indeed trifles: 
<margin>Astrology contains nothing but trifles and fictions.</margin> 
for what does astrology have, except the mere trifles and fables of poets and monstrous fictions? With these they have invented a heaven that is completely full. Indeed, no two classes of men agree more with each other than astrologers and poets, except that they disagree about **Lucifer** and **Vesper** <note>original: "Lucifero & Vespere"; these are the ancient names for the planet Venus when it appears as the Morning Star and the Evening Star, respectively</note>: the poets asserting that on the same day **Lucifer** appears before the rising Sun, he follows the setting Sun—which almost all astrologers deny is possible, except those who place **Venus** above the Sun. This is because stars that are much further from us at their rising seem to rise earlier and fall back later at their setting. But I would have passed over this discord of astrologers regarding the position of the stars or planets, had I not just remembered it; since it belongs not so much to astrologers as to philosophers. 

<margin>The controversy of philosophers regarding the position of stars and planets.</margin> 
For **Plato** places the second sphere, that of the Sun, after the Moon; the **Egyptians** do the same, placing the Sun between the Moon and **Mercury**. **Archimedes** and the **Chaldeans** <note>A term often used for ancient Babylonian astronomers and magicians</note> place the Sun fourth in order. **Anaximander**, **Metrodorus of Chios**, and **Crates** say they establish the Sun as the highest of all, after which they place the Moon, and below these the other wandering and fixed stars <note>original: "errantes inerrantesq;"; 'wandering stars' refers to the planets, from the Greek 'planētēs'</note>. **Xenocrates** thinks all stars move on one and the same surface. There is no less disagreement concerning the Sun, the Moon, and the rest; nor is there any consistency or truth among their opinions about celestial matters. Nor is this surprising, since the very Heaven they scrutinize is the most inconsistent of all things and is most full of trifles and fables. For the twelve signs themselves, and the rest—the northern and southern constellations <note>original: "imagines"; literally 'images' or 'figures'</note>—have ascended into Heaven only through fables. And yet, by these fables astrologers live, deceive, and profit, while the poets who invented them are meanwhile remarkably hungry.

<margin>Judicial astrology</margin>
There remains yet another kind of astrology, which they call **DIVINATORY** or **judicial** <term>Judicial astrology: the practice of predicting future events and human destiny based on the positions of celestial bodies</term>, which deals with the revolutions of the years of the world, with nativities <note>Horoscopes based on the time of a person's birth</note>, with questions, with elections, with intentions and thoughts, with virtues, and toward the knowledge of all future things (even either divine...

### OF VANITY

<margin>
They attribute the works of God to the stars.
</margin>

...from the secret dispositions of providence, events are to be predicted, summoned, avoided, or repelled. From this, the **Astrologers** divine the effects of the Heavens and the stars from the most remote years—even before all memory of things or the times of **Prometheus** <note>In Greek mythology, the Titan who created humanity; here used to denote the deep reaches of pre-history</note>—based on great (as they say) and pre-diluvian <note>original: "ante diluvianis"; referring to the time before the Great Flood of Noah</note> constitutions. They affirm that the effects, powers, and movements of all living beings, stones, metals, herbs, and whatever else was created in these lower realms flow down from these very heavens and stars; they claim that not even the smallest thing can exist or be imagined without depending upon them. These men are truly faithless and no less impious, failing to recognize at least this one fact: that God had already created herbs, plants, and trees *before* the heavens and the stars <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis, where plants were created on the third day, while the Sun, Moon, and stars were created on the fourth.</note>. Indeed, even the most serious philosophers—such as **Pythagoras**, **Democritus**, **Bion**, **Favorinus**, **Panaetius**, **Carneades**, **Posidonius**, **Timaeus**, **Aristotle**, **Plato**, **Plotinus**, **Porphyry**, **Avicenna**, **Averroes**, **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and **Alexander of Aphrodisias**; and furthermore, **Cicero**, **Seneca**, **Plutarch**, and many others who searched for the causes of things through every art and science—never refer us back to these astrological causes. Even if these were true causes, because the courses of the stars and their powers are not clearly known (as is well known to all wise men), they could not give a certain judgment regarding their effects. Nor indeed are there lacking among them men like **Eudoxus**, **Archelaus**, **Cassandrus**, **Hoychilax**, and **Halicarnassus**, who were most skilled mathematicians. These, along with many other more recent and serious authors, admit that it is impossible for anything certain to be found in the science of judgments <term>Judicial Astrology: the practice of casting horoscopes to predict specific future events or human character</term>.

<margin>
Judicial astrology is uncertain.
</margin>

This is because of the innumerable other causes cooperating with the Heavens which must be considered at the same time (as **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note> also commands), and because so many circumstances stand in their way: for instance, customs, manners, education, modesty, government, location, lineage, blood, food, and the freedom and discipline of the mind. For those celestial influences do not "compel" (as they say) but merely "incline" <note>original: "non cogant... sed inclinant"; a central maxim in medieval and Renaissance astrology used to reconcile stellar influence with the Christian doctrine of human free will.</note>. Furthermore, those who have prescribed the rules for these judgments set down things so diverse and so often conflicting regarding the same matter, that it is impossible for a prognosticator to pronounce anything certain from so many various and discordant opinions, unless there resides within him some internal sense of future and hidden things, or an instinct of presage...

<meta>catchword: ...to be (fuis-)</meta>

He cites a long list of ancient authorities who rejected the idea that the stars are the primary causes of earthly events.</summary>

Folio 46.

->OF THE SCIENCES.<-

Or perhaps it is more a hidden and lurking inspiration from a **demon**—which allows one to distinguish between these matters—or by some other means that one is led to adhere now to this opinion, now to another. If anyone lacks this instinct, he cannot be a teller of truth in **astrological judgments** (as **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer whose work was central to medieval European astrology</note> says). Therefore, astrological prediction consists not so much in art as in a certain obscure chance of things. And just as a verse sometimes comes out of game-tablets <note>original: "ludorum codicillis"; likely referring to lots or cards used in games of chance</note> pronouncing the truth, not by art but by luck, so too do **prophecies** come forth from the mind of the **Astrologer**, not by art but by chance. To this **Ptolemy** also testifies, saying, "The science of the stars is from you and from them" <note>original: "Scientia stellarum ex te & ex illis est"; a famous aphorism from the *Centiloquium*, a collection of astrological sayings attributed to Ptolemy</note>, indicating that the prediction of future and hidden things is not so much from the observation of the stars as from the stirrings of the mind.

Therefore, there is no certainty in this art, but it is adaptable to all things according to opinion, which is gathered by conjectures, or estimation, or the imperceptible breath of **demons**, or superstitious luck. This art is nothing other than the deceptive conjecture of superstitious men, who, through long use, have made a "science" out of uncertain things. In this science, for the sake of swindling money <note>original: "emungendae pecuniae"; literally "wiping the nose of money," a Latin idiom for cheating or fleecing someone</note>, they deceive the unskilled, and are themselves deceived at the same time. But if this art is so true and is understood by them, why do so many and such great errors bubble up in their prognostications? If it is not true, do they not vainly, foolishly, and impiously profess a science about things that do not exist or are not understood?

<margin>
The caution of astrologers.
</margin>

But the more cautious among them pronounce only obscure things about the future; they craft ambiguous **prognostications** with technical cunning that can be applied to every matter, time, prince, and nation. Afterward, however, when any of these things has happened, they then gather the causes for it, and after the fact they stabilize old prophecies with new reasons so that they seem to have foreseen it. This is just like **interpreters of dreams**: when they see a dream, they understand nothing for certain; but when something has happened to them afterward, then they fit the dream they saw to what occurred. Furthermore, since it is impossible in such a variety of stars not to always find some well-placed and some poorly-placed, they take the opportunity from these to say what they want, and to whomever they want they grant life, health,

<meta>This page continues the author’s scathing critique of astrologers. Having argued that their "art" is based on luck rather than science, he now shifts to the social and political dangers they pose, citing Roman historians and ancient laws to prove that astrology is a plague upon the state and the source of all superstition.</meta>

->OF VANITY<-

They predict health, honors, wealth, power, victory, health, offspring, friends, marriages, or even priesthoods, magistracies, and the like. But if the stars are ill-disposed toward some, they announce deaths, hangings, disgraces, disasters, exiles, bereavements, illnesses, and calamities—not so much from a wicked art as from wicked impulses. By this unholy curiosity, they draw credulous men to their destruction, often setting peoples and Princes against each other in deadly seditions and wars. 

But if, by chance, their fortune happens to coincide with their prognostications, so that among so many ambiguities one or two truths occur, then they raise their crests <note>A Latin idiom meaning to grow arrogant or boastful, like a rooster raising its comb.</note> and proclaim it most insolently. If, however—as they lie constantly—they are caught in a lie, they excuse it with blasphemy or cover one lie with another, saying: "The wise man rules the stars" <note>original: "Sapientem dominari astris"</note>. Yet in truth, neither do the stars rule the wise man, nor the wise man the stars, but God rules both. Or they claim that the unfitness of the recipient hindered the celestial influences. 

When people demand further proof, they get angry; and those swindlers meanwhile find Princes and Magistrates who believe everything they say and reward them with public salaries.
<margin>Astrologers are harmful to the State.</margin>
In reality, no class of men is more ruinous to the State than these who promise future things from the stars, from inspecting palms, from dreams, and similar devices of divination, and who spread prophecies. Furthermore, they are always hostile toward Christ and all who believe in Him. Regarding them, Cornelius Tacitus <note>A Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) known for his skeptical view of political power and social corruption.</note> complains, saying that the **Mathematicians** <term>Mathematici: in the Roman world, this term specifically referred to astrologers, who were often viewed as political troublemakers, rather than scholars of geometry.</term> (for that is what the common people call them) are "a class of men unfaithful to Princes and deceptive to those who believe in them; they are always forbidden in our city, yet never expelled." 
<margin>Astrology is the source of superstitions.</margin>
Indeed, Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar considered one of the greatest authorities on Roman religion and history.</note>, a weighty author, testifies that all the vanities of superstition have flowed from the bosom of astrology. There was even a tax in Alexandria that astrologers paid called the **Blacennomion** <term>Blacennomion: Derived from the Greek "blakeia" (stupidity), this was a specific tax levied on astrologers because their trade was seen as profiting from the "ingenious stupidity" of others.</term>; it was named for folly because they made profit from ingenious stupidity, and usually only foolish and rash men would consult them. For if human life and fortune are from the stars, why do we fear? Why are we troubled? Since we leave these things to God and the Heavens, who can neither err nor do evil; and since we are...

# OF THE SCIENCES. CCXLVII.

Since we are human, we should not seek more than is proper beyond our powers, but only savor human things. Indeed, since we are Christians who believe in Christ, we leave the hours and moments to God the Father, who has placed them in His own power <note>A reference to the Biblical Book of Acts 1:7, suggesting that timing and the future are divine secrets.</note>. Since our life and fortune are not derived from the stars, does not every astrologer run his course in vain?

But there is a class of men of such timid credulity that, like children at stories of ghosts <note>original: "lemurum"; in Roman mythology, lemures were wandering, often vengeful spirits of the dead.</note>, they fear more and believe more in those things which are not than in those which are. The less possible a thing is, the more they fear it; the less likely it is, the more firmly they believe it. Truly, if there were no astrologers and diviners, these people would perish of hunger. Their foolish credulity—forgetting the past, neglecting the present, and rushing headlong into the future—favors those deceivers so much that, while in other men a single lie would make their word suspect and obscure all their other truths, the opposite is true for these masters of lies: a single accidental truth gains them trust even for their public lies.

Those who trust them most are rendered the most unhappy of all, as those superstitious trifles are accustomed to bring ruin upon their practitioners. Antiquity bears witness to this in the cases of Zoroaster, Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Caesar, Crassus, Pompey, Dionysius, Nero, and Julian the Apostate. Because they were most devoted to these trifles, they perished most miserably in their confidence in them. To those whom the astrologers promised all things joyful, all things turned out mournful. This was true for Pompey, Crassus, and Caesar, to whom they promised that none would die except in old age, at home, and in glory; yet each of them perished badly and prematurely. 

Truly, they are a persistent and backward race of men who profess to foreknow the future, yet are ignorant of the past and the present. While they profess to tell everyone the most hidden secrets, they very often do not know what is happening in their own house or in their own bedroom. Thomas More <note>original: "Morus Anglicus"; the English humanist, author of *Utopia*, and statesman.</note> mocked an astrologer of this kind with this very beautiful epigram:

->All the stars reveal themselves to you, the heavenly Prophet:<-
->And they warn of the future fates awaiting all men:<-
->Yet your wife makes herself public to all men: in truth,<-

<margin>Controversy of the Astrologers concerning judgments.</margin> Furthermore, it is known to all how much the Jews, Chaldeans, Egyptians, Persians, Greeks, and Arabs disagree among themselves regarding these very rules of judgment: and how Ptolemy rejects all the astrology of the ancients, and while <unclear>Anfrodas</unclear> <note>Possibly a corrupted reference to Aphrodisias or an Arabic commentator.</note> defends him, Albumasar <note>A famous Persian astrologer (787–886 AD) whose works were central to medieval European astrology.</note> attacks him, and the Hebrew Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abrahã Auenazre"; a celebrated 12th-century scholar and astrologer.</note> tears all these apart; finally, Dorotheus, Paulus Alexandrinus, Hephaistio, Maternus, Aomar, Thabit, Al-Kindi, Zahel, Masha'allah <note>original: "Messahalla"; an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer.</note>, and almost all others think and opine differently. Since they cannot prove what they say to be true, they defend themselves solely by the reasoning of "experience," yet they do not all agree unanimously even on that.

<margin>Controversy concerning the houses.</margin> Nor do they disagree any less concerning the properties of the <term>houses</term> <note>In astrology, "houses" are twelve divisions of the sky representing different areas of life, such as wealth, health, or marriage.</note> from which they seek the prediction of all events. Ptolemy assigns these in one way, Heliodorus another, Paulus another, Milius <note>Likely Marcus Manilius, author of the "Astronomica."</note> another, Maternus another, Porphyry another, Abenragel another, the Egyptians another, the Arabs another, the Greeks and Latins another, the Ancients another, and the Moderns another. Indeed, it is not yet clear among them in what way one ought to establish the beginnings and ends of these houses; the ancients construct these one way, Ptolemy another, Campanus another, and Johannes Regiomontanus <note>original: "Ioannes de Regio Monte"; a major 15th-century German mathematician and astronomer.</note> another. Whence it happens that they take away credit from their own observations by their own actions, since they ascribe different properties, beginnings, and ends to the same locations. They are an impious race of men, who attribute to the stars what belongs to God alone, and make us—who were born free—the slaves of the stars. Although we know that God created all things good, they teach that some stars are malevolent, authors of crimes, and sources of evil influences, not without the greatest [insult] to God—

Astrologers teach heresies and infidelities.

...differently. And again, with great injustice, they determine that in that divine senate of the heavens, evils and crimes are decreed to be committed; and whatever is perpetrated by us through the fault of our will, or whatever happens in nature outside of its usual order due to the defect of matter, they attribute it all to the stars. Now indeed, they are not afraid to teach the most ruinous heresies and infidelities—namely, by claiming that the gift of prophecy, the power of religions, the secrets of the conscience, command over demons, the power of miracles, the efficacy of prayers, and the state of the future life all depend on the stars, are bestowed by them, and are known through them; this they confess with impious boldness. For they say: when the sign of Gemini is ascending, and Saturn and Mercury are joined under Aquarius in the ninth house <note>The "ninth house" in astrology is traditionally associated with religion, philosophy, and long journeys.</note> of the heavens, a Prophet is born. They claim that for this reason Christ the Lord shone with so many virtues because he had Saturn in Gemini in that place. They even distribute the sects of religions—over which they appoint Jupiter as the primary patron—through the various mixtures of the other stars. Thus, they claim that Jupiter joined with Saturn creates the religion of the Jews; with Mars, that of the Chaldeans <note>Here referring to the ancient Near Eastern practitioners of magic and astrology.</note>; with Mercury, that of the Christians; and with the Moon, that religion which they say is to come, the religion of the Antichrist. They also claim that Moses instituted the Sabbath day as a religious observance for the Jews based on astrological reasons, and therefore that Christians are in error because they do not keep the Sabbath as a day of rest from labor after the manner of the Jews, since that is the day of Saturn <note>Saturday, or *dies Saturni*.</note>. 

Furthermore, they believe that the fidelity of any person, both toward men and toward God, as well as one's professed religion and even the secrets of the conscience, can be detected by the position of the Sun and the third, ninth, and eleventh houses of the heavens. Many authors hand down a great many rules for foreknowing the thoughts and "intentions" (as they call them) of men. They even place the celestial configurations as the primary causes for the miraculous works of Divine Omnipotence—such as the universal flood, the giving of the Law through Moses, and the birth of a child to a virgin. They even fabricate the story that Christ’s death, which redeemed the human race, was the work of Mars. Moreover, they claim that Christ himself, in his miracles, used the "election of hours" <note>A branch of astrology used to find the most auspicious moment to perform an action.</note> so that the Jews would not be able to harm him while he was going up to Jerusalem,

### IX. LXXXIX.

...customs, and they utterly ruin whatever arts of human wisdom exist, since at that time, by what reasoning, by what means, and what should be done, Astrology alone was consulted, and it alone held the scepters of life, of morals, of the State, and of private affairs, as if having authority from Heaven over all things; and all other things that did not acknowledge this patroness were considered as nothing. Truly a most worthy art, which even the Demons once claimed as their own, for the deception of men and as an injury to the divinity. Now indeed, 
<margin>
The heresy of the Manichaeans flowed from astrology.
</margin>
even the heresy of the Manichaeans <note>A major dualistic religion that competed with early Christianity, teaching a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note>, which entirely removes and takes away the freedom of the will, emanated from no other source than the false opinion and doctrine of astrologers regarding fate. From the same source also flowed the heresy of Basilides <note>An early Gnostic religious teacher in Alexandria.</note>, who declared that three hundred and sixty-five Heavens were made in succession and similarity to one another, and that the display of these was the number of the days of the year, assigning to each of them certain principles, powers, and Angels, and fashioning names for them: and that the prince of all is **Abraxas**, which name, according to Greek literature <note>original: "Graecam literaturam". In Greek gematria, the letters of ΑΒΡΑΞΑΣ (Abraxas) add up to 365: A=1, B=2, R=100, A=1, X=60, A=1, S=200.</note>, contains in itself three hundred and sixty-five, namely, as many as the local positions of those Heavens devised by him. These things are told for this reason, so that you may know Astrology is also the mother of heretics. Furthermore, this divinatory Astrology,
<margin>
Astrology rejected and condemned by the scriptures and the Church Fathers.
</margin>
just as all the most brilliant philosophers reject it, so too Moses, Isaiah, Job, Jeremiah, and the other Prophets of the ancient law detest it. And among the Catholic doctors, Augustine judges it should be expelled from the Christian religion; Jerome argues that this is a type of idolatry; Basil and Cyprian laugh at it; Chrysostom, Eusebius, and Lactantius refute it; Gregory, Ambrose, and 
<margin>
The Council of Toledo prohibits divinatory astrology.
</margin>

<margin>
Concerning divination in general.
</margin>
Therefore, among the arts prospering for the sake of profit through divining, **Physiognomy**, **Metoposcopy**, **Chiromancy** <note>Palm reading.</note>, **Geomancy** (about which we have also spoken above), **Haruspicy** <note>Divination by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note>, **Speculatory** <note>Scrying, or looking into mirrors and crystals to see the future.</note>, and **Oneirocritica**—which is the interpretation of dreams—as well as the oracles of those in a frenzy, all claim a place for themselves here. However, all these crafts possess no solid doctrine, nor do they consist of any certain reasons. Instead, they inquire into hidden things either by chance, or by the agitation of a spirit, or by certain apparent conjectures which have been gathered from daily and long-term observations. For all those monstrous arts of divination are accustomed to defend themselves only under the title of "experience," and they extricate themselves from the chains of objections whenever they teach or promise something beyond faith and contrary to reason.

</margin>

**PHYSIOGNOMY.**
</margin>

<margin>CHIROMANCY.</margin>
**CHIROMANCY** <note>Also known as palmistry.</note>, however, imagines seven "mounts" <note>Raised areas at the base of the fingers named after the seven classical planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon.</note> within the palm of the hand, according to the number of the planets. From the lines that are seen there, it presumes to be able to know a person's temperament, their passions, their life, and their fortune through a "linear harmonic correspondence." It treats these as if they were celestial marks <note>original: "stigmata"</note> impressed upon us by God and nature. The proponents of this art claim that God (according to the author of the Book of Job) placed these in the hands of men, so that <margin>Job 37.</margin> each one might know his own works. However, in truth, that holy Prophet was not speaking there of the vanity of Chiromancy, but rather of the freedom of the will. 

Furthermore, the aforementioned <margin>The reasons of the diviners, by which they defend their art.</margin> Diviners defend themselves by arguing that, although they do not judge by the underlying causes of things, they can judge the effects through signs impressed upon them by those same causes. They believe that since like produces like, these signs remain consistent. They claim that Pythagoras once used these arts; he would conjecture the character, nature, and intellect of young men from the lines and features of their face and their entire body. Whomever he judged suitable, he ordered to be received into his teaching. Philostratus records that Pharaotes, the King of the Indians, was accustomed to doing the same. 

Truly, there is no other way we need to refute the error of all these arts than by the fact that they clearly lack any basis in reason. Nevertheless, many grave men among the ancients wrote about these things: Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of Hermeticism.</note>, Alchindus <note>Al-Kindi, a 9th-century Islamic philosopher.</note>, Pythagoras, Pharaotes the Indian, Zopyrus, Helenus, Ptolemy, Aristotle, Al-Farabi, and furthermore, Galen, Avicenna, Rhazes, Julianus, Maternus, Loxius, Philemon, Palaemon, and Constantine the African. Finally, among the Roman leaders, Lucius Sulla and Caesar the Dictator were most devoted to these studies. Among later writers, there were Pietro d'Abano, Albert the German <note>Albertus Magnus.</note>, Michael Scot, Antiochus, Bartolommeo Cocles, Michele Savonarola, Antonio Cermisoni, Pietro de Arca, Andreas Corvus, Tricassus of Mantua, John of Indagine, and many other illustrious physicians. Yet, none of them passed down anything beyond mere conjectures and observations of experience. That there is no rule of truth in those conjectures and observations is manifest from this: they are voluntary fictions, upon which...

# OF VANITY

Even these teachers, though equal in learning and authority, do not agree with one another. For this reason, all those who wish to use these signs to predict things beyond the physical makeup and natural disposition—such as a person's character, their fate, and the emotions of the mind—are raving and completely mistaken. This was clearly proven in Zopyrus's judgment of Socrates <note>Zopyrus, a famous physiognomist, claimed Socrates' face revealed a lustful and dull nature. While Socrates’ friends laughed, the philosopher admitted he was naturally inclined to such vices but had conquered them through study and reason.</note>. Nor should you trust what the grammarian Apion wrote: that a certain Alexander painted portraits so precisely that a Metoposcopus <term>Metoposcopus: a diviner who judges character or predicts the future by examining the lines and features of the forehead.</term> could tell from them the years of a person's past or future death. To know such things through these arts is not so much incredible as it is impossible. But this kind of person, dealers in trifles <note>original: "nugiuendum"</note>, is accustomed to rave in this way by the prompting of evil spirits, who lead them from error into superstition, and from there gradually into a loss of faith.

<margin>
GEOMANCY.
</margin>
**GEOMANCY** also—which we mentioned in our discussion of Arithmetic—consists of casting points, either by chance or by some directed force. From these points, using even and odd numbers, it forms certain figures attributed to the heavenly bodies, which are then used for divination. For this reason, all who write on the subject testify that it is the "daughter of Astrology." There is also another kind of Geomancy, introduced by Almadal the Arab <note>Likely a reference to the *Art Almadel*, a medieval grimoire or book of magic named after its purported Arabian creator.</note>, which divines through conjectures based on similarities—such as the cracking, movement, splitting, or swelling of the earth, whether occurring naturally or caused by heat, drought, or thunder. This practice is also supported by the empty superstition of Astrology, as it observes the specific hours, the phases of the moon, and the rising and positions of the stars.

<margin>
AUGURY.
</margin>
¶ **AUGURY**, of which there are many types, was an art held in great esteem in ancient times. Indeed, it was so respected that the ancients performed nothing related to public or private affairs "inauspiciously" <note>original: "inauspicate," meaning without first consulting the omens or "auspices."</note>. This art is extremely ancient; as Pomponius Laetus records, it passed from the Chaldeans to the Greeks—among whom Amphiaraus, Tiresias, Mopsus, Amphilochus, and Calchas were considered the greatest augurs. From the Greeks, it came to the Etruscans, and from them to the Latins. Romulus himself was an augur and established that magistrates should be confirmed by auguries. Furthermore, Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian who wrote about the early history of Rome.</note> records that the ancient art of augury was practiced even by the Aborigines <note>The earliest inhabitants of central Italy in Roman founding myths.</note> and that Ascanius <note>The son of Aeneas and legendary founder of Alba Longa.</note>, before leading his battle-line against Mezentius, had sought an omen <insert>captasse</insert>,

...to have captured it, which when that fortunate man beheld, he fought and conquered. <note>This likely refers to a general observing a favorable omen before a battle, a common theme in Roman history.</note> Finally, the Phrygians, Pisidians, Cilicians, Arabs, Umbrians, Etruscans, and many other peoples have followed the practice of augury. The Spartans even gave their kings an augur as an assistant and required them to be present at public councils. There was also among the Romans a <margin>The College of Augurs in Rome.</margin> **College of Augurs**. Those who gave credit to this art taught that certain "lights of presage" descend from the celestial bodies upon every living creature in these lower realms. These are established as signs in their movement, position, gesture, gait, flight, voice, feeding, color, labor, and final end. By a certain innate hidden force and a silent agreement with the celestial bodies whose powers they assist, these creatures are said to correspond so closely that they can foretell everything the heavenly bodies have intended to do. 

From this, it is clear that this divination follows nothing but conjectures, taken partly from the "influences" of the stars (as they call them) and partly from certain metaphorical similarities, than which nothing is more deceptive. For this reason, Panaetius, Carneades, Cicero, Chrysippus, Diogenes, Antipater, Josephus, and Philo all mock it. Both the Law and the Church condemn it. Of this same sort are those mysteries of the Chaldeans and Egyptians which the Etruscans once adored, then the Romans, and which even today the superstitious common people worship as if they were oracles.

<margin>SPECULATORIA.</margin>
¶ From the same foundation arises **SPECULATORIA** <term>Speculatoria: the art of observing and interpreting lightning, atmospheric phenomena, and strange natural events.</term>, which interprets lightning bolts, flashes, and other impressions of the elements, as well as omens, portents, and prodigies. Yet it does so through no other way than conjecture and similarity, which is clearly most prone to error, because all these things are natural occurrences rather than prognostications.

<margin>DREAM-WATCHING.</margin>
Next is **ONEIROCRITICA** <term>Oneirocritica: the interpretation of dreams.</term>, which is the interpretation of dreams. Its practitioners are properly called "conjectors," just as Euripides sings:

> He who conjectures well, let him be the best prophet.
> <note>original Latin: "Qui bene coniectat, is uates optimus esto." This is a translation of a famous Greek fragment attributed to Euripides.</note>

Even great philosophers have attributed no small importance to this art—especially Democritus, Aristotle, and his follower Themistius, as well as Synesius the Platonist—relying on those examples of dreams which some chance made true...

# ON VANITY

...[it] caused them to try to persuade others that nothing is dreamed in vain. For he says that just as celestial influences produce various forms in physical matter, so from those same influences, phantasms <note>original: "phantasmata"—mental images or visions</note> are imprinted upon the imaginative power—which is an organic faculty—according to the arrangement of the heavens. These images are consistent with the effects to be produced, especially in dreams. This is because the mind, being then relaxed from external and bodily cares, more freely receives those divine influences. Thus, many things become known to those sleeping in dreams which are hidden from those who are awake. By this reasoning above all, they strive to win over belief in the truth of dreams themselves.

<margin>Controversies regarding the causes of dreams.</margin>
Regarding the causes of dreams, both internal and external, not everyone agrees on a single opinion. For the **Platonists** attribute them to "species" <note>mental forms or patterns</note> and innate notions of the soul. **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> attributes them to the "Last Intelligence," which moves the Moon by means of that light which irradiates the human imagination while people sleep. **Aristotle** refers them to the "common sense," but specifically the imaginative part of it. **Averroes** <note>A medieval Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> attributes them to the imaginative power. **Democritus** [refers them] to "idols" <note>original: "idola"—in ancient atomist theory, these were thin films of atoms shed from the surface of objects that strike the senses.</note> cast off from things. **Albertus Magnus** refers them to a superior influence, mediated through certain forms that continuously flow down from the Heavens. **Physicians** attribute these to vapors and humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</note>. Others attribute them to the emotions and cares of waking life; some **Arab philosophers** to the intellectual power; others say they depend simultaneously on the powers of the soul, the influence of the Heavens, and images [simulacra]. **Astrologers** want them to be caused by their constellations; others refer their causes to the surrounding and penetrating air.

<margin>Interpreters of dreams.</margin>
Furthermore, **Daldianus** and **Artemidorus** <note>Artemidorus Daldianus was a 2nd-century professional diviner; his "Oneirocritica" is the most famous ancient manual on dream interpretation.</note> wrote on the interpretation of dreams, and books are circulated under the name of **Abraham**, whom **Philo** [Judaeus], in his books *On Giants* and *On Civil Life*, asserts was the first to discover the explanations of dreams. There are also other books forged on this matter under the names of **Solomon** and **Daniel**, in which nothing is handed down concerning dreams except "mere dreams" <note>original: "mera somnia"—Agrippa is making a pun here, suggesting the books themselves are nonsense or trifles.</note>. But **Marcus Tullius [Cicero]** himself, in his books on divination, argues with very strong reasons against this vanity and the foolishness of those who put faith in dreams—reasons which I omit listing here.

G iii

They grant the credit of divinity to prophecies, and they think that those who have lost awareness of the present, memory of the past, and all human sense have attained a divine foreknowledge of the future. They believe that the insane and the sleeping see things which the wise and the waking do not know—as if God were closer to them than to those who are sane, awake, understanding, and thoughtful. Unhappy indeed are the men who believe these vanities and obey those impostures, who feed the practitioners of such arts and subject their own intellects and their faith to the appetites <note>original: "uentri"—literally "belly," implying greed or base physical needs</note> of those men. For what else shall we consider "fury" <note>original: "furor"—divine madness or prophetic frenzy</note> but an alienation of the human mind, agitated by evil demons themselves, or led away by unclean spirits through the stars or lower instruments? 

This seems to be what the poet Lucan expressed when he introduces Aruns the Tuscan Seer <note>An Etruscan diviner. # OF VANITY

He will confound all law with a wicked hand of crime;
It shall be called virtue, and it shall endure for many years. <note>This concludes the quotation from Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, Book I, where the poet laments the moral inversion caused by civil war.</note>

Therefore, all these crafts of divination have their roots and foundations in Astrology itself. For whether the body, face, or hands are inspected, or whether a dream or a portent has been seen, or an omen observed, or if a prophetic frenzy <note>original: "furor"—the ancient concept of divine or poetic madness</note> has inspired someone, they consult the casting of a celestial figure <note>a horoscope or birth chart</note>. From the indications of this chart, combined with conjectures based on similarities and signs, they hunt for opinions on what is signified. Thus, all divinations demand the art and practice of Astrology for themselves, so that they admit this is like a necessary key to the knowledge of all secrets. Therefore, it is clear to see how far all these arts of divination are from the truth, because they use principles that are so manifestly false and fashioned with poetic rashness. Since these things neither are, nor were, nor ever shall be, they nevertheless want them to be the causes and signs of the outcomes of things, attributing them to that art in defiance of the plain truth.

<margin>MAGIC.</margin>
¶ This place also requires that we speak of MAGIC: for it is so joined and related to Astrology that he who professes Magic without Astrology achieves nothing, but wanders entirely from the path. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> thinks that Magic draws both its name and origin from the Maguseans. The common opinion is that the name is Persian—a view supported by Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> and Apuleius <note>A Roman writer and philosopher famously accused of using magic to win a wealthy widow</note>—and that in their language it signifies the same as Priest, Wise Man, or Philosopher. Magic, therefore, having embraced all of Philosophy, Physics, and Mathematics, also joins the powers of religions to them. Hence, it also contains within itself Goetia <note>derived from the Greek *goēteia*, meaning sorcery or "low" magic involving spirits</note> and Theurgy <note>meaning "divine work," a form of "high" magic seeking to commune with the divine</note>. For this reason, most people divide Magic into two parts: namely, Natural and Ceremonial.

<margin>NATURAL MAGIC.</margin>
¶ They think NATURAL MAGIC is nothing other than the highest power of the natural sciences, which they therefore call the highest peak of natural philosophy and its most absolute completion. Since it is the active portion of natural philosophy, which produces works by the assistance of natural virtues <note>the inherent powers or "signatures" of natural objects like herbs or stones</note> through their mutual and opportune application—surpassing all capacity for wonder—the Ethiopians <note>A term often used in this period to refer broadly to African peoples, who were historically associated with ancient wisdom</note> especially [practiced it]...

They wish Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin.</note> to have remembered this in his letter to Paulinus, where he says that **Apollonius of Tyana** was either a Magician or a Philosopher, like the followers of Pythagoras. Such were **Iarchas** among the Brahmans, **Thespion** among the Gymnosophists <note>original: "Gymnosphistas"—literally 'naked philosophers,' a group of ancient Indian ascetics known to the Greeks.</note>, **Buddha** among the Babylonians, **Numa Pompilius** among the Romans, **Zamolxis** among the Thracians, **Abaris** among the Hyperboreans, **Hermes** among the Egyptians, and **Zoroaster** the son of Oromasus among the Persians. 

For the Indians, Ethiopians, Chaldeans, and Persians especially excelled in this Magic. For this reason (as Plato relates in the *Alcibiades*), the sons of the Persian kings are imbued with it, so that they might learn to administer and distribute their own Republic according to the image of the world’s Republic <note>This refers to the "Macrocosm," the idea that the state should be governed in harmony with the laws of the universe.</note>. And Cicero, in his books on divination, says that no one among the Persians gains the kingdom who has not first learned Magic. 

Therefore, <term>Natural Magic</term> <note>original: "Magia naturalis"—a branch of science in the Renaissance that sought to use the natural properties of plants, minerals, and stars to produce effects.</note> is that which, having contemplated the powers of all natural and celestial things, and having searched out their <term>sympathy</term> <note>The "sympathy of all things" is the belief that objects in the universe are occultly connected, like two strings on a lute.</note> through careful investigation, brings forth into the open those powers that are hidden and latent in nature. It joins lower things to the gifts of higher things as if by certain allurements through their mutual application to one another; from this, amazing miracles often arise, produced not so much by art as by nature—to which this art shows itself a servant while nature performs the work. 

For the Magi, as the most accurate explorers of nature, by bringing together those things prepared by nature and by applying active things to passive <note>This refers to the Aristotelian concept of 'active' agents (like heat) acting upon 'passive' matter.</note>, very often produce effects before the time ordained by nature. The common people think these are miracles, when they are nevertheless natural works, with only the acceleration of time intervening. This occurs, for example, if someone were to produce roses in the month of March, or ripe grapes; or if one were to make sown beans or parsley <note>original: "petroselinon"</note> grow into a perfect plant within a few hours; and things even greater than these, such as clouds, rains, thunders, the creation of animals of diverse kinds, and many transmutations of things—many of which kind **Roger Bacon** boasts he has performed...

...<note>original: "Bacon pura & naturali magia" — referring to Roger Bacon's writings on natural magic as a legitimate science.</note> **Roger Bacon** on pure and natural magic. Regarding its works, **Zoroaster**, **Hermes**, **Euantes** the king of the Arabs, **Zacharias** the Babylonian, **Joseph** the Hebrew, **Bocus**, **Aaron**, **Zenotenus**, the **Cyranides** <note>A collection of ancient texts on the magical properties of plants, stones, and animals.</note>, **Almadal**, **Thetel**, **Al-Kindi**, **Abel**, **Ptolemy**, **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous polymath and alchemist.</note>, **Zahel**, **Nazabarus**, **Thabit**, **Berith**, **Solomon**, **Astaphon**, **Hipparchus**, **Alcmeon**, **Apollonius**, **Tryphon**, and many others have written. Some of their works are still intact, and many fragments still exist, which at some point came into my hands. Of the more recent writers on Natural Magic, there are few; among those few are **Albertus Magnus**, **Arnald of Villanova**, **Ramon Llull**, **Roger Bacon**, and **Pietro d'Abano**, and the author of the book published under the name **Picatrix** <note>The *Picatrix* is a massive medieval grimoire of astrological magic, originally written in Arabic as the *Ghayat al-Hakim*.</note> for King Alfonso, which nonetheless mixes much superstition with Natural Magic—as others have also done.

<margin>MATHEMATICAL MAGIC</margin>
Furthermore, there are other very keen imitators of nature and most daring investigators who—without using natural virtues but from mathematical disciplines alone, having summoned the influences of the Heavens—promise that they can produce works similar to nature. These are bodies that all either speak, though they do not have animal souls—such as the wooden **Dove of Archytas** <margin>The Dove of Archytas and Boethius's skill in mathematical magic.</margin> <note>Archytas of Tarentum was a Greek philosopher-engineer said to have built a steam-powered flying wooden bird.</note> which used to fly—and the statues of **Mercury** which spoke, and the **Brazen Head** forged by **Albertus Magnus**, which they say spoke. **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher and statesman.</note> excelled in these things, a man of greatest genius and wide-ranging learning; writing to him about such things, **Cassiodorus** said: "Your purpose is to know difficult things and show miracles; by the ingenuity of your art, metals low <note>original: "mugiunt" — to make the sound of a cow.</note>, **Diomedes** trumpets loudly in bronze, a bronze serpent hisses, simulated birds are proven to emit songs, though they do not know how to have their own sweetness of voice. We report small things of him, for whom it is permitted to imitate the Heavens." <margin>Plato.</margin> Regarding these things, I think the saying of the craftsman was written, which we read in **Plato's** eleventh book of the *Laws*: "Art was given to mortals so they might generate certain later things, not indeed participating in truth and divinity, but leading out certain likenesses <note>original: "simulachra" — images or phantom representations.</note> related to themselves." And the Magi, most daring men, have progressed so far as to perpetrate everything, mostly favored by that ancient and powerful serpent... <note>Refers to the Devil/Satan, indicating Agrippa's shift from "Natural Magic" toward "Goetia" or demonic magic.</note>

# OF THE SCIENCES. Fo. LIIII.

...by the promiser of sciences, so that, like apes of him <note>This refers to the common medieval and Renaissance trope of the "Simia Dei" (Ape of God), usually describing the Devil or those who use magic to mimic divine miracles through trickery.</note>, they might strive to emulate God and nature. 

<margin>POISONOUS MAGIC</margin>
¶ There is, furthermore, a species of Natural Magic which they call **POISONOUS MAGIC** or pharmacy <note>original: "pharmaciam." In this period, the term carried a dual meaning of both medicine and sorcery/poisoning.</note>, which is performed with potions, philtres, and various poisonous drugs. We read that **Democritus** <note>A Greek philosopher often associated in later occult traditions with secret natural properties.</note> prepared such things: one to ensure the birth of good, happy, and fortunate children, and another through which we may rightly understand the voices of birds—as **Philostratus** and **Porphyry** relate concerning **Apollonius**. **Virgil** also, speaking of certain herbs from Pontus, said:

> By these herbs I have often seen Moeris become a wolf and hide in the woods,
> often summon souls from the depths of the tombs,
> and seen him move sown harvests from one field to another.

¶ And **Pliny** tells of a certain **Demarchus of Parrhasia** who, during a sacrifice of a human victim by the Arcadians to **Lycaean Jove**, tasted the vitals of an immolated boy and turned into a wolf. Because of this changing of men into wolves, **Augustine** thinks the names **Lycaean Pan** and **Lycaean Jove** <note>From the Greek *lykos*, meaning wolf.</note> were bestowed. The same Augustine relates that while he was in Italy, certain sorceresses—much like **Circe**—gave travelers a poison in cheese that turned them into beasts of burden; after they had carried whatever loads were required, they were restored to human form. This supposedly happened to the father of a man named **Prestantius**. 

But if anyone thinks these are entirely ravings and impossibilities, let him remember how the Holy Scriptures relate <margin>Daniel 4</margin> that King **Nebuchadnezzar** was changed into an ox and lived on hay for seven years, until at last by the mercy of God he returned to being a man. After his death, his son **Evil-Merodach** gave his body to be eaten by vultures, lest he who had already returned from being a beast to a man might one day rise from the dead. **Exodus** <margin>Exodus 7</margin> relates many such things regarding the Magicians of Pharaoh. The **Author of Wisdom** <margin>Wisdom 12</margin> speaks of these—whether Magicians or Poisoners—when he says: *You abhorred them, O God, because they worked horrible deeds against You through their medicines.* I want you to know, moreover, that these Magicians do not only scrutinize natural things, but also those things that accompany nature and in a way go out from it,

# OF VANITY.

<margin>Magic beyond nature.</margin>
...such as motions, numbers, shapes, sounds, voices, harmonies, lights, the passions of the soul, and words. Thus the **Psylli** and **Marsi** <note>Ancient peoples of North Africa and Italy, respectively, who were legendary for their ability to charm and heal the bites of venomous snakes.</note> used to call forth serpents, while others drove them away by subduing them. In this manner, **Orpheus** <note>The mythical Greek musician whose music could move even inanimate objects.</note> calmed the storm for the **Argonauts** with a hymn; and **Homer** relates that **Ulysses'** blood was staunched with words <note>An allusion to the *Odyssey*, where an incantation is used to stop the bleeding of a wound Ulysses received from a boar.</note>. Even in the **Law of the Twelve Tables** <note>The earliest code of ancient Roman law, dating to the 5th century BC.</note>, a punishment was established for those who should "enchant away" the harvests <note>original: "messes excantassent." This refers to the crime of using magic to steal the fertility or the actual crops of a neighbor's field.</note>. It is therefore beyond doubt that Mages, using only words, emotions, and similar things, often produce some marvelous effect—not only upon themselves, but also upon external objects. They believe that all these things pour an innate power into other things, drawing them toward themselves or repelling them away, or affecting them in some other manner. This is thought to be no different than how a magnet draws iron, or how amber draws chaff, or how a diamond and garlic are said to bind the power of a magnet <note>A common ancient and medieval belief that certain substances possessed "antipathy" and could neutralize a magnet's attraction.</note>. Thus, through this gradual and chained sympathy of things, they believe that not only natural and celestial gifts, but even intellectual and divine ones can be received from above. **Iamblichus**, **Proclus**, and **Synesius** <note>Influential Neoplatonist philosophers who integrated mysticism and ritual into their philosophy.</note> confirm this as the opinion of the Mages. Proclus further admits that through sacrifice and magic—specifically through this "consensus" or agreement of things—the Mages were even accustomed to call forth the spirits of the gods. Indeed, some of them have fallen into such insanity that they believe a constructed image <note>A talisman or "animated" statue.</note>, if made according to the various constellations of the stars and at the proper intervals of time, will receive the spirit of life and intellect from the heavenly powers, so that it may answer those who consult it and reveal the secrets of hidden truth. From this, it is clear that this Natural Magic often leans toward **Goetia** <note>Commonly understood as "low" magic or sorcery involving the conjuring of spirits.</note> and **Theurgy** <note>Literally "god-working"; a form of high magic intended to purify the soul and communicate with divine beings.</note>, and is very often ensnared by the deceits and errors of evil demons.

# ON VANITY

...we reconcile and attract divine virtues to ourselves: regarding which the ancient Magi <term>Magi: wise men or practitioners of high magic in the ancient world</term>, having published many volumes, have treated with many rules. The greatest part of all ceremonies, however, consists in maintaining **purity**: first, certainly, of the soul, and then also of the body, and of those things which are around the body—such as the skin, clothes, dwellings, vessels, utensils, offerings, victims, and sacrifices. The purity of these things prepares one for the custom and fellowship of the divine, and it is most earnestly demanded in sacred rites, according to the words of Isaiah: "Wash yourselves <margin>Isaiah 1.</margin> and be clean, and take away the evil of your thoughts." <note>original: "Lauamini & mundi estote"</note> Indeed, because impurity frequently infects both the air and the person, it disturbs that most pure influx of celestial and divine things and puts the pure spirits of God to flight. Yet, sometimes unclean spirits and deceiving powers—wishing to be worshipped and adored as Gods—also demand this purity. Therefore, there is a need for the greatest caution here, concerning which we have discoursed widely in our books on **Occult Philosophy**.

However, while Porphyry <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the nature of spirits</note> disputes many things regarding this **Theurgy** <term>Theurgy: a form of ritual magic intended to invoke the presence of divine beings or gods</term> or "divine magic," he finally concludes that through theurgical consecrations, the soul of a person can indeed be rendered fit for the reception of spirits and Angels, and for seeing the gods; but he utterly denies that a return to God can be provided by this art. Of that school, therefore, are the **Art of the Almadel**, the **Notory Art**, the **Pauline Art**, the **Art of Revelations**, and many other such superstitions <note>these "Arts" refer to specific medieval grimoires or ritual systems</note>, which are all the more destructive precisely because they appear more divine to the unlearned.

¶ But here the words of Pliny occur to me, who says: "there is also another faction of Magic <margin>KABBALAH.</margin> depending upon Moses, and even now upon the Jews, through Iaropea." <note>Pliny the Elder in his Natural History mentions a Jewish branch of magic involving Moses and "Jotape" or "Jochia," which the OCR reads as Iaropea</note> These words remind me of the **Kabbalah** of the Jews, which is a constant opinion among the Hebrews to have been given by God himself to Moses on Mount Sinai. Thereafter, it was handed down only by living voice <note>original: "uiua uoce"</note> through successive degrees to posterity, without written records, until the times of Ezra. This is just as the Pythagorean dogmas were formerly handed down by Archippus and Lysiades, who held schools in Thebes in Greece; in those schools, the disciples, holding the precepts of the teachers in their hearts, used their intellect and **memory** instead of books. So also, certain Jews came to despise written letters...

# OF THE SCIENCES. Folio 57.

They situated this science in memory, observation, and oral tradition, which is why it is called **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: from the Hebrew 'Qabbalah,' meaning 'received tradition'</term> by the Hebrews—named as a reception from one to another by hearing alone. It is an art, as they say, of great antiquity, though its name was not known among Christians until recent times. Indeed, they hand down a twofold science of it: <margin>*The twofold science of Kabbalah.*</margin> one concerning **Bereshit** <note>original: "Bresith"; the Hebrew title for the book of Genesis, meaning "In the beginning"</note>, which they also call **Cosmology**. This explains the powers of created, natural, and celestial things, and expounds the secrets of the Biblical Law through philosophical reasoning. Truly, in this regard, it differs not at all from **Natural Magic**, in which we believe King Solomon excelled. For it is read in the sacred histories of the Hebrews <margin>*3 Kings 4.* <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 4:33.</note></margin> that he was accustomed to discourse from the cedar of Lebanon even to the hyssop; likewise regarding beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish, all of which can display certain magical powers of nature. Moses the Egyptian <note>referring to the 12th-century philosopher Maimonides</note> himself, among later writers, and many **Talmudists** <term>Talmudists: scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</term> followed him in these expositions upon the **Pentateuch** <term>Pentateuch: the first five books of the Bible</term>.

The other science they call **Merkabah** <note>original: "Mercana"; referring to the "Chariot" of Ezekiel's vision</note>, which deals with the more sublime contemplations of divine and angelic virtues, as well as sacred names and seals. It is a kind of **Symbolic Theology** in which letters, numbers, figures, things, names, the tips of letters, lines, points, and accents are all significant of the most profound matters and great secrets. They divide this branch again into two parts: namely into **Arithmancy** <note>literally "number-divination"</note> (which is called **Notarikon** <term>Notarikon: a Kabbalistic method of using the first or last letters of words to form new words or hidden meanings</term>), dealing with angelic virtues, names, and seals, as well as the conditions of demons and souls; and into **Theomancy** <term>Theomancy: a branch of magic or study dealing specifically with the names of God and divine emanations</term>, which scrutinizes the mysteries of the divine majesty, emanations, sacred names, and pentacles. 

They say that whoever knows this science is endowed with wonderful powers, so that whenever he wishes, he may foreknow all future things, command all of nature, have authority over demons and angels, and perform miracles. By this art, they believe **Moses** performed so many signs: turning his rod into a serpent, the waters into blood, and sending frogs, flies, lice, locusts, grubs, fire with hail, blisters, and pestilence upon the Egyptians; slaying every firstborn from man even to the beast; and leading his people out, opening the sea, and bringing forth a spring...

### LV III.
->### OF THE SCIENCES.<-

H ii.

...[of] Christ are able to work, just as their ancient fathers did. But what we experience and see—that by the resolutions (as they call them) of this art, miraculous meanings of great mysteries are often wrested from the sacred letters—all of this is nothing other than a certain game of **Allegories** <note>Symbolic interpretations where characters or events represent deeper moral or spiritual meanings.</note>, which idle men, occupied with individual letters, dots, and numbers (since this language and style of writing easily allow for it), invent and reinvent at their own whim. Although these may sometimes sound like great mysteries, they can prove or demonstrate nothing; rather, according to the words of **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), known as Gregory the Great.</note>, one may disregard them with the same ease with which they are asserted.

The monk **Rabanus** <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Carolingian scholar and archbishop of Mainz, famous for his visual poems.</note> devised many similar things by a similar artifice, but using Latin characters and verses, inserting various images. Whoever reads these verses finds that through any lineaments of the surface and images, they announce some sacred mystery of the history depicted there. No one is unaware that such things can even be wrested from secular literature, if they have read the *Centones* <note>original: "centones"; a literary work made up of quotations from other authors, rearranged to tell a new story.</note> of **Valeria Proba** <note>A 4th-century Roman poet who rearranged the lines of Virgil to tell the story of the Old and New Testaments.</note> composed about Christ from the poems of **Virgil**. All these, and things of this sort, are the speculations of idle men. 

But as for the performance of miracles, I think none of you is so stiff-necked <note>original: "stolidæ ceruicis"; meaning stubborn or foolishly headstrong.</note> as to believe that anything regarding them is possessed through art or science. Therefore, this **Kabbalah** of the Jews is nothing other than a certain most pernicious superstition. At their own whim, they collect, divide, and transfer words, names, and letters placed scattered throughout the Scripture. Making one thing from another, they dismember the truth, constructing speeches, inductions, and parables here and there from their own fictions. They wish to fit the oracles of God to these, defaming the Scriptures and saying their figments consist of them; they slander the law of God, and through impudently extorted calculations of words, syllables, letters, and numbers, they attempt to bring forth violent and blasphemous proofs for their own faithlessness. 

Furthermore, puffed up by these trifles, they boast that they have found and known the ineffable mysteries of God and secrets that are above Scripture. Through these, they do not blush to lie with great audacity, claiming they can prophesy and perform virtues and miracles. But it happened to them as it did to **Aesop's Dog**, who, having left the bread <meta>catchword: relicto (having left behind)</meta>

# ON VANITY

...having left [the meat] and snapping at its shadow, he lost his food; so too this faithless and stiff-necked <note>A biblical idiom for stubbornness, frequently used in 16th-century religious polemics.</note> race of men, always occupied in the shadows of Scripture, and making an assault upon those vanities through their artful but superstitious **Kabbalah**, loses the bread of eternal life, and wastes the word of truth on empty names. 

<margin>Heresies arose from the Kabbalah.</margin>From this Jewish leaven <note>Influence or fermenting source.</note> of Kabbalistic superstition, there arose, I believe, the **Ophites**, **Gnostics**, and **Valentinian** heretics <note>Early Christian sects (2nd–4th century) known for their "Gnosis" or secret knowledge, often involving complex systems of divine emanations.</note>, who themselves also, along with their disciples, devised a certain Greek **Kabbalah**, perverting all the mysteries of the Christian faith. With heretical wickedness, they dragged these mysteries down to Greek letters and numbers, constructing from them a "body" which they call "of truth." They teach that without these mysteries of letters and numbers, the truth cannot be found in the writings of the Gospels, because those writings are varied and in places contradictory to themselves, and written full of parables, so that "seeing they might not see, and hearing they might not hear, and understanding they might not understand" <note>A reference to Matthew 13:13 and Mark 4:12.</note>. Instead, they claim the Gospels were set forth for the blind and the wandering according to the capacity of their blindness and error, but that the sincere truth hidden beneath them was entrusted only to the "perfected," not through writings, but through the successive oral transmission <note>original: "vivae vocis"; the living voice.</note> of the word. 

<margin>Matthew 13 and Mark 4. 1 Corinthians 2.</margin>They believe this to be that **Alphabetical** and **Arithmetical Theology** which Christ secretly revealed to the Apostles, and which Paul says he speaks only among the "perfect." Since these are the most profound mysteries, they claim they were neither written down nor should be written, but should be preserved in silence among the Wise in a hidden place, guarding them within themselves. However, among such people, no one is considered "Wise" unless he knows how to manufacture the greatest monsters of Heresy.

<margin>PRESTIDIGITATION</margin>¶ But let us return to **Magic**, of which a small part is also the art of **PRESTIDIGITATION** <note>original: "PRAESTIGIORUM"; the art of illusions or sleight of hand.</note>, that is, of illusions which occur only according to appearance. By these, Mages produce phantasms and play out many miracles through the frauds of traveling performers <note>original: "circulatoriis fraudibus"; the tricks of mountebanks or street performers.</note>, and they send dreams. This is done not so much by **Goetic** incantations <note>Goetia refers to "low" magic involving the invocation of spirits or demons, often contrasted with Theurgy or "high" magic.</note> and imprecations and the deceits of demons, but also by certain vapors of fumigations, lights, love-potions, eye-salves, bindings, and suspensions. Furthermore, they use rings, images, mirrors, and similar drugs and instruments of the Magical art...

# OF THE SCIENCES. Fo. LX.

->H iij<-

<meta>catchword: to both</meta>

**Prometheus**, **Linus**, **Musaeus**, and **Orpheus**, and furthermore **Homer**, are counted as the first inventors of philosophy. Therefore, what truth can **Philosophy** now offer us, which itself was born from the trifles and fables of Poets? Plutarch proves this with clear evidence, showing that all the sects of philosophers took their beginning from Homer; and Aristotle himself admits that even philosophers are by nature *Philomythos* <note>original: *Philomythos*, a Greek term meaning a lover of stories or fables.</note>, that is, lovers of fables. <margin>Sects of philosophers.</margin> Some report that there are nine sects of philosophers, others ten; but **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar who famously identified hundreds of different philosophical opinions on the "highest good."</note> divided them into a much larger number. But even if someone were to gather all the philosophers into one place, it would still be impossible for them to agree on which sect is better to learn, or whose dogmas should be more obeyed. <margin>Dissensions of philosophers among themselves.</margin> To such an extent they fight and disagree with each other on every point, nourishing this perpetual quarrel through the centuries. And (as **Firmianus** <note>Lactantius, an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero," who wrote the Divine Institutes.</note> says), every sect overthrows all others so that it might confirm itself and its own views, and none grants wisdom to another, lest it be forced to admit its own foolishness. **Philosophy** disputes and offers opinions on everything, but is certain of nothing. Hence, I truly do not know whether to count philosophers among the beasts or among men: they seem superior to beasts because they possess reason and intelligence; but how can they be men, whose reason can persuade them of nothing constant, but always wavers in slippery opinions, and whose intellect is uncertain about all things, having nothing to hold onto or follow? Let us now show this to be the case more extensively.

### PRINCIPLES
<margin>PRINCIPLES</margin>

¶ For first of all, concerning the **Principles** of natural things, upon which this whole faculty is founded, a most bitter battle is fought among the most serious philosophers; and the dispute is still before the judge <note>original: *sub iudice lis est*, a legal metaphor from Horace's Art of Poetry, meaning the matter is still undecided.</note> as to which of them spoke better. They bring forward quite persuasive and invincible arguments for contrary positions. For **Thales of Miletus**, judged the first wise man by the Oracle, would have it that all things consist of water. His listener and successor in the school, **Anaximander**, said the Principles of things were infinite. His student **Anaximenes**, however, asserted that infinite air was the Principle of things. **Hipparchus** and **Heraclitus of Ephesus** said it was fire; to these...

**Archelaus of Athens** <note>A 5th-century BCE philosopher, often called the last of the physical philosophers and the teacher of Socrates.</note> in a certain way agreed with both. **Anaxagoras of Clazomenae** posited infinite principles like minute and confused particles, which were later reduced into order by a **divine mind**. **Xenophanes** held that all things are one, and that this "one" is unchanging. **Parmenides** proposed the hot and the cold, identifying them as fire which moves and earth which gives form. **Leucippus**, **Diodorus**, and **Democritus** argued for the "full" and the "empty" <note>This refers to atoms and the void.</note>. **Diogenes of Apollonia** <note>Original text says "Libertus," likely a transcription error or specific variant for the philosopher known for his theories on air.</note> posited air, yet air that possessed divine reason. **Pythagoras of Samos** established **number** as the principle of all things, and was followed by **Alcmaeon of Croton**. **Empedocles of Agrigento** proposed **strife and friendship** <note>Also translated as Love and Strife, the forces that combine and separate the elements.</note>, and the four elements. **Epicurus** held to **atoms and the void**. **Plato** and **Socrates** looked to **God, Ideas, and Matter**. **Zeno** <note>Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism.</note> looked to **God, matter, and the elements**. **Aristotle** proposed matter driven by an "appetite" for form, achieved through <term>privation</term> <note>The absence or lack of a quality that a thing is naturally supposed to have.</note>, which he himself placed as a third principle. This contradicted what he taught elsewhere: that <term>equivocal things</term> <note>Terms that have different meanings in different contexts.</note> should not be counted among principles. Because of this, other more recent **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school.</note> put a certain "motion" in the place of privation, which compels both matter and form; yet, since motion is merely an <term>accident</term> <note>In philosophy, a quality that is not essential to the existence of a thing.</note>, how can it be a principle of substance? Or who would be the "mover" of that motion? Therefore, the **Hebrew Philosophers** established matter, form, and spirit.

THE 
WORLD.

¶ Furthermore, when they dispute about the **World**, they disagree no less. **Thales** believed in a single World and asserted it was the handiwork of God. **Empedocles** similarly believed in one, but said it was only a tiny particle of the universe. **Democritus** and **Epicurus**, on the contrary, argued that there are **innumerable worlds**. They were followed by their disciple **Metrodorus**, who said there are infinite worlds because their causes are infinite; he argued it was no less absurd for there to be only one world in the universe than for only a single ear of corn to grow in a field.

But **Plato** asserts that it was fashioned by **God** after His own image, and will never cease to be. **Epicurus**, on the contrary, says it will utterly perish. **Democritus** teaches that the **World** was born once and will perish, never to be restored. **Empedocles** and **Heraclitus of Ephesus** assert that the World is not generated and destroyed just once, but is always being generated and destroyed.

Let us discuss a certain matter which they say proceeds primarily from a natural cause—for instance, an **Earthquake**. To this day, they have been unable to find a unanimous explanation for it; instead, having wandered through many theories, **Anaxagoras** said its cause was the <term>ether</term> <note>The upper, pure air or fire in ancient physics.</note>, **Empedocles** said fire, **Democritus** and **Thales of Miletus** said water, **Aristotle**, **Theophrastus**, and **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, the medieval scholastic.</note> said wind or subterranean vapor, **Asclepiades** said a fall or collapse, while **Posidonius**, **Metrodorus**, **Callisthenes**, the **Fates**, **Seneca**, and others, distracted by diverse opinions, have searched for the cause of its effect in vain. For this reason, when the ancient **Romans** felt the earth tremble or were notified of it, they indeed commanded festivals, but they did not decree which of the **Gods** they should be dedicated to, since it was still uncertain by what force and by which of the Gods the earth was being shaken.

they agree even less. For **Crates of Thebes** says there is no soul at all, but that bodies are moved thus by nature. ->### ON VANITY<-

<margin>Bede.</margin>
The opinion of **Bede** <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 673–735 AD), an English monk and influential scholar.</note> the theologian, who, writing upon the Gospel of Mark, says: "The primary seat of the soul," he says, "is not in the brain, according to **Plato**, but in the heart, according to **Christ**." 

<margin>The duration of the soul.</margin>
Regarding the duration of the soul, however, **Democritus** and **Epicurus** say that it will perish together with the body. **Pythagoras** and **Plato** say it is altogether immortal, but having departed the body, it returns to the nature of its own kind. 

The **Stoics**, acting as a middle ground between these, think that the soul will leave the body, but if it be weak—as one that was elevated by no virtues in this life—it dies along with the body. If, however, it was shaped by heroic virtues, they believe it joins the permanent natures and escapes to more sublime seats. 

**Aristotle** says that certain parts of the soul, which have bodily seats, are inseparable from those seats and perish together with them; however, the intellect—which he claims belongs to no bodily organ—is separated from the corruptible as something perpetual. Yet he says nothing so clearly on this that his interpreters do not still dispute the matter. 

**Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>A famous commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD) known for his "materialist" interpretation of the soul.</note> says that **Aristotle** clearly established the soul as mortal. Among our own Christian writers, **Gregory of Nazianzus** <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the early Church (4th century AD).</note> feels the same. Against these, **Plethon** <note>A Byzantine Neoplatonist philosopher who revived interest in Plato in the 15th century.</note> and, from our own ranks, **Thomas Aquinas** fight for **Aristotle**, arguing that he held the correct view regarding the immortality of the soul. 

<margin>Averroes.</margin>
Furthermore, **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian Muslim philosopher.</note>, that distinguished commentator on **Aristotle**, thinks that every man possesses his own soul, but a mortal one. However, the human mind—or let us call it the intellect—he says is eternal in every way, both from its beginning and its end, but it is one for all men, or for the whole human species, which we only make use of during our life. 

<margin>Themistius. The disagreement of theologians regarding the origin of the soul.</margin>
**Themistius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher and statesman who commented extensively on Aristotle.</note>, however, says that **Aristotle** established a single "active intellect" <note>original: "mentem agentem"</note> but a multiple "receptive intellect" <note>original: "capacem"; often called the passive or potential intellect.</note>, and both are perpetual. 

Furthermore, through the works of these philosophers, it has come to pass that a disagreement has arisen even among Christian theologians concerning the origin of souls. Some of them think that the souls of all men were created in Heaven at the beginning of the world, among whom is the most learned **Origen**, one of many. 

**Augustine** also thinks that the soul of the first parent <note>Referring to Adam.</note>, being of heavenly origin, is older than the body, and that after beholding the body as a suitable dwelling for itself, it sought it out by a voluntary motion—though he does not affirm even this with enough consistency...

In this opinion was **Apollinaris**, Bishop of Laodicea, and **Tertullian**, **Cyril**, and the **Luciferians** <note>A 4th-century schismatic group following Lucifer of Cagliari, often criticized by St. Jerome.</note>, against whose heresy **Jerome** disputes.
