For **Epicurus** and **Aristotle** think it is mortal; **Pythagoras** leads it in a circle <note>Refers to metempsychosis, the cycle of reincarnation or transmigration of souls.</note>; and there are those (as **Petrarch** says in a certain place) who contract it to its own body; there are those who even scatter it in the bodies of living things; there are those who return it to heaven; there are those who compel it to live in exile around the earth; there are those who assert the existence of the underworld; there are those who deny it; there are those who think each soul is created individually; there are those who think all souls were created together—thus says he. 

There was also **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a Muslim philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle deeply influenced—and troubled—Christian thought.</note>, who dared to say something even more marvelous: he brought forward (as I have said) the unity of the intellect <note>The controversial "Unicity of the Intellect" theory, which claimed all humans share a single, immortal active intellect.</note>. And so they conclude at last, that individual souls are nothing but parts of the universal soul. 

**Plato** also asserts one soul of the universe <note>The *Anima Mundi* or World Soul.</note>, but others for particular things, as if separately—so that the universe exists animated by its own soul, and likewise particular things separately. Furthermore, some affirm one species of souls; others not one but two, the rational and the irrational; others affirm many, and as many as there are species of animals. **Galen** the physician felt that there are different souls according to different species, and moreover he places many souls in the same body. > I recognized the shield, the burden of my left hand <note>original: "fæuæ" [laevae]. The OCR suggests "fæuæ" (fierce), but the classical source in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* refers to the "left" hand carrying the shield.</note>

¶ Many more authors have written about this **Pythagorean migration** <term>transmigration: the belief that the soul moves from one body to another after death</term>, including Timo, Xenophanes, Cratinus, Aristophon, Hermippus, Lucian, and Diogenes Laertius. Iamblichus and many others, along with **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical works were attributed; he was highly regarded in the Renaissance.</note>, agree that such movements do not happen from humans to unreasoning animals, nor from animals to humans, but only from animals to animals and from humans to humans. Yet there are also Philosophers—among them Euripides (a follower of Anaxagoras) and Archelaus the Physicist, and after them **Avicenna**—who teach that the first humans were born from the earth like vegetables. In this, they are no less ridiculous than the Poets who tell fables about various men springing forth from the teeth of serpents <note>A reference to the myth of Cadmus or Jason, who sowed dragon's teeth that grew into armed warriors.</note>. There are those who deny generation entirely, like **Pyrrho of Elis** <note>The founder of Skepticism, who taught that we cannot know the true nature of things.</note>; and those who even deny motion, like **Zeno**.

<margin>
**METAPHYSICS**
</margin>
¶ But let us proceed further and show that those Philosophers fight one another not only concerning things seen in the nature of reality, but also regarding the figments of their own thoughts. They argue over matters that are supported by no firm principles, where it is not even certain whether they exist or not. These are the things they believe exist without body or matter, which they call **separated forms**. Because these are not found in the nature of things but are thought to be above it, they call them "trans-natural" or **Metaphysics**.

concerning

From this have come those innumerable and everywhere-contradictory opinions concerning the Gods—opinions no less impious than they are unlearned. For **Diagoras of Melos** and **Theodorus of Cyrene** said there was no God at all. **Epicurus**, on the other hand, asserted that God does indeed exist, but is held by no concern for things below us. **Protagoras** said that it could not be known whether God exists or not. **Anaximander** thought the Gods were born, rising and falling at long intervals. **Xenocrates** said there were eight Gods. **Antisthenes** said there were many popular Gods, but only one natural God, the supreme craftsman of the whole. Indeed, many of them fell into such insanity that they manufactured with their own hands the Gods they would worship—such as the statue of **Bel** among the Assyrians. ### BOOK V ON THE ORIGINS <note>original: "STIRPIVM LIB. V." While *stirpium* usually refers to plants or roots in a botanical sense, here it likely refers to the "roots" or "lineages" of human thought and error.</note>

<margin>Cicero, Book 1 of *On the Nature of the Gods*.</margin>
Trismegistus in his *Asclepius* <note>A dialogue attributed to Hermes Trismegistus concerning the nature of the divine and the universe.</note>. Speaking of the divine essence, **Thales of Miletus** said that God was the "Mind" who formed all things from water; **Cleanthes** and **Anaximenes** said God was the air. **Chrysippus** called God a natural power endowed with reason, or a divine necessity; **Zeno** called God a divine and natural law. **Anaxagoras** defined God as an infinite mind, moving of its own accord. **Pythagoras** thought God was a soul extended through and traveling through the nature of all things, from which all living beings draw their life. **Alcmaeon of Croton** said the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars were Gods. **Xenophanes** wished for everything that exists to be God. **Parmenides** established a certain "stephane" <note>original: "stephanem" from the Greek *stephanē*, meaning a crown or wreath.</note>—that is, a crown or orb of light—as God. **Aristotle**, as if a sufficient knowledge of the Gods could be obtained from the movement of the Heavens, devised Gods out of their nature; at one moment he attributes divinity to the mind, at another he calls the heat of the Sky "God," then he establishes the World itself as God, and then again he places another God over it. **Theophrastus** follows this same inconsistency. I pass over what was judged by Strato of Lampsacus, Aristo the disciple of Zeno, Plato, Xenophon, Speusippus, Democritus, Heraclides, Diogenes of Babylon, Hermes Trismegistus, Cicero, Seneca, Pliny, and the rest, whose opinions nevertheless do not depart far from those already recited.

I could also run through the rest of their disputes and their linguistic monstrosities concerning **Ideas**, **bodies**, **atoms**, **hyle** <term>hyle: the Greek term for "wood" or "timber," used philosophically to mean raw, unformed matter</term>, **matter**, **form**, **the vacuum**, **the infinite**, **eternity**, **fate**, **transcendentals**, the **introduction of forms**, the **matter of the Heavens** (whether the stars consist of the elements or of the **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence: the "quintessence" or ether, which Aristotle believed made up the celestial bodies, distinct from earth, water, air, and fire</term> which Aristotle introduced), and similar things which provide material for argument, opinion, and doubt to insane men. But I think I have shown enough how nothing is agreed upon among the Philosophers concerning the Truth itself. The closer anyone is brought to these men, the further they are from the Truth itself, and the more they wander from the Catholic religion.

¶ As for the rest, if there is any **MORAL PHILOSOPHY** or discipline regarding behavior (as some prefer to call it): I judge that this consists not so much in the petty reasonings of Philosophers as in varied experience, custom, observation, and the social interaction of common life. It is changeable according to the opinion of times, places, and men. Threats and flattery teach it to children, while laws and punishment teach it to adults. Innate diligence adds some things to men which cannot be taught, but which grow—rightly or wrongly—according to the usage of the times and the agreement of men. Thus it happens that what was once a vice is now considered a virtue, and what is a virtue here is a vice elsewhere; what is honorable to one is shameful to another, and what is just to us is unjust to others, according to the opinions or laws of each time, place, and social standing.

In counsel, the Italian is farsighted, the Spaniard astute, the Frenchman thoughtless, and the German useful. Toward foreigners, the Italians are dutiful, the Spaniards calm, the French mild, and the Germans rustic and inhospitable. In conversation, the Italians are prudent, the Spaniards cautious, the French gentle, and the Germans overbearing and intolerable. In conducting business, the Italians are circumspect, the Germans industrious, the Spaniards vigilant, and the French anxious. In warfare, the Italians are energetic but cruel...

Spaniards are clever and rapacious, Germans are fierce and for-hire <note>original: "venales" — referring to the German reputation as mercenary soldiers in this period.</note>, and the French are high-minded but headstrong. The Italians are distinguished by their literature, the Spaniards by their navigation, the French by their civility, and the Germans by their religion and mechanical arts. But let us turn our discourse to those who have handed down the study of these matters to us in their writings:

<margin>Against the opinion of philosophers regarding the learning of the sciences. Genesis 1. <note>Though the margin cites Genesis 1, the text refers to the Tree of Knowledge in Genesis 2 and 3.</note></margin>
These men have certainly performed the office of the serpent; they have given us that fruit by the eating of which we learn to know good and evil. For this is their first pestilent opinion: that good and evil must not be unknown. They say that only then will men better follow virtue and flee from vice. But how much more certain and useful—how much more blessed—would it be, not only to avoid doing evil, but to be entirely ignorant of it? Who does not know that we were all made miserable by the very fact that the first parents of the human race learned what was good and what was evil? For that reason, perhaps this error might be forgiven the philosophers, if they did not also teach us the worst evils and most shameful vices under the names of virtues and goods.

<margin>The sects of moral philosophers.</margin>

At the end of this work, they conclude that Aristotle was Christ’s precursor in natural matters, just as John the Baptist was His precursor in matters of grace <note>original: "gratuitis" — referring to the Scholastic attempt to harmonize Aristotelian logic with Christian revelation.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique of human wisdom, moving from the personal failings of Aristotle to the broader confusion among philosophers regarding the nature of the "highest good" and the foundation of virtue. # OF THE SCIENCES #

-> Fo. LXVIII. <-

Dionysius the Babylonian, and Antisthenes, and all the Stoics—agreeing in some way with many of our own theologians—are still debating the connection between the virtues, and what that common foundation of happiness <note>original: "felicitatis fundamentum"</note> might be, in which all virtues must converge. For unless they all flow together into one, they can by no means make a person happy, even if only a single one were missing. Furthermore, since the virtues are disparate and, in a sense, at odds with one another—such as generosity <note>original: "liberalitas"</note> and thrift, greatness of soul and humility, mercy and justice, or contemplation and the busy work of frequent ministry, and many others of this kind—unless they all meet in harmony within one person, they might be judged not as virtues, but as vices.

Ambrose and Lactantius, following Macrobius and Plato’s *Republic*, believe that justice <note>original: "iustitiam"</note> is that thing in which all virtues must meet. Others suggest temperance, which imposes a limit on all things; others suggest piety, as Plato does in his *Epinomis*; others suggest charity, without which there is no progress in the virtues, as Paul feels <margin>1 Corinthians 13.</margin> <note>Agrippa refers to the famous passage: "If I have not love, I am nothing."</note>. Thomas Aquinas, Henry of Ghent, Duns Scotus, and others still argue over these points. 

But let us return: others have placed happiness in fortune, such as Theophrastus; but Aristotle placed it in fortune when joined with the primary virtues—or rather, in pleasure, though disguised by the "goods" of the virtues, as if Epicurus did not also defend his own pleasure with those same goods. Finally, the rest of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note> placed it in speculation. 

The philosopher Herillus, Alcidamus, and many of the Socratics thought the highest good was knowledge <note>original: "scientiam"</note>. Truly, the Tyberini people, neighbors to the Chalybes <note>Ancient tribes of the Black Sea region noted by classical geographers.</note> mentioned by Apollonius and Pomponius, said that luxury and laughter were the highest happiness. There are also those who placed the highest good in silence. 

The Platonists, however, along with their masters Plato and Plotinus—always savoring of the divine—located happiness in union with the Highest Good. Bias of Priene placed it in wisdom; Bion and Borysthenes in prudence; Thales of Miletus in a great heap of these things; Pittacus of Mytilene in doing well; and Cicero in freedom from all affairs—though this can be found in God alone. I pass over the remaining "plebeian" philosophers who did away with happiness altogether, such as Pyrrho of Elis <note>The founder of Greek Skepticism, who argued that certain knowledge is impossible.</note>.

Eurylochus and Xenophanes, and those who placed supreme happiness in glory, honor, power, leisure, wealth, and similar things: such as Periander of Corinth and Lycophron, and those of whom the <margin>Psalm 143</margin> Psalmist speaks: *Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity; whose sons are like new plantations in their youth, their daughters fashioned and adorned like the likeness of a temple, their storehouses full, overflowing from one to another; their sheep are fruitful, multiplying in their pastures, their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passing away, nor any cry in their streets. They called the people blessed who have these things.* <note>Agrippa is quoting Psalm 144 (143 in the Vulgate). He uses it to illustrate how worldly prosperity is often mistaken for true happiness by "vain" men.</note>

Now they also feel differently about pleasure, which, as you heard above, Epicurus considers the highest good. On the contrary, Archytas of Tarentum, Antisthenes, and Socrates call this the highest evil. However, Speusippus and some of the Old Academics <note>Followers of Plato's school before it turned toward skepticism.</note> said that pleasure and pain were two evils, opposed to each other, but the good was that which was in the middle between them. Zeno judged pleasure to be neither good nor evil, but indifferent. Critolaus the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle’s school.</note> and Plato say that pleasure is evil, the bait <note>original: "escam"</note> and the parent of many evils. It would be far too long to bring forward the opinions of everyone concerning happiness, or to make a heap out of those with which others have filled so many books. For Augustine mentions that two hundred and eighty-eight opinions on these matters were collected by Marcus Varro. We think it enough to have recited the more famous ones here.

But let us now see how these things agree with Christ, and it will appear that happiness and blessedness <term>beatitudo: A state of supreme spiritual joy or "blessedness," often contrasted with "felicitas" or earthly happiness.</term> are not acquired by us through Stoic virtue, nor through Academic purification, nor through Peripatetic speculation, but through faith and grace in the word of God. For you have heard how some of the philosophers place happiness or blessedness in pleasure; but Christ places it in hunger and thirst. Others place it in integrity, fame, and the greatness of a name; but Christ in being cursed and in the hatred of men. Others in primal instincts, health, joy, and freedom from pain; but Christ in weeping and mourning. Others in prudence and knowledge and...

# OF THE SCIENCES #

...in moral virtues. But Christ placed it in innocence, simplicity, and purity of heart. Others place it in fortune, but Christ in mercy. Others in the glory of war and the subjugation of lands, but Christ in peace. Others in honor and pomp, but Christ in humility, calling the meek blessed. Others in power and victory, but Christ in persecution. Others in riches, but Christ in poverty. Christ teaches that absolute virtue is not acquired except by grace given from above; the Philosophers teach that this is prepared by one’s own strengths and by habit. Christ teaches that every concupiscence <term>concupiscence: an intense desire or lust; in this context, the internal inclination toward sin even before an act is committed</term> is a sin. Conversely, the Philosophers count it among "middle things" <note>original: "medias res" — things considered morally neutral in themselves</note> which are judged as neither virtues nor vices, but they argue these become virtues if one is affected by them with moderation. Christ teaches that one must deserve well of all, that even enemies must be loved, loans should be given freely, vengeance should be taken on no one, and that one should give to everyone who asks. Conversely, the Philosophers suggest this only for those who repay a benefit with a benefit; otherwise, they say it is permitted to be angry, to hate, to contend, to wage war, and to practice usury. Furthermore, they—with their "free will," the "dictate of right reason," and "natural light"—gave us the Pelagian Heretics <note>A group following Pelagius, who taught that human nature is not indwellingly sinful and that salvation can be achieved through good works without divine grace.</note>. Indeed, all moral philosophy (according to Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) who frequently critiqued pagan philosophy</note>) is false and empty, neither instructing one in the duties of justice nor confirming the duty and reasons of man; finally, it is so repugnant to divine law and to Christ himself that its glory is owed to none other than Satan.

The parts of

¶ To this philosophy also belongs POLITICS, which is the art of administering the Commonwealth. And indeed, there are three species: namely, Monarchy, which is the rule of one; Aristocracy, which is the rule of the few, but of the noble, the wealthy, or the "best men"; and Democracy, which is the rule of the common people or the populace. Related to these are Tyrannies, Oligarchy, and Anarchy. But which of these is to be preferred is not yet agreed upon among writers. For those who argue that Monarchy excels fortify their opinion with examples from nature, saying that just as in the universe there is one supreme God, in the stars there is one Sun, one King among the bees, one Leader in the flocks, one Ruler in the herds, and the Cranes follow one: so in a Commonwealth there ought to be one King...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on political governance, specifically comparing the merits of Monarchy, Aristocracy, and Democracy. It follows the previous critique of moral philosophy by applying similar skepticism to the structures of human law and power.</meta>

# ON VANITY #

...as if a head, from which the members should by no means dissent. This form <note>referring to Monarchy, discussed on the previous page</note> was approved above others by Plato, Aristotle, and Apollonius, to whom our own Christian writers, Cyprian and Jerome, subscribe. 

Those who extol Aristocracy <term>Aristocracy: a form of government in which power is held by the nobility or a small "best" class</term>, however, say that nothing is better for administering great affairs than the consultations of many of the best men agreeing as one. For from many of the best, the best counsels must necessarily arise. They argue that no single person is wise enough on their own, as this is a gift of God alone. Solon, Lycurgus, Demosthenes, Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>, and nearly all those ancient Lawgivers, even Moses, also subscribe to this opinion. <margin>A saying of Plato.</margin> Plato also agrees with them, saying that a Republic and city seem to be established in the best and happiest state when they are ruled by Wise men—to which we might also add, if it pleases, by noblemen, since this opinion is confirmed by the consensus of many. 

Those who preferred a popular Republic <note>Democracy</note> have called it by the most beautiful name of all: Isonomia <term>Isonomia: equality of political rights or equality before the law</term>, which is to say, the equality of Law. For there, everything is brought into the common interest, and all counsels taken by the multitude—in whom, without doubt, all things reside—are more certain. Finally, they say "the voice of the people is the voice of God" <note>original: "vox populi, vox dei"</note>; hence, whatever pleases everyone, and whatever is established by the common consent of the people, must be presumed to be the best and most just, as if ordained by God Himself. 

Finally, they say this regime is safer than that of the aristocrats, because it is least subject to sedition. For the people never, or only rarely, disagree among themselves, while the aristocrats do so greatly and most frequently. Furthermore, in a popular government, there is complete equality and liberty, oppressed by the tyranny of none, where there are equal grades of honor and no one stands above his neighbor; rather, each individual and the whole multitude take turns ruling and being ruled. This form was praised above others by Otanes the Persian <note>Otanes: a Persian noble who, according to Herodotus, advocated for democracy after the death of Cambyses</note>, Euphrates, and Dion of Syracuse. Today we see the Venetians and the Swiss <note>original: "Heluetios"</note> flourishing above all the principalities of the Christian world through this Democracy, obtaining the praise of wisdom, the power of riches, the palm of victory, and justice. Indeed, the Republic of the Athenians, which once ruled most widely and powerfully, was governed by Democracy alone, and all things were done by the people and among the people.

### OF THE SCIENCES. Folio LXX. ###

And the Romans, having formerly experienced all these forms of administration, acquired the greatest part of their empire under a popular Democracy; nor were they ever in a worse state than under kings and the "best men" <term>Optimates: the traditionalist senatorial majority of the late Roman Republic</term>, and they were at their absolute worst under the emperors, under whom all their power suffered shipwreck. Therefore, which of these three forms is better or more preferable cannot easily be decided, since each has its own advocates and opponents. 

For kings, who are permitted to do all things according to their whim with impunity, very rarely rule well, nor do they ever reign without the noise of wars. Royalty also carries within itself this pestiferous evil: that even those who were once considered the best of men, approved by the consensus of all, as soon as they have attained the throne, they become insolent—as if granted a license to sin—and turn out to be the worst of villains. This was seen in Caligula, Nero, Domitian, Mithridates, and many others. Indeed, the Holy Scriptures reveal this even in Saul, David, and Solomon—kings chosen by God. Among all the kings of Judah, scarcely a few are approved; among the kings of Samaria, none at all. 

But even those who today are held as Kings, Emperors, and Princes seem to think they were born and appointed not for the people, the citizens, the commoners, or for justice, but for the protection and strengthening of the nobility. They rule in such a way that the fortunes of all citizens seem not to have been entrusted to their guardianship, but given over to their plunder and devastation. They take everything from everyone and use their subjects according to their whim, and sometimes even for their mere pleasure. They abuse the power granted to them from above against their subjects, burdening the citizens with forced loans, the commoners with indictments, others with exactions, and the rest with various taxes upon taxes, without measure and without end. 

If any more modest rulers waive these burdens, they do so not for the common good, but for their own convenience; they allow their subjects to prosper only so that they themselves may prosper, ensuring they have something to seize whenever they wish. Furthermore, so that they may hunt for the reputation of justice, they strictly ordain laws, but they merely clothe their greed and cruelty in the name of justice. They afflict those guilty of transgression with terrible punishments, the stripping of honors, and enormous fines. In this, they are no better than Tyrants, in that they desire as many people as possible to be transgressors; for just as the crimes...

...then popular rule: Aristotle also, in his *Ethics*, considers the administration of the people to be the worst form, but the rule of one man to be the best. <margin>The common people: a leader of errors.</margin> For the common people are the leader of errors, the mistress of perverse customs, and a vast heap of evils. They can be bent neither by reasons, nor by authorities, nor by persuasions; they do not understand reason, they despise authority, and they are indeed unteachable and obstinate toward persuasion. Their habits are most inconstant, always desiring new things and hating the present. They cannot be restrained by the teaching of the wise, the discipline of the fathers, the authority of magistrates, nor the majesty of princes. Among the masses, the advice of the wise is never heard without danger or in vain, for the folly of the multitude almost always prevails. 

This is well known in the case of **Socrates** and his opinion on the Gods given to the Athenians; <note>Socrates was famously sentenced to death by the Athenian democracy on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth.</note> in **Capys the Trojan** regarding the introduction of the wooden horse; <note>In Virgil's *Aeneid*, Capys was among those who warned the Trojans not to bring the Greek horse into the city.</note> in **Magius of Campania** when he advised that Hannibal should not be received into the city; <note>Decius Magius was a leader in Capua who remained loyal to Rome and unsuccessfully opposed the city's alliance with Hannibal during the Second Punic War.</note> in **Lucius Aemilius Paullus** when he refused to join the Battle of Cannae; <note>Aemilius Paullus was the Roman consul who advised against engaging Hannibal at Cannae, but his co-consul Varro insisted on the disastrous battle.</note> and finally, in so many predictions of the Lord's prophets which were not at all heeded by the Jewish people. 

Therefore, how could the statutes of the people and the decrees of the commoners be good, when that popular multitude is almost always ignorant of what is best? This is partly because the greater part of them are manual laborers <note>original: "manuaria sint opifices"</note>, and partly because they do not rely on the reason of justice and equity, but on numbers—in which there are always more evil men than good. Nor is judgment guided by an exact weighing of things, but by the zeal and number of the crowd, as **Pliny the Younger** says: "For opinions are counted, not weighed." <note>original: "Numerantur enim sententiæ, non ponderantur." From Pliny’s *Epistles*, referring to the flaw in voting where every vote is equal regardless of the voter's wisdom.</note> For in a popular consultation, it is not what seems best to the wiser, but what seems best to the many that holds the greatest power. Among them, since all are held equal to one another, nothing is so unequal as equality itself. Thus, by the indiscriminate impulse of the common people, nothing is established healthily, and none of those things that have collapsed into a worse state are restored to a better one. Rather, even those institutions that were once excellent are instead thrown into confusion and abolished by the license of the common people.

<margin>IMAGES.</margin>
Not all peoples since ancient times have accepted the wondrous worship of **IMAGES**. Indeed, the Jews (as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a famous 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> relates) dreaded nothing more than idols; they fashioned no image of what they worshipped, nor of those whose memory they held dear. For the Law of God through Moses forbade them from making idols, placing them in temples, or worshipping before them. Among the Seres <note>The "Seres" was the name used by ancient Greeks and Romans for the people of North China, famous for silk.</note> (according to Eusebius), it was even provided by law that they should not venerate idols. Also, in the temples of the Romans, according to Clement and Plutarch, we read that by the decree of Numa <note>Numa Pompilius was the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many religious rites.</note>, for one hundred and seventy years from the founding of the City, no image—neither sculpted nor painted—was seen. Augustine also testifies to the same, citing Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro was a prolific Roman scholar.</note>, whose words, he says, clearly attest that there was no idol of the Gods in the City for one hundred and sixty years; and it happened thereafter that, because of the multitude of images and statues, the worship of religion was neglected and held in contempt. The Persians also (according to Herodotus and Strabo) did not erect statues. Among the Egyptians, however, there was the greatest impiety and foolishness in these matters, which then spread to all nations. This corrupt custom of the nations and false religion, when they themselves began to be converted to the faith of Christ, [affected] our own [religion] as well...

...infected religion, and introduced into our Church statues, images, and many sterile ceremonies of pomp, none of which existed at all among those first and true Christians. From this, we began to bring the mute statues of our Saints into our temples and to place them upon the altars of God with great venerations; and while we consider it a sin for a man—who is the true image of God—to climb up there <note>The author contrasts the living human "image of God" with the lifeless wooden or stone statues that were granted higher physical placement in the church.</note>, we instead move senseless statues to those spots. Before them, we bow our heads, press kisses, offer candles, hang up votive offerings <term>anathemata: items hung in a church in fulfillment of a vow, like small silver limbs or paintings of miracles</term>, attribute miracles, and buy pardons. Finally, we make pilgrimages to them, make vows to them, worship them, and all but adore them. It cannot be expressed how much superstition—if not to say idolatry—is fostered among the unrefined and unlearned common people regarding these images, while the Priests wink at these things, receiving no small profit from them. And here they defend themselves with the words of Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I (the Great), who famously defended images as a tool for teaching the illiterate.</note> saying:

> Images are the books of the common people <note>original: "Imagines esse libros uulgi"</note>, so that the memory of events can be retained; in these, those who have not learned letters may read, and by the sight of them, they may be drawn to the contemplation of God.

But these are merely the human excuses of Gregory. Although that holy man may approve of images, he does not approve of their worship. However, the commands of the forbidding God are quite different: for it does not befit us to learn from the "book" of the forbidden image, but from the Book of God, which is the book of the Scriptures. Therefore, he who desires to know God should not seek him from the images of painters and sculptors, but (as John says) <margin>John 5.</margin> search the scriptures, which bear witness of him. And those who do not know how to read, let them hear the word of scripture: <margin>Rom. 10.</margin> for their faith (as Paul says) comes from hearing, and Christ <margin>John 10.</margin> says in the Gospel of John:

> My sheep hear my voice.

Furthermore, if as Christ says, <margin>John 6.</margin> no one can come to him unless the Father draws him, and no one comes to the Father except through Christ himself, why do we take away the glory from God by attributing it to pictures and statues, as if they had the power to draw us into the contemplation of God? Added to this is the immoderate worship of **RELICS**: for we confess, nor can anyone deny, that the relics of the Saints are holy, and that they will one day shine with the glory of eternity, and therefore are to be honored by us with the highest reverence.

# OF THE SCIENCES

LXXIIII.

...to be cultivated. Let us even admit that the saints themselves—though they hear those who piously invoke them in all places—are nevertheless [venerated] more where they have some of their relics as a pledge. But because there is not the same certainty for all such things (since the same pledges of the same saints are believed to be held in various different places), it must follow that the confidence of one group or the other is foolish. Therefore, lest we fall into idolatry or superstition, it is safer not to fix our faith on visible things, but to worship the Saints in spirit and truth through our Lord Jesus Christ, imploring their help. Thus, we have no relics more certain or more worthy than the sacrament of the body of Christ, which is the only **Holy of Holies** <term>Sanctum Sanctorum: a term originally referring to the inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle, here applied to the Eucharist</term> preserved in all our Temples. We venerate and adore Christ present before us; for although he is present everywhere, he is also present there bodily.

<margin>Greedy Priests.</margin>
But the greedy priestly class—greedy men—seeking material for their own avarice not only from wood and stone, but even from the bones of the dead and the relics of the Holy Martyrs, have made these into instruments for their own plunder. They exalt the tombs of the Confessors <note>Confessors are saints who suffered for the faith but were not martyred.</note> and expose the relics of martyrs; they observe the people's touching and kissing of them; they adorn their idols and decorate their festivals with great pomp. They preach that those men were holy and extol them with great praise, yet they flee far away from the actual lives of those they praise so highly.

<margin>Matthew 23. Duties distributed among the Saints.</margin>
Did not the Savior speak to such men? "Woe to you who build the tombs of the Prophets, being like those who killed them." <note>A reference to Matthew 23:29-31, where Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for honoring dead prophets while persecuting living ones.</note> Furthermore, in the manner of the pagans, they distribute specific duties to the saints themselves: this one, like Neptune <note>Roman god of the sea.</note>, is to help with the dangers of the waters; that one, like Jupiter <note>King of the Roman gods, associated with the sky.</note>, strikes with lightning, or with Vulcan <note>Roman god of fire and metalworking.</note>, controls fire; another takes care of the crops like Ceres <note>Goddess of agriculture.</note>, and another presides over the harvests like Bacchus <note>God of wine and theater.</note>. Even the common women have their own Goddesses from whom they seek children, as if from Lucina <note>Goddess of childbirth.</note> or Venus <note>Goddess of love.</note>, and who, like Juno <note>Queen of the gods and protector of marriage.</note>, might appease or take vengeance on angry husbands. Now truly there are even those who make it their business to recover thefts and things lost or strayed; and there is no kind of disease that does not have its own Physician among the "Gods." This is the reason why actual Physicians are helped less than Lawyers <note>original: "Causidici," meaning advocates or trial lawyers.</note>, since no legal dispute is so small...

<meta>This page continues the author’s discussion on the transition from proper religious devotion to what he considers superstitious practices. # OF VANITY

...so just that it might find some **Saint** <note>original: "Diuum"</note> as a patron. But just as our soul expresses different acts through different limbs, and those limbs receive different powers according to the diversity of their arrangements—as the eyes receive sight and the ears hearing—so our Lord **Jesus Christ**, in his **mystical body** (of which he himself is the soul), administers and distributes the various gifts of his grace in these lower regions through his various saints, as if through limbs adapted for this very purpose. Individual saints are allotted a specific duty of cooperation, and individuals impart certain graces. According to this multiform distribution of graces—partly revealed to men and partly reached through conjecture—we implore the saints with various prayers and invocations. Indeed, we believe that just as Christ redeemed our death by his own death—in whose death "holy deaths" began and the deaths of all the faithful are sanctified—so the **Martyrs**, who died tormented by a specific kind of disease or a similar torture, can free us from that very thing, as if they had suffered it on our behalf.

<margin>
It is ridiculous that something is attributed to Saints based on the etymology of their names.
</margin>

And that indeed has a reason that is not invalid; however, those who ascribe these powers based on a similarity of names, a confusion of words, or through similar futile inventions are to be laughed at. For example, the Germans attribute the **falling sickness** <term>falling sickness: a historical term for epilepsy</term> to Saint **Valentine** because his name [in German] suggests "falling" <note>This is a linguistic pun: the German name "Valtin" or "Valentin" was phonetically associated by the author with the word "fallen" (to fall)</note>, and the French assign those suffering from **dropsy** <term>dropsy: an old medical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</term> to Saint **Eutropius** because of the similar sound of the word <note>The sound of "Eutrope" was associated with "hydrops," the Greek/Latin word for dropsy</note>.

<margin>
The miracles of Saints are not to be mocked.
</margin>

I wish, therefore, to detract nothing here from divine power or the merits of the Saints. For anyone who thinks wrongly about Christian piety and the miracles of the Saints is impious. But it is also superstitious and wicked for men to sweep monstrous lies into history like poetic trifles and propose them to the simple-minded as if they were **oracles** <note>In this context, "oracles" refers to divine truths that must be believed without question</note> to be believed, insisting upon them with great clamor. Those who have faith in these fables and dreams are likewise most foolish.

<margin>
To revile the moderate veneration of the Saints is a heresy.
</margin>

And here I want you to know that just as the excessive worship of images is **idolatry**, so the stubborn detestation of them is **heresy**; for which the Emperors **Philippicus** and **Leo III** <note>These 8th-century Byzantine emperors were famous "Iconoclasts" who ordered the destruction of religious images</note> were once condemned. So also, just as the abuse of **relics** is an execrable crime, so the irreverence toward them is a detestable heresy, which once in [Vigilantius...] <note>The page ends on a catchword referring to Vigilantius, a 4th-century priest who famously opposed the cult of relics and was criticized by St. Jerome.</note>

<margin>The German heresy.</margin>
The heresy of Vigilantius <note>original: "Vigilãtia"; Vigilantius was a 4th-century priest who opposed the veneration of relics and saints</note>, born of a Gaul and defeated by Jerome, has now begun to sprout again among our neighbors in Germany, together with the "breakers of images" <note>iconoclasts</note>.

<margin>**TEMPLES**.</margin>
Furthermore, let us now speak of **TEMPLES**. We know that this was once the greatest superstition of the Pagans <note>original: "Gentilium"</note>, who built their own temples for each of their gods. In imitation of them, Christians later began to dedicate temples to their own "gods" <note>original: "suis Diis"; the author likely refers to the saints here, implying their veneration had become akin to pagan polytheism</note>. Yet many nations were entirely without temples, and it is said that <margin>Xerxes burned the temples.</margin> Xerxes once, on the advice of the Magi, burned down all the temples throughout Greece, because he thought it impious and wicked to enclose the gods themselves within walls. Truly, concerning temples, <margin>Zeno.</margin> Zeno of Citium <note>the founder of Stoicism</note> once philosophized in these words, saying: "It is not at all necessary to build shrines and temples; for nothing should be rightly considered sacred, nor held as holy, which men themselves have constructed." Among the Persians there were once no temples; among the Hebrews, however, in the entire nation, there was only a single religious temple, built by Solomon in Jerusalem. Concerning this, however, we read in <margin>Isaiah 66.</margin> Isaiah: "Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is this house that you will build for me?" And <margin>Acts 7.</margin> Stephen the first martyr says: "Solomon built him a house, but the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands." And in <margin>Acts 17.</margin> Paul the Apostle says to the Athenians: "God does not dwell in temples made by hands; since he is the Lord of Heaven and Earth, he is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything."

He teaches, however, that human nature and men themselves—provided they are pure, pious, holy, religious, and devoted to God—are the temples most acceptable to God, just as when <margin>1 Corinthians 3.</margin> writing to the Corinthians he says: "You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God will dwell in you. For the temple of God is holy, which you are." Furthermore, <margin>The primitive church had no temples.</margin> Origen himself confesses in his work *Against Celsus* that in our earliest religion—from the very cradle of the Christian faith and for a long time after the passion of Christ—no temples were built for our sacred rites. He teaches through many arguments that such buildings are not at all appropriate for Christians for the true worship of God and true religion. And Lactantius says: "Temples for God are not to be built by piling up stones to a great height,"

To this is added the proud magnificence of their structure, upon which a vast amount of sacred money and alms are poured out daily. As we said before, these funds should instead sustain the many "poor of Christ"—who are the true temples and images of God—who are endangered by hunger, thirst, heat, cold, labor, weakness, and poverty.

<margin>Isaiah 66</margin>

This was done so that the Church should not serve the days, but rather the days should serve the Church.

<margin>For what purpose feast days were instituted.</margin>
Therefore, days were established by the Fathers in the Church during which it is proper for the common people to abstain from all external business and bodily labors. This allows them to serve God more freely, to find leisure for prayers and contemplations, to attend divine services and sermons on the Word of God, and to engage in whatever else is done at that time for the benefit of eternal salvation. 

But that distorter of equity, the overthrower of all order and beauty, and the author of all evils—the Devil—strives tirelessly to demolish whatever the Holy Spirit builds. He has nearly destroyed even this fortress, to the point where the greatest part of the Christian people spends this sacred leisure of feast days not in prayer, nor in hearing the Word of God, nor in the other things for which they were established. 
<margin>The abuse of feast days.</margin>
Instead, they spend it on every kind of corruption of good morals and Christian doctrine: in dances, in comedies, in stage-plays, in songs, in games, in heavy drinking, in processions, in spectacles, and in whatever worldly and fleshly works are contrary to the Spirit and to holiness. 

It is just as Tertullian <note>an early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known for his rigorous moral stance</note> said concerning the festivals of the Caesars: they are accustomed then to perform a "great duty" by bringing out robes and dances into public, feasting street by street, making the city smell like a tavern, forcing the throat with wine, and running together in competition toward insults, impudence, and the lures of lust. Thus is public joy expressed.

# OF VANITY

...through public disgrace: Are we not then deservedly to be condemned, we who celebrate the solemnities of Christ and his saints with such rituals? <note>The author is likely referring to the rowdy or worldly ways feast days were celebrated in the 16th century, which he views as a perversion of their intended purpose.</note> Furthermore, regarding feast days—aside from the insane blasphemy of the **Manichaeans** <note>Followers of Mani who held dualistic views of good and evil</note> and the pestilent dogmas of the **Cataphrygians** <note>Another name for the Montanists, an early Christian movement known for its prophetic claims and strict asceticism</note>—we find that either no heresies or very few have arisen from them. At that time, **Polycrates**, the Bishop of Asia, among other most excellent men, resisted him. Moreover, **Irenaeus**, the Bishop of Lyons, although he himself celebrated Easter according to the Roman rite, nevertheless dared to rebuke Pope Victor with great freedom, calling him a disturber of the peace for having cut off Churches that were not erring in faith, but only differing in certain rituals from the Roman Church—an act contrary to the example of his predecessors. 

Subsequently, many decrees of councils and Popes, as well as the arguments of the Fathers and what are called the **Ecclesiastical Computations** <note>original: "Ecclesiastica computa"; the complex mathematical and astronomical systems used to calculate the date of Easter</note>, have been issued. Yet, even to this day, they have not been able to establish the same, true day of Easter throughout the entire world. To this very day, the business remains undecided and debated, even after consulting astrologers about the reformation of the **Calendar**. It is truly a worthy thing <note>This is intended sarcastically.</note> that for the sake of the stubborn religiousness of a single Roman Pontiff, the Church should suffer such a shipwreck. 

<margin>CERE MONIES</margin>

Finally, among the components of religion, not the least are the displays of rites and ceremonies: in garments, in vessels, in lights, in bells, in organs, in singing, in fragrances, in sacrifices, in gestures, in precious pictures, in the choice of foods and fasts, and similar things. These are received with great admiration and veneration by the unlearned common people and by men who notice nothing except what is placed right before their eyes. **Numa Pompilius** <note>The legendary second king of Rome, traditionally credited with establishing the city's religious institutions</note> was the first to ordain ceremonies for the Romans. For God does not wish to be worshipped through bodily actions, sensory works, or carnal cults, but in spirit and truth through **Jesus Christ**. Therefore, this is the true worship of God, violated by no defilement of external and carnal rites, just as **John** says in instructing us: God is a spirit, and those who wish

I do not deny how, just as in the **Synagogue** of old with **Moses** and **Aaron**, and subsequently the other **High Priests** <term>Pontifices: used here to refer to the Jewish religious leaders and later Christian bishops</term>, **Judges**, and **Prophets**, down to the **Scribes** and **Pharisees**, so it was later done in the **Church** by the **Apostles**, **Evangelists**, **Bishops**, **Priests**, and **Teachers**. Furthermore, although ceremonies have produced no heresies against the faith, they have nonetheless introduced innumerable **sects** into the **Church** and have been the greatest and sole seeds of schisms. It was because of this that the **Greek Church** was first cut off from ours: because they did not consecrate the host in unleavened bread, but in leavened bread <note>The "Azymes" controversy regarding the type of bread used in the Eucharist was a major factor in the Great Schism of 1054</note>, even though we admit that they truly consecrate it. 

Afterward, the **Bohemian Church** <note>The Hussites or Utraquists of Bohemia</note> was also separated, because according to the ancient rite and against the prohibitions of more recent **Popes**, they offered the **Eucharist** under both kinds <note>The practice of giving laypeople both the bread and the wine, rather than just the bread</note>.

For whoever has not been called by the **Spirit of God** to the great office of God and the dignity of the **Apostleship**, like **Aaron**, and who has not entered through the door, which is **Christ**, but has climbed into the Church from elsewhere through the window—through the favors of men, through purchased votes <note>A reference to the practice of simony, or buying church offices.</note>, or by the command of **Princes**—this man is surely not a vicar of Christ and the **Apostles**, but a thief and a robber, and a vicar of **Judas Iscariot** and **Simon the Samaritan** <note>original: "Simon Samaritanus," referring to Simon Magus, from whom the term "simony" is derived (Acts 8).</note>.

But as the ancient constitutions have gradually fallen from their majesty, and with the more recent **Pontifical law** gaining strength through damnable custom, many such Pontiffs and Apostles now ascend the seat of Christ as once the **Scribes** and Pharisees sat upon the seat of **Moses**: those who speak and do not act, binding heavy burdens upon the shoulders of the people, while they themselves are unwilling [to move them] with a finger...

...they would have parried the arrows of Fortune, and secure from all worldly dangers and civil troubles, they eat an idle and begged bread instead of that acquired through labor, sleeping secure and without worry. This is what they then call "Gospel poverty" <note>original: "Euāgelicam paupertatē"</note>: to feed on the labor of others in idleness and beggary. 

And while they profess the highest humility, walking in cheap clothing—like barefoot peasants, or like actors, or net-gladiators <note>original: "retiarii"; a type of gladiator who fought with a net, here used to mock their "costumes"</note>, girded with ropes like captured thieves, with their whole heads shaved like fools—their hoods, with ears and bells, make them look like jesters and Shrovetide masks <note>original: "laruis carnis priuialibus"; referring to the masks worn during the pre-Lenten carnival season, implying their religious life is a hollow performance</note>. Although they claim to take on all these signs of lowliness and rejection for the sake of Christ and religion, they are actually overcome by ambition. They translate every aspect of their lifestyle into the most arrogant titles, boasting of being called **Groomsmen** <note>original: "Paranymphi"; technically a wedding attendant, used here to mock their vanity in claiming titles of honor</note>, **Rectors**, **Guardians**, **Presidents**, **Priors**, **Vicars**, **Provincials**, **Archimandrites** <note>a title for a superior of a monastery or a group of monasteries in Eastern Christianity</note>, and **Generals**. 

Indeed, no class of men seems more hungry for the highest rank than they are. There is no lack of many evil things that could be said about them. However, there have already been those who preached against them with such great insults that they have brought into contempt not only many honest and holy fathers of upright life, but even the very rules of holy living established by the Church Fathers. 

Therefore, I do not wish to say anything here to insult those who walk rightly in their holy callings, following in the footsteps of those holy Fathers and aspiring to the heights of perfection. I admit that their rules and professions are holy; I admit that to this day there are **Holy Monks**, **Holy Mendicant Brothers** <note>friars who originally committed to a life of poverty and begging</note>, **Holy Anchorites** <note>religious recluses who live in isolation</note>, and **Holy Canons Regular**. 

Yet among these, there are many unfaithful men, scoundrels, and apostates who disfigure the profession of religion. It is my purpose to show that no religious order has ever been so pure that a stain of error and malice has not crept in. For we read of apostate angels, and how the first brothers were murderers <note>referring to the biblical story of Cain and Abel</note>, of wicked prophets, traitorous Apostles, and faithless disciples of Christ. Among the **Roman Popes** as well, there have been many schismatics, scoundrels, and even, at times, **Heretics**...

Finally, with this art of pandering as their guide, many have climbed from the lowest social rank to the highest degree of nobility: this man prostituted his wife and was made a Senator; that one prostituted his daughter and was created a Count. They think that through these arts of begging and notable deceits of fraud, they offer to God and the saints most pleasing sacrifices, whenever they are burdened with prey in this manner at great cost to the people and detriment to the State, fattening up their own idle attendants, while utterly setting aside, neglecting, and despising those very works of mercy under the pretext of which such great gifts are bestowed upon them. Apuleius once mocked the story of these men in his *Golden Ass* regarding the Priests of the Syrian Goddess <note>In Apuleius's Roman novel, the priests of Cybele are depicted as traveling charlatans who use religious fervor to hide their thefts and debauchery.</note>. To these are added very many from the number of the mendicant brothers and the Beguards <note>The Beguards (Beghards) were a lay religious group in the Middle Ages; while many were sincere, they were often accused of heresy and hypocrisy by critics like Agrippa.</note> (as they call them), who, having cast behind them the holiness of their professions, have exchanged piety for profit. It is as if they had professed religion for no other reason than that, under the title of poverty, they might be permitted to fly everywhere with impudent begging; and with a hardened face <note>original: "perfricata fronte," a Latin idiom for being shameless or "brazen-faced."</note>, with troublesome hypocrisy, to scrape together money from everywhere, to be ashamed of no profit, and with notable sycophancy <term>sycophantia</term> <note>deceitful flattery or trickery</note> in the choir, in the marketplace, in temples, in schools, in halls, in palaces, in public and private conversations, in confessions, in disputations, in sermons, from the benches, from the chairs, from the pulpits, from the rostrums, to scatter among the common people by the arts of their impudence. They sell the merchandise of <term>indulgences</term> <note>Certificates sold by the Church to reduce punishment for sins; a central grievance of the Reformation.</note>, measure out their own good deeds for sale, and extort the plunder of ill-gotten gains from merchants, usurers, and from noble robbers. They swindle coins from dull citizens, the unlearned rabble, and superstitious old women; and, following the example of the serpent in Eden, they first entice foolish little women and through them prepare an entrance for themselves to deceive the men. While displaying poverty with the affected worthlessness of their garments and proclaiming with loud shouting that money is to be despised and ambition shunned, they themselves care for nothing more than to possess as much money as possible; and for that reason they travel over sea and dry land <meta>circumeunt,</meta>

<summary>Agrippa delivers a scathing critique of mendicant friars and religious orders, accusing them of using the pretext of holy poverty to plunder the poor and live in idle luxury. He compares their behavior to the fraudulent priests of antiquity and the serpent in the Garden of Eden.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Agrippa's scathing critique of the mendicant (begging) orders. # ON VANITY

They go about, penetrating the houses and shops of all, and they do not administer sacred things except for a fee. They demand alms tyrannically, as if they were a tax; they mix themselves into everyone’s business, piece together poorly matched marriages, tamper with wills, settle disputes, and "reform" holy virgins. But all these things they do only for their own profit. These are the "brotherly" arts <note>original: "artes fratricæ" — a pun on "frater" (brother/friar), implying these are the specific tricks of the friars</note>, by which most of them have grown to such authority that they are a terror to the Popes and Monarchs themselves. They have amassed wealth greater than the riches of merchants and the treasures of Princes, and with many thousands of gold coins they have purchased miters and hats <note>The "mitra" (miter) of a bishop and "capella" (hat) of a cardinal</note>, and they have sought the Papacy itself with huge sums of money. Such is the power of that religious begging!

And while they possess vast sums of money, many of them meanwhile pretend to display true poverty and a perfection greater than that of the Gospels. They might not touch money with their bare fingers, but they have their own "Judas" who carries their purses and renders their accounts <note>A common criticism: friars avoided the "sin" of touching money by having a lay person handle it for them</note>. Meanwhile, they dare to say—just as Peter and John did—<margin>Acts 3</margin> "Silver and gold have I none" <note>original: "argentum & aurum non est mecum" — quoting Acts 3:6</note>. But if they were not lying in this, and if their word were faithful, they would also have the right to say, "Arise and walk." Then, together with the blessed father Francis <note>St. Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan Order</note>, stripped of both money and clothing, they would command the creatures and be obeyed. They would turn water into wine, cross rivers with dry feet, make rabid wolves tame, silence the chirping of swallows by a single command, make the falcon act like a rooster to wake them, command the fire, and perform many miracles of that kind which that holy man performed. 

But they do not do these things—all those who say, "Lord, Lord" <note>Referring to Matthew 7:21</note>. Like Stoic apes <note>A metaphor for those who mimic the outward appearance of virtue without the inner reality</note>, they wear only the external signs and garments of Christ and Francis, but they do not observe their will and testament. Long ago, Richard, Bishop of Armagh <note>Richard FitzRalph (d. 1360), a famous opponent of the mendicant orders</note>, and Malleolus, Provost of Zurich <note>Felix Hemmerlin (d. 1460), a Swiss cleric and critic of the friars</note>, and John, Bishop of Chartres <note>John of Salisbury (d. 1180), known for his critiques of ecclesiastical corruption</note>, and many others have written against them or mentioned them. Their writings would be more tolerable if they had not condemned this religious begging so much, but only its abuse. But let enough be said of these things for now, so that we may proceed to further matters.

# OF THE SCIENCES

<page-num>XCV</page-num>
<header>OF THE SCIENCES.</header>

<margin>ECONOMICS AND ANOMALOUS ARTS</margin>
Included under the administration of the Republic is also **ECONOMICS**, which is a certain domestic form of a Republic and nothing other than a private Monarchy. But there are several types: one is royal or courtly, another satrapic <note>The household of a high official or provincial governor</note> or military, another public or communal—whether belonging to a convent or a guild—and finally, another is private or monastic. This, therefore, teaches how the wife, children, relatives, family, and servants are to be ruled; how the home and possessions are to be protected and expanded; and from where expenses are to be scraped together. Furthermore, it includes whatever cunning exists regarding revenues, coinage, tolls, taxes, tithes, usury, interest, monopolies, and whatever means of acquiring profit and new taxes through new arts and inventions.

Moreover, it deals with guilds, alliances, lawsuits, and war; since all these things have neither limit nor rule, they are therefore called **Anomalous** <note>original: "Anomala" — things that follow no law or rule</note>. For this reason, Economics cannot truly be called an art or a science, but rather a domestic discipline consisting of human opinion, use, custom, prudence, or even cunning. To this are referred all sedentary crafts <note>original: "sellularia opificia" — trades performed while sitting, often looked down upon by aristocrats as unmanly</note> and all the mechanical arts, which consist of work with linen, wool, wood, iron, bronze, and various metals. It also includes servile services: barbers, bath-keepers, innkeepers, and the manifold ways of acquiring a living and expanding one's private estate. These do not pertain to the authority of leadership, nor are they entirely useful for the governance of the Republic; they observe nothing divine, nothing noble <note>original: "liberale" — befitting a free man</note>, and nothing heroic. The number of such trades is so great they cannot be counted, and all of these are indeed servile. Many are even held in infamy for certain reasons: for instance, charioteers, sailors, and innkeepers are considered infamous for the vice of talkativeness, because they delight in fables and spread rumors. Likewise barbers, bath-keepers, and shepherds are so judged: for the fable of Midas <note>The king with donkey ears whose secret was whispered into a hole by his barber</note> and the history of Sulla besieging Athens <note>Barbers were often sources of military intelligence or leaks</note> made the former infamous, while the little story of Barrus <note>Likely a reference to a character in Horace's satires known for his boasting</note> did the same for the others. Likewise, singers, flute-players, and lute-players are mercenary men who play musical instruments at banquets for the pleasure of others and are thus held in infamy. But of all, the life of sailors is both the most unhappy and the worst; their dwelling is like a prison, and their food is most harsh and even filthy...

...[he is] tossed about, wearing filthy garments, and suffering the lack of all comforts; in perpetual exile, always wandering, fugitives, knowing no rest, always tossed by the fury of the winds and uncertain waves, always subject to heat, cold, rain, lightning, hunger <note>original: "fauis" — likely a transcription error for "fame" (hunger)</note>, thirst, and squalor. Added to these are the Scylla, Charybdis, Syrtes, and Symplegades <note>These are legendary and real maritime hazards: Scylla and Charybdis were a monster and whirlpool; the Syrtes were dangerous sandbanks off Africa; the Symplegades were "clashing rocks" at the Bosphorus</note>, and so many hostile dangers of the sea; furthermore, storms, than which nothing is more grim and horrible, and with all these and many other evils a continuous danger to life. And since Sailors are the most unhappy of all men, they are at the same time the most wicked of all mortals. 

But among so many Mechanical arts, Commerce, Agriculture, Warfare, Medicine, and Law-pleading hold the more powerful parts, of which we shall speak in order below: But first I will discuss the general foundations of Economics. 

<margin>
PRIVATE
ECONOMICS
</margin>

The whole power of **PRIVATE ECONOMICS** lies in marriage, whence Metellus Numidicus <note>Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus, a Roman censor of the 2nd century BC known for his stern moral views</note> the Censor, when he was exhorting the Roman people to take up marriage, said: "If we could be without a wife, Citizens <note>original: "Quirites" — the formal name for Roman citizens in their civil capacity</note>, we would all lack that trouble: but since nature has so arranged it that it is possible to live neither with them comfortably enough, nor without them in any way, we must consult for our perpetual safety rather than for brief pleasure." Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author who preserved this speech in his book "Attic Nights"</note> recounts this: for no house or domestic affair can stand and endure without a wife: for without a wife neither can progeny be extended, nor an heir be called, nor an inheritance be named, nor can there be kinsmen, nor a family, nor can one be called a father of the family <note>original: "paterfamilias" — the legal head of a Roman household with absolute authority</note>.

<margin>
A house without a wife is deserted.
</margin>

He who does not have a wife does not have a home, because he does not establish a home, and if he has one, he stays in it like a traveler in an inn. He who does not have a wife, even if he is most wealthy, has almost nothing which is truly his own, because he has no one to whom he can leave it, nor anyone in whom he can trust. All his things lie open to snares: servants rob him, partners defraud him, neighbors despise him, friends neglect him, and relatives lie in wait for him. The children, if he has any outside of marriage, are a disgrace to him, and he can leave them neither the family name, nor the images of his ancestors <note>original: "auorum imagines" — wax masks of ancestors displayed by noble Roman families to demonstrate their lineage</note>, nor his wealth by the established laws; and he himself is at once driven away from all public duties and honors by the consensus of all legislators: for he is not worthy to rule a city who has not learned to rule a home.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of household management, arguing that a man cannot lead a state if he cannot manage his own home. It frames marriage as the foundation of a happy life and the training ground for public leadership.</meta>

Fol. XCVI.

->**OF THE SCIENCES**<-

...nor can anyone govern a **Republic** <term>Respublica: the state or the "commonwealth," derived from the Latin for "public affair"</term> who has never understood private and domestic matters, which are the truest model and image of the state. The Greeks knew this well. When Philip of Macedon <note>Philip II, the father of Alexander the Great</note> sought to pacify the Greeks while they were at odds, and Gorgias of Leontini <note>A famous Greek Sophist and rhetorician</note> recited a book on Greek harmony at the Olympic games, the crowds mocked them, responding with one voice: why should those men strive to make others live in harmony when they could establish no peace in their own homes? For at home, Philip had a son and wife who were constantly quarreling, and Gorgias had a wife and a maidservant at odds. Because their presumed wisdom and authority could not settle domestic brawls, the Greeks did not think they could wisely settle external discords. Therefore, if a man is placed in charge of a city and a Republic but does not know how to rule himself, his home, and his private affairs, he is clearly appointed under a bad omen.

Finally, this is the only state of life in which a man—in loving his wife, educating his children, ruling his family, protecting his possessions, governing his home, and propagating his lineage—can lead the most happy life of all. In this state, if any burden or labor should fall upon him (and many do, for truly no life lacks its own cross), this is surely that unique "light burden and sweet yoke" <note>An allusion to the words of Jesus in Matthew 11:30</note> found in marriage—provided that the spouses are such that they were joined by God himself, and not by greed, pride, deceit, fraud, or insane lust. Thus, a man should leave his father, mother, children, brothers, and kinsmen to cling to his wife, whose love ought to surpass the affection for all others. So it was that Hector, seeing that Troy <note>original: "Ilium"</note> was about to be destroyed, was not touched by concern for his parents, his brothers, or even himself as much as he was for his dear wife. For thus he says in the works of Homer:

> Indeed I do not doubt that great Troy shall fall,
> and Priam, and the people of Priam, mighty in arms, shall perish.
> But it is not the care for the people, nor for my dear mother,
> nor does the heart of King Priam gnaw at me so much,
> nor the fate of my brothers—though many and noble men
> shall lay down their lives in the dust beneath the enemy sword—
> as much as the care for you, my dearest wife, torments me.
> <note>original: Latin verse translation of Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 6, where Hector speaks to his wife Andromache</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on domestic life and marriage. While the previous page highlighted marriage as a potential source of supreme happiness and a training ground for leadership, this page shifts to the "vanity" or the darker side of domestic life: the many trials of marriage and the failures of child-rearing.</meta>

### ON VANITY

<margin>Many evils accompany marriage.</margin>
The many evils of marriage: such as those **Socrates** once enumerated, including perpetual anxiety, tormenting jealousy, a web of complaints, the reproach of a dowry, the heavy-browed arrogance of in-laws, the judgmental whispers of neighbors, various expenses, and the uncertain outcomes of children. Sometimes there is childlessness, the extinction of the family line, a foreign heir, and innumerable sorrows. Added to this is the fact that there is no "trial period" for a wife; one must take her as she comes. Whether she turns out to be pleasant, or foolish, or of perverse character, or proud, or filthy, or deformed, or unchaste—whatever the vice may be, it is only learned after the wedding, and is thereafter scarcely ever corrected.

<margin>Examples of perverse marriages.</margin>
There are no small number of examples of unfortunate marriages: **Marcus Cato the Censor** <note>Also known as Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman famous for his strict morality</note>, easily the foremost man of the Roman Republic in his time, who had scarcely an equal in war or peace, married the young daughter of a certain poor and obscure man named **Salonius** when he was already an old man. Because she behaved defiantly, he lost all authority in his own home. **Tiberius** <note>The second Roman Emperor</note> had as his wife **Julia**, the daughter of Augustus, who was infamous for her blatant adulteries; because he dared neither to punish her, nor report her, nor divorce her, nor keep her, he was forced to withdraw to Rhodes, not without infamy to his reputation and danger to his life. **Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher** <note>The Emperor Marcus Aurelius</note>, having taken **Faustina**, the daughter of Antoninus Pius, as his wife, was forced to keep that adulterous woman so as not to lose her dowry and the right to rule <note>Aurelius famously joked that if he divorced his wife, he would have to return her dowry—which was the Empire itself</note>. Truly, however, all these inconveniences arise not so much from the fault of the wives as from the husbands: for a wicked wife does not usually happen to anyone except a bad husband. **Varro** philosophized about this in **Gellius** <note>Aulus Gellius, author of "Attic Nights," quoting the scholar Marcus Terentius Varro</note>, saying: "A wife’s vice is either to be removed or endured: he who removes it makes her more agreeable to himself; he who endures it makes himself a better man." We have spoken more extensively on these matters in our declamation *On the Sacrament of Matrimony*.

<margin>The poor upbringing of sons.</margin>
Now indeed, the education of children does not turn out well for everyone. Very many of them are disobedient or rebellious toward their parents; others are even hostile to them. Some turn out to be insane and senseless; others dull and thick-headed. Still others spend their lives rushing headlong into every vice, overturning their inheritance through luxury, lust, and gambling. Some are parricides <note>Those who kill their parents</note>, such as **Alcmeon** and **Orestes** <note>Figures from Greek mythology</note>, and **Publicius Malleolus**, who killed his mother. Even **Artaxerxes** himself...

# TESTIMONIES. XCVI
N
<meta>catchword: Stealthily</meta>

**Mnemon** <note>Artaxerxes II Mnemon, King of Persia, whose later reign was marred by the horizontal violence of his many sons competing for the throne</note>, having sired fifteen <note>Historical sources usually cite Artaxerxes II as having over 100 sons; the text here specifies fifteen</note> children from her, put a great many of them to death because they were plotting against him. Wherefore **Euripides** said not unskilfully—and our **Bernard** <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic and church leader</note> took up the idea—that it is a good thing to remain unknown and be without children. Even **Augustus**, the most fortunate Emperor, was often forced on account of his daughter and granddaughter <note>Both named Julia, both were exiled by Augustus for scandalous adultery</note> to cry out that verse from **Homer**:
*Would that I had remained unmarried and died childless.*
<note>original: "Coniuge non ducta natis utinam caruiſſem." A Latin translation of Hector's rebuke to Paris in the Iliad.</note>

<margin>Servants</margin>
Regarding servants, **Euripides** also says: no enemy in the home is greater, nor worse, nor more useless than a servant. And **Democritus** says: A servant is a necessary possession, but not a sweet one. And <margin>Petrarch</margin> **Petrarch** wrote somewhere: I knew I lived with dogs, but I did not know I was a hunter until I was warned: Servants are called dogs; they are biting, they are gluttonous, they are thieves. <margin>Plautus</margin> **Plautus**, in *Pseudolus*, expresses their natures in these words: A race of whip-bearing men, in whose minds nothing occurs so as to act rightly; but when the occasion is given—seize, plunder, snatch—this is their work, so that you would rather leave wolves among sheep than these guards at home. And **Lucian**, in *Palinurus*, says: the curses of servants against their masters are always ready, as are thefts, deceptions, flight, arrogance, negligence, drunkenness, greed, sleepiness, slowness, and laziness. Hence that well-known Proverb: <margin>Proverb</margin> We have as many enemies at home as we have servants. But we often do not have them as enemies so much as we *make* them so: when we are proud, greedy, insulting, and cruel toward them, and we put on the minds of Tyrants at home, and we wish to exercise our will upon servants not as much as is fitting, but as much as we please. Regarding them, the servant **Strophilus** speaks thus in **Plautus's** *The Pot of Gold*:

> Masters treat their servants unjustly,
> And servants now obey their masters unjustly,
> Thus it happens on neither side as would be just to happen.
> The larder, the kitchens, the store-rooms,
> The stingy old men lock with a thousand keys,
> Which they will scarcely grant even to their legitimate children,
> But the thieving, fickle, and cunning servants
> Unlock for themselves what was shut with a thousand keys.

Many Republics in the past have endured enormous evils from servants; this is testified by the "Servile Wars" <note>A series of slave revolts in the late Roman Republic, the most famous led by Spartacus.</note> described by many historians. However, the city of Volsinii <note>An ancient Etruscan city in Italy.</note>, once opulent in wealth and adorned with fine morals and laws, formerly offered a miserable spectacle of the insolence of servants. When they began to treat their servants with loose reins and too much familiarity—even occasionally admitting them into their councils—eventually a few of them dared to enter the senatorial order. Soon, they occupied the entire Republic. They ordered wills to be written according to their own whim, and they forbade the banquets and gatherings of free-born citizens. They took the daughters of their masters as wives. Finally, they enacted a law that their violations of widows and unmarried women alike should go unpunished, and that no free-born maiden should marry unless one of their number had first tasted of her chastity. Thus a most wealthy city, which was considered the head of Caria <note>The author here appears to conflate the Etruscan Volsinii with a city in Caria (modern Turkey), likely drawing on historical accounts by Valerius Maximus or Orosius.</note>, fell into a deep pit of injury and disgrace because of excessive indulgence and clemency toward servants. For when the discipline of servants is removed, as **Aristotle** says in his *Politics*, masters fall into ambushes, just as the Helots <note>An enslaved population in Sparta who frequently revolted.</note> did to the Spartans, and the Penestae <note>A class of serfs in ancient Thessaly, Greece.</note> to the Thessalians. It remains for us to briefly explain **ROYAL MANAGEMENT**, that is, the life of the court.

<margin>
ROYAL 
MANAGE-
MENT.
</margin>
The Court is, in truth, nothing other than a college of Giants <note>In this context, "Giants" refers to the mythological rebels against the gods—monstrous, arrogant, and lawless figures.</note>—that is, a gathering of noble and famous scoundrels, a theater of the worst henchmen, a school of the most corrupt morals, and an asylum for execrable crimes. There, pride, arrogance, vanity, greed, lust, luxury, envy, anger, drunkenness, violence, impiety, malice, treachery, deceit, malignity, cruelty, and whatever other vices and corrupt habits exist anywhere else, live, command, and reign. There, the violations, rapes, adulteries, and fornications of Princes and Nobles are treated as mere games; there, even the mothers of Princes and Kings are sometimes the procuresses for their own sons; there, the storms of all crimes rage.
