### OF THE SCIENCES
N n
<meta>catchword: to loathe</meta>

...and an unspeakable shipwreck of all virtues. Every honest man is oppressed there, while the worst of men are promoted. Simple folk are mocked, the just suffer persecution, and the bold and reckless are raised up. Only those who prosper there are the flatterers, whisperers, detractors, informers, slandering sycophants, liars, slayers of reputation <note>original: "famicidæ"—literally "fame-killers," referring to those who destroy a person’s good name through gossip.</note>, schemers, inventors of evil, and all the rest of that stormy rabble for whom the most perverse crimes are a profession.

Their entire life is most foul; whatever ferocity exists anywhere among the most hideous beasts seems to have flowed into this courtly herd as if into a single body. Here is the ferocity of the Lion, the cruelty of the Tiger, the grimness of the Bear, the rashness of the Boar, the pride of the Horse, the greed of the Wolf, the stubbornness of the Calf, the deceit of the Fox, the shifting cunning of the Chameleon, the spottedness of the Leopard, the biting nature of the Dog, the despair of the Elephant, the vengeance of the Camel, the timidity of the Hare, the lewdness of the Goat, the filthiness of the Pig, the foolishness of the Sheep, the stupidity of the Donkey, and the buffoonery of the Monkey. 

In that place are raging Centaurs, there are destructive Chimeras, there are mad Satyrs, there are foul Harpies, there are wicked Sirens, and two-formed Scyllas. There are horrid Ostriches <note>original: "Strutiones." In the medieval and Renaissance imagination, the ostrich was often classified as a monstrous hybrid because it was a bird that could not fly.</note>, there are voracious Griffins, and greedy Dragons; whatever fatal monsters and unhappy omens nature ever shuddered at are gathered there to live and be seen. There, every kind of virtue suffers its own executioners and tyrants. In short, one must either persist in wickedness, malice, and impiety, or one must depart the court: 

> "He who wishes to be pious must depart from the court" <note>original: "exeat aula qui vult esse pius." A famous quotation from the Roman poet Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, expressing the belief that true morality is impossible in the presence of political power.</note>.

<margin>The Court is fatal to cities.</margin>
No more deadly evil can befall cities than the Court of a powerful Prince. When it moves, it is like a comet foretelling all manner of evils, or like a most contagious plague; wherever it attaches itself, it brings a most ruinous slaughter. Wherever it migrates from, it leaves behind the incurable traces of its poison, much like the bite of a rabid dog. It is accompanied by a perpetual high cost of living, as everyone within it strives to snatch a profit by hiking the prices of goods—prices which can never afterwards be lowered, resulting in great loss. It is also accompanied by a luxury in food, by which, through the introduction of foreign delicacies, the people themselves begin **to loathe** <note>This completes the thought from the catchword "fastidire" on the original Latin page.</note> their native foods.

# DE VANITATE
### OF VANITY

...begins to loathe [honest work], and everywhere indulging in taverns and gluttony, shamefully consumes his own affairs. Pride also follows as a companion; while the citizens and their wives try to imitate it, every household borrows the pattern and habit of its own arrangement from the court. They pour out everything they own into clothing and pomp; a corruption of morals follows, and with the introduction of the worst vices, a most ruinous evil takes hold.

Indeed, when the Court <term>Aula</term> <note>original: "Aula" — while literally "hall," it refers here to the entire royal household and its traveling entourage.</note> finally departs from a city, alas, what a foul tail it leaves behind! Some men find their wives have been seduced; others find their daughters deflowered or even carried off as harlots; others find their sons led astray, and others find their male and female servants corrupted. Why say more? There is great mourning, and the entire face of the city is changed, becoming like the face of a harlot.

I know a certain famous city of the Gauls <note>Likely referring to Paris, which Agrippa knew well.</note> so perverted by this cause that there is scarcely a modest matron to be found, and daughters are hardly ever married as virgins. Indeed, to have been a palace prostitute is considered the highest honor, and the older matrons act as procurers <term>Lenae</term> <note>The Latin "Lena" refers to a female pimp or procuress, often a stock character in Roman comedy.</note> for the younger ones. This shame has become so prevalent that there is no room for modesty; even the husbands themselves hardly care about their wives' prostitution,
<margin>Genesis 12</margin>
provided that—as Abraham said to Sarah—it may be well with them because of the women, and they may live sumptuously by their favor. <note>A cynical reference to Genesis 12:13, where Abraham asks Sarah to pose as his sister so he will be treated well by the Egyptians.</note>

<margin>NOBLE COURTIERS</margin>
->**NOBLE COURTIERS**<-

The people of the court are of two kinds. The first rank is held by the Satraps—I mean those noble "Thrasos" <term>Thrasones</term> <note>original: "Thrasones" — a reference to Thraso, the boastful, vainglorious soldier from Terence’s play *The Eunuch*.</note> who are driven mad by pride, luxury, and pomp. They are dressed in purple and fine linen <term>bysso</term>, in embroidery and gilded garments, surrounded by every variety of finery, men whom:

> Harlots please, and a mincing, swaying gait;
> With loose hair, and so many new names for clothes.

These men break all their strength in the service of Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love, used here to signify sexual indulgence.</note>. Furthermore, they possess an ingenious gluttony and taste; they seek refinement in all things, feast splendidly, and give and receive banquets. Among such men, it is often considered a point of pride if they squander so much at a single illustrious wedding feast that they must then shamelessly go around to the tables of others for three whole months. To these men there flock from all sides lyre-players, flute-players, and every kind of musician, mimes, actors, parasites <note>original: "Parasitae" — professional guests who provide flattery and entertainment in exchange for a meal.</note>, harlots, pimps, dancers, hunters, and such-like monstrous people. They also maintain dogs, horses, wolves, deer, <unclear>bears</unclear>, hawks, and other birds of prey, monkeys and parrots, and whatever other monsters and disgraces of nature there may be.

<margin>The conversations of courtiers.</margin>
Bears, Lions, Leopards, Tigers. Their conversations are
mere trifles and idle stories: they disparage, they inform on others, they
babble, they lie, or they mix the false with the true. Some
tell many tales about dogs, about hunts, about the scope of the
forest, about the winding paths of the thickets, and about the

about military service, and about their own brave deeds. If 
an envious rival is present, he will break up the conversations of 
others by shouting them down, inserting other trifles, and 
he will insolently narrate his own exploits, which he thinks will 
bring him praise. Another often convicts this man of lying and 
explodes in various scoffs: from this, the entire conversation of the 
banquet frequently ends in anger and insults, and as if in the

until they draw blood. Thus, in the banquets of these courtiers, the 
guests often return with scars, as if they seemed to be

<margin>The discipline of courtiers.</margin>
Furthermore, the highest discipline of these men is to observe the 
timings of Princes, so that they do not press anything upon them 
at an inopportune moment. They do not take these timings from 
the stars, from the Heavens, or from the astronomical calendars <term>Ephemerides</term> <note>Tables used by astrologers to track the positions of celestial bodies.</note>, but from

...[he] will not dare <note>Continuing from the previous page, describing the arrogant courtier.</note>, so that all may fear him; he will trample his inferiors, despise his equals, and look down on his superiors. He demands honor and adoration even through insult; he is entirely swollen with pride, uplifted, and strives for power:

> Virtue is the freedom for crimes, and the highest power. 
> <note>original: "Libertas scelerum est uirtus & summa potestas" — A quote from the Roman poet Lucan's *Pharsalia*, suggesting that for the powerful, "virtue" is simply the license to do as they please.</note>

Anyone who does not smile at him, or does not applaud him even when he has done wrong, is immediately considered guilty: for he will be judged either to envy the man's fortune or to have failed in his duty to him. Nor are these men hostile only to their equals and inferiors at such times, but they are often most ruinous even to their own Princes. Under the guise of severity, prudence, correction, and counsel, they flatter them most destructively, and very often drive them into unspeakable crimes, just as Curio incited Caesar in the works of Lucan. <note>Gaius Scribonius Curio was a Roman politician who, according to the poet Lucan, urged Julius Caesar to cross the Rubicon and begin the Civil War.</note>

of honesty.

> "Why has a lingering power now held back your strengths?" 
> "We complain; did you lack confidence in us?" 
> "While this warm blood remains in our breathing bodies," 
> "And while strong arms are able to hurl spears," 
> "Will you endure the degenerate toga and the rule of the Senate?"
> <note>original: "Quid iam lenta tuas tenuit potentia uires..." — Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book I. These lines represent the voice of an advisor urging a leader toward tyranny and war.</note>

Alexander the Great had similar instigators, who would further inflame him—already raging by his own nature—into greater wars and slaughters. Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, also had such counselors <note>In the Bible, Rehoboam rejected the advice of elder statesmen in favor of his young companions, leading to the rebellion of the ten tribes of Israel.</note>; and the Princes of our own age have them too. Catering to their masters' desires, they prepare and urge them toward every crime; or they dissuade them in such a way that they actually push them more strongly, by offering reasons so futile and weak that, by admitting they are defeated by the Prince's counter-arguments, they confirm the error of the gullible ruler. In both cases they deceive so skillfully that they cannot be accused of wrongdoing, but instead earn favor despite their treacherous betrayal. Today, Francis, the King of the French <note>Francis I (reigned 1515–1547), a contemporary of the author.</note>, has such advisors—men far too ready for evil counsel—who would willingly drive him into all treachery and tyranny against the Emperor <note>original: "contra Cæsarem" — referring to the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V, the great rival of Francis I.</note>, and meanwhile they are considered the best and most faithful of men.

# ON VANITY

<margin>
The manners of courtiers raised to honors.
</margin>

...should they take up an office, or obtain custody of the treasury, or have the various accounts of the tax census committed to them. And now, having emerged from the narrow straits of their labors, no service of theirs is any longer free of charge, but they henceforth hold everything for sale at a price. With their manners changed along with their new honor, they forget everything that lies behind them; leaning toward what is ahead, they despise their former state and lust for what is further still. Contracted by greed for prey, they turn everything toward the noise of profit. They are stingy with their faith but prodigal with their words, equally flattering and treacherous, obscure in their speech and as ambiguous as oracles. Whatever they see, whatever they hear, whatever is said, whatever is done—they interpret it all in the worst possible way. They trust only themselves, love only themselves, and are wise only for themselves. They believe in no one's loyalty or friendship and cultivate no fellowship except for the sake of profit. They prefer their own advantage to all else. Friends, guests, relatives, and associates—anyone who does not bring them profit—they despise like sterile trees. If one of their former comrades happens to meet them, they pass by as if they do not even know them. If one of those friends implores them for help, they feed him abundantly with words and promises, promising more than they perform; but if you bring nothing with you, they leave you destitute of help and even despoil you of your cause. They hold every favor for sale and despise every virtue. They break the praises of others with diverse opinions and skillfully disparage them behind their backs. They themselves praise no one without an exception, just as that Orator said of Julius Fortunatus: "I admit he is a brave man and one who is known to have acted vigorously in many matters; however, I would certainly wonder how he escaped a trial for extortion <note>original: "iudicium repetundarum" — a legal term for the recovery of extorted funds from corrupt officials.</note> before just judges, if his power of eloquence were unknown to me." Having obtained authority close to their Princes and Kings, they amass riches equal to Princes and build royal palaces, while meanwhile those more noble Courtiers squander all their own means on harlots, on dice, on hunts, on horses, on banquets, on pageants, on clothes, and on pride, wasting away their lands, castles, possessions, and patrimonies. These the commoners then buy, succeeding into the place of the nobles by these most wicked arts of theirs.

# ON VIRGINITY

->DE VIRGINITATE<-
<note>While the heading reads "On Virginity," the text itself is a biting satire on the lack of modesty and the corrupting influence of courtly life on young women.</note>

...is first built and composed of the greatest and most sumptuous stones. Yet, if you search for a God within, you will find either a Monkey, or a Stork, or a Goat, or a Cat. <note>Agrippa is using a popular Renaissance metaphor: Egyptian temples were magnificent on the outside, but inside they housed animals instead of "true" gods. He compares courtly women to these temples—beautifully dressed but morally vacant.</note> So it is with those girls and ladies of the court who, from their earliest age and tenderest years, are nourished in soft leisure, in dances, and in every luxury. Imbued with the worst teachings from those courtly books of love and most depraved histories—tales of luxury, lust, adultery, fornication, and panderings, along with comedies, trendy jests, and songs—most destructive habits have flowed into them as if from a wet-nurse. These include levity, insolence, arrogance, peevishness, impudence, obscenity, contention, contradiction, stubbornness, revenge, cunning, craftiness, petulance, talkativeness, boldness, and shameful lust. They have tongues for which silence is a punishment; they have lips armed for every kind of talkativeness, with which they produce most idle and foolish speeches, which are not rarely annoying to those forced to listen. For what shall we imagine they speak of among themselves for so many hours, if not foolish and idle things? They discuss how the hair is to be arranged, how it is to be combed, how the hair is to be dyed, how the face is to be rubbed <note>A reference to the use of cosmetics and exfoliants, which Agrippa viewed as deceitful.</note>, how a garment is to be folded, with what pomp one should walk, when to rise, when to lie down, and in what clothing it is lawful to appear. They obsess over who should yield place to another, how many bows are required for a greeting, who is permitted or forbidden to receive a kiss, and whether they should be carried by ass, horse, chair, carriage, or litter. They talk of who may wear gold, gems, coral, necklaces, earrings, bracelets, rings, or collars, and they read the rest of the trifles of the Semiramises. <note>Semiramis was a legendary Queen of Assyria, often cited in this period as a symbol of both immense power and excessive, decadent luxury.</note> Nor are there lacking older matrons to tell stories of how many suitors once loved them, with what gifts they were honored, and with what flatteries they were courted.

Sometimes they stuff their conversation with untimely quips or the most impudent lies. Nor are there lacking among them the most intense hatreds and sharpest quarrels, calumnies, detractions, slanders, and whatever...

# OF THE SCIENCES. Folio 102.

...the hair should be braided or the face painted. Then follow the **vices of a wicked tongue**: they have alluring eyes, faces, and smiles full of charms; they use nods and gestures full of lewdness; they have tricks and words by which they entice and deceive their suitors to extort little gifts. <margin>Cunning used to extort gifts</margin> Whether it be a ring, a gemstone, a necklace, or a small chain—whatever it is—they steal it away with flatteries or wring it out with prayers. In return, they give kisses, sweet touches, embraces, and private conversations, which are their public merchandise and the very fuel of courtly love. I am ashamed to report the shameful acts often committed in secret within the bedchamber, an insult to nature even under the cover of hallowed marriage <note>original: *consecrato Hymeneo*; Agrippa is likely alluding to "unnatural" sexual acts or contraceptive practices common in his cynical view of the court.</note>. They believe that once they have put on their clothes, they have covered and hidden everything. With what kind of faith and integrity, therefore, can we expect such women to behave toward their husbands later? Oh, with how much grief do they afflict good spouses, while they constantly throw their noble lineage, their dowry, their beauty, or the marriages of others in their husbands' faces!

<margin>Proud boastings of noble ladies against their husbands</margin>
They overwhelm their men with quarrels and insults, forever complaining; they despise a domestic and frugal table and reproach their husbands for lacking courtly luxury. Accustomed to delicacies and pomp, they exhaust their husbands' wealth through their ambition for ornaments, ruin their households, and sometimes drive their miserable husbands toward shameful and evil ways of making money. They lie in wait for these men day and night with a thousand frauds, pretenses, betrayals, and hypocrisy. I remain silent regarding outside lovers, secret adulteries, substituted births <note>original: *supposititios partus*; the practice of faking a pregnancy or swapping infants to ensure an inheritance or title.</note>, and offspring conceived from another’s seed. For if they once turn toward hatred, they prepare either jealousy or poisons. For these are the familiar arts of wicked women (as Jerome says in his writing *Against Jovinianus* <note>St. Jerome's *Adversus Jovinianum* was a famous late 4th-century defense of virginity that contained many arguments against the difficulties of marriage.</note>): deceits, frauds, poisonings, harmful drugs, and the vanities of magic.

<margin>The arts of evil women. Ecclesiasticus 25.</margin>
Thus Livia <note>Likely referring to Livia Drusilla, wife of Augustus, often accused in antiquity of poisoning her family members.</note> killed her husband, whom she hated too much; Lucillia destroyed hers out of jealousy. One deliberately mixed hemlock; the other, being wicked, offered a draught of madness in place of a love potion. Thus it is safer, as the book of Ecclesiasticus <note>Ecclesiasticus 25:16. A book of the Biblical Apocrypha/Deuterocanon, also known as the Wisdom of Sirach.</note> says, to dwell with a lion and a dragon than with a wicked woman. Whoever desires to have an obedient wife should not take such a courtly lady. And whatever woman wishes to have an honest husband should not marry a man of the court. But my speech has already run on too long with my tongue; yet I have said it, and now I cannot un-say it.

# OF VANITY.

But I will place my hand over my mouth <note>original: *ponam manum meam super os meum*; a biblical expression from Job 40:4, signifying silence or the end of a particular argument.</note> and add no more to this topic. Instead, now departing from the Court, let us examine the remaining parts of Household Management <note>original: *Oeconomiæ*; in the 16th century, "Economy" referred to the governance of a household, estate, or family, rather than just finance.</note> and those disciplines which are deemed the more important among the mechanical arts: Commerce, Agriculture, Warfare, and the rest.

<margin>COMMERCE</margin>
**Commerce** itself is indeed a most cunning seeker of hidden profits, a clearly greedy whirlpool of plunder, never happy in the enjoyment of what it possesses, but always most miserable in its desire for seeking more. Nevertheless, most people have judged it to be of no small help to the State, suitable for forging friendships between foreign Kings and Peoples, very useful for the private lives of men, and in a way, necessary. Indeed, Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman author of Natural History.</note> believes it was invented for the sake of providing a livelihood. For this reason, many illustrious and wise men did not disdain to practice it—among whom (according to Plutarch) were Thales, Solon, and Hippocrates.

But just as we admit some sciences and arts for the sake of pleasure, value others for their labor, pursue others for virtue and honor, and venerate others for truth and justice; yet not all of those which are necessary, profitable, pleasant, or laborious are for that reason immediately honorable, praiseworthy, or just. Thus the practices of Merchants, Shopkeepers, Usurers, Bankers, and Money-changers <note>original: *Trapezitarum* and *Collybistarum*; specialized terms derived from Greek for those who exchange currency or manage tables of finance.</note> are necessary, useful, and laborious; nevertheless, they are called illiberal, sordid, and dishonest gains, because in them it is laborious frauds, not arts, that are bought and sold. This indeed (as Cicero says) is the duty not of fit, simple, noble, just, or good men, but of the versatile, obscure, cunning, deceitful, and crafty.

<margin>The customs of merchants and shopkeepers</margin>
For all merchants buy in one place so that they may sell elsewhere at a higher price and above the principal, and he is considered "better" who profits more. It is common for them everywhere to lie, swear false oaths, cheat, and deceive; nor is any method of profit considered shameful by them.

<margin>The Law of Merchants</margin>
Indeed, they even claim that the law allows them to deceive those making contracts with them, up to half the "just price." <note>This refers to the legal doctrine of *laesio enormis*, which allowed a contract to be rescinded if the price was less than half the true value. Agrippa suggests merchants used this as a legal "safe zone" to cheat people up to that limit.</note> Nor can there be any doubt that, since their entire lives are devoted to gain and riches, they commit many shameful acts and frauds worthy of punishment. ### OF VANITY

...having amassed money, they outdo some, preempt others, and deter others by raising the price of goods; thus they alone buy everything, which they then sell alone at the highest price according to their own whim. Not infrequently, they are stuffed with massive debt; having established a home elsewhere, and after their credit has collapsed and they have fled their native soil, they become fugitives. Returning late or never, they defraud their creditors and drive them to despair and the noose <note>Meaning suicide by hanging, a common trope in Renaissance anti-merchant literature.</note>. These are the ones who entangle and pillage citizens with <term>handwritten notes of debt</term> <note>original: *Cheirographis*; formal documents acknowledging a debt, used here as a metaphor for legal traps.</note> and obligations. They plant the roots of debt so deep, laborious, mournful, and inevitable that they cannot be pulled out; instead, they sprout in circles and, germinating debt from debt, they suffocate and overturn cities. Meanwhile, being incessantly devoted to interest and usury, they devour the substance of the whole common people. They themselves sometimes clip the coins <note>The illegal practice of shaving metal from the edges of gold or silver coins to steal the bullion value.</note>, and they always increase or decrease the value of money however it seems to lead to their own profit, not without detriment to the whole Commonwealth. Having spied out the secrets of Princes, the counsels of cities, and the rumors of the fatherland, they report them to enemies. Sometimes, for a negotiated fee, they even plot against the lives of Princes. There is nothing they will not attempt, do, produce, or keep for sale out of a lust for money. Their entire way of life is nothing but lies, theatrical coloring, clouds of words, spying, traps, frauds, and manifest deceptions.

<margin>In Carthage, merchants had private places.</margin>
For this reason, the Carthaginians established separate lodgings for merchants, nor did they wish them to be shared with the citizens. However, the road to the marketplace was open to them, but even a glimpse of the naval yards and the more secret places of the city was not permitted.

<margin>The Greeks excluded merchants.</margin>
The Greeks, moreover, did not receive them within their cities at all; instead, so that the citizens might be immune from any suspicion of danger, they established the marketplace for vendibles not far from the <term>city boundaries</term> <note>original: *pomœriis*; the sacred or legal boundary of a city.</note>. Many other nations prohibited merchants from approaching them because they would deprave their morals. The people of Epidaurus (according to Plutarch), when they noticed their citizens were becoming wicked through the dishonest commerce of the Illyrians, feared that from the contagion of foreigners and the corruption of their citizens' morals, a revolution would be stirred up in the state. They therefore chose one grave and circumspect man from the whole multitude of citizens each year to go to the Illyrians and... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "que" indicates the next page likely begins with "quem," referring to this chosen man.</note>

Folio 113.
### OF THE SCIENCES.

...so that each person might purchase and contract whatever his own people had ordered. <margin>Plato against merchants</margin> Plato censures merchants because they corrupt the best morals; he believes that in a well-constituted Commonwealth, it should be provided by law that the luxuries of foreign nations are not brought into the City. He also suggests that no citizen younger than forty years old should travel abroad, and that foreigners should be sent back to their own people. This is because, through the contagion of such strangers, citizens unlearn the ancient frugality of their fathers and their traditional customs, beginning to hate them instead. It is for this reason alone that cities are often rendered most wretched, being utterly defiled with every kind of fornication, adultery, luxury, and lust. <margin>Lyons and Antwerp</margin> Lyons <note>original: *Lugdunum*</note> and Antwerp <note>original: *Antuerpia*</note>, the most famous merchant emporiums of today, provide examples of this in themselves. <margin>Aristotle against merchants</margin> Aristotle himself also commands that every care be taken so that cities are not corrupted by the mingling of newcomers. Merchants, though they are necessary, are not to be received into the number of citizens; he detests them most of all because they delight in lies, harass the markets in cities, stir up riots, and sow discord. <margin>Merchants prohibited from magistracy</margin> Indeed, among most Republics there was an ancient law that no merchant should hold a Magistracy, nor be admitted into the senate or the council. <margin>Trade condemned</margin> Furthermore, trade has been plainly condemned by theological opinions and prohibited to all true Christians by the Canon decrees, with the authorities being George, Chrysostom, Augustine, Cassiodorus, and Leo. For, as Chrysostom says: "A merchant cannot please God." Therefore, let no Christian become a merchant; or if he wishes to be one, let him be cast out <note>original: *pronunciatur*; meaning formally declared an outcast or excommunicated</note> from the Church. Augustine also says that merchants, much like soldiers, cannot perform true penance. <margin>THE OFFICE OF THE TREASURY. Tax collectors.</margin>

#### TAX COLLECTORS

Not much better than merchants are the **TAX COLLECTORS** <note>original: *Quaestores*; in this context, Agrippa refers to public treasurers, tax-gatherers, or fiscal agents</note>, a certain thievish breed of men. For the most part, they are of a servile and mercenary nature—men who have hired out their labor for a small pittance, or who are coarse and lazy, yet bold and impudent. They have learned nothing except certain thin crafts, such as it is fitting for such men to know: namely, writing and calculating. Most of all, however, they have learned formulas for stealing—which are by no means unskilled, and are more ingenious than those sought out by common, vulgar bandits. Therefore, they are the most thievish of all men who live...

...they are most thievish <note>original: *furacisimi*</note>, and by their fingers alone—with which the wealthy calculate talents and millions—they are so sticky, and imbued with infinite hooks and barbs, that all money, no matter how light, fleeting, or slippery, like eels and snakes, as soon as it is touched by them, it sticks immediately and cannot easily be pulled away. <margin>The arts of the Treasurers for acquiring wealth</margin>
Moreover, the Treasurers themselves take interest, extort gifts, and plunder by procrastinating on debts. They collude with Captains, calculate falsely, forge hand-written documents <note>original: *cheirographa*</note>, and break open letters with counterfeit seals. They subtract something from the coinage, and sometimes corrupt it with false metal; therefore, they are great friends with Alchemists and are mostly followers of that art, or if they lack the talent, they are at least supporters.

<margin>Cicero's saying regarding Treasurers</margin>

The beginning of **TYRANNY** came from hunting, because tyranny found no more suitable author than one who—through the slaughter and butchery of wild beasts and the wallowing in blood—had learned to despise both God and nature. Nevertheless, the Kings of the Persians practiced this as the truest meditation on the affairs of war,

<margin>
Hunting practiced among the Persians.

because hunting contains something warlike and fierce. It provides pleasure through ravenous dogs, the cornered beast, the spilling of blood, and the tearing of entrails. Meanwhile, the cruel hunter watches a most bitter death as if it were a joke with the greatest delight, and he laughs. He then leads the unhappy prey home in the manner of a triumph—whether it was laid low by his army of dogs or by the deception of his snares—accompanied by a great crowd. There, a funeral-like butchery is prepared, and the beast is carved up with "solemn gestures" <note>original: *cheironomia* — a Greek term for the art of rhythmic hand gestures, used here to describe the ritualistic and performative way meat was carved after a hunt</note> and prescribed terms (for it is not considered lawful to do otherwise). This is surely a notable foolishness and a notable war; while they set their minds to it, they cast aside their humanity and become beasts themselves. By a prodigious perversity of character, they are changed into the natures of wild animals, much like Actaeon <note>In Greek mythology, the hunter Actaeon was transformed into a stag by the goddess Diana and subsequently devoured by his own hounds</note>. Many of them have broken out into such madness that they have become enemies of Nature itself, just as the fables tell of Dardanus.

<margin>
The inventors of hunting.
</margin>
The inventors of so unfortunate an art are said to have been the Thebans, a people notorious for fraud, theft, and perjury, and detested for their parricides and incests. From them, the rules of this exercise were passed to the Phrygians, a people equally shameful, yet foolish and frivolous; for this reason, the Athenians and the more serious Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> people held them in contempt. But later, after the Athenians had revoked the law forbidding hunting and admitted the art and its practice publicly into their Republic, it was then that Athens was first captured. Because of this, I marvel that hunting was commended by **Plato** himself, the Prince of the Academies, unless perhaps it was the honesty of the outcome, or its purpose, or necessity that commended this pleasure. For example, Meleager <note>A hero of Greek myth who led a group of noble hunters to kill the Calydonian Boar</note> slew the Calydonian Boar—that great destroyer—not for his own pleasure, but for the utility of the Republic, freeing his fatherland from a ravaging beast. And **Romulus** <note>The legendary founder of Rome</note> used to hunt stags, not for the sake of pleasure, but out of the necessity of feeding himself and his companions.

<summary>Agrippa condemns hunting as the historical root of tyranny and moral decay, arguing that the cruelty required for the sport strips men of their humanity. He traces the practice from the Persians and "shameful" Thebans to the fall of Athens, contrasting recreational hunting with the necessary hunting performed by heroes like Meleager and Romulus.</summary>

### ON VANITY

<margin>FOWLING.</margin>
There is also another exercise of hunting which they call **FOWLING**, which is indeed of less cruelty, but of no less vanity. From this, the "Fowlers" are named, who clearly either hunt birds or play by means of birds—as the Prophet Baruch says—with the birds of the sky. <margin>Baruch 3.</margin> <note>original: "Baruch 3" — Referring to Baruch 3:17, which mentions those who "have their pastime with the fowls of the air."</note> They say the author of this practice was Ulysses, <margin>Ulysses as the author of fowling</margin> who they tell us was the first to bring birds, armed and trained for the hunt, into Greece after the fall of Troy. This was supposedly done to provide a consolation of new pleasure for those who, having lost their parents, felt the heavy toll of the Trojan War; nevertheless, he commanded his son Telemachus to live his life free from this practice. Eventually, these exercises—which are in truth servile and mechanical <note>In the Renaissance, "mechanical" arts were manual trades, considered inferior to the "liberal arts" suitable for a free and educated mind.</note>—have been elevated so high that today, while all liberal studies are set aside, they are the very first elements and steps of nobility. With these activities as their guides, men reach the highest rank of the nobility. Today, the very life of Kings and Princes—and even, O grief! the religion of Abbots, Bishops, and other overseers of the Church—is entirely caught up, I say, in hunting. In this, they chiefly test themselves and display their "virtue":

<margin>Virgil, Book 4.</margin>
> And they pray that, among the listless cattle,
> a foaming Boar might be granted to their vows,
> or that a tawny Lion might descend from the mountain.
<note>original: "Spumantenq; dari pecora inter inertia uotis / Optant Aprum, aut fuluum deſcendere monte Leonem" — A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (4.158-159), describing the young Ascanius’s desire for a real challenge while hunting.</note>

And those who ought to be examples of patience daily seek to find something to conquer and hunt. Furthermore, animals that are by nature free and which, by the decree of law, belong to those who take them, are instead usurped by the tyranny of the nobles through their own reckless prohibitions. Farmers are driven away from their own newly-plowed fields; estates are taken from the rustics; the forests are closed to the farmers and the meadows to the shepherds, all so that the pastures of wild beasts may be increased for the bloodshed and delights of the Nobles. Only the Nobles are permitted to eat these beasts; if any tenant or farmer should taste them, he is made guilty of treason <note>original: "maiestatis reus" — a legal term for "lese-majesty" or crimes against the dignity of the state/sovereign.</note> and becomes prey for the hunter alongside those very beasts. If we search the scriptures, certainly in the sacred writings and even in the histories of the Heathens, we read of no saint, no wise man, and no philosopher who was a hunter. We find many shepherds, however, and some fishermen. And Augustine says this art <margin>Hunting forbidden to the clergy.</margin> is the most wicked of all; the holy councils of Elvira and Orleans prohibited and condemned this practice among the clergy. In the sacred Canons, it is not only prohibited to hunters...

# OF THE SCIENCES. Fo.CVII.

...[to] them the ascent to holy orders is denied, and even the rank of the highest priesthood, once attained, is taken away. In these same writings it is read <margin>Gen. 25</margin> <note>The marginalia in the original says Gen. 1, but the story of Esau the hunter is found in Genesis 25:27.</note> that **Esau** was a hunter because he was a sinner; nor indeed does Holy Scripture ever use the word "hunting" in a positive sense. Therefore, let it be ambiguous to no one that hunting itself is a reprobate thing, which has been driven out and condemned by the whole assembly of wise and holy men.

In ancient times, when men lived in innocence, <margin>The friendship of men with beasts is peace.</margin> no animals fled from them, none were hostile, and none were harmful; all were subject to them and offered obedience. Manifest examples of this are found even in later times among those who led the most excellent lives, showing how they proved superior to the snares of wild beasts. Just as <margin>Dan. 6</margin> <note>The marginalia says Dan. 4, but Daniel in the lions' den is in Daniel 6.</note> **Daniel** did with the lions, and the <margin>Acts 28</margin> **Apostle Paul** with the viper; a raven fed the **Prophet Elijah** <margin>1 Kings 17</margin> <note>original: "3 Re. 17" — In the Latin Vulgate Bible, the books of Kings are numbered differently; 3 Kings corresponds to 1 Kings in modern English Bibles.</note> and the hermits **Paul** and **Anthony**, while a doe fed **Saint Giles**. The **Abbot Helenus** commanded a wild ass and the beast obeyed, carrying the holy man's burdens; he even commanded a crocodile, and was carried by it across a river.

Many anchorites <term>anchorite</term> <note>A religious recluse who lives in total isolation to focus on prayer.</note> lived in the deserts and stayed in the dens and caves of wild animals, fearing neither lions, nor bears, nor serpents. For with sin, the harm of animals, as well as their persecution and flight, entered the world, and the arts of hunting were devised. For (as **Augustine** says in his third book *On Genesis*) animals were not produced from the beginning as poisonous, hostile, and troublesome to the human race, but after sin they were established as hostile and enemy. This was done by divine decree as a punishment for the unjust rebellion of our first parents. A decree of this kind was <margin>Gen. 3.</margin> pronounced to the serpent when God said: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring." From this sentence arose the struggle of hunting—that is, the war of men against other animals.

But let us now return to the matter: many have written about these aforementioned arts of <margin>Agriculture</margin> **AGRICULTURE**, herding, fishing, hunting, and fowling: Kings **Hiero**, **Philometor**, **Attalus**, and **Archelaus**; the generals **Xenophon** and **Mago**; and the poet **Oppian**. Furthermore: **Cato**, **Varro**, **Pliny**, **Columella**, **Virgil**, **Crescentius**, **Palladius**, and many more recent authors.

### OF THE VANITY OF AGRICULTURE

**Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> considers nothing better, nothing more abundant, nothing sweeter, and nothing more worthy of a free man than these rural pursuits. Not a few have placed the highest good and the peak of happiness in this life; hence **Virgil** calls farmers "fortunate," and **Horace** <note>original: "Oratius"</note> calls them "blessed." For this reason, the Delphic oracle pronounced a certain **Aglaus** to be the happiest man, because while cultivating a small estate in Arcadia, he never left it; thus, having very little desire, he experienced the minimum of evil in his life.

<margin>Agriculture is the curse of God. Genesis 3.</margin>
But miserable men, who think so highly of **Agriculture**, are ignorant that this pursuit is actually the result of sin and the curse of the Most High God. For casting man out from the **Paradise of Pleasure** <note>The Garden of Eden.</note>, He sent him into the fields, saying to the transgressor **Adam**: *Cursed is the earth in your work; in labor you shall eat from it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the field; in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken.* 

But none feel this more than the Farmers and Overseers, who—while they plow, sow, harrow, prune, dig, reap, harvest, gather the vintage, feed the herds, shear, hunt, and fish—lose their bread after many labors when the fields are devastated by hail and storms. One man’s sheep or oxen die or are driven off by soldiers; another loses a wild beast or a fish. At home, the wife wails, the children weep, and the whole family hungers; yet they return again to their doubtful labor with uncertain hope. Before this curse, there would have been no need for the artful cultivation of the earth, nor for pasturing, fishing, hunting, or fowling. For the earth was meant to produce all things spontaneously, both winter and summer fruits, always flowering with sweet scents and a woven mantle of greenery. Finally, the earth would have sprouted nothing harmful: no herb pestilential with poison, and no tree useless through the fault of sterility.

<margin>The water-snake, which Lucan calls the violator of water.</margin>
The venom of water-snakes <note>original: "natrix"</note>, vipers, and other reptiles was even withheld from them, as **Bede** <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar.</note> assures us. Man himself, having obtained lordship over all living creatures, would have commanded even the wild beasts as if to place burdens upon oxen and cattle; the fish of the sea and the birds would have flown to him at his nod. Furthermore, soon after being born, man would have obtained the use and exercise of all his limbs, and without bodily...

# [OF THE] SCIENCES
**Folio 108.**

...[without] coverings, without roofs, without stored provisions, and without medicines, man would have led a most happy life, since all things would have been supplied to him of their own accord (as that Poet says):

->The earth gave food to the children, the warmth was their clothing, and the grass their bed.<-

<margin>Sins have made all things enemies to man.</margin>
But the harm of sin and the necessity of death have made all things hostile to us. Now the earth produces nothing without our labor and sweat; instead, it generates lethal and poisonous things, as if openly reproaching us for the fact that we live. Nor do the other elements act any more mildly toward us: the sea overwhelms many with raging storms and swallows them with monstrous beasts; the Air fights against us with thunder, lightning, tempests, and the plague of pestilence. The Heaven also conspires for our destruction. And now even the animals are professedly hostile to us.

<margin>Proverb.</margin>
And even man himself, as is said in the Proverb, is a wolf to man <note>original: "homini lupus est." A famous phrase from the Roman playwright Plautus, meaning humans are naturally predatory toward one another.</note>. Unclean spirits surround us, tempting us with innumerable allurements of crimes, so that they may drag us into the dark pits of punishment to be perpetually tormented by eternal fires and dire tortures. And from this it is clear that **Agriculture**—along with its attachments of herding, fishing, and hunting—is nothing but the loss of the best things, an invention of evils, and a remedy for the inconveniences of life. Through these, we attempt to escape, or rather mitigate, the infertility of the earth, the poverty of our food, and the cold (by the wearing of skins), having been warned of our mortal fate.

But Agriculture would have no small praise as a necessity of our calamity if it had remained within these boundaries, and had not stepped beyond them to teach the cultivation of so many prodigious roots of plants, and so many portentous graftings and metamorphoses <note>The author views the hybridization and grafting of plants as an "unnatural" distortion of God’s creation.</note> of trees. Furthermore, it teaches how to join horses with donkeys, and wolves with dogs, thus procreating mules and **Lyciscas** <note>original: "Lyciscas." A term used by ancient writers like Virgil and Pliny for a hybrid offspring of a wolf and a dog.</note> and other monstrous animals against the law of nature.

<margin>The *Lycisca* is a monstrous dog, surely born from the mating of a wolf and a dog, from which it also takes its name.</margin>
But it also teaches how to confine in aviaries, fishponds, enclosures, and prisons those creatures to whom nature assigned the free sky, seas, and lands—even fattening them in a labor-house <note>original: "ergastulo." Traditionally a Roman prison for slaves, used here to describe the cramped conditions of livestock.</note> after their eyes have been put out or their limbs mutilated. Then, in the use of linen, wool, hides, and silk <note>original: "bombyce."</note>, and those things which nature granted for the clothing of men, it has devised so many arts of weaving, dyeing, and similar crafts, intended for nothing but luxury and pride, and very often even for the [perniciem] <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the next page begins with "perniciem," meaning "destruction" or "ruin."</note>

...devised for our destruction. Even Pliny complains about the single example of flax <note>original: "de uno lino." Pliny the Elder, in his *Natural History*, famously lamented that flax, used to make sails, allowed man to pursue his own destruction at sea.</note>, which is born from a tiny seed; first a plant, it soon becomes a sail, carrying the world to and fro with the lightest breath of wind. It forces men themselves—as if it were not enough to perish on land—to die in the waters and be devoured by sea monsters. I pass over a thousand decreed observances of Farmers, Shepherds, Fishermen, Hunters, and Bird-catchers, which are not so much foolish and ridiculous as they are superstitious and contrary to divine law. By these practices, they claim they can turn away storms, make sowings fertile, repel all harmful things, drive away wolves and wild beasts, halt fleeing animals, catch fish and birds with their hands, and ward off the diseases of cattle. These things were written with great credulity and seriousness by those "wise" men whom we named above.

<margin>MILITARY SERVICE.</margin>
But let us now pass from Farmers to SOLDIERS, whom Vegetius <note>A 4th-century Roman writer whose work *De Re Militari* was the standard military manual for centuries.</note> says are more suited for battle when chosen from the fields. Cato also asserts that the bravest men and the most strenuous soldiers are born from their ranks. Indeed, as the holy scriptures testify, <margin>Gellius, Book 4.</margin> that first fighter, Cain, was a Farmer and a hunter. And Janus and Saturn, those most warlike and ancient Gods, lived this life on earth along with Agriculture. Therefore, the military art seems by no means to be despised, which (as Valerius says) brought forth the leadership of Italy for the Roman Empire, granted the sovereignty of many cities, great kings, and most powerful nations, opened the jaws of the Black Sea and the gulfs of the ocean, and delivered the shattered barriers of the Alps and Mount Taurus. Scipio Africanus himself, according to Ennius, boasts that through the blood and slaughter of enemies he opened a path to Heaven for himself; Cicero agrees with him, saying that Hercules ascended to the Heavens by the same path.

<margin>The invention of the military art. The gamble of military service.</margin>
The Spartans <note>original: "Lacedæmonij."</note> are said to have been the first to hand down this art. Hence Hannibal, when about to perish in Italy, called Sparta the leader of arms. With this art as a guide, kingdoms and empires were established, and when it was neglected, even the most powerful were again demolished. For into the hands of reckless Commanders fell warlike Numantia, most ornate Corinth, proud Thebes, learned Athens, holy Jerusalem, and Carthage herself, the rival of the Roman Empire; and finally even the most powerful

**Indeed:** <note>original: "Roma" in OCR; likely a transcription error for the Latin "Imo," meaning "Indeed" or "Furthermore," which fits the rhetorical transition.</note> This art, written with more human blood than even the laws of Draco <note>Draco was a 7th-century BC Athenian legislator whose laws were famously harsh, said to be written in blood rather than ink.</note>, teaches one how to elegantly arrange the order of battle, to conveniently draw up the front line, to attack the enemy, to press on, to crowd them, to surround them, to strike to the left and right, to fight at the signals of the commanders, to advance the step, to withstand an assault, to resist those who press forward, to crush those who retreat, to deal blows, to avoid those dealt, or to catch them on a shield and despise them, and to rise up more fiercely against the enemy, to charge on horseback, to urge on with spurs, to guide with the reins, and to wheel about in every direction, to hurl missiles, to brandish lances, to hurl spears: to attack the faces, sides, and backs of the enemy as place and time permit, nor to think of flight until victory is despaired of; but to pursue those who flee, to slaughter, capture, disarm, plunder, and overthrow them, to lead back one's own, to gather them again, to restore the army, and when victory is despaired of, to let the soul turn toward the hope of vengeance, and all the remaining duties of soldiers and commanders. 

It also instructs on preparing fleets, building fortresses, fortifying camps, placing garrisons, constructing ramparts, piling up earthworks, clearing ditches, digging tunnels, manufacturing engines of war, selecting weapons, besieging walls, transporting supplies, devising tricks, laying ambushes, and knowing how to use various stratagems. The end goal of the military art. What war is. What soldiers are.

Hence, war is nothing other than a collective homicide and robbery by many, nor are soldiers anything other than mercenaries and, in a Republic, armed bandits of destruction. <margin>Praisers of warfare.</margin>
And yet, that divine Plato praised this art, and he ordered that boys should learn it and that adults should immediately be handed over to armed military service; and Cyrus, that most famous King, used to say it was no less necessary than Agriculture. Even Augustine and Bernard <note>St. Augustine of Hippo and St. Bernard of Clairvaux, both influential Church Fathers who developed theories of "Just War."</note>, Catholic Doctors in the Church, have approved of it in certain places, and the Papal decrees do not condemn it, even though Christ and the Apostles feel quite differently:

<margin>
Christ and the Apostles forbid warfare.
Sects of sacred soldiers.
The weapons of Christ.

Finally, even with Christ resisting, warfare has obtained no small favor in the Church, with so many sects and orders of "sacred soldiers" <note>A reference to military religious orders like the Knights Templar, Hospitallers, or the Teutonic Knights.</note> having arisen, whose entire religion is situated in blood, in slaughter, in robbery, and in piracy, under the pretext of defending and enlarging the faith. It is as if Christ wished his Gospel to become known—not by the preaching of the word, but by arms; not by the confession of the heart and martyrdom, but by the display and threat of weapons, as well as by the slaughter and carnage of men. Nor is it enough for these "Soldiers" to bear arms against Turks, Saracens, and Pagans, unless they also lead fleets against Christians on behalf of Christians.

<margin>Battles for the Papacy.</margin>
Ultimately, war and military service produce many Bishops, and it is not rare for the High Papacy itself to be fought over. As that holy Bishop of Zamora <note>original: "Camorenſis." This is then called the "constancy of martyrs," if there has been brave fighting for the Chair [of St. Peter] accompanied by a great slaughter of Christians.

<margin>Writers of the military art.</margin>
Xenophon, Zenocrates, Onosander, Cato the Censor, Cornelius Celsus, Ignius, Vegetius, Frontinus, Aelian, Modestus, and many more ancient authors have written about the military art. Among the more recent are Volturinus, Nicolaus the Florentine, James Count of Parisiis, and a few others. These are the teachers of the art, but they are speculative teachers—not nearly as dangerous as the practitioners. Truly, the titles and honors are not the ranks of students—such as the **Bachelor's**, **Master's**, or **Doctorate**—nor are they merely the terms by which they are called: **Emperors**, **Dukes**, **Counts**, **Marquesses**, **Knights**, **Captains**, **Centurions**,

### OF THE SCIENCES. Folio CX.

Centurions, Deans, Standard-bearers, and similar titles of nobility

born from ambition or injustice: but they are truly robbers, burglars, kidnappers, assassins, thieves, the sacrilegious, gladiators, rapists, pimps, fornicators, adulterers, traitors, embezzlers, cattle-rustlers, gamblers, blasphemers, poisoners, parricides, arsonists, bandits, pirates, tyrants, and their like. <margin>The badges of warfare.</margin> 
The badges of warfare, moreover, are not purple robes, necklaces, rings, or tiaras: but rather wounds upon the breast and bodies deformed by scars. 
<margin>The practice of warfare.</margin> 
Its practice is never joined to anything but the destruction and grief of many; it is the ruin of morals, laws, and piety, and is diametrically opposed to Christ, to blessedness, to peace, to charity, to innocence, and to patience. 
<margin>The rewards of warfare.</margin> 
Its rewards are the "glory" of nobility won by the shedding of human blood, and the expansion of empire through the lust for ruling and possessing, resulting in the perpetual damnation of many souls. For since the end of every war is victory, no one can be a victor unless he is a 
<margin>The wretched death of soldiers.</margin> 
murderer, and no one is defeated unless he has perished miserably. Therefore, the death of soldiers is the worst of all, with sin bringing a foul epitaph upon them. Furthermore, those who kill are wicked, even if the war is considered "just": for they do not fight for the sake of justice, but for the sake of profit and plunder. Thus, they are wicked murderers of those they kill; and if any are justly slain by them,

<meta>catchword: they themselves (ipsi)</meta>

<summary>Agrippa presents a scathing moral condemnation of soldiers, stripping away the "noble" titles of military rank to reveal a class of men he defines as essentially criminal and demonic. He argues that the very nature of warfare—its practice, badges, and rewards—is fundamentally incompatible with Christian virtue and results in the spiritual damnation of its practitioners.</summary>

<margin>
NOBILITY
</margin>
Those very men who have killed, positioning themselves into the rank of executioners, have earned this title of nobility; and although the laws otherwise rage with punishments against robbers, arsonists, plunderers, murderers, and assassins, such men are held as noble and honorable under the name of the Military. ¶ Therefore, NOBILITY has its origin in the Military—that is to say, a fame of lineage acquired through vigorous butchery <note>original: "strenua carnificina"</note> from the blood and slaughter of enemies, confirmed by public reward, and graced with public marks of honor. From this source, among the Romans, were born so many types of crowns—civic, mural, siege, and naval—and so many military gifts: bracelets, spears, horse-trappings, collars, rings, statues, and images, with which the first beginnings of nobility were inaugurated.

<margin>
Carthaginians.
Iberians.
Scythians.
Macedonians.

Carmanians.

Honor denied to those to whom it is owed incites many against their country.

What Nobility is.
</margin>
Among the Carthaginians, men were gifted with as many rings as the number of battles they had participated in. The Iberians used to erect as many obelisks around the tomb of the deceased as the number of enemies he had slain. Among the Scythians, at a famous banquet, it was only permitted for those who had killed an enemy to receive the cup passed around. Among the Macedonians, there was a law that those who had slain no enemy should be girded with a halter <note>A rope or noose, used here as a badge of shame for those who had not seen combat.</note> as a reproach for their ignobility. Among the people of Carmania, it was not permitted for any man to take a wife who had not first brought the head of a slain enemy to the King. Furthermore, the very indignation of not receiving a deserved honor led many who had served vigorously in the military to turn against their homeland to subvert its liberty: examples of this are Coriolanus, the Gracchi, Sulla, Marius, Sertorius, Catiline, and Caesar. If, therefore, we now seek the first beginnings of nobility, we will find it born from nefarious treachery and cruelty; if we look at its progress, we will find it increased here by mercenary service and highway robbery. Indeed, if we also seek the origin of kingdoms and empire, we encounter the impious parricides of brothers or parents, fatal marriages, and fathers driven from their kingdoms by their children, or Princes murdered, to whom an oath of loyalty had been sworn. But let us now examine nobility itself from its very roots <note>original: "à primis unguibus," literally "from the first fingernails," an idiom meaning to examine something thoroughly from the start.</note>: In truth, it is nothing other than robust wickedness, and a status—a blessing sought only through crime—and the inheritance of the worst of all sons. That this is so, first Holy Scripture, then also the ancient and more recent histories...

From them, some buy their nobility for money; others have now earned it through pimping, others by poisoning, and others by parricide. is about to fall into the bondage of lust. It would be too long in this place to review the beginnings of all Kingdoms and to run through all the histories of antiquity. I have described this matter, which I have touched upon here in a summary fashion, in a larger volume elsewhere, where I expressed nobility itself in its true colors and features with exactness. There, I showed that there has not been, nor is there, any kingdom or notable principality in the world that did not begin with parricide <note>original: "parricidio"; used here to mean the murder of a ruler or close kin to seize power</note>, treason, perfidy, cruelty, slaughter, murder, and other horrendous crimes—the "arts," I say, of nobility. Since these are its heads, we can easily recognize what the other members of that beast are like; they are all prone and practiced in violence, robbery, slaughter, hunting, lust, and every kind of luxury. 

If anyone wants to become noble, let him first become a **hunter**; this is the first element of nobility. Then, let him become a **mercenary soldier** and hire out his murders for a price: this is the true "virtue" of nobility, in which if he shows himself to be a brave robber, there is no greater glory of nobility. He who is unfit for these things, let him buy nobility with money, since it is even for sale. Or if he cannot do that, let him play the parasite to Kings, or intrude himself by some other courtly fraud, and act as a pimp <note>original: "Lenonem"</note> for palace harlots, or prostitute his wife or daughters to the Prince, or satisfy the lust of the ladies himself, or marry a royal prostitute, or take their illegitimate daughters as wives—this is the highest rank of nobility, for indeed one body is made with them. These are the paths, these the ladders, these the steps by which one ascends to the peak of nobility by a shortcut. 

Those who wish to seem more well-born than others and the noblest of all in their kind, boast of ancestors such as no one would not despise—namely foreigners, **Trojans**, or **Macedonians**, wandering with no fixed home, and deserters covered in a thousand wicked deeds. And yet, if it please the Lord <note>original: "dñs" (dominus)</note>, one must praise and extol this nobility of theirs, which had such wicked origins. <margin>Baldwin, Count of Flanders.</margin>
They had wicked origins: incest, debauchery, kidnapping, adultery, and the like. Thus Baldwin, because he kidnapped Judith <note>Judith of Flanders, daughter of the Frankish King Charles the Bald, was kidnapped (or eloped) with Baldwin I in 861 AD</note>, daughter of Charles the Bald, was created the first Count of Flanders. <margin>The four duties of the noble.</margin>
Furthermore, there are four principal duties of these nobles, in which all their happiness is situated. The first of these is greed <note>original: "rapacitas"</note>, by which, contrary to law and equity, they hold, seize, and possess. The second is pleasure, by which they grow insolent in every kind of luxury and lust. The third is liberty, by which, having despised the laws and surrounded by the forces of violence, they do everything according to their whim. The fourth is ambition, by which, puffed up beyond their lot and status, they seek higher things through every possible crime. Finally, the adequacy of all nobles is proven if they know the art of hunting, if they have been more damnably trained in dice <note>original: "alea"</note>, if they demonstrate the strength of their bodies with enormous cups [of drink], if they prove their natural vigor with numerous acts of Venus <note>original: "Venere"; a common Renaissance euphemism for sexual exploits</note>, if they squander their money boldly and vigorously, and if—devoted to pride, luxury, and every kind of intemperance, and being enemies to virtue—they forget that they were born and that they must die. They are considered even more noble if this plague has flowed from fathers to sons and has been introduced by great ancestors, as in:

<margin>Juvenal, Satire 14.</margin>
> If the ruinous dice please the old man, the heir also plays
> While still wearing the *bulla* <note>a locket worn by free-born Roman children</note>, and shakes the same in his little dice-box <note>original: "fritillo"</note>.

### OF VANITY

# OF THE SCIENCES. Folio CXVIII.

They claim a reputation for themselves out of greed; while they take from one, they give as a gift to another—generous plunderers. As the ancients wrote of Sylla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla (c. 138–78 BC), a Roman dictator known for seizing property from his enemies to reward his supporters.</note>, they strive to enrich some through the injury of others, while they themselves remain forever poor in the midst of their daily robberies. Therefore, they hunt for the name of justice and piety while they willingly take up the complaints of the poor and support their causes against the wealthy; but they only help those afflicted people until they have, in the meantime, drained the pockets of the richer sort. For their intention is not to benefit the poor, but to harm the rich—which is easier for any of them to do than to be of use. Under this shadow of justice and piety, they often arrogant such great license to themselves that they bring violence upon cities and the more powerful, harassing them with public hostility. Where no one could hope for pardon under the authority of the law, these men achieve glory under the pretext of nobility. Like the Giants of old <note>In mythology, the Giants (Gigantes) were symbols of lawless, god-defying arrogance.</note>, they glory in their sins. Just like evil demons, they seek everywhere for ways to do harm; they are thought to be most helpful only when they finally cease from doing injury. They act so that they are a terror to everyone and loved by none. 

<margin>Psalm 49</margin>
<note>This refers to Psalm 49:18 in the Latin Vulgate (Psalm 50 in modern English), which rebukes those who keep company with thieves and adulterers.</note> They take their portion with all the wicked and shameful. Those who entrust themselves to their protection, they plunder and oppress. No class of men is more pestilential to cities than these nobles who, pleasing only themselves as if they were more "well-born" than the rest, are always swelling with a proud spirit. Regarding them, Aristophanes <note>The ancient Greek playwright.</note> gave no bad advice when he said: 

<margin>The saying of Aristophanes.</margin>
"One ought not to raise a lion in the city; but if it has been raised, one must obey it." <note>original: "non oportere in Vrbe nutrire Leones, ſin autem alti ſunt, obſequi illis oportere." This is a famous quote from the play *The Frogs*, originally applied to the general Alcibiades.</note> Oppressed by the tyranny of these men, the Swiss <note>original: "Heluetij"</note> once killed all the nobles and uprooted their entire lineage from the fatherland. Through this remarkable slaughter of the nobility, they achieved a celebrated name for their own valor along with their liberty, by which they have happily ruled and governed for more than four hundred years to this day; they have always hated this breed of noblemen. 

<margin>Tyrant-killers were once pleasing to the people.</margin>
Formerly, no one was more pleasing to the people, nor deemed worthy of greater rewards, than those who killed tyrants and their attendants and henchmen—even their innocent children. Indeed, even the legal experts <note>original: "Iuriſconſulti"</note> teach that sometimes the innocent can be rightly killed, if it should greatly benefit

<meta>This page continues Agrippa's critique of the ruling class. Following the previous page's discussion on how the nobility exploits the poor and hides behind a veneer of "justice," the author now explores the moral justification for removing tyrants and argues that the very concept of "nobility" is rooted in destruction and uselessness, mirroring the most predatory aspects of the natural world.</meta>

<header>OF VANITY</header>

For the Republic, once a Tyrant is extinguished, it is also necessary to slaughter his children, lest a new Tyranny sprout from the guilty root: just as the Greeks, after the destruction of Troy, killed Hector's son Astyanax <note>In Greek mythology, the young son of Hector was thrown from the city walls to prevent him from later seeking revenge for Troy.</note> so that no opportunity for renewing the war might remain. Let us read the historians of ancient times: Titus Livy, Josephus, Hegesippus, Quintus Curtius, Suetonius, Tacitus, Serenus, and the rest. It has always been permissible to plot against Tyrants, permissible to deceive them, and most honorable to kill them—even to remove them by poison. In this manner, Tiberius, the third Emperor from Julius <note>Tiberius (r. 14–37 AD) was the third in the line of the Caesars after Julius Caesar and Augustus. Historical accounts of his death vary, with some suggesting he was smothered or poisoned.</note>, was destroyed. But while poisoning has always been a detestable crime, the world judged the poison by which he was extinguished to be life-giving. Even the Holy Scriptures attest to these things in the cases of Eglon, <margin>Judges 3 & 4.</margin> Sisera, and Holofernes, who were slain by Ehud <note>original: "Aioth"</note>, Jael, <margin>Judith 13 <note>original: "31"</note></margin> and Judith. It was permitted even before God to shake off the yoke of Tyrants by whatever deed; and all those through whose actions an afflicted people was liberated are honored in the sacred annals of the Bible as ministers of God.

Now truly, we do not doubt that nobility is evil, not so much by habit and custom as by its very nature. Indeed, among the Birds and Four-legged animals, <margin>Noble Birds.</margin> none hold the prerogative of nobility except those that are not just troublesome to other living things (including humans), but are even deadly. Such are Eagles, Vultures, Falcons, Hawks, Crows, Kites, Ostriches, and the mythical Harpies, Griffins, Sirens, and similar monsters. <margin>Noble Beasts.</margin> By a similar logic, Tigers, Lions, Wolves, Leopards, Bears, Boars, Dragons, Serpents, and Toads are considered "noble." Among the trees, none <margin>Noble Trees.</margin> (or very few) are held sacred to the Gods or considered noble unless they are either sterile or bear no fruit edible to humans, such as the Oak, the Winter Oak, the Beech, the Laurel, and the Myrtle. Among <margin>Noble Stones.</margin> stones, it is not the marble, nor the building stones, nor the millstones, but the gems—which provide no practical utility to humans—that are considered most noble. So too in metals: silver is quite ruinous, and gold is more harmful than iron; yet they are held as nobler, and deemed worthy of the slaughter and the waste of human blood for which nations fight. ¶ And from this proceeded that heroic art and philosophy of **HERALDRY** <note>original: "**HERALDORVM**"</note>, <margin>**HE**<br/>RAL<br/>DRY.</margin> in judging and distributing those shields of the nobility.

Fol. CXIX.

### ->BOOK THREE<-

...completely occupied with such matters, they believe it a sin and an act of madness to carry upon their armor the image of a beast of burden, a calf, a sheep, a lamb, a capon, a hen, a goose, or any of those animals which are necessary for the service or use of mankind. Instead, they feel it necessary to derive the <term>insignia: symbols or heraldic devices used on coats of arms to identify noble families</term> of their nobility from cruel beasts and rapacious wild animals. 

Thus, the Romans chose the Eagle, the most rapacious of all birds; the Phrygians chose the Sow, a most destructive animal; the Thracians chose Mars <note>The Roman god of war</note>; the ancient Goths chose the Bear; and the Alans, when invading Spain, chose the Cat—an animal both rapacious and fraudulent. The ancient Franks chose the Lion, as did the Saxons; but later, the Franks dwelling in Gaul <note>Modern-day France</note> took up Toads, while the Saxons chose the Horse, a warlike animal. The Cimbri carried the Bull as a sign of their strength and hardiness. For King Antiochus, the symbol was an Eagle carrying a Dragon in its talons; for Pompey, it was a Lion bearing a sword; for Attila, it was a crowned Goshawk <note>original: "Astur"</note>. 

Indeed, not even the Romans themselves, to whom the Geese keeping watch on the Capitoline hill provided salvation against the Gauls <note>Referring to the legend where the honking of sacred geese alerted the Romans to a night attack by the Gauls in 390 BC</note>, could be induced by so great a benefit to include the Goose among their insignia. There are some who perhaps admit the Rooster and the Goat to their shields, provided it is agreed that these animals are proud and lecherous—which are also the primary "gifts" of the nobility. For the same reason, they accept the Peacock, because of its vanity, and the Hoopoe, which seems to possess something of a royal quality and wears a crown. Nor does it hinder their nobility that it builds its nest in excrement; for 

<margin>Vespasian’s dirty proverb.</margin>

the Emperor Vespasian himself once collected a tax even from urine, remarking that "profit has no bad odor" <note>original: "lucri non esse malum odorem." This is the origin of the famous Latin phrase *pecunia non olet* (money does not smell).</note>. Now, many small animals also hold a place of privilege in these images of the nobility, provided they are evidence of someone's downfall; otherwise, they are not to be admitted. In this number are Rabbits, Moles, Frogs, Locusts, Mice, Serpents, Venomous Spiders, and Millipedes, by which—according to the authority of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman natural historian</note>—it is believed that peoples were once driven away and cities destroyed. 

For these same reasons, we would most gladly grant to them Gnats, Bedbugs, Flies, and even—if they wish—Blisters, Rot, Ulcers, and Plagues; for with these things, long ago, 

<margin>Exodus 8</margin>

Egypt was scourged under Pharaoh and Moses.

Insignia of the Gods

And these <term>insignia: heraldic symbols</term> of arms—depending on how they express cruelty, plunder, violence, strength, rashness, and the other "virtues" of the nobility—are judged by the Heralds to be more noble than others. However, those shields that lack these things and instead display milder subjects, such as Trees, Flowers, Stars, and the like—such as Apollo’s lyre or Mercury’s <term>caduceus: a staff entwined by two serpents</term>—or are distinguished only by a variety of colors, are considered much more recent and less noble than the former. This is because they are not judged to have been won by any military fortitude, or by any other artistry of blood and slaughter.

Yet it is a wonder what foolish wisdom these cloaked Heralds display in these matters, as they play the astrologer, the philosopher, and even the theologian, while they assign murky brown and black to Saturn.
<margin>
The foolish commentaries of Heralds concerning colors.
</margin>
Because of this, they attribute perseverance, silence, and patience to that color. To the sapphire or azure color, they want to signify faith—or, according to the opinion of the French, zeal—placing Jupiter in charge of it. In red, they show forth anger and vengeance, owing to the dominion of the furious Mars. The golden-yellow color is dedicated to the Sun; they say that because of the value of its metal and the Sun’s most lucid splendor, it signifies desire and joy. They place Venus in charge of purple and green. They say that purple, with its rosy glow, signifies a smiling love; but the French attribute the cunning of betrayal to it. Green, however, by everyone's consensus, denotes hope; for when the fields turn green, fruit is hoped for. The color white is attributed to the Moon, which, since it is simple without any mixture, yet easily susceptible to every mixture, they want to signify purity, simplicity, and fitness.

...is varied, so all those colors express the variety of the soul: just as ash-colored <note>original: "cinericius"</note>, being closer to black, signifies distress; flesh-colored, as if of diluted blood, signifies a hidden grief of the soul, or a secret and concealed thought; while straw-colored <note>original: "palearis"</note>, both bright and dark like falling leaves and withering grass, signifies despair and suspicion. It would be a long task to recount the kind of nonsense <note>original: "nanias"; literally "trifles" or "silly funeral songs," used here to mock the triviality of the claims</note> they invent here from humors, temperaments, seasons of the year, months and days, the corners of the world and the winds, zodiac signs, planets, plants, stones, and even the very sacraments and mysteries of the Church—forcing nearly the entire Book of Revelation to conform to these fables of theirs. 

And such is that "Heroic Philosophy" of the Heroic Heralds. I was about to make an end of this business, had it not occurred to me that I had passed over the origin of Heralds; therefore, it pleases me to append this to my discourse. 

<margin>Origin of Heralds</margin> Aeneas Sylvius <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini (1405–1464), a renowned humanist who became Pope Pius II</note> derives the name of "Heralds" from "Heroes." For Heroes were veteran soldiers, and it is fitting that they alone should be Heralds; thus "Herald" is a Teutonic word meaning an old man in arms, or a veteran soldier. But today, certain idle men, <term>caduceatores: ancient messengers or peace envoys who carried a staff</term>, and messengers—even <term>fecials: Roman priests who acted as heralds to declare war and peace</term> who have never served in war—obtain this office. Yet the privileges and duties of Heralds have lasted from the most ancient ages until this very <margin>The Founder of Heralds</margin> day. Their first founder was Father Liber <note>Another name for the god Bacchus or Dionysus</note>, who, after conquering India, initiated them into these your rites, saying: 

> “Today I release you from the labors and service of war; <margin>The Duties of Heralds</margin> I wish you to be veteran soldiers and to be called Heroes. Your duty shall be to advise the State, to expose the wicked <note>original: "fontes"; likely a transcription error for "sontes" (the guilty)</note>, and to praise the upright. You shall be free from all other duties. Wherever in the nations or lands you may come, Kings will give you food and clothing; you shall be more honored among all people; Princes will offer you <term>xenia: ritual gifts given to guests</term> and entrust their affairs to you. Your words shall be trusted; you shall abhor lies; you shall pass judgment on traitors; those who mistreat women, you shall mark as infamous; in every land you shall have liberty, and your passage and residence shall be secure. If anyone should trouble you or any of your number by word or deed, he shall be struck down by the sword.”
