<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s discussion on the origins of Heralds, specifically tracing the legendary and legal precedents supposedly established by great ancient and medieval monarchs to justify the high status (and, in his view, the vanity) of the heraldic office.</meta>

# ON VANITY

Alexander the Great granted these privileges of **Heroes** <note>original: "Heroum priuilegijs"; here referring to the veteran soldiers who served as heralds</note> for a long time: that they might use gold, purple, and scarlet garments, and military cloaks <note>original: "paludamentis"; the cloak worn by Roman commanders</note>; furthermore, that they could carry Royal arms and insignia wherever in the world or among whatever nations they might be. If anyone should strike them with a hand or weary them with a word, that person—with their goods confiscated—was to be held guilty of a capital crime. Aeneas <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, mentioned on the previous page</note> reports that Thucydides, Herodotus, Didymus, Megasthenes <note>original: "Megastoneum"</note>, and Xenophon all record the same.

<margin>
Augustus's edict concerning Heralds.
</margin>
Thirdly, Octavian Augustus, having established the Roman monarchy, honored them with this law: "Whoever you are who has served in the military with us for ten years, provided you are forty years old—whether you earned your pay <note>original: "stipendia"</note> as a horseman or a foot soldier—be free from military service hereafter. Be a **Hero** and a veteran soldier. Let no one bar you from the city, the forum, the temple, hospitality, or home. Let no one charge you with a crime, impose a burden upon you, or seek money from you. If you commit any fault, look only to the Emperor’s vengeance <note>original: "Cæsaris uindictam"; meaning they were subject only to the Emperor's personal jurisdiction</note>. Whatever shameful acts men commit, let them fear you as their judge and messenger, whether they be private citizens or princes. Whatever you say or affirm, let no one prove false. Let all paths and places be free and open to you. In the palaces of princes, let there be a table of food and drink for you. Receive a daily stipend from the public treasury to maintain yourself and your house. The woman you take as a lawful wife shall be preferred above all other women. Whomever you reproach or call infamous, let that man be rejected and infamous. As a **Hero**, carry the arms, insignia, names, and ornaments that befit Kings. Whatever you wish to say or do, do it anywhere among the clans, places, and nations. If anyone does you injury, let him lose his head <note>original: "ceruice careto"; literally "be without a neck"</note>."

<margin>
Charlemagne concerning Heralds.
</margin>
Lastly, Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolus Magnus"</note>, after the title of the Empire was transferred to the Germans and after the Saxons and Lombards were conquered, being called Caesar and Augustus, granted them this honor, saying: "My soldiers, you shall be called **Heroes**, the companions of Kings and the judges of crimes. Live hereafter free from labor; advise Kings in the name of the public; correct shameful deeds; favor women; help orphans; surround Princes with your counsel; and seek food, clothing, and pay from them. If anyone denies these, let him be inglorious and infamous. If anyone brings injury upon you, let him acknowledge himself guilty of high treason <note>original: "reum se maiestatis"; the crime of violating the majesty of the sovereign</note>..."

Fol. cxxi.

<insert>**MEDICINE**</insert>

...but we warn you, lest you stain so much honor and such great privilege, earned by the just labor of wars, by drunkenness, or buffoonery, or any other vice; lest what we bestow upon you for glory should turn to your punishment—the right to exact which, should you perhaps overstep, we reserve perpetually for ourselves and our successors, the Kings of the Romans. And such is the "magnificence" of the Heralds, whom the ancient custom of the times considers great because they are permitted to disparage even the greatest men with impunity.

¶ But now let us hasten from Military Service and Nobility to **MEDICINE**, which is itself also a certain art of homicide, entirely mechanical, even though it presumes it can be elevated by the title of "Philosophy." It even ambitions for the seats next to **Theology**, above **Jurisprudence** <note>Law or legal science</note>, which is the source of the greatest contention between Physicians and Jurists. For the Physicians argue: since there are three types of goods in order—those of the soul, the body, and fortune—the Theologian cares for the first, the Physician for the second, and the Jurist for the third. From this, they claim that the middle seats are owed to the Physicians above the Jurists, insofar as the strength and health of the body surpass the riches of Fortune.

<margin>
The witty response of a certain judge concerning the precedence of medicine and law.
</margin>
But a certain Judge <note>original: "Praetor"</note> settled this dispute with a witty question: he asked those litigants what custom and order was observed in leading criminals to execution—which one went first and which followed, the **Thief** or the **Executioner**? When they responded that the Thief goes first and the Executioner follows, he gave his sentence: "Therefore, let the Jurists go first, and let the Physicians follow." He was noting the notorious robbery of the former, and the reckless homicides of the latter. 

But let us return to Medicine. There are many sects <note>original: "hæreses"; in this context, it refers to schools of thought or medical denominations</note> within it. There is one they call the Rational, or Sophistic, or Dogmatic school, which Hippocrates, Diocles, Chrysippus, Caristinus, Praxagoras, and Erasistratus followed. Galen also approved of this school much later; following Hippocrates above all others, he reduced the entire art of healing to the recognition of causes, the knowledge of signs, the qualities of things, and the various temperaments and degrees of bodies. But since this sect deals more with words than with things themselves, it is, I admit, a significant part of Natural Philosophy; but for healing...

<meta>This page continues the critique of the medical profession. The previous page ended with a judge asking a witty question about the precedence of physicians over jurists. This page begins by concluding that theoretical or "Rational" medicine is useless for the sick, before categorizing the more practical branches of the field.</meta>

->### ON VANITY<-

...nevertheless, it is not particularly necessary for the sick—not to say it is even destructive—insofar as it relegates the health and well-being of men to certain twisted sophisms <note>Clever but fallacious arguments used to deceive</note> rather than to sincere medicines that might actually heal diseases. Being occupied with scholastic syllogisms <note>Formal logical arguments used in medieval universities</note>, this field is ignorant of solitudes, forests, and gardens, and knows nothing of herbs and medicines. For this reason, Serapion <note>Serapion of Alexandria (3rd century BCE), a founder of the Empirical school of medicine</note> declared that this **Rational Medicine** <term>Rational Medicine: A school of thought (also called Dogmatism) that relied on theory and logic regarding the hidden causes of disease, rather than just clinical observation.</term> had nothing to do with the art of healing.

<margin>The twofold operational medicine.</margin>
There is, therefore, another faction of Medicine that is entirely mercenary and mechanical, and from which, even to this day, Physicians take their name. For this reason, they call it "operational" medicine, which is divided into the **Empirical** and the **Methodical**. It is of this branch that we speak here. They call it **Empirical** from "experiments" <note>The Latin *experimentis* here refers to practical experience and clinical observation</note>. Its leaders were Serapion, Heraclides, and both the Apollonii; these were followed later among the Latins by Marcus Cato, Caius Valgius, Pomponius, Leneus, Cassius Felix, Aruntius, Cornelius Celsus, and Pliny, along with many others.

From this foundation, Hierophilus of Chalcedon later constructed the **Methodical** school. From long experience—the mistress of all things—he reduced medicine to certain rules. These were afterwards proven with the strongest arguments by Asclepiades, Themiso, and Archigenes. However, it was Thessalus the Italian who fully embraced it; according to Varro, he did away with all the decrees of his predecessors and, as if seized by a certain madness, spoke out against all the physicians of the previous age.

<margin>Arab physicians.</margin>
After these men, many "barbarian" philosophers of foreign nations wrote on the subject. Among them, the glory of the **Arabs** grew to such an extent that they seemed to many to be the very inventors of this art. Indeed, they would easily seem able to claim that title for themselves, were it not for the original Greek and Latin names they used, which indicate the true origin of the art. Hence, the volumes of Avicenna, Rhazes, and Averroes <note>Influential Islamic scholars whose medical texts were standard in Europe for centuries</note> have been received with authority equal to the books of Hippocrates and Galen. They have gained such trust that if anyone presumes to heal a person without following their decrees, he is seen as openly squandering the public health.

<margin>Controversy</margin>
However, although these factions of Physicians are few, there is no less contention and "battle of opinions" among them than there is among the Philosophers. For concerning sperm—which is the genital seed—hear with what "old wives' reasonings" they contend: Pythagoras says it is the foam of the most useful blood...

<margin>The physicians on sperm.</margin>
...called it the foam of the blood, or the most useful byproduct of food. <meta>catchword: as</meta>

Gentile da Foligno and Giacomo da Forlì, not without a notable error, teach that excrement is produced in the stomach. Asclepiades and his followers, however, believe that foods are not digested, but rather that raw materials are distributed throughout the whole body; they further say that the doctrines of all their predecessors are vain and superfluous. I pass over their judgments of urine—not yet perfectly understood by them—and the incomprehensible intervals of the pulse. <margin>Hippocrates' error.</margin> Indeed, even Hippocrates, whom they worship as a God, does not only differ from others in many respects but also erred shamefully. For in his book *On the Nature of the Child*, he says: "The bird is generated from the yellow <note>The yolk</note> of the egg, but receives nourishment and growth from the white within the egg." Aristotle proves this false in his book *On Animals* and in his book *On the Generation of Animals*, arguing against Alcmaeon, who agreed with Hippocrates; Aristotle concludes: "The origin of the chick is in the white, while food is sought from the yellow through the umbilical cord." Pliny also adheres to this opinion, saying: "The animal itself takes its body from the white liquid of the egg; its food is in the yellow." Is not even that aphorism of Hippocrates a lie? "A woman does not suffer from gout unless her menstruation has ceased," <note>original: "Mulier non podagrisat, nisi mēstrua illi defecerint"</note> even though many women who still have their monthly flow suffer from gout.

<margin>OPERATIVE MEDICINE.</margin> ¶ Furthermore, the entire **OPERATIVE** <note>The practical application of medicine, as opposed to theory</note> art of healing is built upon no other foundation than deceptive experiments, and is strengthened by the thin credulity of the sick. It is no less poisonous than beneficial, such that very often—and almost always—there is more danger from the physician and the medicine than from the disease itself. This is something the very "Princes" of this art frankly admit: namely Hippocrates, saying: "This art is difficult, and experiment is deceptive"; <note>A reference to Hippocrates' first aphorism: "Life is short, art is long, opportunity fleeting, experiment treacherous, judgment difficult."</note> and Avicenna saying: "The faith and hope of the sick person toward the physician and the medicine often achieve more than the medicine itself does with the physician"; and Galen: "It is difficult to find a remedy that is greatly profitable without simultaneously being harmful in some way." And some other among them says: "The knowledge of medicines is delightful, like all other things that consist of art and rules, but the practice of medicine is a matter of chance." Let the fortunate sick go then, and put their trust in dangerous experiments and chance! But as Pliny says, so sweet is the hope each person has for themselves...

...so that he might be held in great authority and simultaneously be admired, he makes a point of observing specific hours and attaching physical amulets and charms <note>original: "alligationes suspensionesq;"</note>. He does not administer medicines or potions except by the Mathematical Ephemeris <note>A set of tables used by astrologers to determine the positions of celestial bodies; here the doctor is using astrology to time the taking of medicine to appear more scientific or mystical</note>. Furthermore, he arrogates power over the pharmacist for himself and orders that all things be dispensed in his presence. He cleverly pretends to choose the finest spices and ingredients, though he often does not know how to distinguish the counterfeit from the true, and is completely ignorant of the things themselves beyond their names.

<margin>
Doctors prolong
illnesses for
the rich.

If the patient is rich or of great authority, then to gain more profit and fame for himself, he prolongs the disease as much as possible and restores health only gradually, even if he were able to drive out the illness at once with a single medicine. Sometimes, indeed, having worsened the disease with his own medications before removing it, he brings the man to the very brink of death, so that he may then be proclaimed to have delivered him from a most severe and dangerous sickness. 

But if a patient ever falls into his hands struggling with a more serious disease, and the doctor recognizes it as a terminal evil with a doubtful outcome, then he resorts to these stratagems: with a stern face he prescribes laws for living, orders unusual things, forbids accustomed ones, criticizes what is offered, denounces what is shown, threatens death while promising life, and demands great rewards. If he doubts the outcome, he advises that a college <note>A formal consultation or assembly of multiple physicians</note> be summoned and requests a partner, so that he may treat the patient more securely—or, as is often the case, kill him more cautiously—lest another doctor arriving later, who might restore the sick man alone, should snatch away the fame, praise, and profit for himself. 

If things go badly for the patient, or if he kills him unexpectedly through remarkable ignorance, the doctor excuses himself by claiming it was a suffocating flow of catarrh <note>In the humoral theory of the time, "catarrh" was a fluid believed to drop from the brain into the body; a "suffocating" flow was a common excuse for sudden death</note> or some other similar sudden accident and incurable case. He then sharply accuses the patient of disobedience, or the guardians of negligence; he blames his colleagues, or shoves the fault onto the pharmacist. In this way, he ensures that no sick person appears to have died except by their own fault, and no one appears to have recovered except by the physician’s blessing.

doctors.
</margin>

Antiquity tells the fable that he was the first discoverer of Medicine, begotten from the mind of Jove and destined for the earth through the life-force of the Sun. Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work 'De Medicina'</note>, however, admits he was a man, though later received into the number of the Gods. Many others assert that he was born of a meretricious and incestuous union with Coronis, a beautiful but lowly woman, whom the Priests in the temple of Apollo often subjected to adulterous embraces; it was they who fashioned him as the son of a God. Everyone, however, agrees on this: that this God was so wicked that there was need of Jove’s lightning bolt to restrain him. Concerning this, <margin>Lactantius on Aesculapius.</margin> Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) who often critiqued pagan mythology</note> wrote thus to the Emperor Constantine: "Aesculapius himself, born not without the shame of Apollo, what else did he do worthy of divine honors, except that he healed Hippolytus? He certainly had a more famous death, for he deserved to be struck by lightning by God" <note>original: "Aesculapius & ipse non sine flagitio Apollinis natus, quid fecit aliud diuinis honoribus dignum, nisi quod sanauit Hippolytum? mortem sane habuit clariorem quod à Deo meruit fulminari"</note>.

But in truth, doctors are the most wicked, most discordant, most envious, and most lying of all men. Indeed, they all disagree with one another to such an extent that no doctor can be found who approves a prescription written by another without some exception, addition, or change. On the contrary, he will tear it apart and bite at it, purely so that he himself does not appear to be the lesser doctor; he feels he must detract something even from another’s best counsel, or add something to those things which are already often far too numerous. <margin>Proverb. The controversy of doctors.</margin> Hence, it has finally turned into a Proverb: *The envy and discord of doctors.* For whatever one approves, the other laughs at, and there is nothing certain among them. All their promises are but "flying trifles" and mere lies. Because of this, when the common people wish to point out someone as a notorious liar, they say to him: "You lie like a doctor." The highest effort of their wits is turned toward this: that in the pursuit of thinking up new things, the correct deeds of the ancients are neglected and condemned.

They are arrogant, and what is more, they even accuse those who have died of "intemperance" <note>Overindulgence or lack of self-control in diet or lifestyle.</note>. By night and day, the horrifying images and shadows of the sick haunt their imaginations, and countless homicides disturb their consciences. Their whole exercise is spent in stinking, squalid places and base cares, consisting of an obscene craftsmanship. For the sake of infamous profit, they are always hanging around the bedpans, sewers, and latrines of the sick, nesting in human excrement like the filthy **hoopoe** bird <note>original: "upupa"; a bird which in medieval bestiaries was famously said to build its nest out of dung.</note>. Do you not see them daily, how they pace about the city with their fingers ringed, in their wide, pale robes, and with troubled or pallid faces? With a headlong and most wretched pace, in hope of a little profit, they run from apothecary to apothecary, searching and begging. Whenever someone offers urine to be inspected or a dung-basin, they are the most keen-scented of all men—flocking like hooded vultures to carcasses, so these men flock to excrement. <margin>Epithets for physicians in Old Comedy.</margin>For this reason, he calls the physician a <term>Scatophagus</term> <note>From the Greek *skatos* (dung) and *phagein* (to eat).</note>, a term signifying those who feed on the leftovers of food. From this come the terms <term>Scatomancy</term>, <term>Uromancy</term>, and <term>Drimymancy</term> <note>Divination by means of dung, urine, and pungent fluids like sweat or tears.</note>, which are the names for the divinations or prognostications physicians derive from feces and urine. Even today, many people 
<margin>Physicians excluded from the tables of refined people.</margin>
exclude physicians—along with midwives and executioners—from their tables and banquets, or will only receive them with separate linens and cups. In this regard, one might rightfully be angry at the detestable custom of many Princes who admit such pestilential men to their tables. Not only do they allow them into their bedchambers in the morning, but also into daily gatherings, where they are always infected with the fresh, plague-like vapors of the sick. Indeed, once a physician is invited to a banquet, even amidst the food and wine, he will discourse upon dung, urine, sweat, pus, vomit, and menstrual blood. He will treat of epilepsy, leprosy, internal organs, the itch, and plagues, and by the filthiness of his speech, he will turn a banquet otherwise prepared with the most elegant delicacies into an occasion for nausea. 

<margin>The physician is unfit for civil business.</margin>Admit the physician also, if you wish, to your civil consultations; you will find nothing more inept or tasteless. This is perhaps because the discipline of physicians (as their own **Conciliator** <note>A reference to the famous medieval physician Pietro d'Abano, known as "The Conciliator" for his attempts to reconcile Greek and Arabic medicine.</note> says) is not concerned with virtues or good morals, and because (as he also says) a naturally honest physician must be of bad character <note>An ironic or paradoxical claim often attributed to the profession in satirical works.</note>. We know that in many cities it was provided for by public decrees and popular votes that physicians should not be admitted to councils nor hold magistracies. This was perhaps not so much because they are inept, frivolous, and ill-mannered, but because they are always filthy. Through their constant handling of the sick and their waste, they are so contagious that they defile not only those who come near them, but even the very benches they sit upon and the marble they touch. <note>This epigram mocks the idea that even an indestructible stone statue would succumb to a doctor's meddling.</note>

<margin>The consultations of physicians regarding the sick.</margin>
When they gather for their medical consultation to examine what the patient may have urinated or excreted that night—acting like the **Ephors of Sparta** <note>The Ephors were high-ranking Spartan magistrates who exercised strict, often harsh, oversight over the kings and citizens.</note> about to pronounce a sentence of life or death—it is a wonder, yet a lamentable one, how they then engage in wretched altercations around the patient’s bed. No two of them agree, as if they were hired not to cure, but to debate. 
<margin>A saying of Menander.</margin>
Indeed, to the sick person himself—to whom (according to the Greek verse of **Menander**, which in Latin says: *A talkative doctor is a second disease to the sick man* <note>original: "Medicus garrulus ægrotanti alter morbus."</note>) almost all speech is annoying—they offer their orations rather than their aid. In a scholarly fashion, they produce several **aphorisms** <term>Aphorisms: Short, pithy statements of medical principles, specifically those of Hippocrates.</term> for their own ostentation, which they keep always ready for any use. They invoke **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, **Avicenna**, **Rhazes**, **Averroes**, the **Conciliator** <note>Pietro d’Abano (c. 1250–1316), a famous physician and philosopher known as "The Conciliator" for attempting to reconcile Greek and Arabic medicine.</note>, and their other "Gods"—whose names and titles are enough for them to win trust and a reputation for learning among the ignorant common folk. After they have fought for a long time over causes, signs, symptoms, humors, and the **critical day** <term>Critical day: In medieval medicine, specific days of an illness (like the 7th or 14th) when a patient was expected to either recover or die.</term> in a serious but undecided discord, they finally settle on the remedy—which ought to have been the head and tail of the entire business—with a most cold and indifferent decree. Because of their mutual envy, none of them is willing to share his "secrets" (as they call them) with his rivals, as if what they gave to others would perish for themselves. Instead, they fall back on the common **methodical** practice; and if that fails them, they flee to **empirical** trial as if to a "sacred anchor" <note>The "sacred anchor" (sacram ancoram) was a classical proverb for a last resort.</note>, so that where reason did not restore the patient, recklessness might help. They say it is better to try a risky remedy than none at all. 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 10</margin>
If they are less favorable toward the patient, or if (as **Ecclesiasticus** says) a "lingering sickness" weighs him down, they abandon him to **prognostics** <note>Predictions of the outcome of a disease.</note>, saying: "Hippocrates forbids giving medicine to those who are beyond hope." Or, if they are a little more religious, they cast the blame for the disease upon one of the Saints, or they prescribe the final "medicine," which is: **"Take one Notary, seven witnesses, and add a priest."** <note>The author jokes that the doctor's final "prescription" is for the patient to write their last will and testament and receive the last rites.</note>

Rhazes’ wicked counsel.
</margin>
...with as much blessed water and oil as is sufficient, and set your house in order, for you shall die. <note>This phrase refers to the performance of Last Rites—extreme unction—and the biblical warning given to King Hezekiah in Isaiah 38:1: "Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live."</note> From this, **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>—well aware of both the gullible stupidity of the sick and the argumentative ignorance of physicians—offered advice to both the patient and the doctor that was not without caution. He suggests in his *Aphorisms* that only one physician should be chosen. For, he says, the error of a single man does not bring about great infamy, and the benefit one doctor achieves is highly praised; however, he who employs a great many doctors falls into the greatest of errors. This is what Rhazes says. That ancient inscription upon a monument also bears witness to this: that he perished because of a "crowd of doctors." There is also that Greek proverb:

<margin>
Proverb.
</margin>
*The entrance of many doctors has destroyed the sick man.* <note>original: "Multorum Medicorum introitus ægrum perdidit."</note> There is also that saying of the dying Emperor **Hadrian**: *A crowd of doctors destroys a Prince.* Therefore, there is no advice more useful for preserving life and health than to abstain from doctors. For the health of the body is owed to God, not to physicians. For this reason,

<margin>2 Chronicles 16</margin>
**Asa, King of Judah**, was rebuked by the Prophet of the Lord because, in his illness, he did not seek the Lord but instead trusted in the art of physicians. <note>Referencing 2 Chronicles 16:12, where King Asa is criticized for turning to doctors rather than God for a foot ailment.</note> Those who surrender themselves to the advice of such men cannot truly be healthy; for no life is more wretched than that which is led under the reliance on their "aid." Grant it to be true—let the physicians know (and would that they truly did know!) all the powers and potencies of the elements, roots, herbs, flowers, fruits, seeds, and even of animals and minerals, and of all things that mother Nature produces—yet they still cannot make a man immortal with all these virtues. Nay, they cannot even do the lesser thing: always cure a man suffering from even the slightest disease. Oh, how often has a medicine that ought to have helped failed to do so? How often has that which ought to have been purged remained? How often, when the patient suffers a relapse, must he be treated all over again? And finally, after much labor and expense, either then or shortly after—even with the doctors standing right there—the patient must die. What hope then is left for us in doctors, if, as their own **Hippocrates** says, *experience is fallacious*? <note>original: "experientia fallax." This is from the very first of Hippocrates' Aphorisms.</note> What certainty can physicians promise, if it is true what **Pliny** writes: that no art is more inconstant than medicine, and none is more frequently changed?

<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s critique of the medical profession, shifting from the danger of having too many doctors to the historical and practical benefits of having none at all. He argues that health is better maintained through nature and simple experience than through the complex, guesswork-based treatments of professional physicians.</meta>

### OF THE SCIENCES. Book VI.
<note>page number CXVII (117)</note>

<margin>
Many nations live without physicians. A **Spartan** aphorism.
</margin>
Many nations once were, and still are, living without physicians; we see these people remain robust well beyond a decrepit age and live for more than a hundred years. This is quite the contrary to those more "delicate" peoples who live by the promises and efforts of physicians, who for the most part grow old and perish in middle age. Indeed, the physicians themselves are more often ill than other men, and almost always sickly, dying at a premature age. Hence, that **Spartan** <note>original: "Lacon," referring to the inhabitants of Laconia, of which Sparta was the capital.</note> responded to someone saying, "You have no illness," by saying, "**Because I do not use a physician.**" And when the same man said again, "You have become an old man," he replied, "**Because I never used a physician,**" showing that there is no more certain way to health and old age than to have lacked physicians. If anyone should say that many have recovered by the help of physicians, we shall answer that, on the contrary, even more have died for whom the labor of physicians was of no use. We shall throw back at those restless people that "little net" <note>original: "verriculum," likely referring to a short, catching verse or epigram.</note> of **Ausonius** <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310–395 AD), a Roman poet and teacher.</note>: *To escape...*

<margin>
The **Arcadians** did not use physicians.
</margin>
*...by the help of Fate, and not the Physician.* <note>original: "Euadere Fati ope non Medici."</note> For in olden times, the **Arcadians** <note>Inhabitants of a mountainous region of the Peloponnese, often associated with a simple, pastoral lifestyle.</note> did not use manufactured medicines; rather, as **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the "Natural History."</note> records, they used spring milk, because at that time the herbs are most swollen with life-giving juices and the richer pastures would provide healing. They chose cow's milk above all others because cows in the spring truly eat every kind of herb. The **Spartans**, as well as the **Babylonians**, **Egyptians**, and **Lusitanians** <note>People of Lusitania, roughly modern Portugal.</note> (as **Herodotus** and **Strabo** <note>Ancient Greek historians and geographers.</note> testify), rejected all physicians. Instead, they would carry the sick out into the marketplaces and streets, so that those who had escaped a similar disease—or knew how someone else had escaped—might advise them with the remedies they had experienced themselves. They judged

<margin>
Experience is of the greatest value for the method of curing.
</margin>
(as **Cornelius Celsus** <note>A Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work "De Medicina."</note> also asserts) that nothing contributes more to the method of healing itself than experience. It is well known that the most learned physicians are very often defeated by a rustic **old woman**, who achieves with a single plant or a little herb what the most famous physicians could not do with all their precious and elaborate drugs. For while they—confounding the patient with inexplicable and monstrous mixtures (even though Nature has given so many things, any one of which might suffice as a remedy)—strive to drive out diseases through a composite combination of diverse things, they proceed more by guesswork than by cause or reason. They make the whole art of healing nothing but chance and conjecture. Whereas this benefit of a single, simple medicine...

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous leaf, concluding the word "medicine" [medicinæ] and further contrasting the "vanity" of professional doctors with the simple, natural wisdom of common folk.</meta>

# ON VANITY

...of [medicine], knowing the power and quality of plants, and having been proven by the solid forces of Nature, resolves difficult illnesses. On the other hand, those professional physicians seek out expensive ingredients from the furthest reaches of India or Gades <note>Modern-day Cádiz, Spain, then considered the edge of the western world.</note>—persuading the public that if a thing is not costly, it cannot be useful—and they promise a health that is for sale at a great price. 

But this natural way finds health in the easiest, commonly available domestic plants, which everyone can easily grow in their own gardens; it does not so much "promise" health as restore it. Furthermore, these doctors are taught from deceitful books and illustrated manuals; they take up the very difficult work of healing with a certain bold recklessness and refined chatter for the sake of profit. 

By contrast, the simple method contemplates and learns from the earth and fields every single plant—their colors, shapes, tastes, smells, and varieties—and having tested what they can do in diseases and other conditions, it gives the most certain remedies to everyone for free.

<margin>
Physicians have been taught many things by simple women.
</margin>

Even the most eminent of the Physicians themselves confess that they have learned many excellent remedies from simple women <note>original: "mulierculis," a diminutive for women, often used dismissively by elites, but Agrippa uses it here to show that even "unlearned" women possess greater practical knowledge than the "learned" doctors.</note>, remedies worthy of being inserted into their own books and passed on to posterity as superior. For example, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians in history.</note> praises a medicine against headache that was handed down to him by a woman. 

But if Medicine, which ought to bring about a balanced temperament of health, consists in the proportion and balance of things relative to one another—both among themselves and with the qualities of the body to which they are given—then consider this: the most diligent care of the ancient Physicians was spent in proportioning and mixing medicines through just and harmonic weights <note>Early medicine used a system of "degrees" (hot, cold, moist, dry) and believed drugs had to be balanced like musical harmonies to match a patient's temperament.</note>, leaving it to those who followed to proportion these to the bodies of the sick. 

What boldness and impudence is this, then, not only to change these ancient proportions, but to add to them, or to neglect and ignore them entirely? Whence it happens that just as a harmonious mixture of a drug should bring health, so its dissonance induces pain, shivering, a worsening of the disease, and sometimes even death. 

Therefore, a simple country woman <note>original: "rustica Anus," literally a rustic old woman or "crone."</note> heals more safely with one or two garden plants and a medicine perfected by nature’s work, than that Physician with his monstrous, expensive drugs forged from doubtful conjecture. Many most excellent Philosophers and Physicians were of that same opinion: namely, that one should not heal except with the simplest things.

Fo. CXXVIII.

->OF THE SCIENCES.<-

<margin>Simple medicines.</margin>
From this, those who have scrutinized and tested the powers of **simples** <note>Medicines made from a single ingredient, usually a plant, rather than a complex mixture.</note> have left behind for us, their posterity, excellent volumes. Such were the books written by **Chrysippus** on Cabbage, **Pythagoras** on the Squill <note>A flowering bulb used in ancient medicine as a diuretic or heart stimulant.</note>, **Marchion** on the Radish, **Diocles** on the Turnip, **Phanias** on the Nettle, **Apuleius** on Betony, and many other ancients who wrote on other plants. But those "apothecary doctors" <note>original: "officinarum Medici." Agrippa refers to physicians who rely on the complex, expensive recipes prepared in pharmacies rather than using raw nature.</note> of the shops not only disregard these authors, but even mock them—calling those who study simple ingredients "simpletons" <note>A pun on the word "simples." In Latin, "simplices" can mean both "unmixed medicines" and "simple-minded people."</note>. Therefore, I say that those physicians who heal through simple remedies are not only to be consulted, but I dissuade no one from following them. Truly, however, I advise that those worshippers of the apothecary shops should be fled from and driven away as if they were sorcerers and evildoers. They trade in our misfortunes with their monstrous compositions and cast lots <note>original: "mittunt sortes," meaning they gamble or use guesswork with the patient's life.</note> over our lives.

For since compound medicines must be forged from many different and conflicting species, it is impossible—or at least extremely difficult—for a doctor to determine anything certain about them, except by mere opinion, estimation, and conjecture. Since there are often innumerable ingredients, each of which might seem helpful on its own, the doctor merely piles together whatever chance or a fluke of memory happens to offer him at that moment, or whatever he feels inclined toward by some other internal or hidden instinct. Hence it happens that the power and effect of that compound drug come not so much from the potency of the simple ingredients, but from the doctor’s own fortunate or unfortunate whim—insofar as he is led to choose these things over others by some hidden influence, whether natural, celestial, demonic, or purely accidental. And this is what is commonly said, and what they themselves admit: that one doctor is more "fortunate" than another, and very
<margin>One doctor is luckier than another in curing the sick.</margin>
frequently the unlearned one is more successful than the learned. Indeed, I have seen and known a most literate physician who was so "unlucky" that out of many sick people, scarcely a few escaped alive from his hands. I knew another, a mere **smatterer** <note>original: "semiscialum," someone with only a superficial or half-learned knowledge.</note>, who successfully cured almost all his patients, even many who had been abandoned by others as hopeless cases. Furthermore, I remember reading about a doctor in whose hands any nobles or great lords who fell would survive, yet all the commoners and 
peasants...

<meta>This page continues Agrippa's scathing critique of the medical profession. Having previously praised simple herbal remedies, he now attacks "apothecary medicine" as a form of legalized poisoning, citing Roman history and classical philosophy to argue that physicians are often more dangerous than the diseases they claim to treat.</meta>

### OF THE VANITY OF SCIENCES

<margin>The Romans once drove the physicians out of the City.</margin>
...that the peasants should perish or be gravely endangered. It is easy now to see that this apothecary medicine <note>original: "officinariam Medicinam," referring to the commercial medicine sold in shops/pharmacies.</note>, in which the physician’s luck carries more weight than his learning, is entirely—or for the most part—a form of sorcery <note>original: "sortilegam," literally "lot-casting" or divination, implying that the doctors are merely gambling with the lives of their patients.</note>. Therefore, it should be driven far away and condemned as if it were the work of poisoners and assassins.

Accordingly, the Romans once, under Cato the Censor, drove all physicians out of both the City of Rome and all of Italy. They loathed the physicians' deadly lies and cruelty, seeing that they clearly killed many more than they cured. Furthermore, being most skilled in poisons, these doctors could easily be led by hatred, ambition, or greed to administer poison instead of a remedy and, for a promised fee, plot against men's lives. Such was the case with the physician of Pyrrhus—whether he was Timochares, as Gellius claims, or Nicias, as others say—who promised Fabricius that he would kill his master <note>King Pyrrhus of Epirus.</note> with Medicine. Fabricius detested such a crime and, although Pyrrhus was his enemy, warned him by letter to beware of his doctor. Regarding this, Claudianus says:

> The Romans always despised the servants of crimes,
> When the physician promised to mix harmful poisons for his Master;
> Fabricius sent the fraud, now exposed, back to the King:
> For though he sought him in hostile war, he refused
> To commit a wickedness by the hand of a servant.

<margin>Pliny.</margin>
Cato writes similar things about Greek physicians in his letters to his son, as recorded by Pliny: "They have sworn among themselves to kill all 'Barbarians' <note>To the Greeks of that era, Romans were considered barbarians.</note> with Medicine, but they do this very thing for pay, so that they might be trusted and thus more easily destroy us." Shortly after, Pliny adds: "From this come many plots concerning wills, and indeed even adulteries in the houses of Princes," as was evident in the case of Eudemus <note>The physician Eudemus was famously implicated in the poisoning of Drusus Caesar, son of the Emperor Tiberius, after being seduced by Drusus's wife, Livia Julia.</note> with Livia, the wife of Drusus Caesar.

<margin>Socrates according to Plato.</margin>
Even Socrates himself, in the works of Plato, forbade the multiplication of physicians in the city. It would be expedient even to this day for the Republic if there were none, or very few, and if a law existed to punish their malice—arising from both ignorance and negligence—as a capital crime. For it is a capital matter, and it makes no difference whether it was through unskillfulness or neglect, folly or malice, that a physician has wrongly or intentionally offered poison instead of a drug and brought a man into the danger of his life. And it is not (as Pliny says) that for a physician, a man...

<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s vitriolic attack on the medical profession. He has just finished arguing that physicians are essentially state-sanctioned killers, comparing them unfavorably to the Romans who once banned them for their cruelty and greed.</meta>

### OF THE SCIENCES. Folio CXXIX.

<margin>A comparison of the Physician with the executioner.</margin>
...to have killed a man was a matter of the highest impunity. They certainly share one common honor with the Executioner: namely, to kill men for a fee. And while the law establishes punishment for homicide for everyone else, granting no one impunity, these men alone receive rewards for it. However, there is this difference: the Executioner only kills the guilty by a judicial sentence, whereas the Physician, beyond any judgment, slays even the innocent. Therefore, it was not without good reason that the constitutions of the Popes <margin>The practice of medicine is prohibited for Clerics acting as physicians.</margin> barred the Clergy from practicing medicine. For the medical art is such a bloody business that if it were lawful for Priests and Clerics to practice Medicine, it would also be lawful for them to act as Executioners. 

Nor should it be thought that Portius Cato imprudently once banned Physicians from the City. This was because they are always hunting for fame in this science through some novelty; then, when they are ashamed to bring nothing new and yet cling to the footsteps of others, they conduct experiments through deaths. They learn their art through our dangers, trafficking in our lives. They prolong the illnesses of wicked men <note>original: "malarum hominum," likely referring to the physicians' corrupt clients or perhaps a typo for "malorum," meaning "illnesses" or "evils."</note> which could be removed in a very short time, and not rarely even worsen them for greater profit. To counter this fraud, among the Egyptians, Physicians treated the bodies of the sick at the patients' own risk for the first three days, but after the third day, they did so at their own risk <note>Meaning the physician became legally liable, or even faced the death penalty, if the patient died after the third day of treatment.</note>.

<margin>APOTHECARIES</margin>
¶ And now also, following their Coans <note>Referring to the followers of Hippocrates of Cos, the father of medicine.</note>, they call them Apothecaries and <term>Pharmacopolas</term> <note>translated from Greek: "medicine sellers" or pharmacists.</note>. As the proverb says, their labels promise remedies, but their jars contain poisons—or, as Homer sings, "mixed drugs, many healthful and many harmful." Since these men have no desire to suffer financial loss, they compel us to buy our own death with a great sum of money. Meanwhile, <margin>Pharmacists provide one thing for another.</margin> they offer one thing instead of another, or mix in rotten, aged, and spoiled drugs, often giving a deadly potion instead of a life-saving one. They sell plasters, eye-salves, ointments, lozenges, and other drugs that have long since been touched by decay, traded only for the profit of the shops and concocted from the dregs and filth of the ingredients themselves. Being unable to distinguish these things, they trust <margin>On foreign merchants and their lies.</margin> foreign merchants <note>original: "barbaris," often referring to non-Latin/Greek speaking traders, particularly Arab or Levantine merchants who supplied the spice and drug trade.</note> who corrupt everything with frauds and adulteration. I could also show here their pernicious disagreements concerning <term>Simples</term> <note>Individual medicinal herbs or minerals used as ingredients, as opposed to "compounds."</note> which they use, their knowledge of medicines, and their errors concerning the names of medicinal things...

But today, the simples are neglected and not even recognized. 

<margin>Note the pernicious origins of error in the State caused by Physicians and Pharmacists.</margin>
Medicines are produced only from those two "lights" of the <term>Apothecaries</term><note>Early pharmacists.</note> and the "treasury of the Druggists," namely the <term>Antidotaries</term><note>Reference books containing recipes for medicinal compounds.</note> of <term>Mesue</term> and <term>Nicolaus</term><note>Johannes Mesue and Nicolaus Salernitanus were the standard medieval authorities on pharmacy.</note> and others, adorned with painted and gilded titles. And so it happens that while these Physicians, looking after their own leisure, entrust the lives of men to the reliability of the Apothecaries—and the Apothecaries, without letters and without knowledge, trust in barbarian merchants—they mix things together for the profit of the shop, resulting in much more danger from the medicine than from the disease. Fol. CXXX.
### OF THE SCIENCES.

[...they] may receive; and it would greatly benefit the health of men and the Republic
<margin>Agrippa</margin> to completely forbid all foreign and exotic drugs (which, moreover, are increased to such a great price by thieving merchants to the detriment of the Republic), and to bring all physicians into order, and to restrain the pharmacists, and to prescribe a law for them, such as
<margin>A law once prescribed for pharmacists in Rome.</margin> 
Nero is read to have enacted in Rome while it was still in a better state; by which law they are compelled to use only those drugs which our own world produces, since these are more suited to each of our natures, as well as being far fresher, more choice, and obtainable with less difficulty, expense, and danger. For as for foreign things, the greatest part is suspect, as they are very often sophisticated, adulterated, rejected, or suffocated in the ship, or submerged in the bilge-water, or corrupted by age, or collected at an improper time or place (from which very often the greatest danger looms). For immature <term>colocynth</term><note>original: "coloquintida"; also known as bitter apple, a powerful and potentially toxic purgative.</note> draws out blood and kills, and that which grows solitary or unique is poison. Similarly, the male <term>agaric</term><note>A type of wood-rotting fungus used in ancient medicine, specifically the "Larch agaric."</note> is deadly, and that which is old is ruinous. All <term>scammony</term><note>A resin from the root of Convolvulus scammonia, used as a harsh laxative.</note> is sophisticated; likewise with <term>Lemnian earth</term><note>A medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos, historically stamped with a seal (terra sigillata) to guarantee its authenticity.</note>, and trust in the seals has perished. Now, I ask you, what necessity is there to use these foreign things, if our own land produces the same or similar things of equal efficacy? Or is it not exceptionally foolish to prefer to seek from India what we have at home? Thinking that neither our own land nor sea suffices, preferring foreign things to our native ones—a sumptuous frugality—and preferring difficult things to those easily acquired, even those imported from the very ends of the earth. Can no one heal the spleen without <term>ammoniacum</term><note>A medicinal gum resin derived from a Persian herb.</note>? Nor the liver without sandalwood? Or, if we lack <term>bdellium</term><note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum resin similar to myrrh.</note>, will no one cure internal ulcers? Nor will anyone heal the head without musk and ambergris? Nor the stomach without mastic and corals? If these foreign medicines were suited to our bodies, nature (which has provided abundantly for all) would beyond doubt have ensured that these grew among us as well. Did our fathers not live both as long and more healthily than those people? These are therefore the trifles of lazy physicians, who do not seek out our own resources, and the fabrications of pharmacists, who seek not the common health, but

# OF VANITY

<margin>Jeremiah 8:22<note>The margin in the original text reads "Hier. 4," but the quote "Is there no balm in Gilead?" is found in Jeremiah 8:22.</note></margin>
...they seek the profit of their own trade, persuading us that only the most expensive things are of much use. For this they are rebuked through the prophet Jeremiah: *Is there no balm in Gilead? Or is there no physician there?*<note>original: "Nunquid nō est resina in Galaad, aut Medicus non est ibi." This biblical reference suggests that remedies are often available locally if one only looks.</note> Nature produces and tempers herbs for every land and region, for its own people, its own climate, its own sky, and its own age. Granted, certain plants in different places and times may have sharper powers; nevertheless, in any time and climate, they perform the same work according to the location and the temperament of the people. We might allow those expensive and exotic plants to have greater powers, but we should believe them to be healthy only for the people of the climate in which they were created and produced.

But there are also the robberies of the <term>Empirics</term><note>The "Empirics" were a school of medical thought that relied on observation and experience rather than theory, but in Agrippa's time, the term was often used to describe unlearned "quacks."</note> who persuade us that certain monstrous drugs and things exotic to the practice of healing can contribute much, and that our health cannot be maintained without them, testing their own inventions at the expense of the miserable. Hence, they mix vipers, serpents, and all kinds of most noxious reptiles into their <term>antidotes</term><note>Specifically "Theriac," a famous universal antidote of the era that often contained viper flesh.</note>; and as if remedies were failing them, they work human fat into ointments, and offer human flesh preserved with spices—which they call <term>mummy</term><note>original: "mummia." This refers to the gruesome medieval and Renaissance practice of using pulverized human remains as medicine.</note>—to be eaten by men, a wicked crime against Nature.

### SURGERY

<margin>
Surgery
was the
first of the 
healing
arts to be
used.
</margin>
There remains **SURGERY**, the other part of Medicine, which cures the external faults of the body. Its works are manifest and its remedies more secure, for the counsels of the rest of the Physicians are blind. Surgeons see and feel what they are doing, and they change, apply, and remove things as the opportunity arises. Among all the arts of healing, this was the first to come into use. For since men of old exercised themselves in wars and inflicted wounds upon one another, they began to seek remedies for them. They thought that the evils one man had inflicted on another could also be cured by men. However, they estimated other diseases and the torments of the internal organs to be born from the wrath of the Gods, and thus incurable by natural powers. <margin>The inventor of Surgery.</margin> Therefore, the first inventor of Surgery was **Apis**, King of the Egyptians; or, as **Clement of Alexandria** would have it, an even older man, **Mizraim**, the son of **Ham** and grandson of the great **Noah**. But **Aesculapius** was the first to write on the medicine of wounds.

# OF THE SCIENCES. 1131.

Next, those who stood out in <unclear>my</unclear> view were Pythagoras, Empedocles, Parmenides, Democritus, Chiron, and Paeon. Pliny recounts that Archagathus of Peloponnese first practiced this art in Rome; however, because of his severity in cutting and burning, he was publicly called a "wound-healer" <note>original: "vulnerarium"</note>, but the name soon turned into "butcher" <note>original: "carnificem"</note>. Eventually, the whole art was held in loathing and driven out. Thus, Surgery <note>original: "Cheirurgia"</note> is no less famous for the authority of the excellent men of other medical factions, yet it is infamous for the uncleanness of its virulent filth and its cruelty, sticky with blood.

<margin>ANATOMY.</margin>
¶ Yet **ANATOMY** exceeds even this in cruelty. It is a theatrical butchery practiced by both pharmacists and surgeons, wherein they once dissected criminals condemned to public death while they were still alive and breathing, with most savage tortures. But today, out of reverence for the Christian religion, they have become a little milder; having first killed the man—either by their own hand or the executioner’s—upon the dead corpse they then proceed with these sacrificial rites. Tearing the human body apart, they search and peer into the position, order, measurement, workings, nature, and every hidden part of each limb, so that they might learn from it how and in what places to apply cures. This they do with such diligence and a spectacle that is horrendous, abominable, and no less impious.

<margin>VETERINARY MEDICINE.</margin>
¶ There is still another practice of medicine which they call **VETERINARY MEDICINE**, which treats the diseases of brute animals. It is far more certain and useful than the others, and was invented, as they say, by Chiron the Centaur <note>A figure in Greek mythology known for his wisdom and medical skill, often considered the father of veterinary science.</note>, and illustrated by the most noble writers: Columella, Cato, Varro, Pelagonius, and Vegetius <note>These are prominent Roman authors who wrote on agriculture and the care of livestock.</note>.

<margin>Our doctors are unlearned in veterinary matters.</margin>
Yet these ring-wearing doctors <note>original: "annulati"; referring to the rings worn by doctors of high status or academic rank.</note> of ours do not consider this a matter of modesty, but rather they are utterly ignorant of it and despise it. They are so fastidious that, like the hoopoe bird <note>In medieval lore, the hoopoe was believed to feed on or nest in human dung; Agrippa uses this metaphor to mock doctors who focus only on human waste for diagnosis but find animal care beneath them.</note>, they delight in nothing but human filth. Thus, if someone should ask them for a medicine for his donkey or his ox, he would soon receive an insult instead of a remedy, as if it did not pertain to them to know how to heal not only men, but also other animals—especially those that bring benefit to humans. For this reason, King Alfonso of Aragon once [hired] two most experienced doctors of medicine for his horses and dogs...

<margin>
DIETARY MEDICINE.
Asclepiades abolished drugs.
</margin>
¶ There remains still **DIETARY MEDICINE**, of which Asclepiades stood out as the leader above the rest. He, having largely abolished the use of drugs, reduced the whole art of Medicine to a regimen of living: to the quantity and nature of foods, and the seasonings of side-dishes. Other Physicians do not entirely disagree with him, but they believe that one needs the other—regimen sometimes needing drugs, and drugs likewise needing the logic and measure of regimen. From this, they command, forbid, curse, and accuse foods and drinks which God created, and they establish unobservable rules of diet; and 

<margin>
The diet they prescribe for others, they do not keep themselves.
</margin>
the very foods they forbid others from even tasting modestly, they themselves devour just as pigs devour acorns <note>original: "tanquam porci glandes devorant"</note>. The laws of living they prescribe for others, they themselves are the first of all to transgress—not so much out of negligence as by design. For if they themselves had to live according to these dietary decrees of theirs, they would suffer no small loss of health; but if they permitted the sick to live by the laws of nature, just as they themselves live, they would feel the loss of their money.

<margin>
Ambrose on the diet of Physicians.
</margin>
Indeed, concerning these practitioners of diet, Ambrose says: "The precepts of Medicine are contrary to the divine condition, for they call one away from fasting, they do not permit one to study by lamplight <note>original: "lucubrare," referring to nighttime study or vigils</note>, and they lead one away from the intensity of meditation. Thus, he who gives himself over to Physicians denies himself to himself."

<margin>Bernard.</margin>
And Bernard, writing upon the *Song of Songs*, says: "Hippocrates and Socrates teach how to save souls in this World; Christ and his Disciples teach how to lose them. Which of the two do you wish to follow as Master?" He makes himself manifest who disputes that this is for the eyes, this for the head, this for the stomach—

### CHAPTER XXXII.

<margin>
The culinary art, medicine’s flatterer.
</margin>
They say it harms the stomach, that legumes <note>Beans, peas, and lentils.</note> are "windy" <note>original: "ventosa"; meaning they cause gas.</note>, cheese burdens the stomach, milk harms the head, and the chest cannot endure the drinking of water. Why is this so? It has come to the point where, in all the rivers, fields, gardens, and cellars, you can scarcely find anything you are permitted to eat. But let us grant that these words of Ambrose and Bernard <note>St. Ambrose and St. Bernard of Clairvaux, who wrote strictly on asceticism and fasting.</note> were spoken only to monks, whose lot it perhaps is not to have as much concern for their health as for their religious profession. But for laypeople, a concern for health is not unbecoming, nor is a variety of foods and side-dishes or a certain elegance of the table. Dietary Medicine promises the first—a reasoned health—but the **CULINARY ART**, the discipline of preparing food and drink, provides the second. Wherefore Plato calls this art "the flatterer of medicine," and many count it as a part of Dietary Medicine; though Pliny, Seneca, and the rest of the medical schools admit that a vast multitude of diseases are birthed from a variety of over-refined foods.

<margin>
THE CULINARY ART.
</margin>
¶ Therefore the **CULINARY ART** is very convenient, and not at all dishonorable, provided it does not exceed the limits of moderation. Indeed, this reasoning has led even the greatest and most self-controlled men to not blush at writing about cooking and the seasoning of side-dishes.

<margin>
Writers on the culinary art.
</margin>
Among the Greeks: Pantaleon, Mithecus, Epiricus, Zophon, Hegesippus, Pazanius, Epaenetus, Heraclides of Syracuse, Tyndaricus of Sicyon, Simonactides of Chios, and Glaucus of Locri. Among the Romans: Cato, Varro, Columella, Apicius, and from the more recent authors, Platina.

<margin>
Asiatic luxury.
</margin>
The people of Asia, however, were always so luxurious and intemperate in these matters that their very name passed into a nickname for gluttons and spendthrifts, whom we thereafter call *Asotae* <note>meaning "prodigals" or "the lost ones."</note>. From this (as Titus Livius reports), after the victory in Asia, foreign luxuries flowed into the City of Rome. It was then that feasts first began to be prepared with greater care and expense; then the Cook, who to the ancients was the cheapest of slaves both in estimation and use, began to rise in price and value. Though still dripping with sauce <note>original: "iure madens"; a pun on "jus" meaning both law and sauce.</note> and stained with soot from the kitchen, he was received with his pots, pans, ladles, mortars, and spits into the halls of learning; and what had been a lowly service began to be considered an art, whose entire concern is to hunt down from every possible source the [inducements...]

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ancient culinary experts, shifting from a list of Greek authors to the specific delicacies they prized and the Roman reaction to such decadence. It specifically highlights the figure of Apicius and the failed attempts to curb gluttony through legislation.</meta>

...the attractions of gluttony, and delicacies of food to satisfy deep-seated **gormandizing**, sought out from every corner of the world. Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author known for his "Attic Nights," a collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note> enumerates many of these from the works of Varro: specifically, peacock from Samos, Phrygian hazel-hen, cranes from Melos, kid from Ambracia, young tunny-fish from Chalcedon, lamprey from Tartessus, hake from Pessinus, oysters from Tarentum, scallops from Chios, elops-fish from Rhodes, parrotfish from Cilicia, nuts from Thasos, Egyptian dates, and Iberian acorns. All these culinary "institutions" were devised for the wicked indulgence of satiety and the wantonness of luxury.

<margin>Apicius, the head of the culinary art.</margin>
However, **Apicius** <note>Marcus Gavius Apicius, a legendary Roman gourmet of the 1st century AD, whose name became synonymous with luxury.</note> claimed the glory and fame of this art for himself above all others. As a result, his name became a title (according to Septimius Florus); by a kind of imitation of the naming of Philosophers, cooks were called "Apicians" after him. Concerning this man, **Seneca** <note>The Stoic philosopher who famously critiqued Roman decadence.</note> left this written record: "Apicius," he said, "lived in our memory, and in that City—from which philosophers were at one time ordered to depart as corrupters of youth—he professed the science of the **cookshop** <note>original: "popinæ"; refers to the low-status taverns or kitchens associated with excess.</note> and infected the age with his teachings." **Pliny** also most severely called him the "deepest abyss of all spendthrifts." In short, so many instruments of gluttony, so many provocations of lust, and so many varieties of side-dishes were devised and perfected by the ingenuity of those "Apicians," that it eventually became necessary to restrain the luxury of the kitchen by prescribed laws.

<margin>Laws against the luxury of the kitchen.</margin>
For this reason, those ancient **Sumptuary** and **Food Laws** <note>Laws intended to limit private spending on banquets and expensive foods to maintain moral discipline.</note> were passed: namely, the Orchian, Fannian, Didian, Licinian, and Cornelian laws, the Law of Lepidus, and the Law of Antistius. Moreover, **Lucius Flaccus** and his colleague, serving as Censors, removed **Duronius** from the Senate because, as a Tribune of the Plebs, he wished to repeal a law passed to restrain the expenses of banquets. Indeed, how impudently did Duronius mount the rostrum to say: "Reins have been cast upon you, Citizens, which must in no way be endured; you are bound and fettered by the bitter chain of servitude. For a law has been given which commands you to be frugal; let us therefore cast away that rule, which is covered in the rust of horrid antiquity!"

<margin>The gluttony and luxury of our age.</margin>
"For what need is there for liberty, if those who wish to perish in luxury are not permitted to do so?" There were many other such edicts, all of which have now become obsolete and utterly abolished, so much so that no age has ever indulged in greater care for gluttony and luxury than our own; which...

# ... CONCERNING TEMPERANCE AND SOBRIETY ...

For its sake—as **Musonius** <note>Musonius Rufus, a 1st-century Stoic philosopher known as the "Roman Socrates," who advocated for a simple diet.</note> says, and after him our own **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the Church Father who frequently wrote on the virtues of fasting and asceticism.</note>—we traverse lands and seas. So that honeyed wine and precious food may pass through our throats, we sweat through the labors of an entire lifetime. There are now so many **cookshops** <note>original: "popinæ"</note> among us, so many dens of vice, so many taverns for parasites and harlots, where men are destroyed by greediness, drunkenness, and lust. Often, and not without great detriment to the State, they devour and consume their entire inheritances. 

So many types of dishes have now been devised, so many seasonings for delicacies, and so many laws, rites, and ceremonies of the table—matching those of the Asians, Milesians, Sybarites, and Tarentines <note>Ancient groups legendary in the Roman world for their soft living and indulgence.</note>. Furthermore, the sumptuous banquets of **Sardanapalus**, **Xerxes**, and the Emperors **Claudius**, **Tiberius**, **Vitellius**, **Heliogabalus**, and **Gallienus**, and those other ancient gluttons (whom historians record as surpassing all other nations and men in the delights, luxury, and pleasure of the cookshop), would seem utterly filthy, unrefined, and rustic if they were compared with our current banquet preparations. 

Moreover, nothing is achieved by the elegance of food and drink unless there is also abundance to the point of loathing—an abundance that would intoxicate even **Hercules** (who, it is said, often used the same vessel as both his boat and his drinking cup) and would satisfy the hunger of **Milo of Croton** or the "glutton" of **Aurelian**. 

<margin>The voracity of Hercules, Milo, and the glutton of Aurelian.</margin> 
Of these, Milo was accustomed to eating thirty loaves of bread at a single dinner in addition to other foods. The other man, in one day before the table of the Emperor Aurelian, devoured an entire wild boar, a hundred loaves of bread, a sheep, and a piglet; he also drank more than a large jar's worth of liquid through a funnel. 

These practices are today most widely accepted in those rustic public feasts, Church dedications, and their other festivals. You would say the **orgies of Bacchus** <note>The Roman god of wine, associated with wild, unrestrained festivals.</note> were being celebrated: for there, everything is defiled by madness, blood, and the many-fold disgraces of gluttony and drunkenness. There you might behold the "Banquets of the Centaurs" <note>A mythological reference to a wedding feast that devolved into a violent brawl; a metaphor for a party turning into a fight.</note>, from which no one returns without a scar. There you would see such voracity as **Ovid** describes regarding **Erysichthon** <note>The original text reads "Erichthone," but refers to Erysichthon, a king cursed by Ceres with insatiable hunger.</note> in this poem:

<margin>Metamorphoses, Book 8.</margin>
> Without delay, what the sea, what the land, what the air produces,
> He demands; and with the tables set before him, he complains of hunger,
> And seeks feasts within feasts: and what would be enough for cities,
> And what could suffice for a whole people, is not enough for one man.

# ON VANITY

<meta>Catchword: ra & (from the word pestifera)</meta>

> He desires more, the more he sends down into his belly;
> And just as the sea receives rivers from all the earth,
> Yet is not satisfied with the waters and drinks up foreign streams;
> And just as ravenous fire refuses no fuel,
> And burns countless torches, and the greater the supply 
> Given to it, the more it seeks, and is made more voracious by the very crowd of food;
> So do the lips of the profane **Erysichthon** <note>The Latin text reads "Erichthonis," likely a variant of Erysichthon, the King of Thessaly whom the goddess Ceres cursed with insatiable hunger in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*.</note>
> Receive and demand all banquets at once; in him, all food
> Is a cause for more food, and a void is always created by eating.

<margin>The voracity of Albinus.</margin>
<margin>The gluttony of Maximinus.</margin>
¶ There were once among the Greeks, and then also among the Romans, athletes who were most voracious men; but their infamy was eventually surpassed even by men of consular rank and Emperors. For **Albinus** <note>Clodius Albinus, a Roman usurper and rival to Septimius Severus in the late 2nd century.</note>, who once held power in Gaul, devoured at a single dinner one hundred peaches, ten melons, five hundred dried figs, three hundred oysters; and the Emperor **Maximinus** <note>Maximinus Thrax, a 3rd-century emperor known for his massive physical size and legendary strength.</note>, who succeeded **Alexander**, the son of **Mamaea**, ate forty pounds of meat in a single day and drank an amphora of wine—an amphora contains forty-eight pints <term>sextarios</term> <note>A 'sextarius' was a Roman unit of volume roughly equal to a modern pint or half-liter.</note>.

<margin>The luxury of Geta.</margin>
<margin>Sicknesses arising from gluttony.</margin>
The Emperor **Geta** <note>The younger brother of Caracalla, famously murdered by him.</note> is also recorded as being of such ruined luxury that he ordered feasts to be brought out according to the alphabet <note>A decadent whim where all dishes in a single course began with the same letter.</note> and gorged himself in three-day banquets. Now indeed, what crime is more impious, when God and Nature prepared food and drink for us for the sake of health and strength, yet we instead abuse those things through various culinary tricks for the sake of pleasure? We gorge our bodies beyond the capacity of human nature, contracting incurable diseases as a result. From this, we clearly see the truth of what **Musonius** <note>Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher who argued that a simple diet was the foundation of self-control.</note> says: that slaves are more robust than their masters, peasants than city-dwellers, the poor than the wealthy—and indeed everyone who uses cheaper and more common food is sturdier, healthier, and stronger than the rest. They tolerate labor better, are less exhausted by it, and fall ill very rarely. Nor do those grave illnesses—such as dropsy <term>hydrops</term>, gout <term>podagra</term>, skin diseases <term>morpheæ</term>, colic <term>colica</term>, and the like—torment anyone more than those who, despising a simple diet, live out of the workshops of kitchens. On the contrary, we see those who are content with a simple diet remain healthier. **Cornelius Celsus** <note>A 1st-century medical writer whose work 'De Medicina' was rediscovered during the Renaissance.</note> also agrees with this, stating that for a human, the most useful food is simple; a piling up of flavors is pestilential and...

<summary>This page contrasts the insatiable hunger of the mythological Erysichthon with the historical gluttony of Roman Emperors like Albinus and Maximinus. It concludes with a moral and medical argument that simple diets lead to better health, whereas culinary excess causes chronic diseases like gout and dropsy.</summary>

-># OF THE SCIENCES<-
->Folio 134<-

...[pestife]rous and seasoned foods are useless for twond reasons: first, because more is consumed than is proper due to their sweetness; second, because they are more difficult to digest. Furthermore, many very serious men and authors have detested these goads of gluttony and the artificial pleasure of fine delicacies.

<margin>Religion, not gluttony. Ephesians 5.</margin>
But there are others who, in the name of **Religion** <note>The author refers to Ephesians 5:18, "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is luxury."</note>, detest not only gluttony and luxury but even some foods that God created for eating. They abstain from meat, yet in the matter of wine—in which (as the Apostle says) there is luxury—they are more capacious than the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Epicurus, popularly (though often unfairly) associated with a life of sensory pleasure and indulgence.</note>. They claim to be abstaining and fasting when they have filled themselves with every kind of fish and the very best wine; for these things they carry about "armed" lips, tongues, teeth, and bellies, but not their money-purses. But enough of these; let us move from this culinary kitchen to the **Geberic** <note>original: "Gebericam". Named after Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), the famous 8th-century polymath and father of chemistry/alchemy.</note> kitchen—that is, the Alchemical one—which boils away no less wealth than a tavern.

<margin>ALCHEMY</margin>
¶ **ALCHEMY**, therefore—whether it should be called an art, or a fraud, or a pursuit of nature—is truly a remarkable and unpunished imposture. Its vanity easily betrays itself by the fact that it promises things that nature can in no way endure or achieve, since no art can overcome nature, but only imitate it and follow it at a long distance; for the force of nature is much stronger than that of art. Moreover, Alchemy is:

> An art suspected by the good, an art hated by many,
> It makes even the practitioners of the art hated;
> So many clearly appear as liars,
> Who, being idle, frustrate both themselves and others alike.

¶ While they attempt to change the species of things, they even presume to manufacture a certain "blessed stone" of the **Philosophers** (as they call it). By this, in the manner of **Midas** <note>The mythological king of Phrygia who was granted the wish that everything he touched would turn to gold.</note>, all bodies touched by it would be instantly changed into gold or silver. Indeed, they even strive to bring down from the highest and inaccessible heavens a certain **fifth essence** <term>quinta essentia</term> <note>The "quintessence" or ether, believed by alchemists to be the pure element of the celestial bodies, capable of curing all diseases and granting immortality.</note>. By this, they promise us not only riches greater than those of **Croesus** <note>The King of Lydia renowned for his vast wealth.</note>, but also—by casting off old age—rejuvenation, perpetual health, and almost immortality along with their vast wealth.

> But nowhere among so many who busy themselves with such things
> Does anyone appear who, in fact, proves 
> Such great miracles.

Laws are the <unclear>do</unclear>gma of all the wise, because those ancient Legislators—in order to win authority for their decrees among the unrefined common people—feigned that they were taught by the Gods to prescribe those very laws. Thus, for the Egyptians, **Osiris** claimed to be taught by **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio," referring to the god Hermes Trismegistus</note>; **Zoroaster** <note>The founder of Zoroastrianism</note> for the Brastians and Persians by **Oromasus** <note>Ahura Mazda</note>; **Charondas** for the Carthaginians by **Saturn**; **Solon** for the Athenians by **Minerva**; **Zamraites** among the Arimaspi by a good deity; **Zamolxis** <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae</note> for the Scythians by **Vesta**; **Minos** for the Cretans by **Jupiter**; **Lycurgus** for the Spartans by **Apollo**; and **Numa Pompilius** for the Romans by the Nymph **Egeria**. Behold, you see now in what manner this <term>Jurisprudence</term> <note>The science or philosophy of law</note> arrogates empire to itself over all other sciences and exercises a Tyranny; and how it prefers itself to all remaining disciplines as if it were the first-born of the Gods, despising them as cheap and empty.
