# BOOK XVII. TITLE II.
<warning>The image is a bit dark and the top header is partially faded/cut off.</warning>

...established property as its own. From this, so many lawsuits have flowed among men that—as the laws themselves testify—more legal cases have been created than there are names for actual things. For since men were naturally prone to disagreement, it was necessary, as the saying goes, to proclaim laws for the sake of maintaining justice. This was done so that the audacity of the wicked might be restrained, innocence might be kept safe among the dishonest, and the good might live in peace among the bad.

And these are the principles of that so-distinguished Law, in which the legislators have been almost countless:

<margin>Legislators of various nations.</margin>
The first of these was **Moses**, who wrote laws for the Jews, at which time **Cecrops** also brought laws to the Egyptians. After him, **Phoroneus** was the very first of all to give laws to the Greeks. Later, **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus"</note> gave laws to the Egyptians. Then came **Draco** and **Solon** for the Athenians, and **Lycurgus** for the Spartans. **Palamedes** was the first to establish the Laws of War for the judgment of an army.

For the Romans, however, **Romulus** was the first to establish laws, which were called <term>curiate laws</term> <note>Latin: *curiatae*; laws passed by the earliest Roman assembly, the *Comitia Curiata*</note>. After him, **Numa Pompilius** established religious laws, and the subsequent Roman Kings each gave their own laws in succession. All of these were later recorded in the books of **Papirius**.

<margin>Papyrian Civil Law.</margin>
From this, the **Papyrian Civil Law** took its name. After these, the Law of the **Twelve Tables** appeared, as well as the **Flavian Law**, the **Aelian Law**, the **Hortensian Law**, and the **Honorary Law** of the <term>Praetor</term> <note>A Roman magistrate who had the power to issue edicts that supplemented or modified existing law</note>. Likewise, there were <term>Plebiscites</term> <note>Latin: *Plebiscita*; laws passed by the common people's assembly</note>, <term>Senatusconsults</term> <note>Latin: *Senatusconsulta*; decrees or advice from the Roman Senate</note>, the Law of the Magistrates, and Custom. Finally, the power of establishing Law was given to the Prince <note>the Emperor</note>. Beyond these were those countless jurists, a good portion of whom were included in the "second law on the origin of Law" <note>referring to a specific historical title in Justinian's *Digest*</note>.

Indeed, if any tried to reduce the Civil Law into a single volume, **Gnaeus Pompey** was the first to attempt it. Next was **Gaius Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar</note>, but both were prevented by civil wars and untimely deaths, and so they could not complete the task. At last, **Constantine** renewed those ancient laws, and **Theodosius the Younger** compiled them into the code named after him. Finally, **Justinian** published this Code which is in use today. However, the entire authority of Civil Law rests with the people and the Princes; for Civil Law is nothing other than what men desire by common consent.

<margin>What Civil Law is.</margin>
Hence, **Julianus** <note>Salvius Julianus, a famous Roman jurist</note> says that the Laws bind us for no other reason than that they have been accepted by the judgment of the people. Who by common...

# ON VANITY

...by common consent, transferred all command and power to the Prince <note>Referring to the *Lex Regia*, where the Roman people theoretically transferred their sovereignty to the Emperor</note>. From this, whatever has pleased the People and the Prince possesses the force of Law, whether through custom or through legal constitutions—even if it appears to be an error or a falsehood. For "common error makes the law" <note>original: "communis error facit ius"</note>, and a matter once judged is accepted as the truth.

**Ulpian** <note>One of the most influential Roman jurists</note> taught us this in these very words: that a man must be accepted as free-born <note>term: *ingenuus*; a person born free, never having been a slave</note> if a legal sentence has been passed to that effect, even if in reality he was a freedman <note>term: *libertinus*; a former slave who has been manumitted</note>, because a judged matter is accepted as the truth.

In the writings of the same man, we read of a certain **Barbarius Philippus**. Although he was a runaway slave, he sought the praetorship <note>a high-ranking magistracy</note> at Rome. Having performed the duties and finally being recognized for what he was, it was nevertheless decided that none of the actions he performed under the cover of such high dignity should be changed.

And elsewhere, an old countryman is worshipped as a god <note>original: "in numen veneratur"</note> by the authority of the Emperor, an argument which the legal expert is commanded to prove from the Emperor's own words. **Paulus** also, the most learned of Roman legal consultants, says that today, because of the custom of the Emperors, if a silver candelabra is listed as "silver," it belongs to the category of silver and not to the category of "household goods," since error makes Law.

The same author openly admits regarding Laws and Decrees of the Senate <note>original: "Senatusconsultis"</note> that a reason cannot be given for everything established by our ancestors. From this, we now know that all the wisdom of Civil Law depends solely upon the opinion and will of men, urged by no other reason than the integrity of morals, the convenience of living, the authority of the Prince, or the force of arms. If Law exists as a preserver of the good and an avenger of the wicked, it is a good discipline; but if otherwise, it is a most wretched thing, because of the injustices committed when a magistrate or Prince is negligent, or when he tolerates or approves of them.

<margin>The opinion of Demonax</margin>
Furthermore, it was the opinion of **Demonax** <note>A Greek Cynic philosopher</note> that all laws were useless and superfluous, since they are enacted neither for the good nor for the bad; for the former do not need laws, while the latter are made no better by them.

Moreover, since **Cato** admits in the writings of **Livy** that scarcely any law can be passed that is convenient for everyone, and from which it does not very often happen that equity fights against the rigor of the Law: **Aristotle** himself, in his *Ethics*, defines equity as follows:

<margin>CANON LAW.</margin>
**CANON LAW** or Pontifical Law, which to most might seem most holy, yet it shadows the ingenious prescriptions of its own greed and the formulas for plundering with a facade of piety. This is the sole ambition and lust of all the Roman Pontiffs: namely, the establishing of new Canons. 

<margin>The Pope commands the Angels.</margin>
Their arrogance grew to such a point that it commanded the Angels of the Heavens, and presumed to commit robbery by snatching prey from hell, and to lay a hand upon the spirits of the dead. Even against the divine law—by interpreting, declaring, and disputing—they sometimes exercised a Tyranny, lest anything be lacking or taken away from the fullness of their power. 

<margin>Clement's bull</margin>
Did not **Pope Clement**, in a bull <note>an official papal document, named for the "bulla" or lead seal attached to it</note> which to this day is still kept under lead seal in the archives of privileges at Vienna and Poitiers <note>original: "Vienæ, Limonis, Pictauiū"</note>, command the Angels of Heaven that they should lead into eternal joys the soul of a pilgrim traveling to Rome for the sake of indulgences who died [on the way], having been absolved from purgatory? Furthermore, he said: "We do not wish that the punishment of hell be inflicted upon him in any way." Beyond this, he granted to those signed with the cross <note>referring to Crusaders or those taking specific vows</note> that they could, according to their wishes, snatch three or four souls they desired from purgatory. 

<margin>The school of Paris corrected the Pope’s temerity.</margin>
This erroneous and intolerable temerity—not to say near heresy—the school of Paris then openly detested and corrected. But perhaps they regret today that they did not interpret that hyperbolic zeal of Clement with some pious commentary, so that the matter might stand rather than perish, since nothing changes in the reality or authority of the Supreme Pontiff because of their affirming or denying. For his Canons and Decrees have so [bound] all of Theology itself...

...has so bound them, that no theologian, however obedient, dares to decree anything, much less to hold an opinion or debate anything different from the Papal Canons, without a formal protest and "By Your Leave," <note>original: "Venia"; meaning permission or a request for pardon for speaking</note> just as Martial sings concerning Rufus:

We have learned that the "goods of the Church" are not only Gospel doctrine, the fire of faith, and contempt for the world, but taxes, tithes, offerings, collections, purple robes, miters, gold, silver, gems, estates, and money. <margin>Mark 11 and Luke 19</margin>
—to make the house of prayer into a den of thieves. <note>References to Jesus cleansing the Temple of money-changers</note> This goes so far that the Pope can depose Bishops without cause; he can give away what belongs to others; he cannot commit <term>simony</term> <note>the practice of buying or selling sacred things or Church offices</note>; he can grant dispensations against a vow, against an oath, and even against natural law, and no one has the right to say to him: "Why do you do so?" They say he can, moreover, for some "grave cause," grant dispensations against the entire New Testament, and even drag a third part of the souls of the faithful (or more!) into hell with him.
<margin>The duties of Bishops in this age.</margin>
The duty of Bishops, meanwhile, is no longer to preach the Word of God, but to confirm children with a slap on the cheek, <note>Refers to the traditional "alapa," a light blow on the cheek given during the sacrament of Confirmation to signify strength in faith</note> to confer holy orders, dedicate temples, baptize bells, consecrate altars and chalices, and bless vestments and images. As for those who possess a higher intellect than this, they leave such tasks to I know not what "titular" bishops, <note>Bishops who held the title of a defunct diocese and often performed the ceremonial duties of wealthy, politically-active prelates</note> while they themselves serve as ambassadors for Kings, preside over royal chapels, or accompany Queens—being excused from their service for some "great and weighty cause"...

### OF THE SCIENCES. Folio 139.

...they might worship God in Temples and magnificently honor the King in Courts. From these same sources have come those legal tricks by which, today, Bishoprics and <term>benefices</term><note>A church office that provides an income</note> are bought and sold without the official name of <term>simony</term><note>The illegal buying or selling of spiritual things, such as church offices or sacraments</note>.
<margin>of benefits:</margin>
From these also come whatever other marketings and monopolies exist in favors, pardons, indulgences, dispensations, and similar formulas of plunder. By these means, a price is set even for the remissions of sins freely given by God Himself, and profit is squeezed from the punishments of the lowly. Moreover, to this law we owe that forged <term>Donation of Constantine</term><note>A forged Roman imperial decree by which the Emperor Constantine supposedly transferred authority over Rome and the western part of the Roman Empire to the Pope; a key document used to justify Papal political power</note>, although in truth and by the witness of the Word of God, neither should Caesar abandon his own rights, nor should the Clergy usurp for themselves the things that belong to Caesar. But out of many laws of ambition, pride, and tyranny, I shall mention only a few here to give credit to what we have just said.
<margin>Some chapters of the tyrannical book.</margin>
Scrutinize, therefore, if you please, in the ancient <term>Decretals</term><note>Letters of the Pope that formulate decisions in canon law</note> the chapter "You have indicated" <note>original: "Significasti"</note>, etc.; the chapter "Venerable" <note>original: "venerabilem"</note> concerning elections; the chapter "Customarily" <note>original: "solite"</note> concerning superiority and obedience; the chapter "Since formerly" <note>original: "cum olim"</note> concerning privileges; the chapter "If the Supreme Pontiff" <note>original: "Si summus Pontifex"</note> concerning the sentence of excommunication; the chapter "Among others" <note>original: "Inter cætera"</note> concerning the office of the ordinary judge. Then, in the sixth book of the Decretals, which that tyrant of Popes, Boniface VIII, compiled, see what he says in its prologue, and in the first chapter on the immunity of Churches. Nor let that most arrogant <term>Clementine</term><note>A collection of canon law issued by Pope Clement V</note> "Pastoral" yield to those, regarding the sentence and the matter judged. Along with the <term>Extravagant</term><note>Papal decrees not included in the main organized collections</note> of John XXII, which begins "Of the Roman Church" <note>original: "Ecclesiæ Romanæ"</note>, and another by the same "Over the nations" <note>original: "super gentes"</note>; and the Extravagant of Boniface VIII, "One Holy" <note>original: "Unam Sanctam"</note>. Finally, from the compilation of <term>Gratian</term><note>A 12th-century jurist who created the first systematic collection of canon law</note> we encounter: Chapter "If the Lord" <note>original: "Si curus"</note>, distinction 13; Chapter "If all" <note>original: "Si omnis"</note>, distinction 18; Chapter "Thus all" <note>original: "Sic omnes"</note>, etc. Indeed, Chapter "In memory" <note>original: "In memoriam"</note>, Chapter "If of the Romans" <note>original: "Si Romanorum"</note>, distinction 19; Chapter "All" <note>original: "Omnes"</note>, distinction 22; Chapter "To you, Lord" <note>original: "Tibi domino"</note>, distinction 63; "Constantine" <note>original: "Constantinus"</note>, distinction 96; and Chapter "When" <note>original: "Quando"</note>, distinction 86, and the Commentary <note>original: "Glossa"</note> in the same place; and Chapter "If the Pope" <note>original: "Si Papa"</note>, distinction 40. <header>ON VANITY</header>

...converting and sometimes adulterating those things which are said elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures, and shaping and adapting them to fit those inventions of theirs; from this source were born those "Concordances of the Bible and the Canons," as they call them.

<margin>
Titles of plunder.
</margin>
To these are added so many titles of plunder: concerning <term>Palliums</term><note>A woolen vestment conferred by the Pope upon archbishops; the "plunder" refers to the heavy fees charged for them</note>, Indulgences, <term>Bulls</term><note>Official papal edicts or charters</note>, Confessionals, Indults and <term>Rescripts</term><note>Formal written answers from the Pope or a ruler to a legal question or petition</note>, Wills, Dispensations, Privileges, Elections, Dignities, <term>Prebends</term><note>The portion of a cathedral's revenue granted to a member of the clergy as a salary</note>, Religious houses, Sacred buildings, Immunities, the Court, Judgments, and other such things.

<margin>
Canon Law is inconsistent.
</margin>
Finally, Canon Law itself is the most inconsistent of all things, more changeable than <note>original: "Proteo atque Cameleonte"</note> Proteus or the Chameleon, and more tangled than the <term>Gordian knot</term><note>An ancient metaphor for a complex or unsolvable problem</note>. Even the Christian religion—at whose origin Christ put an end to ceremonies—now possesses more ceremonies through this Canon Law than the Jews ever had in the past. With the weight of these added, the "light and easy yoke of Christ" has now been made the heaviest of all, and Christians are compelled to live more by the prescriptions of the Canons than by the Gospel itself.

<margin>
What both branches of law concern.
</margin>
¶ Now, the entire expertise of both branches of Law <note>Civil Law and Canon Law</note> is concerned with nothing but decaying, fragile, fleeting, vain, and profane business, the commerce and insults of the common crowd, as well as murders, thefts, pillaging, robberies, factions, conspiracies, injuries, and destruction. To these are added the perjuries of witnesses, the falsifications of scribes, the <term>prevarications</term><note>Acting in a misleading or evasive way to delay a legal process</note> of lawyers, the corruptions of judges, the ambitions of counselors, and the robberies of governors. By these, widows are oppressed, orphans are brought low, the honest are exiled, the poor are trampled, the innocent are condemned, and as it says in Juvenal:
> *He grants pardon to the ravens, but the census harasses the doves.* <note>original: "Dat veniam Corvis, vexat censura Columbos." A quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal meaning the guilty escape while the innocent are punished.</note>

And blind men, the very things they thought they could avoid through Laws and Canons, they immediately prepared for themselves and fell into. For these Laws and Canons are not from God, nor do they lead to God, but have proceeded from the corrupted nature and character of men, and were devised for gain and greed.

...most [wicked] and fraudulent, craftily adorned with a persuasive cover. This is nothing other than knowing how to soothe the Judge with persuasion and to use him at one's every whim; to know how to invent and reinvent any Laws whatsoever for one's own pleasure by using laws or convenient <term>glosses</term><note>Interpretive notes or commentaries on legal texts that often twisted the original meaning</note>, or to escape them by any wicked evasions, or to prolong a fraudulent lawsuit. They cite Laws in such a way that equity is perverted, and build up the authority of the glossators so that the sense of the Law and the mind of the Legislator are subverted. In this art, it is of great importance to shout loudly, and to be bold, clamorous, and shameless in litigation.

<margin>Who is the best advocate.</margin>
And he is considered the best of Advocates who entices more people into litigating, and drives them into court with the promised hope of winning the suit, stimulating those entangled in his counsel. He is a master of <term>vain appeals</term><note>Legal maneuvers used to delay a case without merit</note>, an excellent <term>rabula</term><note>A "pettifogger" or "brawling lawyer"—someone who argues loudly and aggressively rather than with logic</note> and quarrelsome instigator, who can shout anything with his wordiness and the strength of his tongue. Furthermore, anyone can prefer one cause over another through the tricks of the courts, and in this way make true and just things appear doubtful and wicked: and to defeat, pervert, and overthrow Justice itself with its own weapons. Among these people:

> Justice is nothing but a public commodity,
> And the Judge who sits on the case approves what he has bought.
<note>original: "Iustitia nihil est nisi publica merces, / At Iudex in causa qui sedet empta probat."</note>

But even those things which are not [real] things—namely, privations and silences—they put up for sale. For just as none of them speaks except for payment, so neither do they keep silent except for a reward, after the pure example of Demosthenes. When he [Demosthenes] asked Aristodemus, an actor of plays, how much pay he had received for acting, and he replied "one talent," Demosthenes said, "But I received more to keep silent." Indeed, the tongue of <term>lawyers</term><note>Latin: "causidicorum" — literally "pleaders of causes"</note> is so damaging that unless it is bound by gifts, it is impossible for it not to cause harm.

<margin>THE ART OF PROCURATION.</margin>
¶ To these lawyers, there are also present for this very purpose **PROCURATORS** and **NOTARIES**, whom they call **Tabelliones** <note>Public scribes or scriveners authorized to draft legal documents</note>. Everyone must patiently endure their injuries, losses, wickedness, and forgeries, since they seem to have obtained for themselves the trust, license, and power of everyone by Apostolic and Imperial authority. And among these, those are the foremost who know how to exceptionally disturb the <term>forum</term><note>The public court or marketplace where legal business was conducted</note>, stir up lawsuits, confuse cases, and substitute...

<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s scathing critique of the legal profession, moving from the general character of advocates to the specific ways that legal documents, commentaries, and "legal experts" undermine the truth and serve only the powerful.</meta>

# ON VANITY

<margin>
**JURISPRUDENCE**
</margin>

They ensure that wills, legal documents, imperial decrees, and charters are used to egregiously mislead, deceive, and—where necessary—perjure and record falsehoods. They dare anything, and in the construction of deceits, frauds, schemes, slanders, snares, traps, ambushes, trifles, evasions, deceptions, and their own <term>Scylla and Charybdis</term><note>A classical metaphor for a situation where one is caught between two equal dangers; here, the "traps" of the law</note>, they allow themselves to be surpassed by no one. Furthermore, no <term>Notary</term><note>In the Renaissance, a notary was a high-status official authorized to draw up contracts and legal deeds</note> is so honest that he can draft what they call a "legal instrument" in such a way that it is not necessary to dispute it in court, should an adversary wish to speak against it. Either the opponent will say something was omitted, or that it is false, or that fraud is hidden within it, or he will raise some other <term>exception</term><note>A formal legal objection intended to stop or delay an action</note> to challenge the credibility of the document or the Notary. And these are those "legal remedies" to which they teach litigants to flee; these are the "watchtowers" by which they say the laws provide help—unless there is someone who prefers to fight and litigate. For a person will possess only as much right as his own power can defend, as the law itself says: *since we cannot be equal to those who are more powerful.* <note>original: "quoniam potioribus pares eſſe nō poſſumus." A cynical take on the reality of legal inequality.</note>

¶ To this we also look upon those vast Giants who, contrary to <term>Justinian’s edict</term><note>The Emperor Justinian (r. 527–565), who codified Roman law, strictly forbade the writing of commentaries on his laws to prevent the very confusion Agrippa describes</note>, have produced for us so many huge and innumerable volumes of <term>glosses</term><note>Brief explanations or interpretations written in the margins of legal texts</note>, commentaries, and expositions, with every one of them interpreting the text in a different way.

<margin>
**Legal experts are lovers of contention.**
</margin>

Furthermore, they have brought forth—with a most unhappy fertility—so many storms of opinions, and such a forest of crafty counsels and legal safeguards. These serve to equip and nourish the wickedness of Advocates, who bind their own sense of shame to the famous "list of names" of those legal experts throughout every sentence and <term>paragraph</term> (as they call them). They act as if truth consisted of confused testimonies dragged from a cesspool of such trifling opinion-mongers, rather than standing on reason itself. Among these people, praise, contention, and discord are held in such high regard that anyone who does not disagree with others—who does not know how to contradict the sayings of others with new opinions, call all settled judgments back into doubt, and adopt well-founded laws for their own fictions through ambiguous expositions—is considered to be poorly educated or not learned at all. Hence, this entire "Jurisprudence" has become a perverted and crafty counsel, a net of iniquity. These are the wits and the arts by which the Christian world is ruled today, and by which Empires, Kingdoms, and the Sovereignty of peoples are established.

### OF THE SCIENCES

<page-num>Folio CXLI.</page-num>

From these rascals are selected the officials of Princes and Popes, as well as those Parliamentary Senators and Presidents. It is as if those who have been unjust <term>Advocates</term><note>Lawyers or legal representatives</note> until now will suddenly become more equitable Judges, though they eventually become the heads of Kingdoms. These men are even formidable to their own Kings, just as the <term>Titans</term><note>In Greek mythology, the Titans were a race of giants who challenged Jupiter (Zeus) for control of the heavens</note> were once to Jupiter. Furthermore, from this group eventually emerge those pot-bellied Arch-scribes of Emperors and Kings, and the purple-clad 
<margin>Chancellors.</margin>
Chancellors, to whom the highest affairs of state are entrusted. They hold everything for sale: the decrees of Princes, gifts, benefits, offices, dignities, <term>rescripts</term><note>Formal written answers from a ruler or pope to a legal question</note>, and diplomas. Beyond this, they trade in divine law, human law, statutes, equity, and honor—everything is a commodity to them, and they compel others to buy from them. At their whim, the friends and enemies of Kings are numbered; according to their own lust for power, they now join nations in treaties, and now again commit them to deadly wars. And although they have climbed from the lowest dregs of the common people to such a peak of dignity through the most filthy <term>prostitution of their voice</term><note>A metaphor for lawyers selling their speech to the highest bidder regardless of the truth</note>, 
<margin>The audacity of legal experts.</margin>
they are carried to such a crime of audacity that they sometimes dare to proscribe Princes, and even without a <term>Decree of the Senate</term><note>original: "Senatusconsulto," referring to formal legislative acts</note> or without a trial, they condemn men to death. They are the authors of changing the states of Kingdoms, while they themselves swell with their thefts and robberies.

¶ Also belonging to this assembly are the **INQUISITORS** of Heretics from the 
<margin>THE ART OF INQUISITION.</margin>
<term>Order of Preachers</term><note>The Dominicans, a Catholic religious order heavily involved in the historical Inquisition</note>. Their jurisdiction ought to be founded entirely upon theological traditions and the Holy Scriptures; however, they exercise it most cruelly based on <term>Canon Law</term><note>The body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority (the Church)</note> and the decrees of the Pope, as if it were impossible for the Pope to err. They leave Holy Scripture itself behind them like a "dead letter" and nothing but a shadow of the truth—indeed, they even cast it far away as if it were (as they say) a shield and bulwark for heretics. Nor do they accept the traditions of the ancient <term>Doctors</term><note>Renowned historical theologians and teachers of the Church</note> and Church Fathers, saying that they "can be deceived and can deceive." Instead, they recognize only the Roman Church which, they claim, cannot err, and of which the Pope is the head. They set the "style of his court" as the target and goal of their faith. When investigating a suspect, they demand nothing else than: "Do you believe in the Roman Church?" If the person affirms this, the Roman Church immediately declares the suspect's original 
<margin>The order of proceeding.</margin>
proposition to be either heretical, or scandalous, or offensive to pious ears, or to the ecclesiastical...

<meta>This page continues the critique of the legal and ecclesiastical systems, specifically shifting from the corruption of state chancellors to the tyrannical methods of the religious Inquisitors who prosecute heresy.</meta>

# ON VANITY

...they condemn him for undermining the power of justice, and soon they compel him to a <term>palinode</term><note>A formal recantation or retraction of a previous statement</note> and a total revocation of his views. If the accused then tries to protect his opinion with the testimony of the Scriptures or other reasons, they interrupt him with a great noise and angry voices. They tell him that he is not dealing with <term>Baccalaureates</term><note>Advanced university students or low-ranking academics</note> or scholars in a classroom, but with Judges at a tribunal. They insist that there is no place there for litigating or disputing, but only for answering simply whether he wishes to stand by the decree of the Roman Church and revoke his opinion. If he does not, they show him <term>bundles of wood and fire</term><note>The "faggots" used for burning heretics at the stake</note>, saying that one must contend with heretics not with arguments and Scriptures, but with flames. Thus, they compel a man—who has neither been convicted of any stubbornness nor taught any better—to abjure his beliefs against his own conscience. If he refuses, they hand him over to the <term>secular court</term><note>The civil legal system, as the Church officially "shed no blood" but handed victims to the state for execution</note> as a deserter of the Church to be burned, saying with the Apostle: <note>original: "Auferte malum de medio ueſtri"</note> *Remove the evil from among you.*
<margin>1 Corinthians 5</margin>
<margin>The former gentleness of the Church and Popes toward those in error.</margin>
Such was the ancient gentleness of the Church and the clemency of the Popes—as <term>Gratian</term><note>The 12th-century jurist who founded the study of Canon Law</note> compiled in the fourth distinction regarding consecration—that they did not even punish with death those who relapsed into Judaism, nor did they inflict the death penalty on blasphemers. Even <term>Berengarius</term><note>Berengar of Tours (d. 1088), a theologian who denied the material presence of Christ in the Eucharist</note> himself, though he relapsed into an abominable heresy, was not only not killed, but was not even deprived of his dignity as an Archdeacon. But today, if a man falls into the smallest error, he is treated as more than a capital criminal, and is sometimes handed over to the fire by these Inquisitors for the slightest offense. Perhaps such severe punishment is necessary for the Church today, provided that in the meantime true piety is not killed along with it. Indeed, the Inquisitors of <term>heretical depravity</term><note>The technical name for the crime of heresy in canon law</note> are sometimes depraved themselves, and can even be heretics themselves; this fact gave the occasion for a new constitution by <term>Clement</term><note>Pope Clement V, who addressed the abuses of the Inquisition at the Council of Vienne in 1311</note>. Therefore, Inquisitors ought to dispute against heretics not through dark arguments and quarrelsome <term>syllogisms</term><note>Logical proofs consisting of three parts; here, Agrippa mocks them as pedantic word games</note>, but through the Word of God concerning the Catholic faith. They should convict the heretic through the Holy Scriptures, and then, according to the teachings of the Canons and the constitutions of the Holy Councils, terminate the business and either lead the accused back to the orthodox faith or declare him a heretic.
<margin>What a heretic is.</margin>
For he is not a heretic who is not rash; nor is he to be considered a supporter of heretics who defends one who is innocent of the crime and not yet condemned...

Fo. CXLII.
### OF THE SCIENCES.

...defends the accused, so that they are not dragged before the tribunal of certain wicked Inquisitors—or rather, ravenous wolves—and into an unsafe place to be torn to pieces. Now indeed, even though it is expressly provided by law that Inquisitors have neither the power of inquiry nor any jurisdiction over any suspicion of heresy, its defense, the harboring of suspects, or the showing of favor, unless it is clearly evident that an expressed and explicitly condemned heresy is involved; nonetheless, these blood-sucking vultures, going beyond the privileges granted to the office of the inquisition and acting against the Laws and <term>Canons</term><note>The body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority (Church law)</note>, thrust themselves into the jurisdiction of the <term>ordinaries</term><note>The local bishops who usually held primary authority over their dioceses</note>. They arrogate to themselves the authority of the Popes in matters that are not heretical, but merely "offensive to pious ears," or scandalous, or in some other way erroneous without actually being heresy.

<margin>The cruelty of Inquisitors toward peasant women. Corrupt Inquisitors.</margin>
Furthermore, they rage most cruelly against poor peasant women. When these women are denounced and accused of <term>sortilege</term><note>Divination or fortune-telling</note> or <term>maleficium</term><note>Harmful magic or witchcraft</note>, even without any prior legal evidence, the Inquisitors expose them to atrocious and enormous tortures until they have extorted confessions of things the women never even dreamed of. Only then do they have something to condemn. These Inquisitors believe they are truly doing their job when they do not cease from their "duty" until the wretched woman is either burned at the stake, or has <term>gilded the hand</term><note>A metaphor for paying a bribe</note> of the Inquisitor so that he might take pity and acquit her as if she were sufficiently "purged" by the tortures. For it is not uncommon for an Inquisitor to change a physical punishment into a monetary one and apply it to the benefit of his own office, which brings them no small profit.

<margin>Peasant women pay a yearly tribute to the Inquisitors.</margin>
They even have many of those wretched women who are forced to pay them a yearly <term>census</term><note>A tax or tribute</note> so that they are not snatched away again for questioning. Furthermore, when the goods of heretics are confiscated by the <term>Fisc</term><note>The public or royal treasury</note>, the Inquisitor takes no small share of the prey. Finally, the mere accusation or denunciation, or even the slightest suspicion of heresy or sorcery—and the very fact of being "cared for" by the Inquisitor—carries a lasting infamy. A person's reputation can only be protected if money is given to the Inquisitor, and that is no small matter. Through this tactic, while I was in Italy, many Inquisitors in the <term>Duchy of Milan</term><note>A northern Italian state where Agrippa lived and practiced as a lawyer and physician</note> harassed many most honorable matrons, even from the nobility, and secretly squeezed huge amounts of money from these fearful and terrified women. At last, when their fraud was discovered by the nobles, they were severely punished, and they hardly [escaped]...

<margin>The Inquisitor Hoogstraten</margin>
...escaped sword and fire. I could relate here the very subtle and more-than-<term>Scotist</term><note>Referring to the followers of Duns Scotus, known for their complex and often pedantic theological distinctions</note> invention of that famous <term>Hoogstraten</term><note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican Inquisitor and major opponent of the Reformation and humanist scholarship</note> and my other fellow citizens of Cologne regarding the investigation of the Jews, and that whole tragedy of <term>Capnio</term><note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a humanist scholar whose Greek nickname "Capnio" means "smoky." <margin>Agrippa's dispute with a certain Inquisitor.</margin>
Once, while I was serving as the Advocate and legal counsel for the Republic of <term>Metz</term><note>Latin: *Mediomatrici*; a city in northeast France where Agrippa served as a legal official</note>, I had a very serious battle with an Inquisitor. This man, acting wickedly, had dragged a poor peasant woman to his place of execution—and to a venue where he had no jurisdiction—based on certain futile and most unjust slanders; he intended not so much to investigate her as to torture her. When I had undertaken her defense and demonstrated from the records themselves that nothing had been alleged that would justify <term>interrogation</term><note>In this context, a judicial euphemism for the use of torture to extract a confession</note>, he resisted me to my face. "There is one thing," he said, "that is more than sufficient: for this woman's mother was once burned as a sorceress." When I argued that this point was irrelevant and that, according to cited laws, a person should not be judged for the act of another—and that even the Judge’s duty should be to reject such an argument—he immediately replied (so as not to seem to speak without reason) by drawing an argument from the inner chambers of the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: *Mallei Maleficarum*; the infamous manual for witch-hunting published in 1486</note> and the foundations of <term>Peripatetic Theology</term><note>A critique of theologians who relied too heavily on Aristotelian philosophy rather than Scripture</note>. He said that it was so because witch-women are accustomed to sacrifice their newborn offspring to demons, and because they often conceive them through intercourse with <term>incubi</term><note>Demons in male form believed to have sexual relations with women</note> demons; therefore, it happens that in such offspring, malice remains rooted as if by an inherited disease. I replied: "Is this the perverse way you, a theologian, act? Do you drag innocent peasant women to torture with these fictions? Do you judge others as heretics with these sophistries? You yourself are no less a heretic in that opinion than <term>Faustus</term> or <term>Donatus</term><note>Famous historical heretics; Faustus was a Manichaean and Donatus founded a schismatic sect</note>. Even if it were as you say, do you not empty the grace of baptism of its power?"

<margin>The power and grace of Baptism.</margin>
"And would the priest say in vain, 'Depart, unclean spirit, and give place to the Holy Spirit,' if the offspring were to remain with the Devil because of the sacrifice of an impious parent? Even if you chose to defend the opinions of those who claim that incubi demons can procreate, surely none of those who assert this has been so foolish..."

...their reasoning was so foolish as to suggest that those **Demons**, together with stolen seed, transmit something of their own nature into the child. Rather, I tell you (I said) in good faith, that from the very nature of our humanity, we are all born as a single <term>mass of sin</term><note>Latin: *massa peccati*; a theological concept, largely from St. Augustine, suggesting humanity is a collective lump of sin due to the Fall</note> and eternal curse, children of perdition, children of the devil, children of God's wrath, and heirs of hell. You see now how this "most sufficient evidence" of yours, as you call it, is by law invalid, by reason empty, and by its very assertion even heretical. The cruel hypocrite burned with rage at these words and threatened to take action against me as a supporter of heretics. But I did not cease to defend that poor woman, and finally, by the power of the law, I snatched her safely from the mouth of that Lion. That bloodthirsty monk stood confused before everyone, forever infamous for his cruelty. Even those slanderers who had betrayed the woman—who were subjects of the Cathedral Chapter of <term>Metz</term><note>A major city in the Lorraine region; Agrippa served as its legal orator</note>—were themselves condemned to a significant fine.

<margin>THEOLOGY.</margin>
¶ It remains now to speak of **THEOLOGY**. I will pass over the theology of the Pagans once described by <term>Musaeus</term>, <term>Orpheus</term>, and <term>Hesiod</term><note>Legendary figures of early Greek poetry and myth</note>, which is widely admitted to be entirely poetic and fabled. <term>Eusebius</term> and <term>Lactantius</term><note>Early Christian authors who wrote polemics against paganism</note> and other teachers of the Christians have long since defeated it with the strongest arguments. Nor will I speak of the theology of Plato and the other philosophers, all of whom we showed above to be masters of error. Instead, let our discussion here be only regarding Christian Theology. It is certain that this depends on nothing but the faith of its teachers, since it cannot fall under the rules of any human art.

<margin>Scholastic Theology.</margin>
But first, let us speak of **Scholastic Theology**, which was forged at the <term>Sorbonne</term><note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris, which Agrippa viewed as a bastion of dry, overly-logical traditionalism</note> in Paris from a certain mixture of divine words and philosophical reasons, a two-formed discipline like the race of **Centaurs**. Furthermore, it was written in a new style of teaching, foreign to the power of the ancient masters, through petty questions and sharp <term>syllogisms</term><note>A form of logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion</note>, without any elegance of speech, and...

...writings, which were otherwise full of judgment and intellect, and which brought no small benefit to the Church for the refuting of Heretics.
<margin>Authors of Scholastic Theology.</margin>
Its authors, and those who excelled in it, were the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1164), whose *Sentences* was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages</note>, Thomas Aquinas, Albert surnamed the Great, and many other excellent men.
<margin>Sophistical Theology</margin>
Furthermore, John [Duns] Scotus was a doctor of subtle intellect, but prone to contention. From this point, Scholastic theology gradually declined into **Sophistries** <note>Clever but fallacious arguments intended to deceive or win a debate rather than find truth</note>, while these more recent "Theosophists" and <term>hucksters</term> <note>Latin: *cauponatores*; literally "innkeepers" or "merchants" who dilute their wine—here meaning those who corrupt the Word of God for profit</note> of God's word, who are only theologians by virtue of a purchased title, have turned such a sublime discipline into a kind of **Logomachy** <note>A "war of words" where the focus is on terminology rather than the underlying reality</note>. They wander through the schools, raising trivial questions, manufacturing opinions, and doing violence to the Scriptures by cloaking them in a foreign meaning with intricate words. They are readier to "toss arguments about" <note>original: *ventilare*</note> than to truly examine them, and they have dared to devise many "seedbeds of quarrels" <note>original: *iurgiorum seminaria*; a pun on "seminary" as both a school and a place where seeds of discord are sown</note>, which provide material for contentious Sophists to fight over.

They abstract "forms," they debate "intellects," and they call mere words "genera" and "species" <note>This refers to the medieval debate between Realists and Nominalists over whether universal categories exist in reality or only in name</note>. While some cling to things and others to names alone, what they grant to one, they attribute to another; others receive these things indifferently, and each student seeks only how they might confirm their own <term>heresy</term> <note>Agrippa uses "heresy" here broadly to mean a private, stubborn opinion or factional stance</note>. Thus, they expose our most holy faith to the laughter and distrust of the wise of this world (a point which even Thomas Aquinas complained about). 

Having left the canonical Scriptures of the Holy Spirit behind their backs, they have chosen for themselves many questions about divine matters that are quite suited for brawling. In these, exercising their wit and consuming their entire lives, they have placed the whole doctrine of Theology into those questions alone. If anyone wishes to resist them by the authority of the **Sacred Letters** <note>The Bible</note>, he is soon to hear: "the letter kills" <note>A common medieval misapplication of 2 Corinthians 3:6 used by Scholastics to dismiss the literal or historical sense of the Bible in favor of their own allegories</note>, it is pernicious, it is useless. Instead, they will say that what lies *hidden* in the letter must be investigated. Turning quickly to interpreting, expounding, glossing, and syllogizing, they clothe the text in any sense other than its own proper, literal meaning. If you press them more sharply, if you urge them, you will receive insults and be called a "jackass" <note>original: *asinus*</note> who does not understand what is hidden in the letter, but like a serpent, you feed only on the earth. To such an extent, none are held as Theologians by them, unless they know how to contend excellently, and to every proposition...

...once he has sworn an oath to some sect, he holds to it with his teeth, defends it stubbornly, and displays its name and brands everywhere. He always has it in his mouth, and glories in being greeted and preferred by its title, such as **Thomists, Albertists, Scotists, or Ockhamists.** <note>These groups are the "schools" of the Middle Ages, named after their founders: Thomas Aquinas, Albertus Magnus, Duns Scotus, and William of Ockham. Agrippa is criticizing how they value their school's brand over Christian unity.</note> For it is not considered honorable enough for these great masters of ours to be called simply "Christians," since that surname is one that any butcher, cook, baker, shoemaker, barber, or camp-follower—and even "little women" and the unlearned common folk—can hold in common with them. 

And these followers, moreover, split amongst themselves in many ways. For some of them, who possess a "sublime wit," wish to seem more skilled than the Prophets and Apostles; they presume that they can find and demonstrate through their own syllogisms <term>syllogism: a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal)</term> those things which are believed by faith alone. They philosophize about divine matters with deplorable questions and contend with a monstrous confidence in various—and sometimes even absurd—opinions. For instance, some distinguish the divine essence from its "relations" by the thing itself, others only by reason; others set up infinite "realities" (as they call them) as if they were Platonic ideas. <note>Agrippa is mocking the incredibly dense metaphysical debates of the time regarding the nature of God's attributes.</note>

Others, in turn, deny and laugh at these things. They fabricate so many monsters concerning God, so many varying forms of the divine power, and so many phantasms and idols of their own thoughts regarding divine things. They tear apart Christ the Savior with the depravity of their opinions, clothing him as if in the various masks of their **Sophisms** <note>In this context, a sophism is a clever but false argument used to deceive.</note>. By their absurd suppositions, they form and reform him like a wax idol into whatever figure they wish, until their doctrine can be seen as mere **Idolatry**.

<meta>This page continues Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa’s critique of the clergy, specifically transitioning from the treacherous behavior of corrupt preachers and inquisitors to a formal discussion of "True Theology." He distinguishes between prophetic revelation and the human labor of interpretation.</meta>

...to profess that they lead the wicked toward salvation, they have instead become hunters of honors. For the purpose of destruction, they hold their mouths like a bow of lies, and their tongues wound like an arrow. But enough about these men; for it is not safe to rebuke them with a freer manner of speech. Indeed, whenever they are provoked, they tend to conspire and drag those who rebuke them before their Inquisitors <term>Inquisitors: officials of the Church tasked with detecting and punishing heresy</term>, hauling them into court and forcing them into a recantation <term>recantation: a formal public withdrawal of one's stated opinions, historically called a "palinode"</term>. They may deliver them to the bundles of wood <note>original: "fasciculis tradere." This refers to the "faggots" or bundles of firewood used to burn heretics at the stake.</note>, or secretly remove them from the world with an offered poison. For they hold this also among the secret symbols of their religion: if anyone attempts to bring scandal upon the religious order, they believe it is right to kill him with a hidden dose of poison, lest the order be defamed if one of their own were to be punished publicly. Therefore, leaving these men behind, let us now hasten toward true Theology. This, too, is divided into two parts: one is prophetic, and the other is interpretive. We shall speak of the latter first.

<margin>INTERPRETIVE THEOLOGY.</margin>
For **INTERPRETIVE THEOLOGIANS** believe that just as grapes, olives, grain, flax, and many other such things grow and ripen through the generosity of nature—from which wine, oil, bread, and cloth are eventually formed by human ingenuity and aid, thus completing the works of nature through human arts—so too were the divine oracles given in an extremely obscure and hidden manner. They are to be explained by our interpretations, not indeed by our own strength or inventions as if they were our own oracles (just as the works of nature require our assistance), but by the Holy Spirit of those very scriptures. 
<margin>1 Corinthians 12.</margin>
<margin>The interpretation of the sacred scriptures.</margin>
This Spirit distributes His gifts to everyone according to His will, and where He wills, making some indeed Prophets and others the interpreters of Prophets. Therefore, this Theology of interpreting divine things does not proceed in the manner of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who relied heavily on logic and categorization</term> by defining, or dividing, or composing—none of which methods reach God, since He can neither be defined, nor divided, nor composed. Instead, it consists of another way of knowing, which stands midway between this world and prophetic vision. This is the matching of truth with our purified intellect, like a key with a lock. Just as the intellect is most hungry for all truths, so it is receptive to all things that can be understood; and for this reason, it is called the potential intellect <term>potential intellect: in Scholastic philosophy, the "intellectus possibilis" is the capacity of the human mind to receive and understand universal concepts</term>. Through this, even if we do not perceive with full light those things which the Prophets bring forth...

<meta>This page continues Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa’s discussion of theology. ->### SOLILOQUY 648<-

...to the Prophets and those who beheld the divine things themselves, a gate is nevertheless opened to us. Through the harmony of truth perceived by our intellect, and from the light that shines upon us from those open inner chambers, we are made much more certain than by the apparent demonstrations, definitions, divisions, and compositions of the Philosophers. It is granted to us to read and understand not with external eyes and ears, but to perceive with better <note>meaning: spiritual or internal</note> senses. With the veil removed and our face revealed, we may draw forth the truth emanating from the **marrow of the sacred scriptures**, which was passed down under various coverings by those who beheld it with true insight. This truth is hidden from the "wise" of this world and from philosophical inquiries; yet we grasp it with such a judgment of certainty that all perplexity is removed.

And since this truth lies hidden in the sacred scriptures in manifold ways, holy and spiritual men have undertaken various and manifold expositions of the sacred scriptures.

For some, proceeding with a gentle course through the **bark of the letter** <note>original: "corticem literæ." A common medieval metaphor where the "bark" or "husk" is the literal surface meaning, and the "marrow" is the spiritual truth within.</note>, hunt for the truth of Scripture by harmonizing the writings—explaining one passage through another based on the order of words, etymologies, properties, and from the power of terms and similar methods to establish a specific meaning. They call this the **Literal Exposition**.

<margin>Moral Exposition.</margin> Others refer whatever has been written to the business of the soul and the works of justice; for this reason, their exposition is called **Moral**.

<margin>Tropological.</margin> Others, through various tropes <term>tropes: figures of speech or metaphorical uses of a word</term> or figures, relate these things back to the secrets of the Church, for which reason their sense is called **Tropological**.

<margin>Anagogical.</margin> Others, devoted to the contemplation of the higher life, refer all things to the secrets of heavenly glory; they call this the **Anagogical Exposition**.

And these are the four expositions of the Theologians practiced in the Church. Besides these, there are yet two others:

One of these relates all things to the cycles of time, the changes of kingdoms, and the restoration of the ages; for this reason, it is called **Typical**. <margin>Typical.</margin> In this method, Cyril <note>likely St. Cyril of Alexandria</note>, Methodius, and Abbot Joachim <note>Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), a mystic famous for his theories on the three ages of history</note> excelled, as well as the more recent Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara <note>A Dominican friar and reformer in Renaissance Florence, executed in 1498</note>.

The other [is found] in the sacred scriptures themselves, [concerning] the nature of the entire universe and the sensible world and its whole...

What Prophetic Theology is.

**Prophetic Theology**, therefore, is that which teaches the unshakable Word of God from intuitive inspiration. Moreover, the authority and arguments by which its truth is corroborated are not the whims of men, nor the usage of long time, nor the devised commentaries of the wise, nor the magnificent decrees of sects, nor **Syllogisms** <term>Syllogism|A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</term>, nor **Enthymemes** <term>Enthymeme|An argument in which one of the premises is kept hidden or implied.</term>, nor inductions, nor obligations, nor insoluble consequences. Instead, they are the divine oracles harmonizing with one another, received in the universal Church with unanimous and stable consent, proven by miracles, wonders, portents, and every kind of sanctity and the trial of life, and by the very testimony of shed blood. We have as teachers of this Prophetic Theology **Moses**, **Job**, **David**, **Solomon**, and most other canonical writers and Prophets of the Old Testament. <margin>Ecclesiastes 1</margin> Did not **Ecclesiastes** speak of this, saying? "What is that which has been? The same as that which has been done. What is that which has been done? The same as that which is to be done. <margin>Nothing is new</margin> There is **nothing new under the sun**, nor can anyone say: 'Behold, this is new,' for it has already preceded us in the ages that were before us. There is no memory of earlier things, nor indeed will there be any remembrance of those things which are to come afterward among those who will exist in the very end." <margin>Ecclesiastes 2.</margin> And a little further down he says: "The learned and the unlearned die together." What shall we say here, then? Except that all sciences and arts are subject to oblivion and death, nor will they remain perpetually in the soul, but together with death they shall pass into death; <margin>Matthew 15 and Mark 7.</margin> as **Christ** said, "every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up," and cast into eternal fire. So far is it from the case that knowledge leads to immortality; <margin>Isaiah 40, 1 Peter 1, Deuteronomy 11, and Jeremiah 11.</margin> for only the **word of God** remains forever. The knowledge of which is indeed so necessary for us that whoever despises it, whoever neglects it, whoever does not hear it (as the Word itself testifies in the Holy Scriptures), God will bring upon him a curse, and perdition, and eternal judgment. It is not, therefore, for you to think that this pertains <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "nere" completes the Latin word "pertinere" (to pertain).</note> to theologians alone—

...deceptions <note>The text likely completes "praestigiae," referring to the arts and sciences as illusions or tricks.</note>, and their end is always evil, so that it has even passed into a Proverb among the common people: *All who are knowledgeable are insane.* This is supported even by Aristotle, who says: *No great science exists without a mixture of madness.* Augustine himself testifies that many have lost their senses through the desire for knowing. Nothing is so repugnant to the Christian religion and faith as science, nor do they tolerate one another less. For we know from Ecclesiastical Histories and are taught by experience itself how, as the faith of Christ gained strength, the sciences fell, so that the greatest and most powerful part of them utterly perished. For those most potent Magic arts vanished so completely that not even a trace remains. Of so many sects of Philosophers, scarcely one remained—the Peripatetic <note>The school of followers of Aristotle, who were known for walking about while teaching.</note>—and even that is not intact.

Indeed, the Church never fared better or rested more securely than when all those sciences were reduced to a narrow scope: when Grammar was found only in a single author like Alexander Gallus <note>Alexander of Villedieu (c. 1175–1240), whose "Doctrinale" was the standard medieval grammar textbook.</note>; when Peter of Spain <note>A 13th-century scholar and later Pope John XXI, famous for his "Summulae Logicales," the standard logic manual.</note> presided over Dialectic <note>The art of logical argument.</note>; when Laurentius Aquilegius <note>An author of "Ars Dictaminis," or the art of formal letter writing and rhetoric.</note> sufficed for Rhetoric; and when the *Fasciculus Temporum* <note>A very popular 15th-century universal history or world chronicle.</note> satisfied the needs of History. For Mathematical disciplines, there was the Ecclesiastical *computus* <note>The method used to calculate the date of Easter and other movable feasts.</note>; and for all other things, Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose "Etymologies" served as the encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note> alone was enough. 

But now, where the skill of languages, the ornament of speaking, and the number of authors have been revived, and the sciences gain strength, the tranquility of the Church is disturbed, and new heresies arise. Truly, there is no class of men less suited for receiving Christian doctrine than those who already have a mind soaked in the opinions of the sciences. For these men are so stubborn and obstinate in their own opinions that they leave no room for the Holy Spirit. They lean upon and trust in their own strength and their own wit so much that they yield to no truth, nor do they admit anything unless they can demonstrate it through Syllogistic reasons <note>Logical arguments consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note>. Those things which they cannot investigate or understand by their own strength and industry, they mock and despise. Therefore, Christ hides this truth from the wise and the prudent, and reveals it to the little ones—those who are surely poor in Spirit, possessing no treasures of the sciences; who are pure in heart, untainted by the opinions of the sciences; and in whose heart, as if on a *tabula rasa* <note>original: "tabula rasa"; a clean slate or an erased wax tablet ready for new writing.</note>...

...nothing has yet been described of those human traditions <note>Continuing the thought from the previous page: "human traditions" refers to the complex man-made laws and academic logic that the author argues distract from true faith.</note>, who are peaceful, not followers of sects, not contentious, nor quarrelsome: <margin>Wisdom 5</margin> those who are attacking the truth with syllogisms <note>Formal logical arguments</note>, and those who suffer persecution for the sake of truth and justice from those contentious Sophists <note>Here used as a derogatory term for academic philosophers who prioritize cleverness over truth.</note>. These humble ones are laughed at as "Blessed Ones" <note>original: "Beatis"—likely used here as a mocking nickname for the simple-minded</note> and "Asses," and are maligned in the Schools, banned from the pulpits, and thrown out of the academies <term>gymnasiis: Greek-style schools of higher learning</term>. Sometimes they are slandered as Heretics; even the death penalty is established against them, and they are deprived of life by dire punishments. 

Thus in Athens long ago, Socrates was taken away by poison, Anaxagoras was sentenced to the ultimate punishment, and Diagoras was accused in a capital case—though he escaped imminent death by swift flight. Among the Prophets of the Hebrews also: Isaiah was sawn in pieces, Jeremiah was overwhelmed with stones, and Ezekiel <margin>Daniel 6; 2 Chronicles 24; 3 Kings 19; Hebrews 11</margin> was slain. Daniel was condemned to the beasts, Amos was killed with a club, Micah was thrown from a precipice, Zechariah was slaughtered at the altar, and Elijah was persecuted by Jezebel, who herself killed many Prophets. Indeed, even that Holy Patriarch Abraham was cast into the Chaldean furnace <note>A tradition from Jewish Midrash, widely known in the Renaissance, which claims Abraham was thrown into a fire by King Nimrod for refusing to worship idols and was miraculously saved.</note>. So too the Apostles and disciples of Christ and infinite Martyrs, witnesses of Christ's divinity, were killed by manifold torments. 

All these died for no other reason than that they thought more holily about God than those "wise men" of the world. Behold, these who are so small and humble in poverty of Spirit, purity of heart, and peace of conscience, ready even to shed their blood for the truth—these, I say, are the ones to whom alone is given that true and deifying wisdom, which brings us into the choirs of the blessed Gods and transforms us into the likeness of the blessed Gods. <margin>Matthew 5</margin> As Christ clearly teaches us this, saying: 

> Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of God. <note>original: "Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam eorum est Regnum Dei."</note> Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. <note>original: "Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum uidebunt."</note> Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. <note>original: "Beati pacifici, quoniam filij Dei uocabuntur."</note> Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice's sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. <note>original: "Beati qui persequutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam, quoniam ipsorum est Regnum Cælorum."</note>

It is therefore better and more useful to exist as unlearned ones <term>idiotas: from the Greek 'idiotes,' meaning a private person or one without professional knowledge, rather than the modern insult</term> and as those knowing nothing at all, and to believe through faith and charity and become close to God, than to be puffed up by the subtleties of the sciences and, through pride, fall into the <margin>Matthew 11</margin> possession of the serpent. Thus we read in the Gospels how...

<margin>Exodus 13</margin> In this way, God himself honored the ass so much that when He commanded every first-born to be killed in sacrifice, He spared only asses along with humans; specifically, He permitted a human to be redeemed by a price, and an ass to be exchanged for a sheep. Moreover, we read in the same author that a Dragon loved a girl of Aetholis; it is also believed by many that the same dragon protected its foster-father and rushed to the sound of his voice when recognized. And in Pliny we read of an Asp that was accustomed to come daily to the table of a certain man; when it perceived that its own offspring had killed the host’s son, it put the young snake to death as a punishment for the violated hospitality, and never returned to that house again out of shame. The same author recounts that a Panther, on account of its cubs being rescued from a pit, showed gratitude to a man and, after leading him out of the wilderness, restored him to the public road. <meta>This page continues Agrippa’s satirical yet profound "Encomium of the Ass." Having previously established the ass's importance in the Old and New Testaments, he now moves into classical legends and hagiography (lives of the saints) to argue that the humble ass is more spiritually perceptive than the arrogant scholar.</meta>

CLVII

### SCIENCES.

It is celebrated that the founders of the Roman city <note>Romulus and Remus.</note>, after being exposed, were nourished by a she-wolf. I pass over the miracles of dolphins, and the recognized kindness and returned gratitude of lions. I say nothing of the Daunian bear and the Tarentine bull tamed by Pythagoras, and many very similar things. But what surpasses the wonder of all prodigies: it is read that Ammonius of Alexandria, the greatest philosopher of his time and teacher of the divine Origen and Porphyry, had an ass as a student of wisdom and a fellow pupil to those men. We also know from the sacred history of the Bible that an ass was once gifted with a prophetic spirit:

<margin>Numbers 22</margin> For when Balaam, a man of knowledge and a prophet, went out to curse the people of Israel, he did not see the angel of the Lord, but the ass saw him, and spoke with a human voice to its rider Balaam. Thus, he says, very often the simple and unrefined layman <note>original: "idiota" — in Agrippa’s time, this referred to a person without formal academic training, rather than a lack of intelligence.</note> sees what the scholar and Doctor, corrupted by human sciences, cannot see.

<margin>Judges 15</margin> Did not Samson, with the jawbone of an ass—the jaw of a young ass—strike down and destroy the men of the Philistines? And being thirsty, he prayed to the Lord, who opened a molar tooth in the jaw of the ass, and living waters flowed out, by drinking which his spirit and strength were refreshed. Did not Christ, through the mouths <note>original: "bucca"</note> of his asses—his simple and unrefined lay apostles and disciples—conquer and strike down all the philosophers of the nations and the legal experts of the Jews, and prostrate and destroy all human wisdom? He offers us, from the jawbone of those asses of His, the waters of life and eternal wisdom. Now indeed, in ecclesiastical histories and the deeds of the Saints, we read of various and many benefits bestowed by divine gift upon diverse animals through their prayers; but we never read of any animal being raised from the dead, except for that ass which the blessed Germanus, Bishop of the Britons <note>St. Germanus of Auxerre (c. 378–448), who was said to have miraculously restored an ass to life during his mission to Britain.</note>, restored to life. By which remarkable miracle it seems to be shown that the ass itself participates in immortality even after this life. From these things which have now been said, it is clearer than the sun that no animal is so capable of receiving the divine as the ass; unless you are turned into one, you will not be able to carry the divine mysteries. This was formerly a custom among the Romans

<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s satirical and theological defense of "holy ignorance." -># ON VANITY<-

...[among the Ro]mans, the name of Christians was such that they were called **Ass-worshippers** <note>original: *Asinarii* — a derogatory term used by pagans who mocked Christians for allegedly worshipping an ass's head; the famous "Alexamenos graffito" depicts this slur</note>, and they were even accustomed to painting the image of Christ with the ears of an ass. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD, who defended Christianity against these specific pagan slanders</note> is a witness to these things. Therefore, let our **Popes** and **Abbots** no longer be indignant, nor consider it a reproach to themselves, if they are called "asses" by those giant elephants of the sciences. Nor let the Christian common people wonder if, among these leaders of the Churches and initiates of our sacred mysteries, the more learned someone is, the more rarely he is valued by the others. For the songs and melodies of nightingales do not suit the ears of asses; and as the proverb says, <margin>Proverb.</margin> the unpleasant and unmusical braying of asses does not harmonize with the lyre. And yet, from the marrow taken out of the bones of asses, the best flutes of all are made, which when filled with breath—just as they far surpass and conquer the most eloquent singing of all birds and the most elegant sounds of any lyre or zither—so these religious **unlearned men** <note>original: *idiotæ* — used here in the classical sense of "laymen" or "private persons" without formal academic degrees, rather than the modern pejorative</note> with their "asinine" blare surpass and excel all the most talkative Sophists. 

So we read that some pagan philosophers came to **Anthony** <note>Saint Anthony the Great, d. 356 AD, a desert hermit famous for his simple, direct holiness despite a lack of formal education</note> for the sake of debating, and having been captured by him with a short speech, they departed with shame and modesty. We also read that a certain simple and unlearned man overcame a most skilled and cunning heretic with few words and brought him back to the faith—a man whom the most learned men and Bishops who had gathered at the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The first ecumenical council of the Church in 325 AD, intended to settle theological disputes</note> could not overcome in a long and very anxious dispute. When he was later asked by his friends how he had yielded to an unlearned man when he had resisted such learned Bishops, he replied that he had easily deceived the Bishops with verbal tricks, but he could not resist this unlearned man, who spoke not from human wisdom but from the Spirit. 

<margin>Matthew 11, Luke 10.</margin> Therefore, you asses—who now, along with your young foals, have been loosed from the darkness of flesh and blood by the command of Christ through his Apostles (the messengers and lecturers of true wisdom in his holy Gospel)—if you desire to attain this divine and true wisdom, which is not of the **tree of knowledge** of good and evil <margin>Genesis 2.</margin> but of the **tree of life**, you must cast aside human sciences and every investigation and discourse of flesh and blood, of whatever...

<meta>catchword: ...kind [illæ]</meta>

<summary>Agrippa argues that the "asinine" simplicity of the faithful is more spiritually potent than the complex logic of scholars, citing Saint Anthony and the Council of Nicaea as proof that the Holy Spirit speaks through the unlearned. He urges believers to reject human "sciences" in favor of the divine wisdom of the Tree of Life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s argument from the previous folio. ### OF THE SCIENCES

<margin>Gen. 1</margin>
...whether these be found in the reasoning of speeches, or in the investigation of causes, or in meditations on works and effects, you will no longer seek them in the schools of Philosophers and the gymnasiums of Sophists; rather, having entered into yourselves, you will know all things. For the knowledge <note>original: *notio* — a term used here to mean an innate spark or concept</note> of all things was created within you. As the Academics <note>Refers to the followers of Plato's Academy, who believed in the theory of "reminiscence"—that learning is actually remembering what the soul knew before birth</note> admit, so the sacred scriptures attest: because God created all things "very good," namely in the highest degree in which they could exist. Therefore, just as he created trees full of fruit, so he created souls—or "rational trees"—full of forms and knowledge. But through the sin of our first parent <note>Adam</note> all things were veiled, and Oblivion, the mother of ignorance, entered in. 
<margin>Gen. 1</margin>
Therefore, remove now, you who can, the veil from your intellect, you who are wrapped in the darkness of ignorance. Vomit up the drink of Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, a river in the underworld; those who drank from it forgot everything. Agrippa uses it here as a metaphor for the spiritual "forgetfulness" of the Fall</note>, you who have intoxicated yourselves with forgetfulness. Wake up to the true light, you who have been soothed by irrational sleep, and soon, with your face revealed, you will transcend from glory to glory. 
<margin>1 John 2</margin>
For "you have been anointed by the Holy One" (as John says) "and you know all things." And again: "you have no need for anyone to teach you, because his anointing teaches you about all things." For he alone is the one who gives speech and wisdom. David, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Daniel, John the Baptist, and many other Prophets and Apostles did not learn their letters; instead, from shepherds, peasants, and commoners <note>original: *idiotis* — referring to those without formal academic training or status</note>, they were made the most learned in all things. Solomon, in the dream of a single night, 
<margin>3 Kings 3</margin>
was filled with the wisdom of all things above and below, as well as with such prudence in conducting affairs that no one was ever his equal. And all these men were mortals, just as you are—and indeed, they were sinners. You might say perhaps that these things have happened to only a very few:

<margin>Virgil, Aeneid 6</margin>
->And the few whom impartial Jupiter loved,<-
->or whom burning virtue carried up to the heavens,<-
->those born of the Gods, were able to do it.<-

<margin>Isa. 59</margin>
¶ But do not despair; the hand of the Lord is not shortened to all those who call upon him and who offer him faithful obedience. Anthony <note>St. Anthony the Great, the "Father of All Monks," who was famously illiterate but considered profoundly wise</note> and that Christian servant Barbarus, through three days of prayer, obtained full knowledge of divine matters (as Augustine testifies). Those, however, who...

<meta>catchword: do not</meta>

<summary>Agrippa argues that all knowledge is innate and was placed in the human soul at creation, but was obscured by the Fall. He claims that divine inspiration, as seen in the Prophets and Saints, is superior to the "vanity" of academic philosophy.</summary>
