<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, shifting from the innate knowledge lost at the Fall to the specific sources where one should now seek truth. Agrippa transitions from the "internal light" to the authority of Scripture as the only reliable substitute for those who lack direct prophetic vision.</meta>

### ON VANITY

If you cannot, alongside the Prophets, the Apostles, and those holy men, look upon these things with a clear and revealed intellect, then you should seek understanding from those who have beheld them with a true vision. From here, a path remains to be sought, as Jerome <note>original: *Hieronymus*; St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the Church Father who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate</note> says to Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, a monk and theologian who was initially a close friend of Jerome but later became his bitter intellectual rival</note>, so that what the Holy Spirit suggested to the Prophets and Apostles, we must seek through the study of writings—of those writings, I say, which were handed down by divine oracles and received by the Church with unanimous consent. We must not seek it in those writings devised by human wits, because these do not illuminate the intellect, but rather cause it to grow dark.

Therefore, we must return to Moses, to the Prophets, to Solomon, to the Evangelists, and to the Apostles. Flashing with every kind of learning, wisdom, morals, languages, prophecies, oracles, wonders, and holiness, they spoke of divine things from God himself, and spoke of lower things in a way that surpasses human ability; they have handed down all the secrets of God and nature to us in a clear light. For all the secrets of God and nature, the whole logic of morals and laws, and all knowledge of past, present, and future things are handed down in the sacred words of the Bible itself.

Where, then, are you rushing so headlong? You who seek knowledge from those who have consumed their entire lives in searching, and have lost both time and effort, yet were never able to find any truth. Oh, fools and godless men, who, setting aside the gifts of the Holy Spirit, labor so that you might learn from treacherous Philosophers and masters of error those things which you ought to receive from Christ and the Holy Spirit! Do you think we can draw knowledge from the ignorance of Socrates? <note>Socrates famously claimed he knew nothing; Agrippa takes this literally to mock the foundation of Greek philosophy</note> Light from the darkness of Anaxagoras? Virtue from the well of Democritus? <note>Democritus famously said that "truth lies at the bottom of a well"</note> Prudence from the insanity of Empedocles? Piety from the barrel of Diogenes? <note>Diogenes the Cynic was said to live in a large ceramic jar or barrel to show his contempt for worldly comforts</note> Sense from the stupor of Carneades and Arcesilaus? <note>Skeptical philosophers who argued that nothing can be known for certain</note> Wisdom from the impious Aristotle and the treacherous Averroës? <note>Averroës was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university education, but often viewed with suspicion by theologians</note> Faith from the superstition of the Platonists?

You are greatly mistaken indeed, and you will be deceived by those who were themselves deceived. But recall yourselves, you who are desirous of truth; depart from the mists of human traditions and take up the true light. Behold, a voice from heaven, a voice teaching from above, showing more clearly than the Sun why you are unfair to yourselves, and why you hesitate to receive wisdom...

<meta>catchword: ...hesitate?</meta>

<summary>Agrippa rejects secular philosophy and the "treacherous" teachings of Greek and Islamic thinkers, arguing that true knowledge of God and nature is found exclusively in the Bible. He contrasts the clarity of the Prophets and Apostles with the "darkness" and "insanity" of human academic tradition.</summary>

--- Page 310 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that divine revelation is the only source of certain knowledge. Having established that the Bible contains all secrets of both the divine and natural worlds, Agrippa now cites specific scriptural authorities—Baruch, Solomon (the "Wise Man"), and the Book of Revelation—to prove that God grants this "true science" to the faithful rather than the merely academic.</meta>

...of those who hesitate? <margin>Baruch 3</margin> Listen to the oracle of Baruch: "This is our God," he says, "and no other shall be compared to him. He found out all the way of knowledge and delivered it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men." <note>original: *Baruch 3:36-38*. This passage was traditionally interpreted by Christian scholars as a prophecy of the Incarnation of Christ.</note> That is to say, he was made flesh, and with an open mouth taught those things which he had previously handed down through the Law and the Prophets in riddles. 

You may well think that these things refer only to divine matters, and not also to these natural things; but listen to what the Wise Man <note>Solomon, traditionally credited with the authorship of the Book of Wisdom.</note> testifies concerning himself: <margin>Wisdom 7</margin> "He himself," he says, "gave me true knowledge of the things that are, so that I might know the organization of the whole world, and the powers of the elements; the beginning, the end, and the middle of times; the alterations of the turning seasons, and the changes of times; the courses of years, and the positions of stars; the natures of living creatures, and the rages of wild beasts; the force of winds, and the reasonings of men; the diversities of plants, and the virtues of roots; and all such things as are hidden and unforeseen, I learned: for wisdom, the worker of all things, taught me." <note>This influential passage suggests that Solomon’s legendary wisdom was a divinely-granted "unified science" covering everything from physics to botany.</note>

For divine knowledge is never-failing; nothing is hidden from it, nothing is added to it, but it encompasses all things. Know, therefore, now, that there is no need for great labor here, but for faith and prayer; not for the study of a long time, but for humility of Spirit and purity of heart; not for the expensive furniture of many books, but for a purged intellect, fitted to the truth like a key to a lock. For a crowd of books burdens the learner rather than instructing him, and he who follows many authors wanders in error with many. 

In the one sacred volume of the Bible, all things are contained and handed down—but on the condition that they are perceived only by those who are enlightened; to others they are parables and riddles, shut tight by the seals you have heard of. Pray, therefore, to the Lord God in faith, hesitating nothing, so that the <margin>Revelation 5</margin> Lamb of the tribe of Judah may come and open the sealed book for you. This Lamb alone is holy and true, he alone has the key of knowledge <term>key of knowledge: *clavis scientiae*; a biblical metaphor for the authority to interpret the mysteries of God</term> and discernment; he who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one can open. 

This is Jesus Christ, the Word and Son of God the Father, and the deifying wisdom, the true Master, made man just as we are, so that he might make us perfect sons of God, just as he himself is, who is blessed for all ages. But lest by speaking longer <note>original: *sermocinando*; this catchword indicates the start of the next page's first sentence.</note>

<summary>Agrippa argues that true knowledge of both the spiritual and natural worlds (astronomy, biology, and physics) is a gift from God found in the Bible. He asserts that faith and divine illumination are superior to the "burdensome" study of many human-authored books.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's famous "De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum" (On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences). The previous page finished the main text by asserting that true wisdom comes from God and the Bible rather than human academic disciplines. This final page provides a closing address to the reader and the printer's colophon.</meta>

->Let this be the end of our discourse.<-

# THE END.

## TO THE READER.

**I**f it is true what Horace <note>original: *Oratius*. Horace (65–8 BCE) was a leading Roman lyric poet.</note> said—that he gains every point who mixes the useful with the pleasant—then for many reasons this book of Agrippa’s <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), the author of this work, was a controversial German polymath, legal scholar, and occult writer.</note> ought to be most pleasing to you. Indeed, you may doubt whether there is more profit or delight in it. For it delights by telling the truth; and by delighting, it recalls the truth—which had been submerged in the well of Democritus—back into the light, as if by a right of restoration. <note>original: *post liminio*. A legal term referring to the restoration of rights to a person returning from exile or captivity. Democritus, the Greek philosopher, famously remarked that "truth lies at the bottom of a well," implying it is difficult to find.</note> It does this while examining all the sciences of all men against that sacred scripture, which was divinely inspired (as the Apostle <note>St. Paul, often referred to simply as "the Apostle" in Renaissance texts.</note> says), as if testing them against a Lydian stone. <term>Lydian stone<gloss>A "touchstone" used since antiquity to test the purity of gold; here, it means a standard for judging the truth.</gloss></term> He explains the matter itself so aptly and skillfully, without any circularity, that no Apelles <note>A renowned painter of ancient Greece, used here as a metaphor for the highest level of artistic or descriptive skill.</note> could have expressed it better with his brush. 

However, if there are some whose ears are so tender that they cannot bear this biting truth with a calm mind, and for that reason begin to speak against it with viperous tongues—thinking perhaps that something has been said with less than due respect for their particular profession—let them remember that they say nothing against the author, but only betray their own wicked conscience. For nothing was written specifically against any one faculty, but generally against them all. Whoever recognizes their own vices, and into whose ear their conscience snarls in secret—as Persius <note>A Roman satirist (34–62 CE) known for his difficult style and moral critiques.</note> says—it is fitting for that person to strive with all their might to correct themselves. If they do not, let them assume nothing was said against them. On the other hand, if anyone is able to bring forth better ideas openly and without envy, let them not doubt that they will find the greatest favor, not only with all scholars but even with the author himself. 

Farewell. From our workshop.

->PARIS, AT THE SORBONNE<-
->BY THE LABOR AND EXPENSE<-
->OF JEAN PIERRE.<-
->In the year 1531. In the month<-
->of February.<-

<summary>This concluding page (colophon) justifies Agrippa's harsh critique of human knowledge by arguing that he uses Scripture as a "touchstone" for truth. It warns readers that taking offense only proves their own guilt and provides the 1531 Paris publication details.</summary>

### OF THE SCIENCES. Folio 54.

<margin>SORCERY</margin>
...by promising these sciences, just as they are like apes to him <note>The author likely refers to how magicians mimic God or Nature, much as an ape mimics a human.</note>, and they strive to rival nature. ¶ There is, moreover, a species of natural Magic which they call **SORCERY** <note>original: "VENEFICAM"</note> or pharmacy, which is accomplished with draughts, love potions, and various medicinal poisons. It is recorded that Democritus prepared such things, by which men are made good, happy, and fortunate, and another by which we might rightly understand the voices of birds, just as Philostratus and Porphyrius relate concerning Apollonius. Virgil also, speaking of certain powerful herbs, said:

*By these I have often seen Moeris become a wolf and hide in the woods, often summon souls from the depths of the graves, and transport harvests to another's field.* <note>original: "His ego sæpe lupum fieri, & se condere syluis / Merim, sæpe animas imis exire sepulchris / Atq; faras alio uidi traducere messes." — Virgil, Eclogue 8.</note>

<margin>Daniel 4</margin>
<margin>Evil-Merodach 1</margin>
<margin>Exodus 7</margin>
<margin>Wisdom 3</margin>
¶ And Pliny relates that a certain Demarchus of Parrhasia, in a sacrifice which the Arcadians performed for Lycaean Jove with a human victim, tasted the entrails of an immolated boy and turned himself into a wolf. On account of this changing of men into wolves, Augustine believes the names were given to Lycaean Pan and Lycaean Jove. The same Augustine relates that while he was in Italy, certain sorceresses <note>original: "feminas magas"</note>, like Circe, by giving a poison in cheese to travelers, turned them into beasts of burden; and after they had carried whatever loads were required, they were restored again to men. He notes that this very thing happened to the father of a certain Praestantius.

But if anyone should think these things are entirely ravings and impossible, let him remember how the Holy Scripture relates that King Nebuchadnezzar was changed into an ox, and lived on hay for seven years, and finally by the mercy of God returned to being a man. After his death, his son Evil-Merodach gave his body to the vultures to eat, lest he should ever rise from the dead, having already returned from a beast to a man. Exodus relates many similar things regarding the Magicians of Pharaoh. Indeed, the Wise Man <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Wisdom in the Apocrypha.</note> speaks of these, whether Magicians or Sorcerers, when he says: *You abhorred them, O God, because they worked horrible deeds against you through their medicines.* <note>original: "Exhorruisti illos deus, quia horribilia opera tibi faciebant per medicamina." — Wisdom 12:4.</note> Furthermore, I want you to know that these Magicians do not only scrutinize natural things, but also those things which accompany and, in a way, depart from nature, such as motions...

<summary>This page explores "Venefica" or sorcery, a branch of natural magic involving potions and transformations. The author cites classical poets like Virgil, historians like Pliny, and biblical accounts of Nebuchadnezzar to argue that such supernatural shifts between man and beast are historically attested.</summary>
